In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, whose surroundings We have blessed, that We might show him of Our signs. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.﴾ ﴿And We gave Moses the Book and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel: "Do not take anyone other than Me as a guardian."﴾ ﴿O descendants of those whom We carried with Noah. Indeed, he was a grateful servant.﴾

His words, ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾: "Subhan" is a verbal noun of "sabbaha" (to glorify), as one says "sabbaha yusabbihu tasbihan wa subhanan," like "kaffara al-yamin" (to expiate the oath) becomes "takfiran wa kufranan." Its meaning is the declaring of Allah free from, and exalted above, every imperfection.

Sibawayh said: the governing verb for it is a verb not derived from its own root, and the implied sense is "I declare Allah free of imperfection (unazzihu Allaha tanzihan)," so "subhanahu" stands in place of "tanzihan." On this view it is like "qa'ada al-qurfusa'" (he sat in the crouching manner) and "ishtamala al-samma'" (he wrapped himself in the garment that covers the whole body). It was also said that it is a proper noun for glorification, like "Uthman" as a man's name, and its accusative status is by an implied verb whose expression is omitted, its estimated form being "usabbihu Allaha subhanan," after which it took the place of the verb and filled its role. We have already presented, in His words ﴿Glory be to You, we have no knowledge except what You have taught us﴾, a portion of the discussion related to "subhan."

As for "al-Isra'" (the night journey): it has been said that it is traveling at night. One says "sara" and "asra," both forms being like "saqa" and "asqa," two dialects. The poet combined both in his verse:

Hayy al-Nadir and the lady of the curtain
Came to me at night, though she was not wont to travel by night.

It has also been said that it is traveling only during the first part of the night. And since the night journey can only take place at night, the explicit mention of the night after it must serve some purpose. It was said that by His words "at night" (laylan) He intended to lessen the duration of the journey, that He took him during part of the night from Makkah to Syria, a distance of forty nights.

The indication of "laylan" for lessening the duration lies in its indefiniteness, which denotes partiality, unlike when you say "sirtu al-layla" (I traveled the night), which conveys that the travel covered the entire night.

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) cited, to show that "laylan" denotes partiality, the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) and Hudhayfah, "min al-layl" (during the night).

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "asra bi-abdihi laylan" is "sayyara abdahu laylan" (He made His servant travel by night), meaning Muhammad. On this view, "asra" means "sayyara," so restricting it to the night has a purpose. He said "bi-abdihi" and did not say "bi-nabiyyihi" (His prophet), "bi-rasulihi" (His messenger), or "bi-Muhammad," in honor of him (ﷺ). The people of knowledge said: had any other name been more noble than this, Allah would have called him by it in this great station and this exalted state:

Do not call me except "O slave of her,"
For it is the most noble of my names.

Calling by names as nicknames among their tribes,
As if names have become some of my names.

﴿From the Sacred Mosque﴾: al-Hasan and Qatadah said: it means the mosque itself, and this is the apparent sense of the Qur'an.

The majority of commentators said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the journey from the house of Umm Hani'. They understood "al-Masjid al-Haram" to mean Makkah, or "al-Haram" (the Sacred Precinct), because each of these encompasses the Sacred Mosque, or because the whole Haram is a mosque.

Then He mentioned the destination to which He took His Messenger (ﷺ), saying: ﴿to the Farthest Mosque﴾, which is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It was called "the Farthest" because of the great distance between it and the Sacred Mosque, and there was no mosque beyond it at that time. Then He described the Farthest Mosque by His words: ﴿whose surroundings We have blessed﴾, with fruits, rivers, prophets, and righteous people. Allah has blessed the surroundings of (p-810) the Farthest Mosque with the blessings of this world and the Hereafter. And in "bараkna" (We have blessed), after "asra" (He took), there is an iltifat (shift) from the third person (absence) to the first person (speech).

Then He mentioned the reason for which He took him, saying: ﴿that We might show him of Our signs﴾, meaning what Allah showed him that night of wonders, among which was covering this long distance in a portion of the night. ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing﴾ of every thing heard, and among that is the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿The All-Seeing﴾ of everything seen, and among that is His Messenger's essence and actions.

The people of knowledge differed as to whether the night journey was with his body (ﷺ) together with his spirit, or with his spirit alone. The majority of the early generations (al-Salaf) and later generations (al-Khalaf) held the first view.

Some people of knowledge held the second view, including Aisha, Mu'awiyah, al-Hasan, and Ibn Ishaq, and Ibn Jarir reported it from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman.

Another group took a detailed position, saying: the journey was with his body, awake, to Bayt al-Maqdis, and to the heaven with his spirit. They used this distinction as evidence, citing His words "to the Farthest Mosque," which He made the endpoint of the journey with his very person (ﷺ). Had the journey from Bayt al-Maqdis to the heaven occurred with his person, He would have mentioned it. What the numerous authentic hadiths indicate is what the majority of the early and later generations held: that the journey was with his body and spirit, awake, to Bayt al-Maqdis, and then through the heavens. There is no need for interpretation that diverts this Qur'anic text and similar wording in the hadiths from its real meaning, and there is no justification for it except mere disbelief and judging by the purely deficient intellects that fail to grasp what is known: that nothing is impossible for Him. Even if it were merely a dream, as those claim who maintain that the journey was with the spirit alone, and that the dreams of prophets are true, the disbelievers would not have denied the Prophet (ﷺ) when he informed them of it, to the point that those whose hearts had not been opened to faith apostatized. A person may see in his sleep what is improbable, even what is impossible, and no one denies this. As for those who hold that the journey was only with the spirit in the form of a dream, relying on His words ﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people﴾, even granting that this vision refers to this journey, the explicit statement here, His words ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾, along with the explicit statements in the numerous authentic hadiths that he was taken on the journey, is no less a basis for interpreting this "vision" in the verse as seeing with the eye. A visual sighting may indeed be called a "vision." And how can this journey be understood as a dream when he (ﷺ) explicitly stated that it occurred between sleep and wakefulness?

The dating of the night journey has also been disputed. It is narrated that it happened one year before the Hijrah to Madinah, and it is narrated that it happened several years before the Hijrah.

The basis for the latter is that Khadijah prayed with the Prophet (ﷺ) and died five years before the Hijrah, or it was said three, or four years. Prayer was not made obligatory until the night of the journey.

Ibn Abd al-Barr used this argument for this view, though the reports from al-Zuhri differ.

Among those who said the night journey was one year before the Hijrah was al-Zuhri in one of his reports, and likewise al-Harbi, who said: the Prophet (ﷺ) was taken on the journey on the night of the twenty-seventh of Rabi' al-Awwal, one year before the Hijrah.

Ibn al-Qasim said in his history: the journey took place eighteen months after his mission.

Ibn Abd al-Barr said: I know of no one among the historians who said the like of this.

It is narrated from al-Zuhri that it took place seven years before his mission, and it is narrated from him that he said: it was five years before his mission.

Yunus narrated from Urwah from Aisha that she said: Khadijah died before prayer was made obligatory.

﴿And We gave Moses the Book﴾, that is, the Torah. It was said that the meaning is: We honored Muhammad with the ascension (mi'raj, the ascent to heaven), and We honored Moses with the Book, and We made it, that is, that Book, or Moses, ﴿a guidance for the Children of Israel﴾ by which they might be guided, ﴿that you not take﴾. Abu 'Amr read it with the ya' (third person), and the rest read it with the ta' (second person), meaning: lest they take.

The meaning is: We gave him the Book for the guidance of the Children of Israel, lest they take ﴿anyone other than Me as a guardian﴾. Al-Farra' said: that is, a trustee over their affairs. It is narrated from him that he said: one who suffices. It was also said: that is, those who rely upon Him in their affairs. It was said: a partner. And the meaning of "wakil" in the lexicon is one to whom affairs are entrusted.

﴿O descendants of those whom We carried with Noah﴾: it is in the accusative case by way of specification (ikhtisas) or address (nida'). He reminded them of His favor upon them within the context of saving their forefathers from drowning. It may also be that the first object of His words "that you not take" is intended, meaning: do not take the descendants of those whom We carried with Noah as a guardian other than Me, like His words: ﴿Nor would He order you to take the angels and the prophets as lords﴾. It was also read in the nominative case, as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as an apposition to the subject of "tattakhidhu" (you take).

Mujahid read it with a fatha on the dhal. Zayd ibn Thabit read it with a kasra on it. The intended meaning of "dhurriyyah" here is all who are on the earth, because they are descendants of those who were in the ark. It was also said: Moses and his people from the Children of Israel. This is what suits the reading in the accusative as an address. The accusative in specification, and the nominative as apposition or predicate, all refer back to the Children of Israel mentioned. As for making the accusative the first object of His words "do not take," the better interpretation is to read "dhurriyyah" as referring to all of the sons of Adam who are on the earth. ﴿Indeed, he was a grateful servant﴾, that is, Noah. Allah described him with abundant gratitude and made it like a reason for what precedes it, to announce that gratitude is among the greatest causes of goodness and among the most excellent acts of obedience, encouraging his descendants to thank Allah.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Amr ibn Shu'ayb from his father from his grandfather, who said: the Prophet (ﷺ) was taken on the journey on the seventeenth night of Rabi' al-Awwal, one year before the Hijrah.

Al-Bayhaqi narrated in al-Dala'il from Ibn Shihab, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken to Bayt al-Maqdis one year before his departure to Madinah.

Al-Bayhaqi narrated the like of it from Urwah.

Al-Bayhaqi also narrated from al-Suddi, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the journey sixteen months before his migration.

Ibn Abi (p-811) Hatim narrated from al-Suddi regarding His words ﴿whose surroundings We have blessed﴾, that he said: We made trees grow around it.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿And We gave Moses the Book and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel﴾, that he said: Allah made it a guidance that brings them out of darkness into light, and made it a mercy for them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿do not take anyone other than Me as a guardian﴾, that he said: a partner.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding His words ﴿O descendants of those whom We carried with Noah﴾, that he said: it is in the form of address: "O descendants of those whom We carried with Noah."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abdullah ibn Zayd al-Ansari, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Those whom We carried with Noah: with Noah there were only four sons: Ham, Sam, Yafith, and Kush. These four sons are the ones from whom this creation descended."

Know that many commentators, such as Ibn Kathir, al-Suyuti, and others, lengthened this section by mentioning the hadiths about the night journey with their varying wordings. There is little benefit in that, since they are well known in their places in the books of hadith. Likewise, they lengthened by mentioning the virtues of the Sacred Mosque and the Farthest Mosque, which is a separate topic. The purpose of books of tafsir is what relates to explaining the words of the Mighty Book, mentioning the occasions of revelation, and clarifying the legal rulings derived from it. Whatever goes beyond this is supplementary, and there is no need for it.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "asra bi-abdihi laylan" is "sayyara abdahu laylan" (He made His servant travel by night), meaning Muhammad. On this view, "asra" means "sayyara," so restricting it to the night has a purpose. He said "bi-abdihi" and did not say "bi-nabiyyihi" (His prophet), "bi-rasulihi" (His messenger), or "bi-Muhammad," in honor of him (ﷺ). The people of knowledge said: had any other name been more noble than this, Allah would have called him by it in this great station and this exalted state:

Do not call me except "O slave of her,"
For it is the most noble of my names.

Calling by names as nicknames among their tribes,
As if names have become some of my names.

﴿From the Sacred Mosque﴾: al-Hasan and Qatadah said: it means the mosque itself, and this is the apparent sense of the Qur'an.

The majority of commentators said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the journey from the house of Umm Hani'. They understood "al-Masjid al-Haram" to mean Makkah, or "al-Haram" (the Sacred Precinct), because each of these encompasses the Sacred Mosque, or because the whole Haram is a mosque.

Then He mentioned the destination to which He took His Messenger (ﷺ), saying: ﴿to the Farthest Mosque﴾, which is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It was called "the Farthest" because of the great distance between it and the Sacred Mosque, and there was no mosque beyond it at that time. Then He described the Farthest Mosque by His words: ﴿whose surroundings We have blessed﴾, with fruits, rivers, prophets, and righteous people. Allah has blessed the surroundings of (p-810) the Farthest Mosque with the blessings of this world and the Hereafter. And in "bараkna" (We have blessed), after "asra" (He took), there is an iltifat (shift) from the third person (absence) to the first person (speech).

Then He mentioned the reason for which He took him, saying: ﴿that We might show him of Our signs﴾, meaning what Allah showed him that night of wonders, among which was covering this long distance in a portion of the night. ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing﴾ of every thing heard, and among that is the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿The All-Seeing﴾ of everything seen, and among that is His Messenger's essence and actions.

The people of knowledge differed as to whether the night journey was with his body (ﷺ) together with his spirit, or with his spirit alone. The majority of the early generations (al-Salaf) and later generations (al-Khalaf) held the first view.

Some people of knowledge held the second view, including Aisha, Mu'awiyah, al-Hasan, and Ibn Ishaq, and Ibn Jarir reported it from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman.

Another group took a detailed position, saying: the journey was with his body, awake, to Bayt al-Maqdis, and to the heaven with his spirit. They used this distinction as evidence, citing His words "to the Farthest Mosque," which He made the endpoint of the journey with his very person (ﷺ). Had the journey from Bayt al-Maqdis to the heaven occurred with his person, He would have mentioned it. What the numerous authentic hadiths indicate is what the majority of the early and later generations held: that the journey was with his body and spirit, awake, to Bayt al-Maqdis, and then through the heavens. There is no need for interpretation that diverts this Qur'anic text and similar wording in the hadiths from its real meaning, and there is no justification for it except mere disbelief and judging by the purely deficient intellects that fail to grasp what is known: that nothing is impossible for Him. Even if it were merely a dream, as those claim who maintain that the journey was with the spirit alone, and that the dreams of prophets are true, the disbelievers would not have denied the Prophet (ﷺ) when he informed them of it, to the point that those whose hearts had not been opened to faith apostatized. A person may see in his sleep what is improbable, even what is impossible, and no one denies this. As for those who hold that the journey was only with the spirit in the form of a dream, relying on His words ﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people﴾, even granting that this vision refers to this journey, the explicit statement here, His words ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾, along with the explicit statements in the numerous authentic hadiths that he was taken on the journey, is no less a basis for interpreting this "vision" in the verse as seeing with the eye. A visual sighting may indeed be called a "vision." And how can this journey be understood as a dream when he (ﷺ) explicitly stated that it occurred between sleep and wakefulness?

The dating of the night journey has also been disputed. It is narrated that it happened one year before the Hijrah to Madinah, and it is narrated that it happened several years before the Hijrah.

The basis for the latter is that Khadijah prayed with the Prophet (ﷺ) and died five years before the Hijrah, or it was said three, or four years. Prayer was not made obligatory until the night of the journey.

Ibn Abd al-Barr used this argument for this view, though the reports from al-Zuhri differ.

Among those who said the night journey was one year before the Hijrah was al-Zuhri in one of his reports, and likewise al-Harbi, who said: the Prophet (ﷺ) was taken on the journey on the night of the twenty-seventh of Rabi' al-Awwal, one year before the Hijrah.

Ibn al-Qasim said in his history: the journey took place eighteen months after his mission.

Ibn Abd al-Barr said: I know of no one among the historians who said the like of this.

It is narrated from al-Zuhri that it took place seven years before his mission, and it is narrated from him that he said: it was five years before his mission.

Yunus narrated from Urwah from Aisha that she said: Khadijah died before prayer was made obligatory.

﴿And We gave Moses the Book﴾, that is, the Torah. It was said that the meaning is: We honored Muhammad with the ascension (mi'raj, the ascent to heaven), and We honored Moses with the Book, and We made it, that is, that Book, or Moses, ﴿a guidance for the Children of Israel﴾ by which they might be guided, ﴿that you not take﴾. Abu 'Amr read it with the ya' (third person), and the rest read it with the ta' (second person), meaning: lest they take.

The meaning is: We gave him the Book for the guidance of the Children of Israel, lest they take ﴿anyone other than Me as a guardian﴾. Al-Farra' said: that is, a trustee over their affairs. It is narrated from him that he said: one who suffices. It was also said: that is, those who rely upon Him in their affairs. It was said: a partner. And the meaning of "wakil" in the lexicon is one to whom affairs are entrusted.

﴿O descendants of those whom We carried with Noah﴾: it is in the accusative case by way of specification (ikhtisas) or address (nida'). He reminded them of His favor upon them within the context of saving their forefathers from drowning. It may also be that the first object of His words "that you not take" is intended, meaning: do not take the descendants of those whom We carried with Noah as a guardian other than Me, like His words: ﴿Nor would He order you to take the angels and the prophets as lords﴾. It was also read in the nominative case, as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as an apposition to the subject of "tattakhidhu" (you take).

Mujahid read it with a fatha on the dhal. Zayd ibn Thabit read it with a kasra on it. The intended meaning of "dhurriyyah" here is all who are on the earth, because they are descendants of those who were in the ark. It was also said: Moses and his people from the Children of Israel. This is what suits the reading in the accusative as an address. The accusative in specification, and the nominative as apposition or predicate, all refer back to the Children of Israel mentioned. As for making the accusative the first object of His words "do not take," the better interpretation is to read "dhurriyyah" as referring to all of the sons of Adam who are on the earth. ﴿Indeed, he was a grateful servant﴾, that is, Noah. Allah described him with abundant gratitude and made it like a reason for what precedes it, to announce that gratitude is among the greatest causes of goodness and among the most excellent acts of obedience, encouraging his descendants to thank Allah.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Amr ibn Shu'ayb from his father from his grandfather, who said: the Prophet (ﷺ) was taken on the journey on the seventeenth night of Rabi' al-Awwal, one year before the Hijrah.

Al-Bayhaqi narrated in al-Dala'il from Ibn Shihab, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken to Bayt al-Maqdis one year before his departure to Madinah.

Al-Bayhaqi narrated the like of it from Urwah.

Al-Bayhaqi also narrated from al-Suddi, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the journey sixteen months before his migration.

Ibn Abi (p-811) Hatim narrated from al-Suddi regarding His words ﴿whose surroundings We have blessed﴾, that he said: We made trees grow around it.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿And We gave Moses the Book and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel﴾, that he said: Allah made it a guidance that brings them out of darkness into light, and made it a mercy for them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿do not take anyone other than Me as a guardian﴾, that he said: a partner.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding His words ﴿O descendants of those whom We carried with Noah﴾, that he said: it is in the form of address: "O descendants of those whom We carried with Noah."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abdullah ibn Zayd al-Ansari, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Those whom We carried with Noah: with Noah there were only four sons: Ham, Sam, Yafith, and Kush. These four sons are the ones from whom this creation descended."

Know that many commentators, such as Ibn Kathir, al-Suyuti, and others, lengthened this section by mentioning the hadiths about the night journey with their varying wordings. There is little benefit in that, since they are well known in their places in the books of hadith. Likewise, they lengthened by mentioning the virtues of the Sacred Mosque and the Farthest Mosque, which is a separate topic. The purpose of books of tafsir is what relates to explaining the words of the Mighty Book, mentioning the occasions of revelation, and clarifying the legal rulings derived from it. Whatever goes beyond this is supplementary, and there is no need for it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 17, verses 4–11 (part 1 of 2):

**"And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book"** (﴿وقَضَيْنا إلى بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ في الكِتابِ﴾). *Qada'* means "informed and told," or "judged and completed." Its root meaning is "to firmly establish a thing and finish with it." It is also said to mean "We revealed." The context supports this, since the verb is followed by *ila* (to) with "Children of Israel." If it meant "informed" or "told," it would be used without *ila* ("qadayna Bani Isra'il"). If it meant "judged," it would take *ala* ("on"). If it meant "completed," it would take *li* ("for"). The "Book" here is the Torah, and its being sent down to their prophet Musa is like its being sent down to them, since they were his people. It is also said that the "Book" is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

Abu al-Aliya and Sa'id ibn Jubayr read *fi al-kutubi* ("in the books").

Isa al-Thaqafi read *latafsudunna* with an opened *ta'* (the second verb form with *ta'* in the first position), and its meaning is close to the reading of the majority, because when they corrupt, they are corrupted within themselves. "Corruption" here means opposing what God prescribed for them in the Torah. "The land" means the land of al-Sham and Bayt al-Maqdis. It is also said to mean the land of Egypt. The *lam* in *latufsidunna* is the answer to an implied oath.

Al-Naysaburi said: or he treated the definitive decree as if it were an oath, as if it were said: "And We swore that you will surely corrupt."

*Marratayn* ("twice") is in the accusative either as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, or as a verbal noun itself governing something not of its own kind. The first time was the killing of Sha'ya, or the imprisonment of Irmiya, or opposing the rulings of the Torah. The second time was the killing of Yahya ibn Zakariyya and the plot to kill Isa.

**"And you will become haughty with great haughtiness"** (﴿ولَتَعْلُنَّ عُلُوًّا كَبِيرًا﴾). This *lam* is like the *lam* before it. That is, you will be arrogant toward obeying God, and you will exalt yourselves over people through oppression and transgression, going beyond all limits in that.

**"So when the promise of the first of them came"** (﴿فَإذا جاءَ وعْدُ أُولاهُما﴾), that is, the first of the two mentioned times, **"We sent against you servants of Ours, of great might"** (﴿بَعَثْنا عَلَيْكم عِبادًا لَنا أُولِي بَأْسٍ شَدِيدٍ﴾), meaning strength in wars and severity at the encounter.

It is said they were Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) and his armies. It is also said they were Jalut (Goliath), or an army from Persia, or an army from Babylon.

**"And they went through the homes"** (﴿فَجاسُوا خِلالَ الدِّيارِ﴾). *Jasu* means they ravaged and roamed. It is said *jasu*, *hasu*, and *dasu* have the same meaning, as mentioned by Ibn Ghurayr and al-Qutaybi.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that they went around among the homes asking whether anyone remained whom they had not killed. He said: *al-jaws* is seeking something thoroughly.

Al-Jawhari said: *al-jaws* is the verbal noun of your saying *jasu khilal al-diyar*, meaning they passed through them as a man searches for news, that is, seeks it. Abu Ubayda also said this.

Ibn Jarir said: the meaning of *jasu* is that they walked among the homes seeking them and killing them, going and coming.

Al-Farra' said: its meaning is that they killed them among their houses, and he recited a verse by Hassan:

*"And among us is the one who met with the sword of Muhammad, and so he roamed among the enemies, across the ranks of the armies."*

Qutrub said: its meaning is that they descended. He recited a poet's verse:

*"So we entered their homes by force, and we returned with their chiefs bound in chains."*

Ibn Abbas read *fa-hasu* with the unpointed *ha'* (ح).

Abu Zayd said: *al-hawsu*, *al-jawsu*, *al-ʿawsu*, and *al-hawsu* all mean roaming at night. It is said that roaming at night is *al-jawasan*, with a vowel on it. Abu Ubayda said this too.

*Khalal al-diyar* was also read as *khalal al-diyar*, and its meaning is the same as *khilal*, which is the middle of the homes.

**"And it was a promise to be fulfilled"** (﴿وكانَ ذَلِكَ وعْدًا مَفْعُولًا﴾), that is, it was certain and unavoidable.

**"Then We gave you the return of victory over them"** (﴿ثُمَّ رَدَدْنا لَكُمُ الكَرَّةَ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾): that is, the dominance, the victory, and the return. This was at the time of their repentance.

It is said this was when Dawud (David) killed Jalut. It is also said it was when Bukhtnassar was killed.

**"And We aided you with wealth and children"** (﴿وأمْدَدْناكم بِأمْوالٍ وبَنِينَ﴾), after the plunder of your wealth and the capture of your sons, until your affairs returned to what they had been.

**"And made you more in manpower"** (﴿وجَعَلْناكم أكْثَرَ نَفِيرًا﴾). Abu Ubayda said: *al-nafir* is the number of men, so the meaning is: more in men than your enemy.

*Al-nafir* is the one who goes out with a man from his tribe, and it is said *nafir* and *nafir* (with an active participle pattern) like *qadir* and *qadir*. It is permitted for *al-nafir* to be the plural of *nafar*.

**"If you do good"** (﴿إنْ أحْسَنْتُمْ﴾), that is, your deeds and words in the manner required of you, **"you do good for yourselves"** (﴿أحْسَنْتُمْ لِأنْفُسِكُمْ﴾), because the reward of that returns to you. **"And if you do evil"** (﴿وإنْ أسَأْتُمْ﴾), that is, your deeds and words, which you performed not in the manner required of you, **"then it is against them"** (﴿فَلَها﴾), that is, *fa-'alayha*.

A similar usage is the poet's verse:

*"So he fell prone upon his hands and his face."*

That is, on his hands and on his face.

Ibn Jarir said: the *lam* here means *ila* ("to"), that is, the evil returns to them, like His saying: **"Because your Lord has inspired her"** (﴿بِأنَّ رَبَّكَ أوْحى لَها﴾), that is, to her.

It is also said the meaning is: for it is the requital or the punishment.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: for it there is a Lord who forgives the evil.

This address is said to be to the Children of Israel who were living in the times mentioned in these verses. It is also said it is to the Children of Israel living in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ). Its meaning is to inform them of what befell their predecessors, so that they would be wary of the same. It is also said it is an address to the polytheists of Quraysh.

**"So when the promise of the second came"** (﴿فَإذا جاءَ وعْدُ الآخِرَةِ﴾), that is, the time came for what they had been promised of the punishment of the second time. The second time was their killing of Yahya ibn Zakariyya, as previously mentioned. The story of his killing is fully given in the Gospel, where his name is Yuhanna (John). A king of their kings killed him because of a woman who urged him to kill him. The name of the king is Lakht, as Ibn Qutayba said. Ibn Jarir said it was Hirudus (Herod).

The answer to *idha* is omitted. Its estimated form is: "We sent them," because the answer of the first *idha* indicates it. **"To make your faces grieve"** (﴿لِيَسُوءُوا وُجُوهَكُمْ﴾) is connected to this omitted answer. That is, they would do to you what would grieve your faces, until the signs of harm appear upon you and the sorrow becomes visible in your faces. It is also said that the faces here means their chiefs.

Al-Kisa'i read *li-nasu'a* with *nun*, meaning that the pronoun refers to God, glorified is He.

Ubayy read *li-nasu'anna* with the emphatic *nun*.

Abu Bakr, al-A'mash, Ibn Wathhab, Hamza, and Ibn Amir read *li-yasu'a* with the *ya'* (third-person) and singular form. Al-Zajjaj said: everything you break and crush, you have *tabbartahu*. The pronoun refers to God or to the promise.

**"And to enter the Masjid"** (﴿ولِيَدْخُلُوا المَسْجِدَ﴾) is joined to *li-yasu'u*, **"as they entered it the first time, and to destroy what they had overcome"** (﴿كَما دَخَلُوهُ أوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ ولِيُتَبِّرُوا﴾), that is, they would ruin and destroy. Qutrub said: they would demolish. From this is the poet's verse:

*"Men are only two kinds: one who works to destroy what he builds, and another who raises up."*

The rest read with *ya'* and a *damma* on the *hamza*, with a *waw* after it, meaning the subject is "servants of Ours." *Ma 'alaw* means what they overcame of your lands, or the duration of their dominance, **"destruction"** (*tatbiran*), that is, annihilation. The verbal noun is mentioned to remove doubt and to confirm the report.

**"It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you"** (﴿عَسى رَبُّكم أنْ يَرْحَمَكُمْ﴾), O Children of Israel, after His retribution against you the second time. **"And if you return, We will return"** (﴿وإنْ عُدْتُمْ عُدْنا﴾), that is, to punishment against you for a third time.

The people of the histories (*ahl al-siyar*) said: then they returned to what was not fitting, which was denying Muhammad (ﷺ) and concealing what had come about his sending in the Torah and the Gospel. So God returned to punishing them at the hands of the Arabs. What happened to the Banu Qurayza, al-Nadir, Banu Qaynuqa', and Khaybar, of killing, captivity, expulsion, imposing the jizya on those who remained, and the imposition of humiliation and destitution, befell them.

**"And We have made Hell a prison for the disbelievers"** (﴿وجَعَلْنا جَهَنَّمَ لِلْكافِرِينَ حَصِيرًا﴾). *Hasir* means a prison, so it is *fa'il* in the sense of *fa'il* or *maf'ul*. The meaning is that they are confined in Hell and never escape from it.

Al-Jawhari said: *hasarahu yahsuruhu hasran* means he constricted him and surrounded him. It is also said: *hasir* means a bed and a cushion. In this sense, *al-hasir* refers to the mat that people spread out.

**"Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright"** (﴿إنَّ هَذا القُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هي أقْوَمُ﴾). That is: the Qur'an guides people to the path that is most upright compared to other paths, and it is the religion of Islam. So *allati hiya aqwamu* is an adjective of an omitted noun, which is "the path."

Al-Zajjaj said: it means "to the state that is the most upright of states," which is the oneness of God and belief in His messengers. Al-Farra' also said this.

**"And gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds"** (﴿ويُبَشِّرُ المُؤْمِنِينَ الَّذِينَ يَعْمَلُونَ الصّالِحاتِ﴾). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *yabashshiru*, with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and a *damma* on the *shin*. The rest read it with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *kasra* on the *shin*, from *al-tabshir*, meaning: he gives good tidings with what it contains of the promise of good, both in the next life and in this life, to the believers, **"that for them is a great reward"** (﴿أنَّ لَهم أجْرًا كَبِيرًا﴾), that is, that for them is.

**"And that those who do not believe in the Hereafter"** (﴿وأنَّ الَّذِينَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالآخِرَةِ﴾), and its rulings that are explained in the Qur'an, **"We have prepared for them a painful punishment"** (﴿أعْتَدْنا لَهم عَذابًا ألِيمًا﴾). This is the punishment of the Fire. This clause is joined to the clause *yubashshiru*, with an implied *yukhbiru* ("he informs"). That is: and he informs that those who do not believe in the Hereafter... It is also said it is joined to His saying *anna lahum ajran kabiran*, and "giving good tidings" means the general sense of informing. Or the intended meaning is its literal sense, and the speech contains a double good tiding to the believers: the first is what they have of reward, and the second is what their enemies have of punishment.

**"And man invokes evil as he invokes good"** (﴿ويَدْعُ الإنْسانُ بِالشَّرِّ دُعاءَهُ بِالخَيْرِ﴾). Here "man" refers to the species, because this supplication comes from some of its individuals, namely a man invoking against himself and his child when he is distressed with something he would not want answered. **"As he invokes for good"** (*duʿa'hu bi-al-khayr*), that is, like his supplication to his Lord for good for himself and his family, such as seeking health, provision, and the like. If God answered his supplication against himself for evil, he would perish. But He did not answer it, out of His grace and mercy. Similar to this is **"And if God were to hasten for people the evil as they seek to hasten the good"** (﴿ولَوْ يُعَجِّلُ اللَّهُ لِلنّاسِ الشَّرَّ اسْتِعْجالَهم بِالخَيْرِ﴾), which has already been mentioned.

It is also said that "man" here refers to the one who says this statement, the disbeliever, who invokes evil upon himself. This is seeking the hastening of punishment, and he invokes for it as good, like the saying of the speaker: **"O God, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment"** (﴿اللَّهُمَّ إنْ كانَ هَذا هو الحَقَّ مِن عِنْدِكَ فَأمْطِرْ عَلَيْنا حِجارَةً مِنَ السَّماءِ أوِ ائْتِنا بِعَذابٍ ألِيمٍ﴾).

It is also said: that he supplicates in seeking the forbidden as he supplicates in seeking the permissible.

The *waw* was omitted from *wa-yadaʿu al-insanu* in the script of the Mushaf, because it is not pronounced, since the unvowelled *lam* follows it, like His saying: **"We will call the guards of Hell"** (﴿سَنَدْعُ الزَّبانِيَةَ﴾), **"And Allah will erase falsehood"** (﴿ويَمْحُ اللَّهُ الباطِلَ﴾), **"And Allah will bring the believers"** (﴿وسَوْفَ يُؤْتِ اللَّهُ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾), and similar.

**"And man has always been hasty"** (﴿وكانَ الإنْسانُ عَجُولًا﴾), that is, created with haste as a nature. From his haste is that he asks for evil just as he asks for good. It is also said that it refers to Adam, peace be upon him, when he rose before the spirit was fully breathed into him. The one that fits the context is the first meaning.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying **"And We decreed to the Children of Israel"**, that he said: "We informed them."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: "We told them."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: "We told them."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him regarding *qadayna ila Bani Isra'il*: "We decreed upon them."

Ibn Asakir in his *Tarikh* narrated from Ali, regarding His saying **"You will surely cause corruption in the land twice"** (﴿لَتُفْسِدُنَّ في الأرْضِ مَرَّتَيْنِ﴾), that he said: "The first was the killing of Zakariyya, and the last was the killing of Yahya."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding the verse that he said: "The first corruption was the killing of Zakariyya, so God sent against them the king of the Nabateans. Then the Children of Israel prepared and raided the Nabateans and took from them, and that is His saying: **'We gave you the return of victory over them'** (﴿رَدَدْنا لَكُمُ الكَرَّةَ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "God sent against them in the first time Jalut, and He sent against them in the second time Bukhtnassar. Then they returned, and God empowered the believers over them."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding *fa-jasu*: "They walked."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him also: "*Tatbiran*: destruction."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Dahhak regarding His saying **"It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you"** that he said: "The mercy that He promised them was the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him: the meaning of *hasiran* is that God made their dwelling place in it.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abd al-Razzaq related from al-Hasan regarding His words ﴿ḥaṣīran﴾ that he said: a bedding and a cushion.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Zayd regarding His words: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ that he said: to that which is most correct.

al-Hakim related from Ibn Mas'ud that he would frequently recite: "Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright, and gives good news of lightening (the burden)," adding "and gives good news of lightening."

Ibn Jarir also related from him regarding His words: ﴿And man has always been hasty﴾ that he said: impatient, having no patience in ease or in hardship.

He began to look at it while it was being created, but his legs remained (uncreated). When it was after 'Asr, he said: 'My Lord, hasten (the creation) before night.' That is His saying: ﴿And man has always been hasty﴾."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 17, verses 4–11 (part 1 of 2):

**"And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book"** (﴿وقَضَيْنا إلى بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ في الكِتابِ﴾). *Qada'* means "informed and told," or "judged and completed." Its root meaning is "to firmly establish a thing and finish with it." It is also said to mean "We revealed." The context supports this, since the verb is followed by *ila* (to) with "Children of Israel." If it meant "informed" or "told," it would be used without *ila* ("qadayna Bani Isra'il"). If it meant "judged," it would take *ala* ("on"). If it meant "completed," it would take *li* ("for"). The "Book" here is the Torah, and its being sent down to their prophet Musa is like its being sent down to them, since they were his people. It is also said that the "Book" is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

Abu al-Aliya and Sa'id ibn Jubayr read *fi al-kutubi* ("in the books").

Isa al-Thaqafi read *latafsudunna* with an opened *ta'* (the second verb form with *ta'* in the first position), and its meaning is close to the reading of the majority, because when they corrupt, they are corrupted within themselves. "Corruption" here means opposing what God prescribed for them in the Torah. "The land" means the land of al-Sham and Bayt al-Maqdis. It is also said to mean the land of Egypt. The *lam* in *latufsidunna* is the answer to an implied oath.

Al-Naysaburi said: or he treated the definitive decree as if it were an oath, as if it were said: "And We swore that you will surely corrupt."

*Marratayn* ("twice") is in the accusative either as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, or as a verbal noun itself governing something not of its own kind. The first time was the killing of Sha'ya, or the imprisonment of Irmiya, or opposing the rulings of the Torah. The second time was the killing of Yahya ibn Zakariyya and the plot to kill Isa.

**"And you will become haughty with great haughtiness"** (﴿ولَتَعْلُنَّ عُلُوًّا كَبِيرًا﴾). This *lam* is like the *lam* before it. That is, you will be arrogant toward obeying God, and you will exalt yourselves over people through oppression and transgression, going beyond all limits in that.

**"So when the promise of the first of them came"** (﴿فَإذا جاءَ وعْدُ أُولاهُما﴾), that is, the first of the two mentioned times, **"We sent against you servants of Ours, of great might"** (﴿بَعَثْنا عَلَيْكم عِبادًا لَنا أُولِي بَأْسٍ شَدِيدٍ﴾), meaning strength in wars and severity at the encounter.

It is said they were Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) and his armies. It is also said they were Jalut (Goliath), or an army from Persia, or an army from Babylon.

**"And they went through the homes"** (﴿فَجاسُوا خِلالَ الدِّيارِ﴾). *Jasu* means they ravaged and roamed. It is said *jasu*, *hasu*, and *dasu* have the same meaning, as mentioned by Ibn Ghurayr and al-Qutaybi.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that they went around among the homes asking whether anyone remained whom they had not killed. He said: *al-jaws* is seeking something thoroughly.

Al-Jawhari said: *al-jaws* is the verbal noun of your saying *jasu khilal al-diyar*, meaning they passed through them as a man searches for news, that is, seeks it. Abu Ubayda also said this.

Ibn Jarir said: the meaning of *jasu* is that they walked among the homes seeking them and killing them, going and coming.

Al-Farra' said: its meaning is that they killed them among their houses, and he recited a verse by Hassan:

*"And among us is the one who met with the sword of Muhammad, and so he roamed among the enemies, across the ranks of the armies."*

Qutrub said: its meaning is that they descended. He recited a poet's verse:

*"So we entered their homes by force, and we returned with their chiefs bound in chains."*

Ibn Abbas read *fa-hasu* with the unpointed *ha'* (ح).

Abu Zayd said: *al-hawsu*, *al-jawsu*, *al-ʿawsu*, and *al-hawsu* all mean roaming at night. It is said that roaming at night is *al-jawasan*, with a vowel on it. Abu Ubayda said this too.

*Khalal al-diyar* was also read as *khalal al-diyar*, and its meaning is the same as *khilal*, which is the middle of the homes.

**"And it was a promise to be fulfilled"** (﴿وكانَ ذَلِكَ وعْدًا مَفْعُولًا﴾), that is, it was certain and unavoidable.

**"Then We gave you the return of victory over them"** (﴿ثُمَّ رَدَدْنا لَكُمُ الكَرَّةَ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾): that is, the dominance, the victory, and the return. This was at the time of their repentance.

It is said this was when Dawud (David) killed Jalut. It is also said it was when Bukhtnassar was killed.

**"And We aided you with wealth and children"** (﴿وأمْدَدْناكم بِأمْوالٍ وبَنِينَ﴾), after the plunder of your wealth and the capture of your sons, until your affairs returned to what they had been.

**"And made you more in manpower"** (﴿وجَعَلْناكم أكْثَرَ نَفِيرًا﴾). Abu Ubayda said: *al-nafir* is the number of men, so the meaning is: more in men than your enemy.

*Al-nafir* is the one who goes out with a man from his tribe, and it is said *nafir* and *nafir* (with an active participle pattern) like *qadir* and *qadir*. It is permitted for *al-nafir* to be the plural of *nafar*.

**"If you do good"** (﴿إنْ أحْسَنْتُمْ﴾), that is, your deeds and words in the manner required of you, **"you do good for yourselves"** (﴿أحْسَنْتُمْ لِأنْفُسِكُمْ﴾), because the reward of that returns to you. **"And if you do evil"** (﴿وإنْ أسَأْتُمْ﴾), that is, your deeds and words, which you performed not in the manner required of you, **"then it is against them"** (﴿فَلَها﴾), that is, *fa-'alayha*.

A similar usage is the poet's verse:

*"So he fell prone upon his hands and his face."*

That is, on his hands and on his face.

Ibn Jarir said: the *lam* here means *ila* ("to"), that is, the evil returns to them, like His saying: **"Because your Lord has inspired her"** (﴿بِأنَّ رَبَّكَ أوْحى لَها﴾), that is, to her.

It is also said the meaning is: for it is the requital or the punishment.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: for it there is a Lord who forgives the evil.

This address is said to be to the Children of Israel who were living in the times mentioned in these verses. It is also said it is to the Children of Israel living in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ). Its meaning is to inform them of what befell their predecessors, so that they would be wary of the same. It is also said it is an address to the polytheists of Quraysh.

**"So when the promise of the second came"** (﴿فَإذا جاءَ وعْدُ الآخِرَةِ﴾), that is, the time came for what they had been promised of the punishment of the second time. The second time was their killing of Yahya ibn Zakariyya, as previously mentioned. The story of his killing is fully given in the Gospel, where his name is Yuhanna (John). A king of their kings killed him because of a woman who urged him to kill him. The name of the king is Lakht, as Ibn Qutayba said. Ibn Jarir said it was Hirudus (Herod).

The answer to *idha* is omitted. Its estimated form is: "We sent them," because the answer of the first *idha* indicates it. **"To make your faces grieve"** (﴿لِيَسُوءُوا وُجُوهَكُمْ﴾) is connected to this omitted answer. That is, they would do to you what would grieve your faces, until the signs of harm appear upon you and the sorrow becomes visible in your faces. It is also said that the faces here means their chiefs.

Al-Kisa'i read *li-nasu'a* with *nun*, meaning that the pronoun refers to God, glorified is He.

Ubayy read *li-nasu'anna* with the emphatic *nun*.

Abu Bakr, al-A'mash, Ibn Wathhab, Hamza, and Ibn Amir read *li-yasu'a* with the *ya'* (third-person) and singular form. Al-Zajjaj said: everything you break and crush, you have *tabbartahu*. The pronoun refers to God or to the promise.

**"And to enter the Masjid"** (﴿ولِيَدْخُلُوا المَسْجِدَ﴾) is joined to *li-yasu'u*, **"as they entered it the first time, and to destroy what they had overcome"** (﴿كَما دَخَلُوهُ أوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ ولِيُتَبِّرُوا﴾), that is, they would ruin and destroy. Qutrub said: they would demolish. From this is the poet's verse:

*"Men are only two kinds: one who works to destroy what he builds, and another who raises up."*

The rest read with *ya'* and a *damma* on the *hamza*, with a *waw* after it, meaning the subject is "servants of Ours." *Ma 'alaw* means what they overcame of your lands, or the duration of their dominance, **"destruction"** (*tatbiran*), that is, annihilation. The verbal noun is mentioned to remove doubt and to confirm the report.

**"It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you"** (﴿عَسى رَبُّكم أنْ يَرْحَمَكُمْ﴾), O Children of Israel, after His retribution against you the second time. **"And if you return, We will return"** (﴿وإنْ عُدْتُمْ عُدْنا﴾), that is, to punishment against you for a third time.

The people of the histories (*ahl al-siyar*) said: then they returned to what was not fitting, which was denying Muhammad (ﷺ) and concealing what had come about his sending in the Torah and the Gospel. So God returned to punishing them at the hands of the Arabs. What happened to the Banu Qurayza, al-Nadir, Banu Qaynuqa', and Khaybar, of killing, captivity, expulsion, imposing the jizya on those who remained, and the imposition of humiliation and destitution, befell them.

**"And We have made Hell a prison for the disbelievers"** (﴿وجَعَلْنا جَهَنَّمَ لِلْكافِرِينَ حَصِيرًا﴾). *Hasir* means a prison, so it is *fa'il* in the sense of *fa'il* or *maf'ul*. The meaning is that they are confined in Hell and never escape from it.

Al-Jawhari said: *hasarahu yahsuruhu hasran* means he constricted him and surrounded him. It is also said: *hasir* means a bed and a cushion. In this sense, *al-hasir* refers to the mat that people spread out.

**"Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright"** (﴿إنَّ هَذا القُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هي أقْوَمُ﴾). That is: the Qur'an guides people to the path that is most upright compared to other paths, and it is the religion of Islam. So *allati hiya aqwamu* is an adjective of an omitted noun, which is "the path."

Al-Zajjaj said: it means "to the state that is the most upright of states," which is the oneness of God and belief in His messengers. Al-Farra' also said this.

**"And gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds"** (﴿ويُبَشِّرُ المُؤْمِنِينَ الَّذِينَ يَعْمَلُونَ الصّالِحاتِ﴾). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *yabashshiru*, with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and a *damma* on the *shin*. The rest read it with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *kasra* on the *shin*, from *al-tabshir*, meaning: he gives good tidings with what it contains of the promise of good, both in the next life and in this life, to the believers, **"that for them is a great reward"** (﴿أنَّ لَهم أجْرًا كَبِيرًا﴾), that is, that for them is.

**"And that those who do not believe in the Hereafter"** (﴿وأنَّ الَّذِينَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالآخِرَةِ﴾), and its rulings that are explained in the Qur'an, **"We have prepared for them a painful punishment"** (﴿أعْتَدْنا لَهم عَذابًا ألِيمًا﴾). This is the punishment of the Fire. This clause is joined to the clause *yubashshiru*, with an implied *yukhbiru* ("he informs"). That is: and he informs that those who do not believe in the Hereafter... It is also said it is joined to His saying *anna lahum ajran kabiran*, and "giving good tidings" means the general sense of informing. Or the intended meaning is its literal sense, and the speech contains a double good tiding to the believers: the first is what they have of reward, and the second is what their enemies have of punishment.

**"And man invokes evil as he invokes good"** (﴿ويَدْعُ الإنْسانُ بِالشَّرِّ دُعاءَهُ بِالخَيْرِ﴾). Here "man" refers to the species, because this supplication comes from some of its individuals, namely a man invoking against himself and his child when he is distressed with something he would not want answered. **"As he invokes for good"** (*duʿa'hu bi-al-khayr*), that is, like his supplication to his Lord for good for himself and his family, such as seeking health, provision, and the like. If God answered his supplication against himself for evil, he would perish. But He did not answer it, out of His grace and mercy. Similar to this is **"And if God were to hasten for people the evil as they seek to hasten the good"** (﴿ولَوْ يُعَجِّلُ اللَّهُ لِلنّاسِ الشَّرَّ اسْتِعْجالَهم بِالخَيْرِ﴾), which has already been mentioned.

It is also said that "man" here refers to the one who says this statement, the disbeliever, who invokes evil upon himself. This is seeking the hastening of punishment, and he invokes for it as good, like the saying of the speaker: **"O God, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment"** (﴿اللَّهُمَّ إنْ كانَ هَذا هو الحَقَّ مِن عِنْدِكَ فَأمْطِرْ عَلَيْنا حِجارَةً مِنَ السَّماءِ أوِ ائْتِنا بِعَذابٍ ألِيمٍ﴾).

It is also said: that he supplicates in seeking the forbidden as he supplicates in seeking the permissible.

The *waw* was omitted from *wa-yadaʿu al-insanu* in the script of the Mushaf, because it is not pronounced, since the unvowelled *lam* follows it, like His saying: **"We will call the guards of Hell"** (﴿سَنَدْعُ الزَّبانِيَةَ﴾), **"And Allah will erase falsehood"** (﴿ويَمْحُ اللَّهُ الباطِلَ﴾), **"And Allah will bring the believers"** (﴿وسَوْفَ يُؤْتِ اللَّهُ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾), and similar.

**"And man has always been hasty"** (﴿وكانَ الإنْسانُ عَجُولًا﴾), that is, created with haste as a nature. From his haste is that he asks for evil just as he asks for good. It is also said that it refers to Adam, peace be upon him, when he rose before the spirit was fully breathed into him. The one that fits the context is the first meaning.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: "We told them."

**"So when the promise of the first of them came"** (﴿فَإذا جاءَ وعْدُ أُولاهُما﴾), that is, the first of the two mentioned times, **"We sent against you servants of Ours, of great might"** (﴿بَعَثْنا عَلَيْكم عِبادًا لَنا أُولِي بَأْسٍ شَدِيدٍ﴾), meaning strength in wars and severity at the encounter.

It is said they were Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) and his armies. It is also said they were Jalut (Goliath), or an army from Persia, or an army from Babylon.

**"And they went through the homes"** (﴿فَجاسُوا خِلالَ الدِّيارِ﴾). *Jasu* means they ravaged and roamed. It is said *jasu*, *hasu*, and *dasu* have the same meaning, as mentioned by Ibn Ghurayr and al-Qutaybi.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that they went around among the homes asking whether anyone remained whom they had not killed. He said: *al-jaws* is seeking something thoroughly.

Al-Jawhari said: *al-jaws* is the verbal noun of your saying *jasu khilal al-diyar*, meaning they passed through them as a man searches for news, that is, seeks it. Abu Ubayda also said this.

Ibn Jarir said: the meaning of *jasu* is that they walked among the homes seeking them and killing them, going and coming.

Al-Farra' said: its meaning is that they killed them among their houses, and he recited a verse by Hassan:

*"And among us is the one who met with the sword of Muhammad, and so he roamed among the enemies, across the ranks of the armies."*

Qutrub said: its meaning is that they descended. He recited a poet's verse:

*"So we entered their homes by force, and we returned with their chiefs bound in chains."*

Ibn Abbas read *fa-hasu* with the unpointed *ha'* (ح).

Abu Zayd said: *al-hawsu*, *al-jawsu*, *al-ʿawsu*, and *al-hawsu* all mean roaming at night. It is said that roaming at night is *al-jawasan*, with a vowel on it. Abu Ubayda said this too.

*Khalal al-diyar* was also read as *khalal al-diyar*, and its meaning is the same as *khilal*, which is the middle of the homes.

**"And it was a promise to be fulfilled"** (﴿وكانَ ذَلِكَ وعْدًا مَفْعُولًا﴾), that is, it was certain and unavoidable.

**"Then We gave you the return of victory over them"** (﴿ثُمَّ رَدَدْنا لَكُمُ الكَرَّةَ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾): that is, the dominance, the victory, and the return. This was at the time of their repentance.

It is said this was when Dawud (David) killed Jalut. It is also said it was when Bukhtnassar was killed.

**"And We aided you with wealth and children"** (﴿وأمْدَدْناكم بِأمْوالٍ وبَنِينَ﴾), after the plunder of your wealth and the capture of your sons, until your affairs returned to what they had been.

**"And made you more in manpower"** (﴿وجَعَلْناكم أكْثَرَ نَفِيرًا﴾). Abu Ubayda said: *al-nafir* is the number of men, so the meaning is: more in men than your enemy.

*Al-nafir* is the one who goes out with a man from his tribe, and it is said *nafir* and *nafir* (with an active participle pattern) like *qadir* and *qadir*. It is permitted for *al-nafir* to be the plural of *nafar*.

**"If you do good"** (﴿إنْ أحْسَنْتُمْ﴾), that is, your deeds and words in the manner required of you, **"you do good for yourselves"** (﴿أحْسَنْتُمْ لِأنْفُسِكُمْ﴾), because the reward of that returns to you. **"And if you do evil"** (﴿وإنْ أسَأْتُمْ﴾), that is, your deeds and words, which you performed not in the manner required of you, **"then it is against them"** (﴿فَلَها﴾), that is, *fa-'alayha*.

A similar usage is the poet's verse:

*"So he fell prone upon his hands and his face."*

That is, on his hands and on his face.

Ibn Jarir said: the *lam* here means *ila* ("to"), that is, the evil returns to them, like His saying: **"Because your Lord has inspired her"** (﴿بِأنَّ رَبَّكَ أوْحى لَها﴾), that is, to her.

It is also said the meaning is: for it is the requital or the punishment.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: for it there is a Lord who forgives the evil.

This address is said to be to the Children of Israel who were living in the times mentioned in these verses. It is also said it is to the Children of Israel living in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ). Its meaning is to inform them of what befell their predecessors, so that they would be wary of the same. It is also said it is an address to the polytheists of Quraysh.

**"So when the promise of the second came"** (﴿فَإذا جاءَ وعْدُ الآخِرَةِ﴾), that is, the time came for what they had been promised of the punishment of the second time. The second time was their killing of Yahya ibn Zakariyya, as previously mentioned. The story of his killing is fully given in the Gospel, where his name is Yuhanna (John). A king of their kings killed him because of a woman who urged him to kill him. The name of the king is Lakht, as Ibn Qutayba said. Ibn Jarir said it was Hirudus (Herod).

The answer to *idha* is omitted. Its estimated form is: "We sent them," because the answer of the first *idha* indicates it. **"To make your faces grieve"** (﴿لِيَسُوءُوا وُجُوهَكُمْ﴾) is connected to this omitted answer. That is, they would do to you what would grieve your faces, until the signs of harm appear upon you and the sorrow becomes visible in your faces. It is also said that the faces here means their chiefs.

Al-Kisa'i read *li-nasu'a* with *nun*, meaning that the pronoun refers to God, glorified is He.

Ubayy read *li-nasu'anna* with the emphatic *nun*.

Abu Bakr, al-A'mash, Ibn Wathhab, Hamza, and Ibn Amir read *li-yasu'a* with the *ya'* (third-person) and singular form. Al-Zajjaj said: everything you break and crush, you have *tabbartahu*. The pronoun refers to God or to the promise.

**"And to enter the Masjid"** (﴿ولِيَدْخُلُوا المَسْجِدَ﴾) is joined to *li-yasu'u*, **"as they entered it the first time, and to destroy what they had overcome"** (﴿كَما دَخَلُوهُ أوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ ولِيُتَبِّرُوا﴾), that is, they would ruin and destroy. Qutrub said: they would demolish. From this is the poet's verse:

*"Men are only two kinds: one who works to destroy what he builds, and another who raises up."*

The rest read with *ya'* and a *damma* on the *hamza*, with a *waw* after it, meaning the subject is "servants of Ours." *Ma 'alaw* means what they overcame of your lands, or the duration of their dominance, **"destruction"** (*tatbiran*), that is, annihilation. The verbal noun is mentioned to remove doubt and to confirm the report.

**"It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you"** (﴿عَسى رَبُّكم أنْ يَرْحَمَكُمْ﴾), O Children of Israel, after His retribution against you the second time. **"And if you return, We will return"** (﴿وإنْ عُدْتُمْ عُدْنا﴾), that is, to punishment against you for a third time.

The people of the histories (*ahl al-siyar*) said: then they returned to what was not fitting, which was denying Muhammad (ﷺ) and concealing what had come about his sending in the Torah and the Gospel. So God returned to punishing them at the hands of the Arabs. What happened to the Banu Qurayza, al-Nadir, Banu Qaynuqa', and Khaybar, of killing, captivity, expulsion, imposing the jizya on those who remained, and the imposition of humiliation and destitution, befell them.

**"And We have made Hell a prison for the disbelievers"** (﴿وجَعَلْنا جَهَنَّمَ لِلْكافِرِينَ حَصِيرًا﴾). *Hasir* means a prison, so it is *fa'il* in the sense of *fa'il* or *maf'ul*. The meaning is that they are confined in Hell and never escape from it.

Al-Jawhari said: *hasarahu yahsuruhu hasran* means he constricted him and surrounded him. It is also said: *hasir* means a bed and a cushion. In this sense, *al-hasir* refers to the mat that people spread out.

**"Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright"** (﴿إنَّ هَذا القُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هي أقْوَمُ﴾). That is: the Qur'an guides people to the path that is most upright compared to other paths, and it is the religion of Islam. So *allati hiya aqwamu* is an adjective of an omitted noun, which is "the path."

Al-Zajjaj said: it means "to the state that is the most upright of states," which is the oneness of God and belief in His messengers. Al-Farra' also said this.

**"And gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds"** (﴿ويُبَشِّرُ المُؤْمِنِينَ الَّذِينَ يَعْمَلُونَ الصّالِحاتِ﴾). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *yabashshiru*, with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and a *damma* on the *shin*. The rest read it with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *kasra* on the *shin*, from *al-tabshir*, meaning: he gives good tidings with what it contains of the promise of good, both in the next life and in this life, to the believers, **"that for them is a great reward"** (﴿أنَّ لَهم أجْرًا كَبِيرًا﴾), that is, that for them is.

**"And that those who do not believe in the Hereafter"** (﴿وأنَّ الَّذِينَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالآخِرَةِ﴾), and its rulings that are explained in the Qur'an, **"We have prepared for them a painful punishment"** (﴿أعْتَدْنا لَهم عَذابًا ألِيمًا﴾). This is the punishment of the Fire. This clause is joined to the clause *yubashshiru*, with an implied *yukhbiru* ("he informs"). That is: and he informs that those who do not believe in the Hereafter... It is also said it is joined to His saying *anna lahum ajran kabiran*, and "giving good tidings" means the general sense of informing. Or the intended meaning is its literal sense, and the speech contains a double good tiding to the believers: the first is what they have of reward, and the second is what their enemies have of punishment.

**"And man invokes evil as he invokes good"** (﴿ويَدْعُ الإنْسانُ بِالشَّرِّ دُعاءَهُ بِالخَيْرِ﴾). Here "man" refers to the species, because this supplication comes from some of its individuals, namely a man invoking against himself and his child when he is distressed with something he would not want answered. **"As he invokes for good"** (*duʿa'hu bi-al-khayr*), that is, like his supplication to his Lord for good for himself and his family, such as seeking health, provision, and the like. If God answered his supplication against himself for evil, he would perish. But He did not answer it, out of His grace and mercy. Similar to this is **"And if God were to hasten for people the evil as they seek to hasten the good"** (﴿ولَوْ يُعَجِّلُ اللَّهُ لِلنّاسِ الشَّرَّ اسْتِعْجالَهم بِالخَيْرِ﴾), which has already been mentioned.

It is also said that "man" here refers to the one who says this statement, the disbeliever, who invokes evil upon himself. This is seeking the hastening of punishment, and he invokes for it as good, like the saying of the speaker: **"O God, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment"** (﴿اللَّهُمَّ إنْ كانَ هَذا هو الحَقَّ مِن عِنْدِكَ فَأمْطِرْ عَلَيْنا حِجارَةً مِنَ السَّماءِ أوِ ائْتِنا بِعَذابٍ ألِيمٍ﴾).

It is also said: that he supplicates in seeking the forbidden as he supplicates in seeking the permissible.

The *waw* was omitted from *wa-yadaʿu al-insanu* in the script of the Mushaf, because it is not pronounced, since the unvowelled *lam* follows it, like His saying: **"We will call the guards of Hell"** (﴿سَنَدْعُ الزَّبانِيَةَ﴾), **"And Allah will erase falsehood"** (﴿ويَمْحُ اللَّهُ الباطِلَ﴾), **"And Allah will bring the believers"** (﴿وسَوْفَ يُؤْتِ اللَّهُ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾), and similar.

**"And man has always been hasty"** (﴿وكانَ الإنْسانُ عَجُولًا﴾), that is, created with haste as a nature. From his haste is that he asks for evil just as he asks for good. It is also said that it refers to Adam, peace be upon him, when he rose before the spirit was fully breathed into him. The one that fits the context is the first meaning.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying **"And We decreed to the Children of Israel"**, that he said: "We informed them."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: "We told them."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: "We told them."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him regarding *qadayna ila Bani Isra'il*: "We decreed upon them."

Ibn Asakir in his *Tarikh* narrated from Ali, regarding His saying **"You will surely cause corruption in the land twice"** (﴿لَتُفْسِدُنَّ في الأرْضِ مَرَّتَيْنِ﴾), that he said: "The first was the killing of Zakariyya, and the last was the killing of Yahya."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding the verse that he said: "The first corruption was the killing of Zakariyya, so God sent against them the king of the Nabateans. Then the Children of Israel prepared and raided the Nabateans and took from them, and that is His saying: **'We gave you the return of victory over them'** (﴿رَدَدْنا لَكُمُ الكَرَّةَ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "God sent against them in the first time Jalut, and He sent against them in the second time Bukhtnassar. Then they returned, and God empowered the believers over them."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding *fa-jasu*: "They walked."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him also: "*Tatbiran*: destruction."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Dahhak regarding His saying **"It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you"** that he said: "The mercy that He promised them was the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding His saying **"And if you return, We will return"** that he said: "They returned, so God sent against them Muhammad (ﷺ), and they now pay the jizya willingly while they are humbled."

Know that the reports have differed in identifying what befell them in the two times, in identifying who God empowered against them, and in the manner of the retribution against them. Not much benefit depends on this.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying **"And We have made Hell a prison for the disbelievers"** (﴿وجَعَلْنا جَهَنَّمَ لِلْكافِرِينَ حَصِيرًا﴾) that he said: "A prison."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him: the meaning of *hasiran* is that God made their dwelling place in it.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abd al-Razzaq related from al-Hasan regarding His words ﴿ḥaṣīran﴾ that he said: a bedding and a cushion.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Zayd regarding His words: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ that he said: to that which is most correct.

al-Hakim related from Ibn Mas'ud that he would frequently recite: "Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright, and gives good news of lightening (the burden)," adding "and gives good news of lightening."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿And man prays for evil as he prays for good﴾ that it means the saying of a person: "O Allah, curse him and be angry with him."

Ibn Jarir also related from him regarding His words: ﴿And man has always been hasty﴾ that he said: impatient, having no patience in ease or in hardship.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Asakir related from Salman al-Farisi that he said: "The first thing Allah created of Adam was his head. He began to look at it while it was being created, but his legs remained (uncreated). When it was after 'Asr, he said: 'My Lord, hasten (the creation) before night.' That is His saying: ﴿And man has always been hasty﴾."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 17, verses 4–11 (part 1 of 2):

**"And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book"** (﴿وقَضَيْنا إلى بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ في الكِتابِ﴾). *Qada'* means "informed and told," or "judged and completed." Its root meaning is "to firmly establish a thing and finish with it." It is also said to mean "We revealed." The context supports this, since the verb is followed by *ila* (to) with "Children of Israel." If it meant "informed" or "told," it would be used without *ila* ("qadayna Bani Isra'il"). If it meant "judged," it would take *ala* ("on"). If it meant "completed," it would take *li* ("for"). The "Book" here is the Torah, and its being sent down to their prophet Musa is like its being sent down to them, since they were his people. It is also said that the "Book" is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

Abu al-Aliya and Sa'id ibn Jubayr read *fi al-kutubi* ("in the books").

Isa al-Thaqafi read *latafsudunna* with an opened *ta'* (the second verb form with *ta'* in the first position), and its meaning is close to the reading of the majority, because when they corrupt, they are corrupted within themselves. "Corruption" here means opposing what God prescribed for them in the Torah. "The land" means the land of al-Sham and Bayt al-Maqdis. It is also said to mean the land of Egypt. The *lam* in *latufsidunna* is the answer to an implied oath.

Al-Naysaburi said: or he treated the definitive decree as if it were an oath, as if it were said: "And We swore that you will surely corrupt."

*Marratayn* ("twice") is in the accusative either as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, or as a verbal noun itself governing something not of its own kind. The first time was the killing of Sha'ya, or the imprisonment of Irmiya, or opposing the rulings of the Torah. The second time was the killing of Yahya ibn Zakariyya and the plot to kill Isa.

**"And you will become haughty with great haughtiness"** (﴿ولَتَعْلُنَّ عُلُوًّا كَبِيرًا﴾). This *lam* is like the *lam* before it. That is, you will be arrogant toward obeying God, and you will exalt yourselves over people through oppression and transgression, going beyond all limits in that.

**"So when the promise of the first of them came"** (﴿فَإذا جاءَ وعْدُ أُولاهُما﴾), that is, the first of the two mentioned times, **"We sent against you servants of Ours, of great might"** (﴿بَعَثْنا عَلَيْكم عِبادًا لَنا أُولِي بَأْسٍ شَدِيدٍ﴾), meaning strength in wars and severity at the encounter.

It is said they were Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) and his armies. It is also said they were Jalut (Goliath), or an army from Persia, or an army from Babylon.

**"And they went through the homes"** (﴿فَجاسُوا خِلالَ الدِّيارِ﴾). *Jasu* means they ravaged and roamed. It is said *jasu*, *hasu*, and *dasu* have the same meaning, as mentioned by Ibn Ghurayr and al-Qutaybi.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that they went around among the homes asking whether anyone remained whom they had not killed. He said: *al-jaws* is seeking something thoroughly.

Al-Jawhari said: *al-jaws* is the verbal noun of your saying *jasu khilal al-diyar*, meaning they passed through them as a man searches for news, that is, seeks it. Abu Ubayda also said this.

Ibn Jarir said: the meaning of *jasu* is that they walked among the homes seeking them and killing them, going and coming.

Al-Farra' said: its meaning is that they killed them among their houses, and he recited a verse by Hassan:

*Khalal al-diyar* was also read as *khalal al-diyar*, and its meaning is the same as *khilal*, which is the middle of the homes.

**"And it was a promise to be fulfilled"** (﴿وكانَ ذَلِكَ وعْدًا مَفْعُولًا﴾), that is, it was certain and unavoidable.

**"Then We gave you the return of victory over them"** (﴿ثُمَّ رَدَدْنا لَكُمُ الكَرَّةَ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾): that is, the dominance, the victory, and the return. This was at the time of their repentance.

It is said this was when Dawud (David) killed Jalut. It is also said it was when Bukhtnassar was killed.

**"And We aided you with wealth and children"** (﴿وأمْدَدْناكم بِأمْوالٍ وبَنِينَ﴾), after the plunder of your wealth and the capture of your sons, until your affairs returned to what they had been.

**"And made you more in manpower"** (﴿وجَعَلْناكم أكْثَرَ نَفِيرًا﴾). Abu Ubayda said: *al-nafir* is the number of men, so the meaning is: more in men than your enemy.

*Al-nafir* is the one who goes out with a man from his tribe, and it is said *nafir* and *nafir* (with an active participle pattern) like *qadir* and *qadir*. It is permitted for *al-nafir* to be the plural of *nafar*.

A similar usage is the poet's verse:

*"So he fell prone upon his hands and his face."*

That is, on his hands and on his face.
