**"And We aided you with wealth and children"** (﴿وأمْدَدْناكم بِأمْوالٍ وبَنِينَ﴾), after the plunder of your wealth and the capture of your sons, until your affairs returned to what they had been.

**"And made you more in manpower"** (﴿وجَعَلْناكم أكْثَرَ نَفِيرًا﴾). Abu Ubayda said: *al-nafir* is the number of men, so the meaning is: more in men than your enemy.

*Al-nafir* is the one who goes out with a man from his tribe, and it is said *nafir* and *nafir* (with an active participle pattern) like *qadir* and *qadir*. It is permitted for *al-nafir* to be the plural of *nafar*.

**"If you do good"** (﴿إنْ أحْسَنْتُمْ﴾), that is, your deeds and words in the manner required of you, **"you do good for yourselves"** (﴿أحْسَنْتُمْ لِأنْفُسِكُمْ﴾), because the reward of that returns to you. **"And if you do evil"** (﴿وإنْ أسَأْتُمْ﴾), that is, your deeds and words, which you performed not in the manner required of you, **"then it is against them"** (﴿فَلَها﴾), that is, *fa-'alayha*.

A similar usage is the poet's verse:

*"So he fell prone upon his hands and his face."*

That is, on his hands and on his face.

Ibn Jarir said: the *lam* here means *ila* ("to"), that is, the evil returns to them, like His saying: **"Because your Lord has inspired her"** (﴿بِأنَّ رَبَّكَ أوْحى لَها﴾), that is, to her.

It is also said the meaning is: for it is the requital or the punishment.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: for it there is a Lord who forgives the evil.

This address is said to be to the Children of Israel who were living in the times mentioned in these verses. It is also said it is to the Children of Israel living in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ). Its meaning is to inform them of what befell their predecessors, so that they would be wary of the same. It is also said it is an address to the polytheists of Quraysh.

**"So when the promise of the second came"** (﴿فَإذا جاءَ وعْدُ الآخِرَةِ﴾), that is, the time came for what they had been promised of the punishment of the second time. The second time was their killing of Yahya ibn Zakariyya, as previously mentioned. The story of his killing is fully given in the Gospel, where his name is Yuhanna (John). A king of their kings killed him because of a woman who urged him to kill him. The name of the king is Lakht, as Ibn Qutayba said. Ibn Jarir said it was Hirudus (Herod).

The answer to *idha* is omitted. Its estimated form is: "We sent them," because the answer of the first *idha* indicates it. **"To make your faces grieve"** (﴿لِيَسُوءُوا وُجُوهَكُمْ﴾) is connected to this omitted answer. That is, they would do to you what would grieve your faces, until the signs of harm appear upon you and the sorrow becomes visible in your faces. It is also said that the faces here means their chiefs.

Al-Kisa'i read *li-nasu'a* with *nun*, meaning that the pronoun refers to God, glorified is He.

Ubayy read *li-nasu'anna* with the emphatic *nun*.

Abu Bakr, al-A'mash, Ibn Wathhab, Hamza, and Ibn Amir read *li-yasu'a* with the *ya'* (third-person) and singular form. Al-Zajjaj said: everything you break and crush, you have *tabbartahu*. The pronoun refers to God or to the promise.

**"And to enter the Masjid"** (﴿ولِيَدْخُلُوا المَسْجِدَ﴾) is joined to *li-yasu'u*, **"as they entered it the first time, and to destroy what they had overcome"** (﴿كَما دَخَلُوهُ أوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ ولِيُتَبِّرُوا﴾), that is, they would ruin and destroy. Qutrub said: they would demolish. From this is the poet's verse:

*"Men are only two kinds: one who works to destroy what he builds, and another who raises up."*

The rest read with *ya'* and a *damma* on the *hamza*, with a *waw* after it, meaning the subject is "servants of Ours." *Ma 'alaw* means what they overcame of your lands, or the duration of their dominance, **"destruction"** (*tatbiran*), that is, annihilation. The verbal noun is mentioned to remove doubt and to confirm the report.

**"It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you"** (﴿عَسى رَبُّكم أنْ يَرْحَمَكُمْ﴾), O Children of Israel, after His retribution against you the second time. **"And if you return, We will return"** (﴿وإنْ عُدْتُمْ عُدْنا﴾), that is, to punishment against you for a third time.

The people of the histories (*ahl al-siyar*) said: then they returned to what was not fitting, which was denying Muhammad (ﷺ) and concealing what had come about his sending in the Torah and the Gospel. So God returned to punishing them at the hands of the Arabs. What happened to the Banu Qurayza, al-Nadir, Banu Qaynuqa', and Khaybar, of killing, captivity, expulsion, imposing the jizya on those who remained, and the imposition of humiliation and destitution, befell them.

**"And We have made Hell a prison for the disbelievers"** (﴿وجَعَلْنا جَهَنَّمَ لِلْكافِرِينَ حَصِيرًا﴾). *Hasir* means a prison, so it is *fa'il* in the sense of *fa'il* or *maf'ul*. The meaning is that they are confined in Hell and never escape from it.

Al-Jawhari said: *hasarahu yahsuruhu hasran* means he constricted him and surrounded him. It is also said: *hasir* means a bed and a cushion. In this sense, *al-hasir* refers to the mat that people spread out.

**"Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright"** (﴿إنَّ هَذا القُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هي أقْوَمُ﴾). That is: the Qur'an guides people to the path that is most upright compared to other paths, and it is the religion of Islam. So *allati hiya aqwamu* is an adjective of an omitted noun, which is "the path."

Al-Zajjaj said: it means "to the state that is the most upright of states," which is the oneness of God and belief in His messengers. Al-Farra' also said this.

**"And gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds"** (﴿ويُبَشِّرُ المُؤْمِنِينَ الَّذِينَ يَعْمَلُونَ الصّالِحاتِ﴾). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *yabashshiru*, with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and a *damma* on the *shin*. The rest read it with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *kasra* on the *shin*, from *al-tabshir*, meaning: he gives good tidings with what it contains of the promise of good, both in the next life and in this life, to the believers, **"that for them is a great reward"** (﴿أنَّ لَهم أجْرًا كَبِيرًا﴾), that is, that for them is.

**"And that those who do not believe in the Hereafter"** (﴿وأنَّ الَّذِينَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالآخِرَةِ﴾), and its rulings that are explained in the Qur'an, **"We have prepared for them a painful punishment"** (﴿أعْتَدْنا لَهم عَذابًا ألِيمًا﴾). This is the punishment of the Fire. This clause is joined to the clause *yubashshiru*, with an implied *yukhbiru* ("he informs"). That is: and he informs that those who do not believe in the Hereafter... It is also said it is joined to His saying *anna lahum ajran kabiran*, and "giving good tidings" means the general sense of informing. Or the intended meaning is its literal sense, and the speech contains a double good tiding to the believers: the first is what they have of reward, and the second is what their enemies have of punishment.

**"And man invokes evil as he invokes good"** (﴿ويَدْعُ الإنْسانُ بِالشَّرِّ دُعاءَهُ بِالخَيْرِ﴾). Here "man" refers to the species, because this supplication comes from some of its individuals, namely a man invoking against himself and his child when he is distressed with something he would not want answered. **"As he invokes for good"** (*duʿa'hu bi-al-khayr*), that is, like his supplication to his Lord for good for himself and his family, such as seeking health, provision, and the like. If God answered his supplication against himself for evil, he would perish. But He did not answer it, out of His grace and mercy. Similar to this is **"And if God were to hasten for people the evil as they seek to hasten the good"** (﴿ولَوْ يُعَجِّلُ اللَّهُ لِلنّاسِ الشَّرَّ اسْتِعْجالَهم بِالخَيْرِ﴾), which has already been mentioned.

It is also said that "man" here refers to the one who says this statement, the disbeliever, who invokes evil upon himself. This is seeking the hastening of punishment, and he invokes for it as good, like the saying of the speaker: **"O God, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment"** (﴿اللَّهُمَّ إنْ كانَ هَذا هو الحَقَّ مِن عِنْدِكَ فَأمْطِرْ عَلَيْنا حِجارَةً مِنَ السَّماءِ أوِ ائْتِنا بِعَذابٍ ألِيمٍ﴾).

It is also said: that he supplicates in seeking the forbidden as he supplicates in seeking the permissible.

The *waw* was omitted from *wa-yadaʿu al-insanu* in the script of the Mushaf, because it is not pronounced, since the unvowelled *lam* follows it, like His saying: **"We will call the guards of Hell"** (﴿سَنَدْعُ الزَّبانِيَةَ﴾), **"And Allah will erase falsehood"** (﴿ويَمْحُ اللَّهُ الباطِلَ﴾), **"And Allah will bring the believers"** (﴿وسَوْفَ يُؤْتِ اللَّهُ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾), and similar.

**"And man has always been hasty"** (﴿وكانَ الإنْسانُ عَجُولًا﴾), that is, created with haste as a nature. From his haste is that he asks for evil just as he asks for good. It is also said that it refers to Adam, peace be upon him, when he rose before the spirit was fully breathed into him. The one that fits the context is the first meaning.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying **"And We decreed to the Children of Israel"**, that he said: "We informed them."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: "We told them."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: "We told them."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him regarding *qadayna ila Bani Isra'il*: "We decreed upon them."

Ibn Asakir in his *Tarikh* narrated from Ali, regarding His saying **"You will surely cause corruption in the land twice"** (﴿لَتُفْسِدُنَّ في الأرْضِ مَرَّتَيْنِ﴾), that he said: "The first was the killing of Zakariyya, and the last was the killing of Yahya."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding the verse that he said: "The first corruption was the killing of Zakariyya, so God sent against them the king of the Nabateans. Then the Children of Israel prepared and raided the Nabateans and took from them, and that is His saying: **'We gave you the return of victory over them'** (﴿رَدَدْنا لَكُمُ الكَرَّةَ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "God sent against them in the first time Jalut, and He sent against them in the second time Bukhtnassar. Then they returned, and God empowered the believers over them."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding *fa-jasu*: "They walked."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him also: "*Tatbiran*: destruction."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Dahhak regarding His saying **"It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you"** that he said: "The mercy that He promised them was the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding His saying **"And if you return, We will return"** that he said: "They returned, so God sent against them Muhammad (ﷺ), and they now pay the jizya willingly while they are humbled."

Know that the reports have differed in identifying what befell them in the two times, in identifying who God empowered against them, and in the manner of the retribution against them. Not much benefit depends on this.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying **"And We have made Hell a prison for the disbelievers"** (﴿وجَعَلْنا جَهَنَّمَ لِلْكافِرِينَ حَصِيرًا﴾) that he said: "A prison."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him: the meaning of *hasiran* is that God made their dwelling place in it.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abd al-Razzaq related from al-Hasan regarding His words ﴿ḥaṣīran﴾ that he said: a bedding and a cushion.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Zayd regarding His words: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ that he said: to that which is most correct.

al-Hakim related from Ibn Mas'ud that he would frequently recite: "Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright, and gives good news of lightening (the burden)," adding "and gives good news of lightening."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿And man prays for evil as he prays for good﴾ that it means the saying of a person: "O Allah, curse him and be angry with him."

Ibn Jarir also related from him regarding His words: ﴿And man has always been hasty﴾ that he said: impatient, having no patience in ease or in hardship.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Asakir related from Salman al-Farisi that he said: "The first thing Allah created of Adam was his head. He began to look at it while it was being created, but his legs remained (uncreated). When it was after 'Asr, he said: 'My Lord, hasten (the creation) before night.' That is His saying: ﴿And man has always been hasty﴾."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on surah 17, verses 12–17 (part 1 of 2):

.
When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the proofs of prophethood and of monotheism (tawhid), He confirmed them with another proof from the wonders of His craftsmanship and the marvels of His creation, so He said: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾. This is because of what they contain of darkness and light, together with their alternation and all the other wonders they comprise, which minds are bewildered in describing. The meaning of their being two signs is that they point to the existence of the Creator and His power. He mentioned the night before the day because it is the origin. ﴿So We effaced the sign of the night﴾, that is, We obliterated its light, though the moon was like the sun in brightness and radiance.
It has been said: among the traces of the effacement is the blackness seen in the moon. It has also been said: the meaning of its effacement is that He, glory be to Him, created it effaced and obscured, and the meaning is not that He effaced it after it had been otherwise. ﴿And We made the sign of the day illuminating﴾, that is, He, glory be to Him, made its sun shining, so that things can be seen by it.
Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and al-Kisa'i said: it is from the saying of the Arabs, "the day became visible (absara al-nahar)", when it reached a state in which it can be seen by. It has also been said: "illuminating (mubsira) for the people", from the phrase "absarahu fa-basura" (he made him see, and he saw).
The first is a description of the day in terms of the condition of its people, and the second is a description of the day in terms of its own condition. The annexation of "sign" (ayah) to "the night and the day" is explicative (bayaniyyah), that is: "We effaced the sign which is the night and the sign which is the day", as in their saying "the self (nafs) of the thing and its essence (dhat)". ﴿That you may seek bounty from your Lord﴾, that is, so that by the whiteness of the day you may reach the disposal of the means of livelihood. The lam (li) is connected to His saying "and We made the sign of the day illuminating", that is: We made it so that you may seek bounty from your Lord, that is, provision, since most of the acquisition of sustenance and fulfilment of needs takes place by day. He did not mention here the rest at night, being content with what He said in another place: ﴿He it is who made the night for you that you may rest therein, and the day to see by﴾. Then He mentioned another benefit in that arrangement, so He said: ﴿And that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾. This is connected to both verbs together: I mean "We effaced the sign of the night" and "We made the sign of the day illuminating", not to one of them alone as with the first (benefit), since the knowledge of the number of years and the reckoning is not possible except through the alternation of the two (new) things and the knowing of days, months and years.
The difference between "number" ('adad) and "reckoning" (hisab) is that "number" is the counting of what has quantity by repeating its like without anything resulting from it, while "reckoning" is the counting of what has quantity by repeating its like in such a way that from a particular group of them a specific limit results, which has a specific name. So the year, for example, if it is viewed in terms of the number of its days, that is the number; and if it is viewed in terms of its being realised and composed of a number of months, and each month being composed of a number of days, and each day composed of a number of hours, and each hour composed of a number of minutes, that is the reckoning. ﴿And every thing We have detailed in detail﴾, that is, everything you need in matters of your religion and your worldly life, We have explained with clear explanation that is not ambiguous, and at that point causes are removed and excuses vanish, ﴿so that whoever perishes may perish upon clear evidence﴾.
For this reason He said: ﴿And every human being – We have fastened his bird (ta'ir) to his neck﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: "the bird" (al-ta'ir) among the Arabs means fortune (al-hazz), and it is also called "lot" (al-bakht). So the "bird" is what befalls the person in eternity, by way of his share of reason, deeds, lifespan, provision, happiness and misery, as if a bird were flying towards him from the nest of eternity and the darknesses of the unseen world, in a flight without end or limit, reaching that person at his appointed time, with no escape and no refuge.
Al-Azhari said: The basis of this is that when God, glory be to Him, created Adam, He knew the obedient of his descendants and the disobedient, so He wrote what He knew of them all, and decreed the happiness of whom He knew to be obedient and the misery of whom He knew to be disobedient. Thus there flew to each of them what he would come to at his creation and origination. That is His saying: ﴿And every human being – We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ (p-٨١٤), that is, what flew to him in the knowledge of God. "In his neck" is an expression for inseparability, like the necklace's inseparability from the neck among the things worn.
Al-Zajjaj said: The mention of the neck is an expression for inseparability, like the necklace's inseparability from the neck. ﴿And We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find laid open﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read (yukhraju), with a fathah on the initial yā' (ya) and a ḍammah on the rā', meaning "the bird comes out for him". "A book" (kitaban) is accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). It is also permissible that the meaning be: "the bird comes out for it, and it becomes a book".
Yahya ibn Wathhab read (yukhrijuhu), with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the rā', that is, God brings it out.
Shayba and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' (read similarly). It is also transmitted from Abu Ja'far (yukhraja), with a ḍammah on the yā' and a fathah on the rā', in the passive form, that is: "and a bird will be brought out for him as a book."
The rest read (wa-nukhriju), with the nūn, so that the one who brings out is God, glory be to Him, and "a book" is the object. Abu 'Amr argued for this reading by His saying "We have fastened" (alzamnahu).
Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan and Ibn 'Amir read (yulaqqahu), with a ḍammah on the yā', a fathah on the lam, and the qāf doubled. The rest read with a fathah on the yā', a sukun on the lam and a light qāf. God, glory be to Him, said (yalqahu manshuran) only to hasten the glad tidings for the good deed and to rebuke for the evil deed.
﴿Read your book﴾, that is, We say to him: "Read your book", or saying to him. It has been said: whoever is able to read will read that book, and whoever is not able to read... ﴿Sufficient is yourself today as a reckoner against you﴾. The bā' in (bi-nafsika) is superfluous, and (ḥasiban) is a specification (tamyiz), that is: reckoning.
Sibawayh said: "ḍarib al-qidah" means "its striker", and "ṣarim" means "ṣarim" (one who cuts). It is permissible that "al-ḥasib" means "sufficient", then it was placed in the position of "witness" and so was construed with "ʿala". "The self" (nafs) means "the person". It is also permissible that "al-ḥasib" means "one who reckons", like "al-sharik" and "al-jalis".
﴿Whoever is guided, is guided only for his own self﴾. God, glory be to Him, made clear that the reward of righteous deeds and the punishment of their opposite belong specifically to their doers and do not pass from him to another. So whoever is guided by doing what God has commanded him and leaving what God has forbidden, the benefit of that returns only to his own self. Whoever strays from the path of truth, not doing what he was commanded and not refraining from what he was forbidden, ﴿then he strays only to his own loss﴾, that is, the harm of his error falls upon his own self and does not go beyond it. So every individual is accountable for himself, rewarded for his obedience and punished for his disobedience. Then He emphasised this statement with the most eloquent emphasis, so He said: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾. "Wizr" means sin. It is said: "wazara yazir wizran and wazratan", that is, a sin. The plural is awzar. "Wizr" also means weight.
From it comes His saying: ﴿They bear their burdens upon their backs﴾, that is, the weights of their sins. The meaning of the verse: no soul bearing a burden shall bear the burden of another soul, until the other is freed from its burden and the first is taken to account for it. Something similar has already been mentioned in Surat al-An'am.
Al-Zajjaj said in explaining this verse: the sinner and the offender are not taken to account for the sin of another. ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾. When He, glory be to Him, mentioned that the guided person is singled out for his guidance and the misguided for his misguidance, and that a person is not held to account for the crime of another, He mentioned that He does not punish His servants except after establishing proof against them by sending His messengers and sending down His books. So He made clear that He did not leave them neglected, nor does He take them to account before the establishment of the proof against them. The apparent meaning is that He does not punish them, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter, except after establishing proof against them by sending the messengers, and this is the view of a group of the people of knowledge.
The majority held that what is negated here is the punishment of this world, not the punishment of the Hereafter.
﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones (amarna)﴾. The commentators differed about the meaning of "amarna" on two views. The first: that what is meant by it is the command which is the opposite of prohibition. On this basis they differed about what was commanded. Most of them say it is obedience and good.
Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, said: its meaning is: "We commanded them to wickedness, so they became wicked." He extended the discussion in establishing this, and those who followed him in tafsir followed him. What he and those who followed him said is opposed by a statement like "I commanded him, but he disobeyed me", for everyone who knows the Arabic language understands from this that the thing commanded is other than disobedience, since disobedience is incompatible with command and contrary to it. Likewise, "I commanded him, so he became wicked" indicates that what was commanded is other than wickedness, since wickedness is an expression for doing the opposite of what was commanded, so that its being wickedness is incompatible with its being commanded and contradicts it.
The second view: the meaning of "amarna" is "We made its affluent ones numerous", that is, We made its wicked ones many.
Al-Wahidi said: The Arabs say "amara al-qawm" when the people increased, and "amarahum Allah" when God increased them.
Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi, Abu Raja', Abu al-'Aliya, al-Rabi', Mujahid and al-Hasan read (ammarna), with the mīm doubled, meaning: We made them rulers who are empowered.
Al-Hasan also, and Qatada, Abu Haywa al-Shami, Ya'qub, Kharija (from Nafi'), Hammad ibn Salama (from Ibn Kathir), Ali and Ibn 'Abbas read (amarna), with the madd and light pronunciation, meaning: We increased its tyrants and its rulers, as al-Kisa'i said.
Abu 'Ubayda said: "amartuhu" with the madd and "amirtuhu" are two dialects with the same meaning, that of increasing. From it is the hadith: "The best of wealth is a commanded (ma'mura) mare", that is, one abundant in offspring and progeny. Ibn 'Aziz also said likewise.
Al-Hasan also, and Yahya ibn Ya'mar, read (amirna) with the short vowel and a kasrah on the mīm, meaning "we did" (fa'alna). This reading is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas.
Qatada and al-Hasan said: the meaning is "We increased."
Abu Zayd and Abu 'Ubayd related something similar, but al-Kisa'i denied it and said: from "increase" only "amarna" with the madd is said.
In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari) it says: Abu al-Hasan said "amira malahu" with a kasrah, meaning "it increased", and "amira al-qawm", meaning "they multiplied". From it is the saying of Labid:
"If they envy, they descend; and if they multiply, a day will come that is for destruction and ruin."
The majority read (amarna) from "command" (al-amr), and its meaning is what we mentioned in the first view. The meaning of (mutrafiha) is the pampered ones whom luxury and ease of life have made insolent. The commentators, in explaining "the affluent" (al-mutrafin), say they are the tyrants who dominate and the unjust kings. He said: they were singled out for mention because whoever else there is follows them. The meaning of (fasaqu fiha) is: they went out of obedience and rebelled in their unbelief, because "fusuq" is going out towards what is more foul. ﴿Then the word became due against it﴾, that is, the punishment became established and certain upon them after their wickedness had become manifest. ﴿So We destroyed it with complete destruction﴾, that is, a great destruction which cannot be fully grasped, because of its severity and the greatness of its impact.
It has been said, in interpreting "We commanded", that it is a metaphor for the command that impels them to wickedness, namely the abundance of blessings bestowed upon them. It has also been said that the meaning of "We intended to destroy a town" is that the destruction of a town was near, and this is a departure from the apparent meaning without any compelling reason for it.
Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned that this is His habitual practice with the past generations, so He said: ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed after Noah﴾ (p-٨١٥), that is, We destroyed many of them. So (kam) is the object of (ahlakna), and (min al-qurun) is an explanation of (kam) and a specification for it, that is: how many peoples disbelieved after Noah, like 'Ad and Thamud, so ruin befell them and the scourge of punishment descended upon them. In this is a warning to the disbelievers of Makkah.
Then He addressed His messenger with what is a deterrent for all people, so He said: ﴿And sufficient is your Lord as one who is Acquainted and Seeing with the sins of His servants﴾. Al-Farra' said: the bā' may be introduced into the nominative only when its bearer is praised by it or dispraised by it, as in your saying "kafaka" (sufficient for you), "akrim bihi rajulan" (what a noble man he is), and "tāba bi-ta'amika ta'aman" (your food is good food). One does not say "qama bi-akhika" while meaning "qama akhuka" (your brother stood).

Al-Bayhaqi in *Dala'il al-Nubuwwah* and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Sa'id al-Maqburi that 'Abd Allah ibn Salam asked the Prophet ﷺ about the dark patch on the moon. He said: "They were two suns. Allah said: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs, then We effaced the sign of the night﴾. So the darkness you saw is the effacement." 

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet ﷺ, a similar report, but longer.

As-Suyuti said: "Its chain is weak (wahin)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif* narrated from 'Ali, regarding His words ﴿then We effaced the sign of the night﴾, that he said: "It is the darkness that is on the moon."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿And We made the sign of the day to give sight﴾, that he said: "Bright." ﴿That you may seek bounty from your Lord﴾: he said: "He made for you a long span (sabh) [of time for movement]."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿We have explained it in detail﴾ (faṣṣalnāhu), that he said: "We made it clear (bayyannāhu)."

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Jarir narrated with a good (hasan) chain from Jabir: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Every person's bird is around his neck.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿We have fastened to every man his bird (ṭā'ir) upon his neck﴾, that he said: "It is his happiness and his misery, and what Allah has decreed for him and against him, and it will cling to him wherever he is."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Anas, regarding His words ﴿his bird﴾, that he said: "His book (kitāb)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "His deed. ﴿And We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find spread open﴾: it is his deed which was recorded, and on the Day of Resurrection there will be brought out for him what was written for him of deeds, and he will read it spread open."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿Read your book﴾, that he said: "On that Day, everyone who was not a reader in the world will read."

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in *al-Tamhid* narrated from 'A'ishah, regarding His words ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, that she said: "Khadijah asked about the children of the polytheists, and he said: 'They are from their fathers.' Then she asked him again after that, and he said: 'Allah knows best what they used to do.' Then she asked him again after Islam had become firmly established, and this verse was revealed: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, and he said: 'They are upon the fitrah (natural disposition),' or he said, 'in Paradise.'"

As-Suyuti said: "Its chain is weak (da'if)."

It is firmly established in the two Sahihs and others that "the Prophet ﷺ was asked, and it was said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, we sometimes strike, during night raids (bayāt), the offspring (dharārī) of the polytheists.' He said: 'They are from them.'" On this matter there are many hadiths and a lengthy discussion.

Ibn Kathir, in his tafsir of this verse, mentioned most of the hadiths related to the children of the polytheists, then quoted the statements of the scholars on the question, so let one refer to him.

Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Ahmad, Ibn Hibban, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Ma'rifah*, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *Kitab al-I'tiqad* narrated from al-Aswad ibn Sari' that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Four will argue on the Day of Resurrection: a man who is deaf and hears nothing; a man who is feeble-minded; a man who is senile; and a man who died during the fatrah (interval between prophets). Then he said: 'Allah will take their covenants that they will obey Him, and He will send to them a messenger saying: Enter the Fire.' He said: 'By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, if they had entered it, it would have been coolness and safety for them. And whoever does not enter it will be dragged into it.'"

Its chain in Ahmad is, thus: "'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah narrated to us: Mu'adh ibn Hisham narrated to us: my father narrated to me, from Abu Qatadah, from al-Ahnaf ibn Qays, from al-Aswad ibn Sari'."

Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Ahmad, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated something similar from Abu Hurayrah, and it is in Ahmad with the chain mentioned above, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, from Abu Rafi', from Abu Hurayrah.

Qasim ibn Asbagh, al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la, and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in *al-Tamhid* narrated from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said," and he mentioned something similar, but in place of "the fool" he said "the mentally deficient (ma'tuh)."

al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul* and al-Tabarani and Abu Nu'aym narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: "On the Day of Resurrection there will be brought the one who was impaired in intellect (mamsuh 'aqlan), the one who died in the fatrah, and the one who died as a child," and he mentioned its meaning at greater length.

Ibn Jarir narrated through the route of Ibn Jurayj, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿We commanded its affluent ones (mutrafiha)﴾, that he said: "To obey Allah, but they disobeyed."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Shahr ibn Hawshab, who said: "I heard Ibn 'Abbas say regarding this verse, ﴿We commanded its affluent ones﴾ with truth, but they opposed it, so destruction (tadmir) became due against them for that."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* narrated from him regarding the verse, that he said: "We empowered their wicked ones, and they disobeyed. So when they did that, We destroyed them with punishment." This is like His words ﴿And thus We placed in every town its greatest criminals, that they might plot therein﴾.

al-Bukhari and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "In the Jahiliyyah, when a tribe (hayy) became numerous, we used to say: 'The Banu so-and-so have been commanded.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on surah 17, verses 12–17 (part 1 of 2):

.
When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the proofs of prophethood and of monotheism (tawhid), He confirmed them with another proof from the wonders of His craftsmanship and the marvels of His creation, so He said: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾. This is because of what they contain of darkness and light, together with their alternation and all the other wonders they comprise, which minds are bewildered in describing. The meaning of their being two signs is that they point to the existence of the Creator and His power. He mentioned the night before the day because it is the origin. ﴿So We effaced the sign of the night﴾, that is, We obliterated its light, though the moon was like the sun in brightness and radiance.
It has been said: among the traces of the effacement is the blackness seen in the moon. It has also been said: the meaning of its effacement is that He, glory be to Him, created it effaced and obscured, and the meaning is not that He effaced it after it had been otherwise. ﴿And We made the sign of the day illuminating﴾, that is, He, glory be to Him, made its sun shining, so that things can be seen by it.
Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and al-Kisa'i said: it is from the saying of the Arabs, "the day became visible (absara al-nahar)", when it reached a state in which it can be seen by. It has also been said: "illuminating (mubsira) for the people", from the phrase "absarahu fa-basura" (he made him see, and he saw).
The first is a description of the day in terms of the condition of its people, and the second is a description of the day in terms of its own condition. The annexation of "sign" (ayah) to "the night and the day" is explicative (bayaniyyah), that is: "We effaced the sign which is the night and the sign which is the day", as in their saying "the self (nafs) of the thing and its essence (dhat)". ﴿That you may seek bounty from your Lord﴾, that is, so that by the whiteness of the day you may reach the disposal of the means of livelihood. The lam (li) is connected to His saying "and We made the sign of the day illuminating", that is: We made it so that you may seek bounty from your Lord, that is, provision, since most of the acquisition of sustenance and fulfilment of needs takes place by day. He did not mention here the rest at night, being content with what He said in another place: ﴿He it is who made the night for you that you may rest therein, and the day to see by﴾. Then He mentioned another benefit in that arrangement, so He said: ﴿And that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾. This is connected to both verbs together: I mean "We effaced the sign of the night" and "We made the sign of the day illuminating", not to one of them alone as with the first (benefit), since the knowledge of the number of years and the reckoning is not possible except through the alternation of the two (new) things and the knowing of days, months and years.
The difference between "number" ('adad) and "reckoning" (hisab) is that "number" is the counting of what has quantity by repeating its like without anything resulting from it, while "reckoning" is the counting of what has quantity by repeating its like in such a way that from a particular group of them a specific limit results, which has a specific name. So the year, for example, if it is viewed in terms of the number of its days, that is the number; and if it is viewed in terms of its being realised and composed of a number of months, and each month being composed of a number of days, and each day composed of a number of hours, and each hour composed of a number of minutes, that is the reckoning. ﴿And every thing We have detailed in detail﴾, that is, everything you need in matters of your religion and your worldly life, We have explained with clear explanation that is not ambiguous, and at that point causes are removed and excuses vanish, ﴿so that whoever perishes may perish upon clear evidence﴾.
For this reason He said: ﴿And every human being – We have fastened his bird (ta'ir) to his neck﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: "the bird" (al-ta'ir) among the Arabs means fortune (al-hazz), and it is also called "lot" (al-bakht). So the "bird" is what befalls the person in eternity, by way of his share of reason, deeds, lifespan, provision, happiness and misery, as if a bird were flying towards him from the nest of eternity and the darknesses of the unseen world, in a flight without end or limit, reaching that person at his appointed time, with no escape and no refuge.
Al-Azhari said: The basis of this is that when God, glory be to Him, created Adam, He knew the obedient of his descendants and the disobedient, so He wrote what He knew of them all, and decreed the happiness of whom He knew to be obedient and the misery of whom He knew to be disobedient. Thus there flew to each of them what he would come to at his creation and origination. That is His saying: ﴿And every human being – We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ (p-٨١٤), that is, what flew to him in the knowledge of God. "In his neck" is an expression for inseparability, like the necklace's inseparability from the neck among the things worn.
Al-Zajjaj said: The mention of the neck is an expression for inseparability, like the necklace's inseparability from the neck. ﴿And We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find laid open﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read (yukhraju), with a fathah on the initial yā' (ya) and a ḍammah on the rā', meaning "the bird comes out for him". "A book" (kitaban) is accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). It is also permissible that the meaning be: "the bird comes out for it, and it becomes a book".
Yahya ibn Wathhab read (yukhrijuhu), with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the rā', that is, God brings it out.
Shayba and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' (read similarly). It is also transmitted from Abu Ja'far (yukhraja), with a ḍammah on the yā' and a fathah on the rā', in the passive form, that is: "and a bird will be brought out for him as a book."
The rest read (wa-nukhriju), with the nūn, so that the one who brings out is God, glory be to Him, and "a book" is the object. Abu 'Amr argued for this reading by His saying "We have fastened" (alzamnahu).
Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan and Ibn 'Amir read (yulaqqahu), with a ḍammah on the yā', a fathah on the lam, and the qāf doubled. The rest read with a fathah on the yā', a sukun on the lam and a light qāf. God, glory be to Him, said (yalqahu manshuran) only to hasten the glad tidings for the good deed and to rebuke for the evil deed.
﴿Read your book﴾, that is, We say to him: "Read your book", or saying to him. It has been said: whoever is able to read will read that book, and whoever is not able to read... ﴿Sufficient is yourself today as a reckoner against you﴾. The bā' in (bi-nafsika) is superfluous, and (ḥasiban) is a specification (tamyiz), that is: reckoning.
Sibawayh said: "ḍarib al-qidah" means "its striker", and "ṣarim" means "ṣarim" (one who cuts). It is permissible that "al-ḥasib" means "sufficient", then it was placed in the position of "witness" and so was construed with "ʿala". "The self" (nafs) means "the person". It is also permissible that "al-ḥasib" means "one who reckons", like "al-sharik" and "al-jalis".
﴿Whoever is guided, is guided only for his own self﴾. God, glory be to Him, made clear that the reward of righteous deeds and the punishment of their opposite belong specifically to their doers and do not pass from him to another. So whoever is guided by doing what God has commanded him and leaving what God has forbidden, the benefit of that returns only to his own self. Whoever strays from the path of truth, not doing what he was commanded and not refraining from what he was forbidden, ﴿then he strays only to his own loss﴾, that is, the harm of his error falls upon his own self and does not go beyond it. So every individual is accountable for himself, rewarded for his obedience and punished for his disobedience. Then He emphasised this statement with the most eloquent emphasis, so He said: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾. "Wizr" means sin. It is said: "wazara yazir wizran and wazratan", that is, a sin. The plural is awzar. "Wizr" also means weight.
From it comes His saying: ﴿They bear their burdens upon their backs﴾, that is, the weights of their sins. The meaning of the verse: no soul bearing a burden shall bear the burden of another soul, until the other is freed from its burden and the first is taken to account for it. Something similar has already been mentioned in Surat al-An'am.
Al-Zajjaj said in explaining this verse: the sinner and the offender are not taken to account for the sin of another. ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾. When He, glory be to Him, mentioned that the guided person is singled out for his guidance and the misguided for his misguidance, and that a person is not held to account for the crime of another, He mentioned that He does not punish His servants except after establishing proof against them by sending His messengers and sending down His books. So He made clear that He did not leave them neglected, nor does He take them to account before the establishment of the proof against them. The apparent meaning is that He does not punish them, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter, except after establishing proof against them by sending the messengers, and this is the view of a group of the people of knowledge.
The majority held that what is negated here is the punishment of this world, not the punishment of the Hereafter.
﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones (amarna)﴾. The commentators differed about the meaning of "amarna" on two views. The first: that what is meant by it is the command which is the opposite of prohibition. On this basis they differed about what was commanded. Most of them say it is obedience and good.
Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, said: its meaning is: "We commanded them to wickedness, so they became wicked." He extended the discussion in establishing this, and those who followed him in tafsir followed him. What he and those who followed him said is opposed by a statement like "I commanded him, but he disobeyed me", for everyone who knows the Arabic language understands from this that the thing commanded is other than disobedience, since disobedience is incompatible with command and contrary to it. Likewise, "I commanded him, so he became wicked" indicates that what was commanded is other than wickedness, since wickedness is an expression for doing the opposite of what was commanded, so that its being wickedness is incompatible with its being commanded and contradicts it.
The second view: the meaning of "amarna" is "We made its affluent ones numerous", that is, We made its wicked ones many.
Al-Wahidi said: The Arabs say "amara al-qawm" when the people increased, and "amarahum Allah" when God increased them.
Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi, Abu Raja', Abu al-'Aliya, al-Rabi', Mujahid and al-Hasan read (ammarna), with the mīm doubled, meaning: We made them rulers who are empowered.
Al-Hasan also, and Qatada, Abu Haywa al-Shami, Ya'qub, Kharija (from Nafi'), Hammad ibn Salama (from Ibn Kathir), Ali and Ibn 'Abbas read (amarna), with the madd and light pronunciation, meaning: We increased its tyrants and its rulers, as al-Kisa'i said.
Abu 'Ubayda said: "amartuhu" with the madd and "amirtuhu" are two dialects with the same meaning, that of increasing. From it is the hadith: "The best of wealth is a commanded (ma'mura) mare", that is, one abundant in offspring and progeny. Ibn 'Aziz also said likewise.
Al-Hasan also, and Yahya ibn Ya'mar, read (amirna) with the short vowel and a kasrah on the mīm, meaning "we did" (fa'alna). This reading is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas.
Qatada and al-Hasan said: the meaning is "We increased."
Abu Zayd and Abu 'Ubayd related something similar, but al-Kisa'i denied it and said: from "increase" only "amarna" with the madd is said.
In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari) it says: Abu al-Hasan said "amira malahu" with a kasrah, meaning "it increased", and "amira al-qawm", meaning "they multiplied". From it is the saying of Labid:

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on surah 17, verses 12–17 (part 1 of 2):

.
When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the proofs of prophethood and of monotheism (tawhid), He confirmed them with another proof from the wonders of His craftsmanship and the marvels of His creation, so He said: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾. This is because of what they contain of darkness and light, together with their alternation and all the other wonders they comprise, which minds are bewildered in describing. The meaning of their being two signs is that they point to the existence of the Creator and His power. He mentioned the night before the day because it is the origin. ﴿So We effaced the sign of the night﴾, that is, We obliterated its light, though the moon was like the sun in brightness and radiance.
It has been said: among the traces of the effacement is the blackness seen in the moon. It has also been said: the meaning of its effacement is that He, glory be to Him, created it effaced and obscured, and the meaning is not that He effaced it after it had been otherwise. ﴿And We made the sign of the day illuminating﴾, that is, He, glory be to Him, made its sun shining, so that things can be seen by it.
Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and al-Kisa'i said: it is from the saying of the Arabs, "the day became visible (absara al-nahar)", when it reached a state in which it can be seen by. It has also been said: "illuminating (mubsira) for the people", from the phrase "absarahu fa-basura" (he made him see, and he saw).
The first is a description of the day in terms of the condition of its people, and the second is a description of the day in terms of its own condition. The annexation of "sign" (ayah) to "the night and the day" is explicative (bayaniyyah), that is: "We effaced the sign which is the night and the sign which is the day", as in their saying "the self (nafs) of the thing and its essence (dhat)". ﴿That you may seek bounty from your Lord﴾, that is, so that by the whiteness of the day you may reach the disposal of the means of livelihood. The lam (li) is connected to His saying "and We made the sign of the day illuminating", that is: We made it so that you may seek bounty from your Lord, that is, provision, since most of the acquisition of sustenance and fulfilment of needs takes place by day. He did not mention here the rest at night, being content with what He said in another place: ﴿He it is who made the night for you that you may rest therein, and the day to see by﴾. Then He mentioned another benefit in that arrangement, so He said: ﴿And that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾. This is connected to both verbs together: I mean "We effaced the sign of the night" and "We made the sign of the day illuminating", not to one of them alone as with the first (benefit), since the knowledge of the number of years and the reckoning is not possible except through the alternation of the two (new) things and the knowing of days, months and years.
The difference between "number" ('adad) and "reckoning" (hisab) is that "number" is the counting of what has quantity by repeating its like without anything resulting from it, while "reckoning" is the counting of what has quantity by repeating its like in such a way that from a particular group of them a specific limit results, which has a specific name. So the year, for example, if it is viewed in terms of the number of its days, that is the number; and if it is viewed in terms of its being realised and composed of a number of months, and each month being composed of a number of days, and each day composed of a number of hours, and each hour composed of a number of minutes, that is the reckoning. ﴿And every thing We have detailed in detail﴾, that is, everything you need in matters of your religion and your worldly life, We have explained with clear explanation that is not ambiguous, and at that point causes are removed and excuses vanish, ﴿so that whoever perishes may perish upon clear evidence﴾.
For this reason He said: ﴿And every human being – We have fastened his bird (ta'ir) to his neck﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: "the bird" (al-ta'ir) among the Arabs means fortune (al-hazz), and it is also called "lot" (al-bakht). So the "bird" is what befalls the person in eternity, by way of his share of reason, deeds, lifespan, provision, happiness and misery, as if a bird were flying towards him from the nest of eternity and the darknesses of the unseen world, in a flight without end or limit, reaching that person at his appointed time, with no escape and no refuge.
Al-Azhari said: The basis of this is that when God, glory be to Him, created Adam, He knew the obedient of his descendants and the disobedient, so He wrote what He knew of them all, and decreed the happiness of whom He knew to be obedient and the misery of whom He knew to be disobedient. Thus there flew to each of them what he would come to at his creation and origination. That is His saying: ﴿And every human being – We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ (p-٨١٤), that is, what flew to him in the knowledge of God. "In his neck" is an expression for inseparability, like the necklace's inseparability from the neck among the things worn.
Al-Zajjaj said: The mention of the neck is an expression for inseparability, like the necklace's inseparability from the neck. ﴿And We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find laid open﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read (yukhraju), with a fathah on the initial yā' (ya) and a ḍammah on the rā', meaning "the bird comes out for him". "A book" (kitaban) is accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). It is also permissible that the meaning be: "the bird comes out for it, and it becomes a book".
Yahya ibn Wathhab read (yukhrijuhu), with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the rā', that is, God brings it out.
Shayba and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' (read similarly). It is also transmitted from Abu Ja'far (yukhraja), with a ḍammah on the yā' and a fathah on the rā', in the passive form, that is: "and a bird will be brought out for him as a book."
The rest read (wa-nukhriju), with the nūn, so that the one who brings out is God, glory be to Him, and "a book" is the object. Abu 'Amr argued for this reading by His saying "We have fastened" (alzamnahu).
Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan and Ibn 'Amir read (yulaqqahu), with a ḍammah on the yā', a fathah on the lam, and the qāf doubled. The rest read with a fathah on the yā', a sukun on the lam and a light qāf. God, glory be to Him, said (yalqahu manshuran) only to hasten the glad tidings for the good deed and to rebuke for the evil deed.
﴿Read your book﴾, that is, We say to him: "Read your book", or saying to him. It has been said: whoever is able to read will read that book, and whoever is not able to read... ﴿Sufficient is yourself today as a reckoner against you﴾. The bā' in (bi-nafsika) is superfluous, and (ḥasiban) is a specification (tamyiz), that is: reckoning.
Sibawayh said: "ḍarib al-qidah" means "its striker", and "ṣarim" means "ṣarim" (one who cuts). It is permissible that "al-ḥasib" means "sufficient", then it was placed in the position of "witness" and so was construed with "ʿala". "The self" (nafs) means "the person". It is also permissible that "al-ḥasib" means "one who reckons", like "al-sharik" and "al-jalis".
﴿Whoever is guided, is guided only for his own self﴾. God, glory be to Him, made clear that the reward of righteous deeds and the punishment of their opposite belong specifically to their doers and do not pass from him to another. So whoever is guided by doing what God has commanded him and leaving what God has forbidden, the benefit of that returns only to his own self. Whoever strays from the path of truth, not doing what he was commanded and not refraining from what he was forbidden, ﴿then he strays only to his own loss﴾, that is, the harm of his error falls upon his own self and does not go beyond it. So every individual is accountable for himself, rewarded for his obedience and punished for his disobedience. Then He emphasised this statement with the most eloquent emphasis, so He said: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾. "Wizr" means sin. It is said: "wazara yazir wizran and wazratan", that is, a sin. The plural is awzar. "Wizr" also means weight.
From it comes His saying: ﴿They bear their burdens upon their backs﴾, that is, the weights of their sins. The meaning of the verse: no soul bearing a burden shall bear the burden of another soul, until the other is freed from its burden and the first is taken to account for it. Something similar has already been mentioned in Surat al-An'am.
Al-Zajjaj said in explaining this verse: the sinner and the offender are not taken to account for the sin of another. ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾. When He, glory be to Him, mentioned that the guided person is singled out for his guidance and the misguided for his misguidance, and that a person is not held to account for the crime of another, He mentioned that He does not punish His servants except after establishing proof against them by sending His messengers and sending down His books. So He made clear that He did not leave them neglected, nor does He take them to account before the establishment of the proof against them. The apparent meaning is that He does not punish them, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter, except after establishing proof against them by sending the messengers, and this is the view of a group of the people of knowledge.
The majority held that what is negated here is the punishment of this world, not the punishment of the Hereafter.
﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones (amarna)﴾. The commentators differed about the meaning of "amarna" on two views. The first: that what is meant by it is the command which is the opposite of prohibition. On this basis they differed about what was commanded. Most of them say it is obedience and good.
Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, said: its meaning is: "We commanded them to wickedness, so they became wicked." He extended the discussion in establishing this, and those who followed him in tafsir followed him. What he and those who followed him said is opposed by a statement like "I commanded him, but he disobeyed me", for everyone who knows the Arabic language understands from this that the thing commanded is other than disobedience, since disobedience is incompatible with command and contrary to it. Likewise, "I commanded him, so he became wicked" indicates that what was commanded is other than wickedness, since wickedness is an expression for doing the opposite of what was commanded, so that its being wickedness is incompatible with its being commanded and contradicts it.
The second view: the meaning of "amarna" is "We made its affluent ones numerous", that is, We made its wicked ones many.
Al-Wahidi said: The Arabs say "amara al-qawm" when the people increased, and "amarahum Allah" when God increased them.
Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi, Abu Raja', Abu al-'Aliya, al-Rabi', Mujahid and al-Hasan read (ammarna), with the mīm doubled, meaning: We made them rulers who are empowered.
Al-Hasan also, and Qatada, Abu Haywa al-Shami, Ya'qub, Kharija (from Nafi'), Hammad ibn Salama (from Ibn Kathir), Ali and Ibn 'Abbas read (amarna), with the madd and light pronunciation, meaning: We increased its tyrants and its rulers, as al-Kisa'i said.
Abu 'Ubayda said: "amartuhu" with the madd and "amirtuhu" are two dialects with the same meaning, that of increasing. From it is the hadith: "The best of wealth is a commanded (ma'mura) mare", that is, one abundant in offspring and progeny. Ibn 'Aziz also said likewise.
Al-Hasan also, and Yahya ibn Ya'mar, read (amirna) with the short vowel and a kasrah on the mīm, meaning "we did" (fa'alna). This reading is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas.
Qatada and al-Hasan said: the meaning is "We increased."
Abu Zayd and Abu 'Ubayd related something similar, but al-Kisa'i denied it and said: from "increase" only "amarna" with the madd is said.
In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari) it says: Abu al-Hasan said "amira malahu" with a kasrah, meaning "it increased", and "amira al-qawm", meaning "they multiplied". From it is the saying of Labid:
"If they envy, they descend; and if they multiply, a day will come that is for destruction and ruin."
The majority read (amarna) from "command" (al-amr), and its meaning is what we mentioned in the first view. The meaning of (mutrafiha) is the pampered ones whom luxury and ease of life have made insolent. The commentators, in explaining "the affluent" (al-mutrafin), say they are the tyrants who dominate and the unjust kings. He said: they were singled out for mention because whoever else there is follows them. The meaning of (fasaqu fiha) is: they went out of obedience and rebelled in their unbelief, because "fusuq" is going out towards what is more foul. ﴿Then the word became due against it﴾, that is, the punishment became established and certain upon them after their wickedness had become manifest. ﴿So We destroyed it with complete destruction﴾, that is, a great destruction which cannot be fully grasped, because of its severity and the greatness of its impact.
It has been said, in interpreting "We commanded", that it is a metaphor for the command that impels them to wickedness, namely the abundance of blessings bestowed upon them. It has also been said that the meaning of "We intended to destroy a town" is that the destruction of a town was near, and this is a departure from the apparent meaning without any compelling reason for it.
Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned that this is His habitual practice with the past generations, so He said: ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed after Noah﴾ (p-٨١٥), that is, We destroyed many of them. So (kam) is the object of (ahlakna), and (min al-qurun) is an explanation of (kam) and a specification for it, that is: how many peoples disbelieved after Noah, like 'Ad and Thamud, so ruin befell them and the scourge of punishment descended upon them. In this is a warning to the disbelievers of Makkah.
Then He addressed His messenger with what is a deterrent for all people, so He said: ﴿And sufficient is your Lord as one who is Acquainted and Seeing with the sins of His servants﴾. Al-Farra' said: the bā' may be introduced into the nominative only when its bearer is praised by it or dispraised by it, as in your saying "kafaka" (sufficient for you), "akrim bihi rajulan" (what a noble man he is), and "tāba bi-ta'amika ta'aman" (your food is good food). One does not say "qama bi-akhika" while meaning "qama akhuka" (your brother stood).
In the verse there is a great glad tiding for the people of obedience and a severe warning for the people of disobedience, because complete knowledge, perfect expertise and penetrating insight require delivering the reward to its deserving person according to his deserving, and this does not preclude abundant grace upon one who is worthy of it. By His being, glory be to Him, "Acquainted and Seeing" is meant that He encompasses the realities of things, outwardly and inwardly, so that no hidden thing is concealed from Him.

Al-Bayhaqi in *Dala'il al-Nubuwwah* and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Sa'id al-Maqburi that 'Abd Allah ibn Salam asked the Prophet ﷺ about the dark patch on the moon. He said: "They were two suns. Allah said: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs, then We effaced the sign of the night﴾. So the darkness you saw is the effacement." 

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet ﷺ, a similar report, but longer.

As-Suyuti said: "Its chain is weak (wahin)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif* narrated from 'Ali, regarding His words ﴿then We effaced the sign of the night﴾, that he said: "It is the darkness that is on the moon."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿And We made the sign of the day to give sight﴾, that he said: "Bright." ﴿That you may seek bounty from your Lord﴾: he said: "He made for you a long span (sabh) [of time for movement]."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿We have explained it in detail﴾ (faṣṣalnāhu), that he said: "We made it clear (bayyannāhu)."

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Jarir narrated with a good (hasan) chain from Jabir: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Every person's bird is around his neck.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿We have fastened to every man his bird (ṭā'ir) upon his neck﴾, that he said: "It is his happiness and his misery, and what Allah has decreed for him and against him, and it will cling to him wherever he is."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Anas, regarding His words ﴿his bird﴾, that he said: "His book (kitāb)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "His deed. ﴿And We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find spread open﴾: it is his deed which was recorded, and on the Day of Resurrection there will be brought out for him what was written for him of deeds, and he will read it spread open."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿Read your book﴾, that he said: "On that Day, everyone who was not a reader in the world will read."

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in *al-Tamhid* narrated from 'A'ishah, regarding His words ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, that she said: "Khadijah asked about the children of the polytheists, and he said: 'They are from their fathers.' Then she asked him again after that, and he said: 'Allah knows best what they used to do.' Then she asked him again after Islam had become firmly established, and this verse was revealed: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, and he said: 'They are upon the fitrah (natural disposition),' or he said, 'in Paradise.'"

As-Suyuti said: "Its chain is weak (da'if)."

It is firmly established in the two Sahihs and others that "the Prophet ﷺ was asked, and it was said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, we sometimes strike, during night raids (bayāt), the offspring (dharārī) of the polytheists.' He said: 'They are from them.'" On this matter there are many hadiths and a lengthy discussion.

Its chain in Ahmad is, thus: "'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah narrated to us: Mu'adh ibn Hisham narrated to us: my father narrated to me, from Abu Qatadah, from al-Ahnaf ibn Qays, from al-Aswad ibn Sari'."
