So the year, for example, if it is viewed in terms of the number of its days, that is the number; and if it is viewed in terms of its being realised and composed of a number of months, and each month being composed of a number of days, and each day composed of a number of hours, and each hour composed of a number of minutes, that is the reckoning. ﴿And every thing We have detailed in detail﴾, that is, everything you need in matters of your religion and your worldly life, We have explained with clear explanation that is not ambiguous, and at that point causes are removed and excuses vanish, ﴿so that whoever perishes may perish upon clear evidence﴾.
For this reason He said: ﴿And every human being – We have fastened his bird (ta'ir) to his neck﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: "the bird" (al-ta'ir) among the Arabs means fortune (al-hazz), and it is also called "lot" (al-bakht). So the "bird" is what befalls the person in eternity, by way of his share of reason, deeds, lifespan, provision, happiness and misery, as if a bird were flying towards him from the nest of eternity and the darknesses of the unseen world, in a flight without end or limit, reaching that person at his appointed time, with no escape and no refuge.
Al-Azhari said: The basis of this is that when God, glory be to Him, created Adam, He knew the obedient of his descendants and the disobedient, so He wrote what He knew of them all, and decreed the happiness of whom He knew to be obedient and the misery of whom He knew to be disobedient. Thus there flew to each of them what he would come to at his creation and origination. That is His saying: ﴿And every human being – We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ (p-٨١٤), that is, what flew to him in the knowledge of God. "In his neck" is an expression for inseparability, like the necklace's inseparability from the neck among the things worn.
Al-Zajjaj said: The mention of the neck is an expression for inseparability, like the necklace's inseparability from the neck. ﴿And We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find laid open﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read (yukhraju), with a fathah on the initial yā' (ya) and a ḍammah on the rā', meaning "the bird comes out for him". "A book" (kitaban) is accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). It is also permissible that the meaning be: "the bird comes out for it, and it becomes a book".
Yahya ibn Wathhab read (yukhrijuhu), with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the rā', that is, God brings it out.
Shayba and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' (read similarly). It is also transmitted from Abu Ja'far (yukhraja), with a ḍammah on the yā' and a fathah on the rā', in the passive form, that is: "and a bird will be brought out for him as a book."
The rest read (wa-nukhriju), with the nūn, so that the one who brings out is God, glory be to Him, and "a book" is the object. Abu 'Amr argued for this reading by His saying "We have fastened" (alzamnahu).
Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan and Ibn 'Amir read (yulaqqahu), with a ḍammah on the yā', a fathah on the lam, and the qāf doubled. The rest read with a fathah on the yā', a sukun on the lam and a light qāf. God, glory be to Him, said (yalqahu manshuran) only to hasten the glad tidings for the good deed and to rebuke for the evil deed.
﴿Read your book﴾, that is, We say to him: "Read your book", or saying to him. It has been said: whoever is able to read will read that book, and whoever is not able to read... ﴿Sufficient is yourself today as a reckoner against you﴾. The bā' in (bi-nafsika) is superfluous, and (ḥasiban) is a specification (tamyiz), that is: reckoning.
Sibawayh said: "ḍarib al-qidah" means "its striker", and "ṣarim" means "ṣarim" (one who cuts). It is permissible that "al-ḥasib" means "sufficient", then it was placed in the position of "witness" and so was construed with "ʿala". "The self" (nafs) means "the person". It is also permissible that "al-ḥasib" means "one who reckons", like "al-sharik" and "al-jalis".
﴿Whoever is guided, is guided only for his own self﴾. God, glory be to Him, made clear that the reward of righteous deeds and the punishment of their opposite belong specifically to their doers and do not pass from him to another. So whoever is guided by doing what God has commanded him and leaving what God has forbidden, the benefit of that returns only to his own self. Whoever strays from the path of truth, not doing what he was commanded and not refraining from what he was forbidden, ﴿then he strays only to his own loss﴾, that is, the harm of his error falls upon his own self and does not go beyond it. So every individual is accountable for himself, rewarded for his obedience and punished for his disobedience. Then He emphasised this statement with the most eloquent emphasis, so He said: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾. "Wizr" means sin. It is said: "wazara yazir wizran and wazratan", that is, a sin. The plural is awzar. "Wizr" also means weight.
From it comes His saying: ﴿They bear their burdens upon their backs﴾, that is, the weights of their sins. The meaning of the verse: no soul bearing a burden shall bear the burden of another soul, until the other is freed from its burden and the first is taken to account for it. Something similar has already been mentioned in Surat al-An'am.
Al-Zajjaj said in explaining this verse: the sinner and the offender are not taken to account for the sin of another. ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾. When He, glory be to Him, mentioned that the guided person is singled out for his guidance and the misguided for his misguidance, and that a person is not held to account for the crime of another, He mentioned that He does not punish His servants except after establishing proof against them by sending His messengers and sending down His books. So He made clear that He did not leave them neglected, nor does He take them to account before the establishment of the proof against them. The apparent meaning is that He does not punish them, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter, except after establishing proof against them by sending the messengers, and this is the view of a group of the people of knowledge.
The majority held that what is negated here is the punishment of this world, not the punishment of the Hereafter.
﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones (amarna)﴾. The commentators differed about the meaning of "amarna" on two views. The first: that what is meant by it is the command which is the opposite of prohibition. On this basis they differed about what was commanded. Most of them say it is obedience and good.
Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, said: its meaning is: "We commanded them to wickedness, so they became wicked." He extended the discussion in establishing this, and those who followed him in tafsir followed him. What he and those who followed him said is opposed by a statement like "I commanded him, but he disobeyed me", for everyone who knows the Arabic language understands from this that the thing commanded is other than disobedience, since disobedience is incompatible with command and contrary to it. Likewise, "I commanded him, so he became wicked" indicates that what was commanded is other than wickedness, since wickedness is an expression for doing the opposite of what was commanded, so that its being wickedness is incompatible with its being commanded and contradicts it.
The second view: the meaning of "amarna" is "We made its affluent ones numerous", that is, We made its wicked ones many.
Al-Wahidi said: The Arabs say "amara al-qawm" when the people increased, and "amarahum Allah" when God increased them.
Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi, Abu Raja', Abu al-'Aliya, al-Rabi', Mujahid and al-Hasan read (ammarna), with the mīm doubled, meaning: We made them rulers who are empowered.
Al-Hasan also, and Qatada, Abu Haywa al-Shami, Ya'qub, Kharija (from Nafi'), Hammad ibn Salama (from Ibn Kathir), Ali and Ibn 'Abbas read (amarna), with the madd and light pronunciation, meaning: We increased its tyrants and its rulers, as al-Kisa'i said.
Abu 'Ubayda said: "amartuhu" with the madd and "amirtuhu" are two dialects with the same meaning, that of increasing. From it is the hadith: "The best of wealth is a commanded (ma'mura) mare", that is, one abundant in offspring and progeny. Ibn 'Aziz also said likewise.
Al-Hasan also, and Yahya ibn Ya'mar, read (amirna) with the short vowel and a kasrah on the mīm, meaning "we did" (fa'alna). This reading is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas.
Qatada and al-Hasan said: the meaning is "We increased."
Abu Zayd and Abu 'Ubayd related something similar, but al-Kisa'i denied it and said: from "increase" only "amarna" with the madd is said.
In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari) it says: Abu al-Hasan said "amira malahu" with a kasrah, meaning "it increased", and "amira al-qawm", meaning "they multiplied". From it is the saying of Labid:
"If they envy, they descend; and if they multiply, a day will come that is for destruction and ruin."
The majority read (amarna) from "command" (al-amr), and its meaning is what we mentioned in the first view. The meaning of (mutrafiha) is the pampered ones whom luxury and ease of life have made insolent. The commentators, in explaining "the affluent" (al-mutrafin), say they are the tyrants who dominate and the unjust kings. He said: they were singled out for mention because whoever else there is follows them. The meaning of (fasaqu fiha) is: they went out of obedience and rebelled in their unbelief, because "fusuq" is going out towards what is more foul. ﴿Then the word became due against it﴾, that is, the punishment became established and certain upon them after their wickedness had become manifest. ﴿So We destroyed it with complete destruction﴾, that is, a great destruction which cannot be fully grasped, because of its severity and the greatness of its impact.
It has been said, in interpreting "We commanded", that it is a metaphor for the command that impels them to wickedness, namely the abundance of blessings bestowed upon them. It has also been said that the meaning of "We intended to destroy a town" is that the destruction of a town was near, and this is a departure from the apparent meaning without any compelling reason for it.
Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned that this is His habitual practice with the past generations, so He said: ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed after Noah﴾ (p-٨١٥), that is, We destroyed many of them. So (kam) is the object of (ahlakna), and (min al-qurun) is an explanation of (kam) and a specification for it, that is: how many peoples disbelieved after Noah, like 'Ad and Thamud, so ruin befell them and the scourge of punishment descended upon them. In this is a warning to the disbelievers of Makkah.
Then He addressed His messenger with what is a deterrent for all people, so He said: ﴿And sufficient is your Lord as one who is Acquainted and Seeing with the sins of His servants﴾. Al-Farra' said: the bā' may be introduced into the nominative only when its bearer is praised by it or dispraised by it, as in your saying "kafaka" (sufficient for you), "akrim bihi rajulan" (what a noble man he is), and "tāba bi-ta'amika ta'aman" (your food is good food). One does not say "qama bi-akhika" while meaning "qama akhuka" (your brother stood).
In the verse there is a great glad tiding for the people of obedience and a severe warning for the people of disobedience, because complete knowledge, perfect expertise and penetrating insight require delivering the reward to its deserving person according to his deserving, and this does not preclude abundant grace upon one who is worthy of it. By His being, glory be to Him, "Acquainted and Seeing" is meant that He encompasses the realities of things, outwardly and inwardly, so that no hidden thing is concealed from Him.

Al-Bayhaqi in *Dala'il al-Nubuwwah* and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Sa'id al-Maqburi that 'Abd Allah ibn Salam asked the Prophet ﷺ about the dark patch on the moon. He said: "They were two suns. Allah said: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs, then We effaced the sign of the night﴾. So the darkness you saw is the effacement." 

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet ﷺ, a similar report, but longer.

As-Suyuti said: "Its chain is weak (wahin)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif* narrated from 'Ali, regarding His words ﴿then We effaced the sign of the night﴾, that he said: "It is the darkness that is on the moon."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿And We made the sign of the day to give sight﴾, that he said: "Bright." ﴿That you may seek bounty from your Lord﴾: he said: "He made for you a long span (sabh) [of time for movement]."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿We have explained it in detail﴾ (faṣṣalnāhu), that he said: "We made it clear (bayyannāhu)."

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Jarir narrated with a good (hasan) chain from Jabir: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Every person's bird is around his neck.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿We have fastened to every man his bird (ṭā'ir) upon his neck﴾, that he said: "It is his happiness and his misery, and what Allah has decreed for him and against him, and it will cling to him wherever he is."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Anas, regarding His words ﴿his bird﴾, that he said: "His book (kitāb)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "His deed. ﴿And We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find spread open﴾: it is his deed which was recorded, and on the Day of Resurrection there will be brought out for him what was written for him of deeds, and he will read it spread open."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿Read your book﴾, that he said: "On that Day, everyone who was not a reader in the world will read."

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in *al-Tamhid* narrated from 'A'ishah, regarding His words ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, that she said: "Khadijah asked about the children of the polytheists, and he said: 'They are from their fathers.' Then she asked him again after that, and he said: 'Allah knows best what they used to do.' Then she asked him again after Islam had become firmly established, and this verse was revealed: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, and he said: 'They are upon the fitrah (natural disposition),' or he said, 'in Paradise.'"

As-Suyuti said: "Its chain is weak (da'if)."

It is firmly established in the two Sahihs and others that "the Prophet ﷺ was asked, and it was said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, we sometimes strike, during night raids (bayāt), the offspring (dharārī) of the polytheists.' He said: 'They are from them.'" On this matter there are many hadiths and a lengthy discussion.

Ibn Kathir, in his tafsir of this verse, mentioned most of the hadiths related to the children of the polytheists, then quoted the statements of the scholars on the question, so let one refer to him.

Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Ahmad, Ibn Hibban, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Ma'rifah*, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *Kitab al-I'tiqad* narrated from al-Aswad ibn Sari' that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Four will argue on the Day of Resurrection: a man who is deaf and hears nothing; a man who is feeble-minded; a man who is senile; and a man who died during the fatrah (interval between prophets). Then he said: 'Allah will take their covenants that they will obey Him, and He will send to them a messenger saying: Enter the Fire.' He said: 'By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, if they had entered it, it would have been coolness and safety for them. And whoever does not enter it will be dragged into it.'"

Its chain in Ahmad is, thus: "'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah narrated to us: Mu'adh ibn Hisham narrated to us: my father narrated to me, from Abu Qatadah, from al-Ahnaf ibn Qays, from al-Aswad ibn Sari'."

Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Ahmad, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated something similar from Abu Hurayrah, and it is in Ahmad with the chain mentioned above, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, from Abu Rafi', from Abu Hurayrah.

Qasim ibn Asbagh, al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la, and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in *al-Tamhid* narrated from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said," and he mentioned something similar, but in place of "the fool" he said "the mentally deficient (ma'tuh)."

al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul* and al-Tabarani and Abu Nu'aym narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: "On the Day of Resurrection there will be brought the one who was impaired in intellect (mamsuh 'aqlan), the one who died in the fatrah, and the one who died as a child," and he mentioned its meaning at greater length.

Ibn Jarir narrated through the route of Ibn Jurayj, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿We commanded its affluent ones (mutrafiha)﴾, that he said: "To obey Allah, but they disobeyed."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Shahr ibn Hawshab, who said: "I heard Ibn 'Abbas say regarding this verse, ﴿We commanded its affluent ones﴾ with truth, but they opposed it, so destruction (tadmir) became due against them for that."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* narrated from him regarding the verse, that he said: "We empowered their wicked ones, and they disobeyed. So when they did that, We destroyed them with punishment." This is like His words ﴿And thus We placed in every town its greatest criminals, that they might plot therein﴾.

al-Bukhari and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "In the Jahiliyyah, when a tribe (hayy) became numerous, we used to say: 'The Banu so-and-so have been commanded.'"

This is because of what they contain of darkness and light, together with their alternation and all the other wonders they comprise, which minds are bewildered in describing. The meaning of their being two signs is that they point to the existence of the Creator and His power. He mentioned the night before the day because it is the origin. ﴿So We effaced the sign of the night﴾, that is, We obliterated its light, though the moon was like the sun in brightness and radiance.
It has been said: among the traces of the effacement is the blackness seen in the moon. It has also been said: the meaning of its effacement is that He, glory be to Him, created it effaced and obscured, and the meaning is not that He effaced it after it had been otherwise. ﴿And We made the sign of the day illuminating﴾, that is, He, glory be to Him, made its sun shining, so that things can be seen by it.
Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and al-Kisa'i said: it is from the saying of the Arabs, "the day became visible (absara al-nahar)", when it reached a state in which it can be seen by. It has also been said: "illuminating (mubsira) for the people", from the phrase "absarahu fa-basura" (he made him see, and he saw).
The first is a description of the day in terms of the condition of its people, and the second is a description of the day in terms of its own condition. The annexation of "sign" (ayah) to "the night and the day" is explicative (bayaniyyah), that is: "We effaced the sign which is the night and the sign which is the day", as in their saying "the self (nafs) of the thing and its essence (dhat)". ﴿That you may seek bounty from your Lord﴾, that is, so that by the whiteness of the day you may reach the disposal of the means of livelihood. The lam (li) is connected to His saying "and We made the sign of the day illuminating", that is: We made it so that you may seek bounty from your Lord, that is, provision, since most of the acquisition of sustenance and fulfilment of needs takes place by day. He did not mention here the rest at night, being content with what He said in another place: ﴿He it is who made the night for you that you may rest therein, and the day to see by﴾. "In his neck" is an expression for inseparability, like the necklace's inseparability from the neck among the things worn.

﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones (amarna)﴾. The commentators differed about the meaning of "amarna" on two views. The first: that what is meant by it is the command which is the opposite of prohibition. On this basis they differed about what was commanded. Most of them say it is obedience and good.
Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, said: its meaning is: "We commanded them to wickedness, so they became wicked." He extended the discussion in establishing this, and those who followed him in tafsir followed him. What he and those who followed him said is opposed by a statement like "I commanded him, but he disobeyed me", for everyone who knows the Arabic language understands from this that the thing commanded is other than disobedience, since disobedience is incompatible with command and contrary to it. Likewise, "I commanded him, so he became wicked" indicates that what was commanded is other than wickedness, since wickedness is an expression for doing the opposite of what was commanded, so that its being wickedness is incompatible with its being commanded and contradicts it.
The second view: the meaning of "amarna" is "We made its affluent ones numerous", that is, We made its wicked ones many.
Al-Wahidi said: The Arabs say "amara al-qawm" when the people increased, and "amarahum Allah" when God increased them.
Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi, Abu Raja', Abu al-'Aliya, al-Rabi', Mujahid and al-Hasan read (ammarna), with the mīm doubled, meaning: We made them rulers who are empowered.
Al-Hasan also, and Qatada, Abu Haywa al-Shami, Ya'qub, Kharija (from Nafi'), Hammad ibn Salama (from Ibn Kathir), Ali and Ibn 'Abbas read (amarna), with the madd and light pronunciation, meaning: We increased its tyrants and its rulers, as al-Kisa'i said.

Al-Hasan also, and Yahya ibn Ya'mar, read (amirna) with the short vowel and a kasrah on the mīm, meaning "we did" (fa'alna). This reading is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas.
Qatada and al-Hasan said: the meaning is "We increased."
Abu Zayd and Abu 'Ubayd related something similar, but al-Kisa'i denied it and said: from "increase" only "amarna" with the madd is said.
In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari) it says: Abu al-Hasan said "amira malahu" with a kasrah, meaning "it increased", and "amira al-qawm", meaning "they multiplied". From it is the saying of Labid:

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned that this is His habitual practice with the past generations, so He said: ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed after Noah﴾ (p-٨١٥), that is, We destroyed many of them. So (kam) is the object of (ahlakna), and (min al-qurun) is an explanation of (kam) and a specification for it, that is: how many peoples disbelieved after Noah, like 'Ad and Thamud, so ruin befell them and the scourge of punishment descended upon them. In this is a warning to the disbelievers of Makkah.

Al-Farra' said: the bā' may be introduced into the nominative only when its bearer is praised by it or dispraised by it, as in your saying "kafaka" (sufficient for you), "akrim bihi rajulan" (what a noble man he is), and "tāba bi-ta'amika ta'aman" (your food is good food). Al-Bayhaqi in *Dala'il al-Nubuwwah* and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Sa'id al-Maqburi that 'Abd Allah ibn Salam asked the Prophet ﷺ about the dark patch on the moon. He said: "They were two suns. Allah said: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs, then We effaced the sign of the night﴾. So the darkness you saw is the effacement." 

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet ﷺ, a similar report, but longer.

As-Suyuti said: "Its chain is weak (wahin)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif* narrated from 'Ali, regarding His words ﴿then We effaced the sign of the night﴾, that he said: "It is the darkness that is on the moon."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿And We made the sign of the day to give sight﴾, that he said: "Bright." ﴿That you may seek bounty from your Lord﴾: he said: "He made for you a long span (sabh) [of time for movement]."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿We have explained it in detail﴾ (faṣṣalnāhu), that he said: "We made it clear (bayyannāhu)."

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Jarir narrated with a good (hasan) chain from Jabir: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Every person's bird is around his neck.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿We have fastened to every man his bird (ṭā'ir) upon his neck﴾, that he said: "It is his happiness and his misery, and what Allah has decreed for him and against him, and it will cling to him wherever he is."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Anas, regarding His words ﴿his bird﴾, that he said: "His book (kitāb)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "His deed. ﴿And We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find spread open﴾: it is his deed which was recorded, and on the Day of Resurrection there will be brought out for him what was written for him of deeds, and he will read it spread open."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿Read your book﴾, that he said: "On that Day, everyone who was not a reader in the world will read."

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in *al-Tamhid* narrated from 'A'ishah, regarding His words ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, that she said: "Khadijah asked about the children of the polytheists, and he said: 'They are from their fathers.' Then she asked him again after that, and he said: 'Allah knows best what they used to do.' Then she asked him again after Islam had become firmly established, and this verse was revealed: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, and he said: 'They are upon the fitrah (natural disposition),' or he said, 'in Paradise.'"

As-Suyuti said: "Its chain is weak (da'if)."

It is firmly established in the two Sahihs and others that "the Prophet ﷺ was asked, and it was said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, we sometimes strike, during night raids (bayāt), the offspring (dharārī) of the polytheists.' He said: 'They are from them.'" On this matter there are many hadiths and a lengthy discussion.

Ibn Kathir, in his tafsir of this verse, mentioned most of the hadiths related to the children of the polytheists, then quoted the statements of the scholars on the question, so let one refer to him.

Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Ahmad, Ibn Hibban, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Ma'rifah*, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *Kitab al-I'tiqad* narrated from al-Aswad ibn Sari' that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Four will argue on the Day of Resurrection: a man who is deaf and hears nothing; a man who is feeble-minded; a man who is senile; and a man who died during the fatrah (interval between prophets). Then he said: 'Allah will take their covenants that they will obey Him, and He will send to them a messenger saying: Enter the Fire.' He said: 'By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, if they had entered it, it would have been coolness and safety for them. And whoever does not enter it will be dragged into it.'"

Its chain in Ahmad is, thus: "'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah narrated to us: Mu'adh ibn Hisham narrated to us: my father narrated to me, from Abu Qatadah, from al-Ahnaf ibn Qays, from al-Aswad ibn Sari'."

Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Ahmad, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated something similar from Abu Hurayrah, and it is in Ahmad with the chain mentioned above, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, from Abu Rafi', from Abu Hurayrah.

Qasim ibn Asbagh, al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la, and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in *al-Tamhid* narrated from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said," and he mentioned something similar, but in place of "the fool" he said "the mentally deficient (ma'tuh)."

al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul* and al-Tabarani and Abu Nu'aym narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: "On the Day of Resurrection there will be brought the one who was impaired in intellect (mamsuh 'aqlan), the one who died in the fatrah, and the one who died as a child," and he mentioned its meaning at greater length.

Ibn Jarir narrated through the route of Ibn Jurayj, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿We commanded its affluent ones (mutrafiha)﴾, that he said: "To obey Allah, but they disobeyed."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Shahr ibn Hawshab, who said: "I heard Ibn 'Abbas say regarding this verse, ﴿We commanded its affluent ones﴾ with truth, but they opposed it, so destruction (tadmir) became due against them for that."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* narrated from him regarding the verse, that he said: "We empowered their wicked ones, and they disobeyed. So when they did that, We destroyed them with punishment." This is like His words ﴿And thus We placed in every town its greatest criminals, that they might plot therein﴾.

al-Bukhari and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "In the Jahiliyyah, when a tribe (hayy) became numerous, we used to say: 'The Banu so-and-so have been commanded.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on surah 17, verses 12–17 (part 1 of 2):

.
When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the proofs of prophethood and of monotheism (tawhid), He confirmed them with another proof from the wonders of His craftsmanship and the marvels of His creation, so He said: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾. This is because of what they contain of darkness and light, together with their alternation and all the other wonders they comprise, which minds are bewildered in describing. The meaning of their being two signs is that they point to the existence of the Creator and His power. He mentioned the night before the day because it is the origin. ﴿So We effaced the sign of the night﴾, that is, We obliterated its light, though the moon was like the sun in brightness and radiance.
It has been said: among the traces of the effacement is the blackness seen in the moon. It has also been said: the meaning of its effacement is that He, glory be to Him, created it effaced and obscured, and the meaning is not that He effaced it after it had been otherwise. ﴿And We made the sign of the day illuminating﴾, that is, He, glory be to Him, made its sun shining, so that things can be seen by it.
Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and al-Kisa'i said: it is from the saying of the Arabs, "the day became visible (absara al-nahar)", when it reached a state in which it can be seen by. It has also been said: "illuminating (mubsira) for the people", from the phrase "absarahu fa-basura" (he made him see, and he saw).
The first is a description of the day in terms of the condition of its people, and the second is a description of the day in terms of its own condition. The annexation of "sign" (ayah) to "the night and the day" is explicative (bayaniyyah), that is: "We effaced the sign which is the night and the sign which is the day", as in their saying "the self (nafs) of the thing and its essence (dhat)". ﴿That you may seek bounty from your Lord﴾, that is, so that by the whiteness of the day you may reach the disposal of the means of livelihood. The lam (li) is connected to His saying "and We made the sign of the day illuminating", that is: We made it so that you may seek bounty from your Lord, that is, provision, since most of the acquisition of sustenance and fulfilment of needs takes place by day. He did not mention here the rest at night, being content with what He said in another place: ﴿He it is who made the night for you that you may rest therein, and the day to see by﴾. Then He mentioned another benefit in that arrangement, so He said: ﴿And that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾. This is connected to both verbs together: I mean "We effaced the sign of the night" and "We made the sign of the day illuminating", not to one of them alone as with the first (benefit), since the knowledge of the number of years and the reckoning is not possible except through the alternation of the two (new) things and the knowing of days, months and years.
The difference between "number" ('adad) and "reckoning" (hisab) is that "number" is the counting of what has quantity by repeating its like without anything resulting from it, while "reckoning" is the counting of what has quantity by repeating its like in such a way that from a particular group of them a specific limit results, which has a specific name. So the year, for example, if it is viewed in terms of the number of its days, that is the number; and if it is viewed in terms of its being realised and composed of a number of months, and each month being composed of a number of days, and each day composed of a number of hours, and each hour composed of a number of minutes, that is the reckoning. ﴿And every thing We have detailed in detail﴾, that is, everything you need in matters of your religion and your worldly life, We have explained with clear explanation that is not ambiguous, and at that point causes are removed and excuses vanish, ﴿so that whoever perishes may perish upon clear evidence﴾.
For this reason He said: ﴿And every human being – We have fastened his bird (ta'ir) to his neck﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: "the bird" (al-ta'ir) among the Arabs means fortune (al-hazz), and it is also called "lot" (al-bakht). So the "bird" is what befalls the person in eternity, by way of his share of reason, deeds, lifespan, provision, happiness and misery, as if a bird were flying towards him from the nest of eternity and the darknesses of the unseen world, in a flight without end or limit, reaching that person at his appointed time, with no escape and no refuge.
Al-Azhari said: The basis of this is that when God, glory be to Him, created Adam, He knew the obedient of his descendants and the disobedient, so He wrote what He knew of them all, and decreed the happiness of whom He knew to be obedient and the misery of whom He knew to be disobedient. Thus there flew to each of them what he would come to at his creation and origination. That is His saying: ﴿And every human being – We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ (p-٨١٤), that is, what flew to him in the knowledge of God. "In his neck" is an expression for inseparability, like the necklace's inseparability from the neck among the things worn.
Al-Zajjaj said: The mention of the neck is an expression for inseparability, like the necklace's inseparability from the neck. ﴿And We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find laid open﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read (yukhraju), with a fathah on the initial yā' (ya) and a ḍammah on the rā', meaning "the bird comes out for him". "A book" (kitaban) is accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). It is also permissible that the meaning be: "the bird comes out for it, and it becomes a book".
Yahya ibn Wathhab read (yukhrijuhu), with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the rā', that is, God brings it out.
Shayba and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' (read similarly). It is also transmitted from Abu Ja'far (yukhraja), with a ḍammah on the yā' and a fathah on the rā', in the passive form, that is: "and a bird will be brought out for him as a book."
The rest read (wa-nukhriju), with the nūn, so that the one who brings out is God, glory be to Him, and "a book" is the object. Abu 'Amr argued for this reading by His saying "We have fastened" (alzamnahu).
Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan and Ibn 'Amir read (yulaqqahu), with a ḍammah on the yā', a fathah on the lam, and the qāf doubled. The rest read with a fathah on the yā', a sukun on the lam and a light qāf. God, glory be to Him, said (yalqahu manshuran) only to hasten the glad tidings for the good deed and to rebuke for the evil deed.
﴿Read your book﴾, that is, We say to him: "Read your book", or saying to him. It has been said: whoever is able to read will read that book, and whoever is not able to read... ﴿Sufficient is yourself today as a reckoner against you﴾. The bā' in (bi-nafsika) is superfluous, and (ḥasiban) is a specification (tamyiz), that is: reckoning.
Sibawayh said: "ḍarib al-qidah" means "its striker", and "ṣarim" means "ṣarim" (one who cuts). It is permissible that "al-ḥasib" means "sufficient", then it was placed in the position of "witness" and so was construed with "ʿala". "The self" (nafs) means "the person". It is also permissible that "al-ḥasib" means "one who reckons", like "al-sharik" and "al-jalis".

God, glory be to Him, made clear that the reward of righteous deeds and the punishment of their opposite belong specifically to their doers and do not pass from him to another. So whoever is guided by doing what God has commanded him and leaving what God has forbidden, the benefit of that returns only to his own self. Whoever strays from the path of truth, not doing what he was commanded and not refraining from what he was forbidden, ﴿then he strays only to his own loss﴾, that is, the harm of his error falls upon his own self and does not go beyond it. So every individual is accountable for himself, rewarded for his obedience and punished for his disobedience. Then He emphasised this statement with the most eloquent emphasis, so He said: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾. "Wizr" means sin. It is said: "wazara yazir wizran and wazratan", that is, a sin. The plural is awzar. "Wizr" also means weight.
From it comes His saying: ﴿They bear their burdens upon their backs﴾, that is, the weights of their sins. The meaning of the verse: no soul bearing a burden shall bear the burden of another soul, until the other is freed from its burden and the first is taken to account for it. Something similar has already been mentioned in Surat al-An'am.

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned that the guided person is singled out for his guidance and the misguided for his misguidance, and that a person is not held to account for the crime of another, He mentioned that He does not punish His servants except after establishing proof against them by sending His messengers and sending down His books. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿And We made the sign of the day to give sight﴾, that he said: "Bright." ﴿That you may seek bounty from your Lord﴾: he said: "He made for you a long span (sabh) [of time for movement]."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿We have explained it in detail﴾ (faṣṣalnāhu), that he said: "We made it clear (bayyannāhu)."

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Jarir narrated with a good (hasan) chain from Jabir: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Every person's bird is around his neck.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿We have fastened to every man his bird (ṭā'ir) upon his neck﴾, that he said: "It is his happiness and his misery, and what Allah has decreed for him and against him, and it will cling to him wherever he is."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Anas, regarding His words ﴿his bird﴾, that he said: "His book (kitāb)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "His deed. ﴿And We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find spread open﴾: it is his deed which was recorded, and on the Day of Resurrection there will be brought out for him what was written for him of deeds, and he will read it spread open."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿Read your book﴾, that he said: "On that Day, everyone who was not a reader in the world will read."

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in *al-Tamhid* narrated from 'A'ishah, regarding His words ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, that she said: "Khadijah asked about the children of the polytheists, and he said: 'They are from their fathers.' Then she asked him again after that, and he said: 'Allah knows best what they used to do.' Then she asked him again after Islam had become firmly established, and this verse was revealed: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, and he said: 'They are upon the fitrah (natural disposition),' or he said, 'in Paradise.'"

As-Suyuti said: "Its chain is weak (da'if)."

It is firmly established in the two Sahihs and others that "the Prophet ﷺ was asked, and it was said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, we sometimes strike, during night raids (bayāt), the offspring (dharārī) of the polytheists.' He said: 'They are from them.'" On this matter there are many hadiths and a lengthy discussion.

Ibn Kathir, in his tafsir of this verse, mentioned most of the hadiths related to the children of the polytheists, then quoted the statements of the scholars on the question, so let one refer to him.

Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Ahmad, Ibn Hibban, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Ma'rifah*, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *Kitab al-I'tiqad* narrated from al-Aswad ibn Sari' that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Four will argue on the Day of Resurrection: a man who is deaf and hears nothing; a man who is feeble-minded; a man who is senile; and a man who died during the fatrah (interval between prophets). Then he said: 'Allah will take their covenants that they will obey Him, and He will send to them a messenger saying: Enter the Fire.' He said: 'By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, if they had entered it, it would have been coolness and safety for them. And whoever does not enter it will be dragged into it.'"

Its chain in Ahmad is, thus: "'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah narrated to us: Mu'adh ibn Hisham narrated to us: my father narrated to me, from Abu Qatadah, from al-Ahnaf ibn Qays, from al-Aswad ibn Sari'."

Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Ahmad, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated something similar from Abu Hurayrah, and it is in Ahmad with the chain mentioned above, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, from Abu Rafi', from Abu Hurayrah.

Qasim ibn Asbagh, al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la, and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in *al-Tamhid* narrated from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said," and he mentioned something similar, but in place of "the fool" he said "the mentally deficient (ma'tuh)."

al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul* and al-Tabarani and Abu Nu'aym narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: "On the Day of Resurrection there will be brought the one who was impaired in intellect (mamsuh 'aqlan), the one who died in the fatrah, and the one who died as a child," and he mentioned its meaning at greater length.

Ibn Jarir narrated through the route of Ibn Jurayj, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿We commanded its affluent ones (mutrafiha)﴾, that he said: "To obey Allah, but they disobeyed."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Shahr ibn Hawshab, who said: "I heard Ibn 'Abbas say regarding this verse, ﴿We commanded its affluent ones﴾ with truth, but they opposed it, so destruction (tadmir) became due against them for that."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* narrated from him regarding the verse, that he said: "We empowered their wicked ones, and they disobeyed. So when they did that, We destroyed them with punishment." This is like His words ﴿And thus We placed in every town its greatest criminals, that they might plot therein﴾.

al-Bukhari and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "In the Jahiliyyah, when a tribe (hayy) became numerous, we used to say: 'The Banu so-and-so have been commanded.'"

[p. 816]

His saying: ﴿Whoever desires the immediate [life]﴾ is an emphasis on what preceded in the sentence ﴿We have fastened to every person his fate﴾ and in the statement about the one who is guided. By *al-ʿājilah* (the immediate) is meant either the immediate benefit or the immediate abode.

The meaning is: whoever desires by his righteous deeds, or by his deeds for the Hereafter, that [immediate benefit], and this includes the disbelievers, the transgressors, those who show off, and the hypocrites, [then] We hasten for him, that is, We hasten for that seeker in it, that is, in that immediate [life]. Then He restricted the one who is hastened with two restrictions. The first is His saying ﴿what We will﴾, that is, what Allah, glorified is He, wills to hasten for him from it, not what that seeker wills. For this reason you see that many of those who seek the immediate [life] desire in this world what they do not attain, and wish for what they do not reach. The second restriction is His saying ﴿for whomever We will﴾, that is, for whomever We will to hasten [it] to from among them, according to what Our will requires. The clause ﴿for whomever We will﴾ is a *badal* (substitute) for the pronoun in ﴿for him﴾, with the preposition repeated, a *badal al-baʿḍ min al-kull* (partial substitution of the whole), because the pronoun refers back to *man* (whoever), which is general. This verse restricts the unrestricted verses, such as His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of this world, We shall give him of it﴾, and His saying: ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment, We will pay them in full for their deeds therein, and they will not be denied therein﴾. It has been said that it was recited as *mā yashāʾu* with the *yāʾ* (third person, "what He wills"). We do not know who recited it this way among the irregular readers (*shādhdh*). According to this reading, it has been said that the pronoun refers to Allah, glorified is He, meaning: what Allah wills; so its meaning is the meaning of the reading with *nūn*. But this is remote, because it contradicts what precedes it, namely *ʿajjalnā* (We hasten), and what follows it, namely ﴿for whomever We will﴾. It has also been said that the pronoun refers back to *man* in His saying ﴿Whoever desires﴾, so that this is restricted by His saying ﴿for whomever We will﴾, meaning: We hasten for him what he wills, but according to Our will. So the one who desires the immediate [life] does not obtain what he wills unless Allah wills that for him.

After all this, behind this empty pursuit, which has no effect except with the two mentioned restrictions, there is the enduring punishment of the Hereafter. For this reason He said: ﴿Then We made Hell for him﴾, that is, We made for him, because of his abandoning what he was commanded to do, which is working for the Hereafter and sincerity free of impurities, the punishment of Hell in its various kinds, ﴿he will burn therein﴾ in a place of *naṣb* (accusative) as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial state), that is, he will enter it, ﴿blamed, expelled﴾, that is, driven away from the mercy of Allah, removed far from it. So this is his punishment in the Hereafter, even though he does not obtain from the world except what Allah, glorified is He, has decreed for him. Where then is the state of this wretched one compared with the state of the God-fearing believer? For he obtains from the world what Allah has decreed for him and willed for him, without anxiety or distress, with the calm of his soul, the tranquility of his heart, and his trust in his Lord. Yet he, along with that, works for the Hereafter, awaiting the reward from Allah, glorified is He, which is Paradise.

For this reason He said: ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter﴾, that is, desires the Hereafter abode by his deeds, ﴿and strives for it its striving﴾, that is, the true striving for it that is fitting for its seeker, which is doing what he is commanded and abstaining from what he is forbidden, sincerely for Allah, unmixed.

And that striving must be according to the legal law, without innovation or caprice, and he must be a believer in Allah with sound faith, because a righteous deed does not earn its doer a reward unless he is a believer; Allah only accepts from the God-fearing. The clause is in a place of *naṣb* as a *ḥāl*. The reference in His saying ﴿those﴾ is to those who desire the Hereafter and strive for it its striving, and its predicate is ﴿their striving is appreciated﴾ with Allah, that is, accepted, not rejected. It has been said: multiplied many times over. So He, glorified is He, considered three matters for the striving to be appreciated: first, the desire for the Hereafter; second, that he strive for it the striving that is due to it; and third, that he be a believer.

Then He, glorified is He, explained the completeness of His kindness and the comprehensiveness of His mercy, and said: ﴿To each We extend, to these and to those, from the gift of your Lord﴾. The *tanwīn* in *kullan* (each) is a replacement (*ʿiwaḍ*) for the omitted genitive complement (*mudāf ilayhi*), and the estimate is: each one of the two groups, We extend, that is, We increase for him from Our gift, continuously without interruption. We provide for believers and disbelievers, for the obedient and the disobedient. The disobedience of the disobedient does not cut off his provision, and what provides extension is what He hastened to the one who desires the world, and what He bestowed in both this life and the next upon the one who desires the Hereafter. In His saying ﴿from the gift of your Lord﴾ there is an indication that this is by pure bounty, and it is connected to ﴿We extend﴾. ﴿And the gift of your Lord is not restricted﴾, that is, not withheld. It is said: *ḥaẓara yaḥẓuru ḥaẓran*, meaning he prevented; and everything that comes between you and something has restricted it from you. ﴿To these﴾ is a *badal* from ﴿to each﴾, and ﴿and to those﴾ is conjoined to the *badal*. Al-Zajjāj said: Allah, glorified is He, informed that He gives both the Muslim and the disbeliever, and that He provides for both of them together, the two groups. So He said: ﴿to these and to those from the gift of your Lord﴾.

﴿Look how We have preferred some of them over others﴾. The address is to Muḥammad ﷺ, and it may be to everyone who has the capacity for reflection and consideration. This sentence confirms what passed of the extension and clarifies it. The meaning: look how We have preferred, in the immediate gifts, some of the servants over others: rich and poor, strong and weak, healthy and sick, intelligent and foolish. That is for a far-reaching wisdom, which minds fall short of grasping. ﴿And the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in preference﴾. That is because the ratio of difference in the degrees of the Hereafter to the difference in the degrees of this world is like the ratio of the Hereafter to this world, and this world has no measure in comparison to the Hereafter. Therefore the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in preference.

It has been said: the meaning is that believers enter Paradise and disbelievers enter the Fire, so the excellence of the believers over the disbelievers becomes apparent. The summary of the meaning is that the difference in the Hereafter and its degrees is above the difference in this world and the ranks of its people therein, in expansion and contraction and similar things.

Then, since He, glorified is He, summarized the deeds of righteousness in His saying ﴿and strives for it its striving, and he is a believer﴾, He began to detail that, starting with the most noble of them, which is monotheism (*tawḥīd*), and said: ﴿Do not set up with Allah another god﴾. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and what is meant is his community, as a stirring and exhortation. Or it is to everyone who is qualified for it and suitable for being addressed by it. It has been said: it is with an implied *qawl* (saying), and the estimate is: say to every responsible person, "Do not set up." The *naṣb* of ﴿you will sit﴾ is as an answer to the prohibition, and the estimate is: let there not come from you a setting-up, so there will be sitting. (p. 817) The meaning of *taqʿud* (you will sit) is "you will become," from the saying of people: he sharpened the blade until it sat, as if it were a ruin. The meaning is not literal sitting, as opposed to standing. It has been said: it is a metaphor for lack of ability to achieve good things, since striving in it can only be done by standing, and inability to stand necessitates being seated from seeking. It has also been said: it is a characteristic of the one who is blamed and forsaken to sit regretful and reflecting on what he has neglected, so sitting according to this is literal. The *naṣb* of ﴿blamed, forsaken﴾ is as the predicate of ﴿you will sit﴾ or as a *ḥāl*, meaning: you will become one who combines the two matters, blame for you from Allah, from His angels, and from His righteous servants, and forsaking for you from Him, glorified is He; or in a state in which you combine the two matters.

Then, since He mentioned what is the greatest pillar, which is monotheism, He followed it with the other rites and laws, and said: ﴿Your Lord has decreed﴾, that is, commanded with a firm command, a definite judgment, and a binding decree, ﴿that you not worship except Him﴾, that is, that you not worship. Thus *an* is *nāṣibah* (governing the subjunctive), and it is possible that it is *mufassirah* (explanatory), with no prohibition.

It is recited as ﴿Your Lord has enjoined (*wa-waṣṣā*)﴾, meaning he enjoined His servants to worship Him alone. Then He followed it with the command of kindness to parents, and said: ﴿and to parents, kindness﴾, that is, and decreed that you be kind to parents, or: and be kind to them both with kindness. It is not permissible for ﴿to parents﴾ to be connected to ﴿kindness﴾, because the verbal noun (*maṣdar*) cannot precede what is connected to it.

It has been said: the reason for mentioning kindness to parents after worshipping Allah, glorified is He, is that they are the apparent cause of the existence of the offspring born between them. In making kindness to the two parents a companion to the monotheism and worship of Allah there is an announcement of the emphasis of their right and attention to their status, which is not hidden. Likewise, in another verse He, glorified is He, made their thanks coupled with His thanks, and said: ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents﴾.

Then He, glorified is He, singled out the state of old age for mention, because it is the state in which the child is most in need of kindness from the offspring compared with other states, and said: ﴿If one of them or both of them reach old age in your presence﴾. *Immā* is composed of *in* (the conditional particle) and *mā* (the indefinite particle of emphasis), to intensify the meaning of the condition. Then the *nūn* of emphasis was added to the verb to increase the affirmation, as if it were said: this condition is something that will certainly happen customarily.

The grammarians said: the condition resembles the prohibition in terms of the jussive mood and non-occurrence, so this is why it is correct for the emphatic *nūn* to enter upon it.

Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read ﴿reach (yablughān)﴾ in the dual. Al-Farrāʾ said: he made it dual because the two parents were mentioned before it, so the verb matched their number. Then he said ﴿one of them or both﴾ as a new sentence. As for the reading ﴿reach (yablughanna)﴾, *aḥaduhumā* (one of them) is a subject independently, and his saying ﴿or both﴾ is also a subject, but not independently; rather by dependence through conjunction. The better view is that, according to the reading ﴿yablughān﴾, *aḥaduhumā* is a *badal* from the pronoun referring to the two parents in the verb, and ﴿both﴾ is conjoined to the *badal*. It is not correct to make ﴿both﴾ a *tawkīd* (emphatic appositive) for the pronoun, because conjunction implies participation.

The meaning of ﴿in your presence (ʿindaka)﴾ is in your care and custody. The singular pronoun in ﴿in your presence﴾ and ﴿do not say﴾ and what follows them is to indicate that each individual among them is forbidden in what is prohibited and commanded in what is commanded.

The meaning of ﴿do not say to them both, "Uff"﴾ is: do not say to either of them in both states, together and separately; the intent is not only the state of being together.

For *uff* there are several dialectal forms: the *hamzah* with *ḍamm* and the three vowels on the *fāʾ*, with and without *tanwīn*, with *kasr* on the *hamzah* and the *fāʾ* without *tanwīn*, *uffī* with *imālah* (vowel inclination), and *uffah* with *hāʾ*.

Al-Farrāʾ said: the Arabs say, "So-and-so is *yata-affaf* (sighs) from a wind he found," meaning he says "uff, uff."

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: *al-uffu* is the wax of the ear, and *al-thuffu* is the dirt of the nails. This is said when something is disgusting; then it became widespread until they used it for everything by which they are harmed.

Thaʿlab narrated from Ibn al-Aʿrābī that *al-affaf* is boredom. Al-Qutaybī said: its origin is that when dust or the like falls on a person he blows on it to remove it, so the sound produced by that blowing is the speaker's saying "uff." Then they extended it, mentioning it at every hated thing that reaches them.

Al-Zajjāj said: its meaning is stench.

Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: *al-uffu* is dirt between the nails, and *al-thuffu* is their clippings.

The summary is that it is a verb-like word (*ism fiʿl*) that expresses annoyance and distaste, or a sound that expresses that. So the child is forbidden from showing anything from himself that indicates annoyance with his parents or distaste for them. By this prohibition, the prohibition of all other things that harm them is understood by *fahwā al-khiṭāb* (the implication of the address) or by its *laḥn* (allusion), as is established in the *uṣūl* (legal theory).

﴿And do not rebuke them (lā tanharhumā)﴾: *al-nahr* is scolding and harshness. It is said: *nahara* and *intahara* when he confronts him with words that scold him.

Al-Zajjāj said: its meaning is: do not speak to them while annoyed, shouting in their faces, and say to them, instead of the *uff* and the rebuke, a noble saying, that is, gentle and kind, the best that can be expressed of gentleness of speech and nobility, together with courtesy, modesty, and decorum.

﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾. Al-Qaffāl mentioned two interpretations of lowering the wing. First: when a bird wants to gather its chicks to it for raising, it lowers its wing for them; so lowering the wing became a metaphor for good management. It is as if He said to the child: take care of your parents by gathering them to yourself, just as they did with you in your childhood.

The second point: when a bird wants to fly and rise, it spreads its wing, and when it wants to descend, it lowers its wing. So lowering the wing became a metaphor for humility and abandoning arrogance. There are two views on the attribution of the wing to humility. The first is that it is like the attribution of Hatim to generosity in your saying "Hatim of generosity" (Hatim al-Ta'i, proverbial for generosity), so the original meaning is "the humbled wing." The second is that it is a metaphor, as if humility were imagined to have a wing, and then lowering was attributed to that wing.

The majority read *al-dhull* (الذُّلِّ) with a *ḍamma* on the *dhāl*, from *dhalla yadhillu dhullan, dhillatan, madhallatan*, so the one who is humbled is *dhalīl*.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr read it with a *kasra* on the *dhāl* (الذِّلِّ), and this is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Asim. It comes from their saying *dābbatun dhalūl* (دابَّةٌ ذَلُولٌ), meaning a tame animal, with the intention of *dhull* (submission), that is, one that is compliant and easy, with no difficulty in it.

The phrase *min al-rahmah* (مِنَ الرَّحْمَةِ) carries the sense of cause, meaning: out of excessive compassion and tenderness toward them, because of their old age and their need today for one who was once the neediest of God's creation toward them. Then it is as if God, glorified is He, said: "Do not be content with your mercy, which has no permanence, but rather [say]: ﴿And say: My Lord, have mercy upon them as they raised me when I was small.﴾" The *kaf* (ك) in *kamā* is in the accusative position as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: mercy like their raising of me, or like their mercy toward me. It has also been said that the intended meaning is not "mercy like mercy," but that the *kaf* indicates the coincidence of the two in existence, so let this [mercy] happen as that [raising] happened.

*Al-tarbiyah* (التَّرْبِيَةُ) means nurturing and growing. The *kaf* may also be causal, meaning: for the sake of their raising me, as in His saying: ﴿And remember Him as He guided you﴾. God, glorified is He, has greatly emphasized the command to honor parents, with an emphasis that makes the skins of the disobedient shiver and their hair stand on end.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Dahhak regarding His saying ﴿Whoever desires the hastened [life]﴾: he said, "Whoever intends by his deed the worldly life, ﴿We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We wish.﴾ That is for him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah* (Hilyat al-Awliya') reported from al-Hasan regarding His saying ﴿each—We extend to them﴾ [the verse]: he said, "Each one, God provides for in this world, the righteous and the wicked."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the verse: he said, "God provides for whoever desires this world, and provides for whoever desires the Hereafter."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Dahhak: "*Mahzūran*: prohibited, forbidden."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported the same from Ibn Zayd.

Al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah* reported from Salman, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "There is no servant who desires to rise a degree in this world, and rises by it, except that God will place him in the Hereafter at a degree greater than it and longer." Then he recited: ﴿And the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in preference.﴾ This is from the narration of Zadhan from Salman. And it is established in the *Sahihayn* (the two Sahih collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim) that "the people of the high degrees will see the people of 'Illiyyin as one sees a star setting on the horizon of the sky."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying *madhmūman* (مَذْمُومًا): he said, "*malūman*: blamed."

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif* reported through the route of Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas that he recited: ﴿*Wa-wassā rabbuka*﴾ (And your Lord enjoined), in place of *wa-qadā* (And your Lord decreed). He said: "The waw and the ṣād have been joined, and you read it as *wa-qadā rabbuka*."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported the same through the route of al-Dahhak from him.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Mani', Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh reported through the route of Maymun ibn Mihran from him, also the same, and added: "Even if it had been revealed as *qadā* (decree), no one would have associated partners with Him."

I say: This would follow only if *qadā* meant completion of the matter. Although that is one of the meanings of the general term *qadā*, as in His saying ﴿The matter has been decided concerning which you both inquire﴾, and His saying: ﴿So when you have completed your rites﴾, and ﴿So when you have finished the prayer﴾, here it means *amr* (command), which is one of the meanings of *qadā*, and command does not necessitate that. For He, glorified is He, has commanded His servants with all that He has made obligatory, and among that is singling Him out in worship and His monotheism, yet that does not necessitate that polytheism never occurs from the polytheists. Among the meanings of the general term *qadā* are other meanings besides these two, such as *qadā* in the sense of creation, as in ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾.

And in the sense of will, as in His saying: ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾.

And in the sense of covenant, as in His saying: ﴿And you were not on the western side when We decreed to Moses the command﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported through the route of 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying *wa-qadā rabbuka*: he said, "*amara*: commanded."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujahid regarding the verse: he said, "*'ahida rabbuka*: your Lord covenanted."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan regarding His saying ﴿And to parents, good treatment﴾: he said, "That means kindness."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid regarding His saying ﴿So do not say to them, "Uff"﴾: "Because of the harm you remove from them, namely the excrement and urine, just as they did not say it about what they removed from you of excrement and urine."

Al-Daylami reported from al-Husayn ibn 'Ali, as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) narration: "If God knew of anything of disobedience less than 'uff,' He would have forbidden it."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Zuhayr ibn Muhammad regarding His saying ﴿And speak to them a noble word﴾: he said, "When they call you, say, 'Here I am for you both (labbayka wa-sa'dayka).'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah regarding the verse: he said, "A gentle, easy word."

Al-Bukhari in *al-Adab* (al-Adab al-Mufrad), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Urwah regarding His saying ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility﴾: he said, "He is gentle toward them, so that he does not refuse them anything they love."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding the verse: he said, "Be submissive to your parents as a slave is submissive to a harsh, severe master."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported through the route of 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And say, "My Lord, have mercy upon them"﴾, then God revealed after this ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were relatives﴾.

Al-Bukhari in *al-Adab al-Mufrad*, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported through various routes from him something similar. Many authentic hadiths about kindness to parents have also been transmitted, established in the *Sahihayn* and elsewhere, and they are well known in the books of hadith.

[p. 816]

His saying: ﴿Whoever desires the immediate [life]﴾ is an emphasis on what preceded in the sentence ﴿We have fastened to every person his fate﴾ and in the statement about the one who is guided. By *al-ʿājilah* (the immediate) is meant either the immediate benefit or the immediate abode.

The meaning is: whoever desires by his righteous deeds, or by his deeds for the Hereafter, that [immediate benefit], and this includes the disbelievers, the transgressors, those who show off, and the hypocrites, [then] We hasten for him, that is, We hasten for that seeker in it, that is, in that immediate [life]. Then He restricted the one who is hastened with two restrictions. The first is His saying ﴿what We will﴾, that is, what Allah, glorified is He, wills to hasten for him from it, not what that seeker wills. For this reason you see that many of those who seek the immediate [life] desire in this world what they do not attain, and wish for what they do not reach. The second restriction is His saying ﴿for whomever We will﴾, that is, for whomever We will to hasten [it] to from among them, according to what Our will requires. The clause ﴿for whomever We will﴾ is a *badal* (substitute) for the pronoun in ﴿for him﴾, with the preposition repeated, a *badal al-baʿḍ min al-kull* (partial substitution of the whole), because the pronoun refers back to *man* (whoever), which is general. This verse restricts the unrestricted verses, such as His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of this world, We shall give him of it﴾, and His saying: ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment, We will pay them in full for their deeds therein, and they will not be denied therein﴾. It has been said that it was recited as *mā yashāʾu* with the *yāʾ* (third person, "what He wills"). We do not know who recited it this way among the irregular readers (*shādhdh*). According to this reading, it has been said that the pronoun refers to Allah, glorified is He, meaning: what Allah wills; so its meaning is the meaning of the reading with *nūn*. But this is remote, because it contradicts what precedes it, namely *ʿajjalnā* (We hasten), and what follows it, namely ﴿for whomever We will﴾. It has also been said that the pronoun refers back to *man* in His saying ﴿Whoever desires﴾, so that this is restricted by His saying ﴿for whomever We will﴾, meaning: We hasten for him what he wills, but according to Our will. So the one who desires the immediate [life] does not obtain what he wills unless Allah wills that for him.

After all this, behind this empty pursuit, which has no effect except with the two mentioned restrictions, there is the enduring punishment of the Hereafter. For this reason He said: ﴿Then We made Hell for him﴾, that is, We made for him, because of his abandoning what he was commanded to do, which is working for the Hereafter and sincerity free of impurities, the punishment of Hell in its various kinds, ﴿he will burn therein﴾ in a place of *naṣb* (accusative) as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial state), that is, he will enter it, ﴿blamed, expelled﴾, that is, driven away from the mercy of Allah, removed far from it. So this is his punishment in the Hereafter, even though he does not obtain from the world except what Allah, glorified is He, has decreed for him. Where then is the state of this wretched one compared with the state of the God-fearing believer? For he obtains from the world what Allah has decreed for him and willed for him, without anxiety or distress, with the calm of his soul, the tranquility of his heart, and his trust in his Lord. Yet he, along with that, works for the Hereafter, awaiting the reward from Allah, glorified is He, which is Paradise.

For this reason He said: ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter﴾, that is, desires the Hereafter abode by his deeds, ﴿and strives for it its striving﴾, that is, the true striving for it that is fitting for its seeker, which is doing what he is commanded and abstaining from what he is forbidden, sincerely for Allah, unmixed.

And that striving must be according to the legal law, without innovation or caprice, and he must be a believer in Allah with sound faith, because a righteous deed does not earn its doer a reward unless he is a believer; Allah only accepts from the God-fearing. The clause is in a place of *naṣb* as a *ḥāl*. The reference in His saying ﴿those﴾ is to those who desire the Hereafter and strive for it its striving, and its predicate is ﴿their striving is appreciated﴾ with Allah, that is, accepted, not rejected. It has been said: multiplied many times over. So He, glorified is He, considered three matters for the striving to be appreciated: first, the desire for the Hereafter; second, that he strive for it the striving that is due to it; and third, that he be a believer.

Then He, glorified is He, explained the completeness of His kindness and the comprehensiveness of His mercy, and said: ﴿To each We extend, to these and to those, from the gift of your Lord﴾. The *tanwīn* in *kullan* (each) is a replacement (*ʿiwaḍ*) for the omitted genitive complement (*mudāf ilayhi*), and the estimate is: each one of the two groups, We extend, that is, We increase for him from Our gift, continuously without interruption. We provide for believers and disbelievers, for the obedient and the disobedient. The disobedience of the disobedient does not cut off his provision, and what provides extension is what He hastened to the one who desires the world, and what He bestowed in both this life and the next upon the one who desires the Hereafter. In His saying ﴿from the gift of your Lord﴾ there is an indication that this is by pure bounty, and it is connected to ﴿We extend﴾. ﴿And the gift of your Lord is not restricted﴾, that is, not withheld. It is said: *ḥaẓara yaḥẓuru ḥaẓran*, meaning he prevented; and everything that comes between you and something has restricted it from you. ﴿To these﴾ is a *badal* from ﴿to each﴾, and ﴿and to those﴾ is conjoined to the *badal*. Al-Zajjāj said: Allah, glorified is He, informed that He gives both the Muslim and the disbeliever, and that He provides for both of them together, the two groups. So He said: ﴿to these and to those from the gift of your Lord﴾.

﴿Look how We have preferred some of them over others﴾. The address is to Muḥammad ﷺ, and it may be to everyone who has the capacity for reflection and consideration. This sentence confirms what passed of the extension and clarifies it. The meaning: look how We have preferred, in the immediate gifts, some of the servants over others: rich and poor, strong and weak, healthy and sick, intelligent and foolish. That is for a far-reaching wisdom, which minds fall short of grasping. ﴿And the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in preference﴾. That is because the ratio of difference in the degrees of the Hereafter to the difference in the degrees of this world is like the ratio of the Hereafter to this world, and this world has no measure in comparison to the Hereafter. Therefore the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in preference.

It has been said: the meaning is that believers enter Paradise and disbelievers enter the Fire, so the excellence of the believers over the disbelievers becomes apparent. The summary of the meaning is that the difference in the Hereafter and its degrees is above the difference in this world and the ranks of its people therein, in expansion and contraction and similar things.

Then, since He, glorified is He, summarized the deeds of righteousness in His saying ﴿and strives for it its striving, and he is a believer﴾, He began to detail that, starting with the most noble of them, which is monotheism (*tawḥīd*), and said: ﴿Do not set up with Allah another god﴾. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and what is meant is his community, as a stirring and exhortation. Or it is to everyone who is qualified for it and suitable for being addressed by it. It has been said: it is with an implied *qawl* (saying), and the estimate is: say to every responsible person, "Do not set up." The *naṣb* of ﴿you will sit﴾ is as an answer to the prohibition, and the estimate is: let there not come from you a setting-up, so there will be sitting. (p. 817) The meaning of *taqʿud* (you will sit) is "you will become," from the saying of people: he sharpened the blade until it sat, as if it were a ruin. The meaning is not literal sitting, as opposed to standing. It has been said: it is a metaphor for lack of ability to achieve good things, since striving in it can only be done by standing, and inability to stand necessitates being seated from seeking. It has also been said: it is a characteristic of the one who is blamed and forsaken to sit regretful and reflecting on what he has neglected, so sitting according to this is literal. The *naṣb* of ﴿blamed, forsaken﴾ is as the predicate of ﴿you will sit﴾ or as a *ḥāl*, meaning: you will become one who combines the two matters, blame for you from Allah, from His angels, and from His righteous servants, and forsaking for you from Him, glorified is He; or in a state in which you combine the two matters.

Then, since He mentioned what is the greatest pillar, which is monotheism, He followed it with the other rites and laws, and said: ﴿Your Lord has decreed﴾, that is, commanded with a firm command, a definite judgment, and a binding decree, ﴿that you not worship except Him﴾, that is, that you not worship. Thus *an* is *nāṣibah* (governing the subjunctive), and it is possible that it is *mufassirah* (explanatory), with no prohibition.

It is recited as ﴿Your Lord has enjoined (*wa-waṣṣā*)﴾, meaning he enjoined His servants to worship Him alone. Then He followed it with the command of kindness to parents, and said: ﴿and to parents, kindness﴾, that is, and decreed that you be kind to parents, or: and be kind to them both with kindness. It is not permissible for ﴿to parents﴾ to be connected to ﴿kindness﴾, because the verbal noun (*maṣdar*) cannot precede what is connected to it.

It has been said: the reason for mentioning kindness to parents after worshipping Allah, glorified is He, is that they are the apparent cause of the existence of the offspring born between them. In making kindness to the two parents a companion to the monotheism and worship of Allah there is an announcement of the emphasis of their right and attention to their status, which is not hidden. Likewise, in another verse He, glorified is He, made their thanks coupled with His thanks, and said: ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents﴾.

Then He, glorified is He, singled out the state of old age for mention, because it is the state in which the child is most in need of kindness from the offspring compared with other states, and said: ﴿If one of them or both of them reach old age in your presence﴾. *Immā* is composed of *in* (the conditional particle) and *mā* (the indefinite particle of emphasis), to intensify the meaning of the condition. Then the *nūn* of emphasis was added to the verb to increase the affirmation, as if it were said: this condition is something that will certainly happen customarily.

The grammarians said: the condition resembles the prohibition in terms of the jussive mood and non-occurrence, so this is why it is correct for the emphatic *nūn* to enter upon it.

Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read ﴿reach (yablughān)﴾ in the dual. Al-Farrāʾ said: he made it dual because the two parents were mentioned before it, so the verb matched their number. Then he said ﴿one of them or both﴾ as a new sentence. As for the reading ﴿reach (yablughanna)﴾, *aḥaduhumā* (one of them) is a subject independently, and his saying ﴿or both﴾ is also a subject, but not independently; rather by dependence through conjunction. The better view is that, according to the reading ﴿yablughān﴾, *aḥaduhumā* is a *badal* from the pronoun referring to the two parents in the verb, and ﴿both﴾ is conjoined to the *badal*. It is not correct to make ﴿both﴾ a *tawkīd* (emphatic appositive) for the pronoun, because conjunction implies participation.

The meaning of ﴿in your presence (ʿindaka)﴾ is in your care and custody. The singular pronoun in ﴿in your presence﴾ and ﴿do not say﴾ and what follows them is to indicate that each individual among them is forbidden in what is prohibited and commanded in what is commanded.

The meaning of ﴿do not say to them both, "Uff"﴾ is: do not say to either of them in both states, together and separately; the intent is not only the state of being together.

For *uff* there are several dialectal forms: the *hamzah* with *ḍamm* and the three vowels on the *fāʾ*, with and without *tanwīn*, with *kasr* on the *hamzah* and the *fāʾ* without *tanwīn*, *uffī* with *imālah* (vowel inclination), and *uffah* with *hāʾ*.
