It has been said: the meaning is that believers enter Paradise and disbelievers enter the Fire, so the excellence of the believers over the disbelievers becomes apparent. The summary of the meaning is that the difference in the Hereafter and its degrees is above the difference in this world and the ranks of its people therein, in expansion and contraction and similar things.

Then, since He, glorified is He, summarized the deeds of righteousness in His saying ﴿and strives for it its striving, and he is a believer﴾, He began to detail that, starting with the most noble of them, which is monotheism (*tawḥīd*), and said: ﴿Do not set up with Allah another god﴾. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and what is meant is his community, as a stirring and exhortation. Or it is to everyone who is qualified for it and suitable for being addressed by it. It has been said: it is with an implied *qawl* (saying), and the estimate is: say to every responsible person, "Do not set up." The *naṣb* of ﴿you will sit﴾ is as an answer to the prohibition, and the estimate is: let there not come from you a setting-up, so there will be sitting. (p. 817) The meaning of *taqʿud* (you will sit) is "you will become," from the saying of people: he sharpened the blade until it sat, as if it were a ruin. The meaning is not literal sitting, as opposed to standing. It has been said: it is a metaphor for lack of ability to achieve good things, since striving in it can only be done by standing, and inability to stand necessitates being seated from seeking. It has also been said: it is a characteristic of the one who is blamed and forsaken to sit regretful and reflecting on what he has neglected, so sitting according to this is literal. The *naṣb* of ﴿blamed, forsaken﴾ is as the predicate of ﴿you will sit﴾ or as a *ḥāl*, meaning: you will become one who combines the two matters, blame for you from Allah, from His angels, and from His righteous servants, and forsaking for you from Him, glorified is He; or in a state in which you combine the two matters.

Then, since He mentioned what is the greatest pillar, which is monotheism, He followed it with the other rites and laws, and said: ﴿Your Lord has decreed﴾, that is, commanded with a firm command, a definite judgment, and a binding decree, ﴿that you not worship except Him﴾, that is, that you not worship. Thus *an* is *nāṣibah* (governing the subjunctive), and it is possible that it is *mufassirah* (explanatory), with no prohibition.

It is recited as ﴿Your Lord has enjoined (*wa-waṣṣā*)﴾, meaning he enjoined His servants to worship Him alone. Then He followed it with the command of kindness to parents, and said: ﴿and to parents, kindness﴾, that is, and decreed that you be kind to parents, or: and be kind to them both with kindness. It is not permissible for ﴿to parents﴾ to be connected to ﴿kindness﴾, because the verbal noun (*maṣdar*) cannot precede what is connected to it.

It has been said: the reason for mentioning kindness to parents after worshipping Allah, glorified is He, is that they are the apparent cause of the existence of the offspring born between them. In making kindness to the two parents a companion to the monotheism and worship of Allah there is an announcement of the emphasis of their right and attention to their status, which is not hidden. Likewise, in another verse He, glorified is He, made their thanks coupled with His thanks, and said: ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents﴾.

Then He, glorified is He, singled out the state of old age for mention, because it is the state in which the child is most in need of kindness from the offspring compared with other states, and said: ﴿If one of them or both of them reach old age in your presence﴾. *Immā* is composed of *in* (the conditional particle) and *mā* (the indefinite particle of emphasis), to intensify the meaning of the condition. Then the *nūn* of emphasis was added to the verb to increase the affirmation, as if it were said: this condition is something that will certainly happen customarily.

The grammarians said: the condition resembles the prohibition in terms of the jussive mood and non-occurrence, so this is why it is correct for the emphatic *nūn* to enter upon it.

Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read ﴿reach (yablughān)﴾ in the dual. Al-Farrāʾ said: he made it dual because the two parents were mentioned before it, so the verb matched their number. Then he said ﴿one of them or both﴾ as a new sentence. As for the reading ﴿reach (yablughanna)﴾, *aḥaduhumā* (one of them) is a subject independently, and his saying ﴿or both﴾ is also a subject, but not independently; rather by dependence through conjunction. The better view is that, according to the reading ﴿yablughān﴾, *aḥaduhumā* is a *badal* from the pronoun referring to the two parents in the verb, and ﴿both﴾ is conjoined to the *badal*. It is not correct to make ﴿both﴾ a *tawkīd* (emphatic appositive) for the pronoun, because conjunction implies participation.

The meaning of ﴿in your presence (ʿindaka)﴾ is in your care and custody. The singular pronoun in ﴿in your presence﴾ and ﴿do not say﴾ and what follows them is to indicate that each individual among them is forbidden in what is prohibited and commanded in what is commanded.

The meaning of ﴿do not say to them both, "Uff"﴾ is: do not say to either of them in both states, together and separately; the intent is not only the state of being together.

For *uff* there are several dialectal forms: the *hamzah* with *ḍamm* and the three vowels on the *fāʾ*, with and without *tanwīn*, with *kasr* on the *hamzah* and the *fāʾ* without *tanwīn*, *uffī* with *imālah* (vowel inclination), and *uffah* with *hāʾ*.

Al-Farrāʾ said: the Arabs say, "So-and-so is *yata-affaf* (sighs) from a wind he found," meaning he says "uff, uff."

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: *al-uffu* is the wax of the ear, and *al-thuffu* is the dirt of the nails. This is said when something is disgusting; then it became widespread until they used it for everything by which they are harmed.

Thaʿlab narrated from Ibn al-Aʿrābī that *al-affaf* is boredom. Al-Qutaybī said: its origin is that when dust or the like falls on a person he blows on it to remove it, so the sound produced by that blowing is the speaker's saying "uff." Then they extended it, mentioning it at every hated thing that reaches them.

Al-Zajjāj said: its meaning is stench.

Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: *al-uffu* is dirt between the nails, and *al-thuffu* is their clippings.

The summary is that it is a verb-like word (*ism fiʿl*) that expresses annoyance and distaste, or a sound that expresses that. So the child is forbidden from showing anything from himself that indicates annoyance with his parents or distaste for them. By this prohibition, the prohibition of all other things that harm them is understood by *fahwā al-khiṭāb* (the implication of the address) or by its *laḥn* (allusion), as is established in the *uṣūl* (legal theory).

﴿And do not rebuke them (lā tanharhumā)﴾: *al-nahr* is scolding and harshness. It is said: *nahara* and *intahara* when he confronts him with words that scold him.

Al-Zajjāj said: its meaning is: do not speak to them while annoyed, shouting in their faces, and say to them, instead of the *uff* and the rebuke, a noble saying, that is, gentle and kind, the best that can be expressed of gentleness of speech and nobility, together with courtesy, modesty, and decorum.

﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾. Al-Qaffāl mentioned two interpretations of lowering the wing. First: when a bird wants to gather its chicks to it for raising, it lowers its wing for them; so lowering the wing became a metaphor for good management. It is as if He said to the child: take care of your parents by gathering them to yourself, just as they did with you in your childhood.

The second point: when a bird wants to fly and rise, it spreads its wing, and when it wants to descend, it lowers its wing. So lowering the wing became a metaphor for humility and abandoning arrogance. There are two views on the attribution of the wing to humility. The first is that it is like the attribution of Hatim to generosity in your saying "Hatim of generosity" (Hatim al-Ta'i, proverbial for generosity), so the original meaning is "the humbled wing." The second is that it is a metaphor, as if humility were imagined to have a wing, and then lowering was attributed to that wing.

The majority read *al-dhull* (الذُّلِّ) with a *ḍamma* on the *dhāl*, from *dhalla yadhillu dhullan, dhillatan, madhallatan*, so the one who is humbled is *dhalīl*.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr read it with a *kasra* on the *dhāl* (الذِّلِّ), and this is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Asim. It comes from their saying *dābbatun dhalūl* (دابَّةٌ ذَلُولٌ), meaning a tame animal, with the intention of *dhull* (submission), that is, one that is compliant and easy, with no difficulty in it.

The phrase *min al-rahmah* (مِنَ الرَّحْمَةِ) carries the sense of cause, meaning: out of excessive compassion and tenderness toward them, because of their old age and their need today for one who was once the neediest of God's creation toward them. Then it is as if God, glorified is He, said: "Do not be content with your mercy, which has no permanence, but rather [say]: ﴿And say: My Lord, have mercy upon them as they raised me when I was small.﴾" The *kaf* (ك) in *kamā* is in the accusative position as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: mercy like their raising of me, or like their mercy toward me. It has also been said that the intended meaning is not "mercy like mercy," but that the *kaf* indicates the coincidence of the two in existence, so let this [mercy] happen as that [raising] happened.

*Al-tarbiyah* (التَّرْبِيَةُ) means nurturing and growing. The *kaf* may also be causal, meaning: for the sake of their raising me, as in His saying: ﴿And remember Him as He guided you﴾. God, glorified is He, has greatly emphasized the command to honor parents, with an emphasis that makes the skins of the disobedient shiver and their hair stand on end.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Dahhak regarding His saying ﴿Whoever desires the hastened [life]﴾: he said, "Whoever intends by his deed the worldly life, ﴿We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We wish.﴾ That is for him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah* (Hilyat al-Awliya') reported from al-Hasan regarding His saying ﴿each—We extend to them﴾ [the verse]: he said, "Each one, God provides for in this world, the righteous and the wicked."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the verse: he said, "God provides for whoever desires this world, and provides for whoever desires the Hereafter."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Dahhak: "*Mahzūran*: prohibited, forbidden."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported the same from Ibn Zayd.

Al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah* reported from Salman, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "There is no servant who desires to rise a degree in this world, and rises by it, except that God will place him in the Hereafter at a degree greater than it and longer." Then he recited: ﴿And the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in preference.﴾ This is from the narration of Zadhan from Salman. And it is established in the *Sahihayn* (the two Sahih collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim) that "the people of the high degrees will see the people of 'Illiyyin as one sees a star setting on the horizon of the sky."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying *madhmūman* (مَذْمُومًا): he said, "*malūman*: blamed."

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif* reported through the route of Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas that he recited: ﴿*Wa-wassā rabbuka*﴾ (And your Lord enjoined), in place of *wa-qadā* (And your Lord decreed). He said: "The waw and the ṣād have been joined, and you read it as *wa-qadā rabbuka*."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported the same through the route of al-Dahhak from him.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Mani', Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh reported through the route of Maymun ibn Mihran from him, also the same, and added: "Even if it had been revealed as *qadā* (decree), no one would have associated partners with Him."

I say: This would follow only if *qadā* meant completion of the matter. Although that is one of the meanings of the general term *qadā*, as in His saying ﴿The matter has been decided concerning which you both inquire﴾, and His saying: ﴿So when you have completed your rites﴾, and ﴿So when you have finished the prayer﴾, here it means *amr* (command), which is one of the meanings of *qadā*, and command does not necessitate that. For He, glorified is He, has commanded His servants with all that He has made obligatory, and among that is singling Him out in worship and His monotheism, yet that does not necessitate that polytheism never occurs from the polytheists. Among the meanings of the general term *qadā* are other meanings besides these two, such as *qadā* in the sense of creation, as in ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾.

And in the sense of will, as in His saying: ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾.

And in the sense of covenant, as in His saying: ﴿And you were not on the western side when We decreed to Moses the command﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported through the route of 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying *wa-qadā rabbuka*: he said, "*amara*: commanded."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujahid regarding the verse: he said, "*'ahida rabbuka*: your Lord covenanted."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan regarding His saying ﴿And to parents, good treatment﴾: he said, "That means kindness."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid regarding His saying ﴿So do not say to them, "Uff"﴾: "Because of the harm you remove from them, namely the excrement and urine, just as they did not say it about what they removed from you of excrement and urine."

Al-Daylami reported from al-Husayn ibn 'Ali, as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) narration: "If God knew of anything of disobedience less than 'uff,' He would have forbidden it."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Zuhayr ibn Muhammad regarding His saying ﴿And speak to them a noble word﴾: he said, "When they call you, say, 'Here I am for you both (labbayka wa-sa'dayka).'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah regarding the verse: he said, "A gentle, easy word."

Al-Bukhari in *al-Adab* (al-Adab al-Mufrad), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Urwah regarding His saying ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility﴾: he said, "He is gentle toward them, so that he does not refuse them anything they love."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding the verse: he said, "Be submissive to your parents as a slave is submissive to a harsh, severe master."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported through the route of 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And say, "My Lord, have mercy upon them"﴾, then God revealed after this ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were relatives﴾.

Al-Bukhari in *al-Adab al-Mufrad*, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported through various routes from him something similar. Many authentic hadiths about kindness to parents have also been transmitted, established in the *Sahihayn* and elsewhere, and they are well known in the books of hadith.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 17, verses 31–33 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls﴾ means: what is in your hearts of sincerity or its absence in all acts of obedience, and of repentance from a sin that you committed or persistence in it. Included within this generality, at the first level of inclusion, is what is in the soul of righteousness and disobedience toward parents. It has been said that the verse is specific to what is due to the two parents of kindness and what is forbidden to children of disobedience. The first view is better, in consideration of the generality of the wording, so the context's indication neither specifies nor restricts it. ﴿If you are righteous﴾ meaning intending righteousness, repentance from sin, and sincerity in obedience, then what has occurred of the sin from which you have repented will not harm you. ﴿Indeed, He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back (to Him) in repentance﴾ (p-819), meaning those who return from sins to repentance, and from lack of sincerity to pure sincerity, forgiving what has passed from them of speech, deed, or belief. Whoever repents, Allah turns to him in repentance, and whoever returns to Allah, Allah returns to him.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the charge concerning relatives other than the parents, after the charge concerning the two of them, saying: ﴿And give the relative his right﴾. The address is either to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as an incitement and a kindling for others of the Ummah, or to everyone among the responsible who is fit for this, as in His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾. By "the relative" is meant the kinsman, and his right is the maintenance of kinship (silat al-rahim) which Allah commanded and repeated the charge concerning. The scholars differ over whether maintenance is obligatory for relatives, or for some of them, such as parents over children and children over parents, which is well known.

What should be relied upon is that it is obligatory to maintain them with what one's ability reaches and as the condition requires. And ﴿the needy﴾ is conjoined to "the relative," and in this conjunction is evidence that the intended "right" is the financial right. And ﴿the wayfarer﴾ is conjoined to "the needy." The meaning: give whoever is characterized by neediness, or by being a wayfarer, his right.

The reality of the needy and the wayfarer has already been explained in al-Baqarah and at-Tawbah.

What is intended in this verse is giving them charity with what one's ability reaches, of voluntary charity, or of what Allah has prescribed for them of obligatory charity, for they are among the eight categories who are the recipients of zakat.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, commanded what He commanded here, He forbade wastefulness, saying: ﴿And do not squander wastefully﴾. Tabdhir is scattering wealth as seed is scattered, however it falls, without deliberately choosing its places. It is the blameworthy extravagance, because it exceeds the limit that is praiseworthy in the law in spending, or it is spending in what is not right, even if it is little.

Al-Shafi'i said: Tabdhir is spending wealth in what is not its right, and there is no tabdhir in doing good.

Al-Qurtubi said after relating the saying of al-Shafi'i: This is the view of the majority.

Ashhab said, from Malik: Tabdhir is taking wealth from its right and placing it in what is not its right, and it is israf, and it is forbidden, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, the squanderers were brothers of the devils﴾. For this clause is a reason for the prohibition of tabdhir. By brotherhood is meant complete similarity, and avoiding similarity to the devil, even in one trait of his traits, is obligatory; how much more so in what is more general than that, as the generality of "similarity" indicates. And extravagance in spending is from the work of the devil, so when any son of Adam does it, he has obeyed the devil and followed him. ﴿And Satan has ever been to his Lord ungrateful﴾, meaning greatly disbelieving, exceedingly rebellious against the truth; because he, with his disbelief, does nothing but evil, commands nothing but evil, and whispers nothing but what has no good in it.

In this verse there is a branding of the squanderers with similarity to the devils, and then a branding of the species of devil as ungrateful. This requires that the squanderer is similar to the devil, and everyone similar to the devil has the ruling of the devil, and every devil is ungrateful; so the squanderer is ungrateful.

﴿And if you turn away from them﴾. It was mentioned shortly before that the origin of this "imma" is composed of the conditional "in" and the indefinite "ma," and that the entry of the emphatic nun on the condition is because it resembles the prohibition. That is: if you turn away from the relative, the needy, and the wayfarer because of a matter that compelled you to that turning away, ﴿seeking mercy from your Lord﴾, meaning for lack of provision from your Lord. But He placed the effect, which is seeking Allah's mercy, in the place of the cause, which is the lack of provision, because one who lacks provision is one who seeks it. The meaning: and if you turn away from them due to lack of provision from your Lord, hoping that Allah will open it to you, ﴿then speak to them a gentle word﴾, meaning an easy, soft word, like a good promise or an acceptable excuse.

Al-Kisa'i said: "Yassartu lahu al-qawl," meaning I made the speech soft for him.

Al-Farra' said: The meaning of the verse is: if you turn away from the petitioner due to poverty and inability, then speak to them a gentle word; promise them a good promise. It is also possible that the meaning is: if you turn away from them and do not benefit them because you lack the ability, then speak to them a gentle word; and what is intended here is not turning away with the face.

In this verse is Allah's instruction to His servants: when a petitioner asks them for what they do not have, how they should speak and with what they should reply. Indeed he spoke well who said:

"If there is no silver one day with which I can be generous to the askers, then I am a supple cane (lenient in character)."

"The askers never lack goodness from my disposition: either a gift, or a fair refusal."

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the etiquette of refusing after the prohibition of squandering, He clarified the etiquette of spending, saying: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it with complete extension﴾. This prohibition encompasses every responsible person, whether the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) as an allusion to his Ummah and as teaching them, or the address is to everyone among the responsible who is fit for it. The intent is the prohibition for a person to withhold in such a way that he constricts himself and his family, and not to expand in spending in an expansion for which there is no need, such that he becomes a spendthrift. So it is a prohibition against both extremes of excess and deficiency.

From this it is established that moderation is legislated, which is the justice that Allah has urged:

"Do not be in it excessive or deficient; both extremes of the way of purpose are blameworthy."

In this verse Allah, glory be to Him, has likened the state of the miser to the state of one whose hand is chained to his neck, such that he cannot use it, and has likened the state of one who exceeds the limit in expenditure to the state of one who extends his hand with an extension by which nothing that hands grasp is held. In this depiction there is eloquent exaggeration. Then He, glory be to Him, clarified the ruin of the two forbidden extremes, saying: ﴿so you sit blamed﴾, before people, because of the stinginess you are in; ﴿and depleted﴾, because of the extravagance you committed, meaning cut off from aims due to poverty. Al-Mahsur, originally, is one cut off from travel, from "hasarahu al-safar" when the journey has exhausted him; and a camel that is ḥasīr is one whose strength has gone so that it cannot rise. From it is His saying: ﴿Your vision will return to you humbled while it is exhausted﴾, meaning dim and cut off. It has been said: its meaning is regretful over what has passed. This speaker derived it from ḥasrah, which is regret. But there is scrutiny in this, because the agent of ḥasrah is ḥasrān, and mahsūr is not said except of one who is blamed.

Then He consoled His Messenger and the believers, that those whom poverty overtakes are not so because of their lowliness before Allah, glory be to Him, but because of the will of the Creator and Provider, saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord extends provision for whom He wills and restricts it﴾, meaning He expands it for some and restricts it for others, for a profound wisdom, not because whoever is given expanded provision is honored with Him, nor because whoever is restricted in provision is despised by Him.

It has been said that it is also possible that what is meant is that expansion and restriction are only from the command of Allah, whose treasuries never run out; as for His servants, it is upon them to be moderate.

Then He justified what He mentioned of expansion for some and restriction for others with His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is ever, of His servants, Acquainted, Seeing﴾, meaning He knows what they conceal and what they make public; nothing of that is hidden from Him. So He is the All-Knowing of their states, the All-Seeing of the manner of their management in their provisions.

In this verse is evidence that He is the Guarantor of His servants' provision, and therefore He said after it: ﴿And do not kill your children out of fear of poverty﴾. Amlaqa al-rajul: the man was left with nothing but al-malaqat, which are large smooth stones.

Al-Hudhali said, describing a hunter:

"There came upon her an Uqayder with a worn garment, when she passed over the smooth stones, he passed."

Al-Uqayder is the diminutive of al-aqdar, who is the short man, and al-khashif of garments is the worn one; sama means passed; and it is said: amlaqa: when he became poor and time stripped what was in his hand.

Aws said:

"And my poverty: calamities are beating upon me."

Allah, glory be to Him, forbade them from killing their children out of fear of poverty, and they used to do that. Then He clarified to them that their fear of poverty, to the point of reaching the killing of children because of it, has no basis; for Allah, glory be to Him, is the Provider of His servants, who provides for the children as He provides for the fathers, so He said: ﴿We provide for them and for you﴾, and you are not providers for them until you do this deed to them. This verse has passed similarly in al-An'am. Then Allah, glory be to Him, justified the prohibition of killing children for that by His saying: ﴿Indeed, their killing has ever been a great sin﴾. The majority read with a kasra on the kha' and sukun on the ta', with a short hamza (khit'an). Ibn 'Amir read (khata'an) with fatha on the kha' and ta' and the hamza shortened. It is said: khati'a fi dinihi khit'an, if he sinned; and akhta'a, if he took a path of error deliberately or not deliberately.

Al-Azhari said: khati'a khiṭa'an, like atha'ama ya'tham ithman, if he deliberately committed error; and akhta'a, if he did not deliberately intend error, akhta'an and khita'an. The poet said:

"Leave me, for I am only in error and rebellion against me, and I have ruined my wealth."

Al-khata' is the noun, standing in place of al-akhta'; it has two forms: the qasr, which is the better, and the mad, which is rare.

Ibn Kathir read with a kasra on the kha' and fatha on the ta' and mad on the hamza. Al-Nahhas said: I do not know a meaning for this reading, and Abu Hatim likewise considered it an error.

al-Hasan read (khata) with fatha on the kha' and ta', tanwin, without hamza.

When He, glory be to Him, forbade killing children, which calls for the extinction of offspring, He mentioned the prohibition of fornication, which leads to that, because of the mixing of lineages it entails. So He said: ﴿And do not approach fornication﴾. In the prohibition of approaching it by engaging in its preliminaries there is a prohibition of it a fortiori, for when the means to a thing is forbidden, the thing sought through it is forbidden by the implication of the address. Fornication has two forms: the mad and the qasr.

The poet said:

"It was an obligation, as you say, just as fornication was an obligation of stoning."

Then He justified the prohibition of fornication with His saying: ﴿Indeed, it was an abomination﴾, meaning ugly, exceedingly ugly, exceeding the limit; ﴿and evil as a way﴾, meaning a wretched path is its path, because it leads to the Fire. There is no disagreement that it is among the major sins. Evidence concerning its ugliness and warning against it has come, which is well known.

When he finished mentioning the prohibition of killing specifically children and the prohibition of fornication, which leads to what killing children leads to of mixing lineages and their instability, He forbade killing souls that are protected in general, saying: ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾. By "the soul which Allah has forbidden" is meant the one He made protected by the protection of religion or the protection of covenant. By "right" which He excepted is what permits killing protected souls originally, such as apostasy and adultery by one who is married, and retaliation against one who kills intentionally with aggression, and what joins these. The exception is incomplete (mufarragh), meaning: do not kill it for any reason except for a reason that is bound with right, or except as those bound with right. The discussion of this has already passed in al-An'am.

**Al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 17, verses 31–33 (part 2 of 2)**

Then He explained the ruling concerning some who are killed unjustly, saying: ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully﴾, meaning, not for any of the causes that legally justify killing him, ﴿We have certainly given his heir authority﴾, meaning, to whoever among his heirs takes charge of his affair if they are present, or to whoever has authority if they are not present. Sultan (authority) here means the power over the killer: if the heir wishes, he may kill him; if he wishes, he may pardon him; and if he wishes, he may take the blood money (diyah). Then, when He had made clear the permissibility of retaliation (qisas) for the one who has a claim to the blood of the one killed, or for what substitutes for retaliation, He forbade him from exceeding the limit, saying: ﴿so let him not commit excess in killing﴾, meaning, let him not go beyond what Allah has permitted him, so that he does not kill two for one, or a group, or mutilate the killer, or torture him.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read لا يُسْرِفْ with the yā' (the third person), meaning the heir (al-waliyy). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read تُسْرِفْ with the tā' (the second person), which is addressed to the first killer and is a prohibition against killing for him, meaning: do not commit excess in killing, O killer, for upon you is retaliation together with what is upon you of the punishment, wrath and curse of Allah.

Ibn Jarir said: the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to the leaders after him, meaning: do not kill, O Muhammad, anyone other than the killer, and let the leaders after you not do so.

In the recitation of Ubayy (Ubayy ibn Ka'b), it is وَلَا تُسْرِفُوا. Then He gave the reason for the prohibition of excess, saying: ﴿indeed, he has been helped﴾, meaning, supported and aided. This refers to the heir, for Allah, glorified is He, has supported him by establishing retaliation for him, by the proofs He has made manifest and the evidences He has clarified, and He has commanded those in positions of authority to assist him and to uphold his right until he obtains it. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the one killed, meaning: Allah has supported him through his heir. It has been said that this verse is among the first of what was revealed of the Qur'an concerning killing, since it is Meccan.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded on the authority of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying ﴿if you are righteous﴾, that he said: it may happen that a hasty act proceeds from the child toward the parent, so Allah said: ﴿if you are righteous﴾, meaning, if the intention is sincere, ﴿then indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back (awwabin)﴾ for the hasty act that proceeded from him.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman recorded from him, regarding His saying ﴿then indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾, that he said: those who return to good.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Hannad, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi recorded on the authority of al-Dahhak regarding the verse, that he said: those who return from sin to repentance, and from evil deeds to good deeds.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿to those who turn back﴾, that he said: to those who obey and do good.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman recorded from him, that he said: to those who repent often (tawwabin).

Al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also recorded from him, regarding His saying ﴿and give the near relative his right﴾, that he said: He commanded him with the most important of rights, and taught him how to act when he has means, and how to act when he does not have means, so He said: ﴿and if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for﴾, meaning, when they ask you and you have nothing, and you await provision from Allah, ﴿then speak to them a gentle word (qawlan maysuran)﴾, which will be, if Allah wills, like a promise (shibh al-'idah).

Sufyan said: a promise from the Prophet (ﷺ) is a debt.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also recorded from him regarding the verse that he said: it is that you maintain ties with the relative, feed the poor, and treat the wayfarer well.

Ibn Jarir recorded on the authority of Ali ibn al-Husayn that he said to a man from the people of Syria: "Have you recited the Qur'an?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then what have you recited in (Surat) Bani Isra'il: ﴿and give the near relative his right﴾?" He said: "And are you the relatives whose rights Allah commanded to be given?" He said: "Yes."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded on the authority of al-Suddi regarding the verse that he said: "The near relatives (al-qurba) are the relatives of the Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib."

I say: There is nothing in the context that indicates this specification, nor has any evidence pointed to it. The meaning of the Qur'anic wording is clear if the address is to everyone among the community who is fit for it, because its meaning is a command to every responsible person who is able to maintain the ties of kinship: that he give them their right, which is the maintaining of ties that Allah has commanded.

If the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), then if it is in the manner of indirect address (ta'rid) to his community, the matter concerning it is as the first. If it is an address to him without indirection, then his community is his example (uswah), so the command to him to give the near relative his right is a command to every individual of his community.

The apparent meaning is that this address is not specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), by the evidence of what comes before this verse, namely His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him﴾, and what comes after it, namely His saying: ﴿and do not spend wastefully (tabdhir) extravagantly﴾, ﴿indeed the wasteful are brothers of the devils﴾.

There are many hadiths with the same meaning as this verse, which indicates the obligation of maintaining ties of kinship.

Ahmad and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, recorded on the authority of Anas that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have much wealth, and a family, and children, and a household. So inform me how I should spend and how I should act." He said: "Pay the obligatory zakat, for it is a purification that purifies you, and join your relatives, and recognize the right of the questioner, the neighbour and the poor." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, reduce it for me." He said: "Then give the near relative his right, and the poor, and the wayfarer, and do not spend wastefully (tabdhir)." He said: "That is enough for me, O Messenger of Allah."

Al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh recorded on the authority of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿and give the near relative his right﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called Fatimah and gave her Fadak."

Ibn Mardawayh recorded on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said: "When ﴿and give the near relative his right﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) granted Fatimah Fadak as a grant."

Ibn Kathir, after citing this hadith of Abu Sa'id, said the following: "This hadith is problematic, even if its chain were sound, because the verse is Meccan, and Fadak was conquered along with Khaybar in the seventh year after the Hijrah, so how can this be reconciled with that?" End of quotation.

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bukhari in al-Adab, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman recorded on the authority of Ibn Mas'ud regarding His saying ﴿and do not spend wastefully (tabdhir)﴾, that he said: tabdhir is spending wealth in other than its right place.

Ibn Jarir recorded from him, who said: "We, the companions of Muhammad, used to say that tabdhir is spending in other than its right."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Bukhari in al-Adab, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman recorded on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿indeed the wasteful (mubadhdhirin)﴾, that he said: they are those who spend wealth in other than its right place.

Al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman recorded on the authority of Ali, who said: "What you spend on yourself and the people of your household without extravagance (israf) or wastefulness (tabdhir) is for you, and what you give in charity is for you. But what you spend for show and reputation (riya' wa sum'ah), that is the portion of the devil."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh recorded on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿so speak to them a gentle word﴾, that he said: it is the promise.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded on the authority of Sayyar Abu al-Hakam, who said: "Wheat from Iraq was brought to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was generous and bountiful, so he distributed it among the people. This reached a group of the Arabs, who said: 'We come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and ask him,' but they found that he had already finished with it. So Allah revealed ﴿and do not make your hand shackled to your neck﴾, meaning, restrained, ﴿nor extend it fully, lest you sit reproached﴾, meaning, the people reproach you, ﴿destitute (mahsuran)﴾, meaning, with nothing left in your hand."

I say: I do not know how this is possible, for the verse is Meccan, and at that time there were no Arabs intending the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), nor was anything being carried to him from Iraq or from what is nearer to him. Moreover, the conquest of Iraq did not take place until after his death (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir recorded on the authority of al-Minhal ibn Amr that a woman sent her son to the Prophet (ﷺ), and she said: "Say to him: clothe me." He said: "I have nothing." She said: "Go back to him and say: clothe me with your shirt." So he went back to him, and he took off his shirt and gave it to her, and then ﴿and do not make your hand shackled to your neck﴾ was revealed, to the end of the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh recorded a similar account on the authority of Ibn Mas'ud.

Ibn Mardawayh recorded on the authority of Abu Umamah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Aisha, and struck with his hand: "Spend what is on the back of my palm." She said: "Then nothing will remain." He said this three times, and then Allah revealed ﴿and do not make your hand shackled to your neck﴾, to the end of the verse.

This is refuted by the fact that he (ﷺ) did not marry Aisha until after the Hijrah.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and do not make your hand shackled to your neck﴾, that he said: by this is meant stinginess (bukhl).

Both of them also recorded from him regarding the verse that he said: this is about expenditure. He says: do not make it shackled; do not extend it except for good, and do not extend it fully, meaning wastefulness, ﴿so you sit reproached﴾, reproaching himself for what he has lost of his wealth, ﴿destitute (mahsuran)﴾, meaning, all his wealth is gone.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded on the authority of al-Hasan regarding His saying ﴿indeed your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾, that he said: He looks after him; if wealth is better for him, He makes him wealthy, and if poverty is better for him, He makes him poor.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿for fear of poverty (imlaq)﴾, that he said: for fear of destitution and want.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him regarding His saying: khit'an (sin), that he said: it means a sin.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded on the authority of al-Suddi regarding His saying ﴿and do not approach fornication (zina)﴾, that he said: on the day this verse (p-822) was revealed there were no prescribed punishments (hudud), and then the hudud came afterward in Surat al-Nur.

Abu Ya'la and Ibn Mardawayh recorded on the authority of Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he recited: "And do not approach fornication; indeed it is an abomination and an evil way, except for those who repent; indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful." This was mentioned to Umar, so he came to him and asked him. He said: "I took it from the mouth of the Messenger of Allah, and you have no work except the trade in the Baqi'."

There are many hadiths warning against the abomination of fornication.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded on the authority of al-Dahhak regarding His saying ﴿and do not kill the soul﴾, to the end of the verse, that he said: this was in Makkah, and the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) was there, and it is the first thing revealed of the Qur'an concerning killing. The polytheists of Makkah used to assassinate the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so Allah said: whoever among the polytheists kills you, let his killing of you not lead you to kill, for his sake, a father, or a brother, or one of his clan, even if they are polytheists. So do not kill anyone except your killer. This was before Bara'ah (Surat al-Tawbah) was revealed. It was also said that this refers to when the command to fight the polytheists was given, and that is His saying: ﴿so let him not commit excess in killing; indeed he has been helped﴾, meaning, do not kill other than your killer. Today, in that same place among the Muslims, it is not lawful for them to kill anyone except their killer.

Al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan recorded on the authority of Zayd ibn Aslam that in the Jahiliyyah, when a man of one tribe killed a man, they would not be satisfied until they killed for him a man of noble status; if their killer was not of noble status, they would not kill the killer but would kill someone else. So they were admonished regarding that by the words of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿and do not kill the soul﴾, to His saying: ﴿so let him not commit excess in killing﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded through the route of al-Awfi on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have certainly given his heir authority﴾, that he said: it is a clear proof from Allah that He revealed, which the heir of the one killed seeks, namely retaliation (qawd) or the blood money (aql); that is the authority.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded through the route of Mujahid on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿so let him not commit excess in killing﴾, that he said: let him not be excessive in killing.

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded through the route of Abu Salih on the authority of Ibn Abbas, also: let him not kill except the killer of his kinsman.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 17, verses 31–33 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls﴾ means: what is in your hearts of sincerity or its absence in all acts of obedience, and of repentance from a sin that you committed or persistence in it. Included within this generality, at the first level of inclusion, is what is in the soul of righteousness and disobedience toward parents. It has been said that the verse is specific to what is due to the two parents of kindness and what is forbidden to children of disobedience. The first view is better, in consideration of the generality of the wording, so the context's indication neither specifies nor restricts it. ﴿If you are righteous﴾ meaning intending righteousness, repentance from sin, and sincerity in obedience, then what has occurred of the sin from which you have repented will not harm you. ﴿Indeed, He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back (to Him) in repentance﴾ (p-819), meaning those who return from sins to repentance, and from lack of sincerity to pure sincerity, forgiving what has passed from them of speech, deed, or belief. Whoever repents, Allah turns to him in repentance, and whoever returns to Allah, Allah returns to him.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the charge concerning relatives other than the parents, after the charge concerning the two of them, saying: ﴿And give the relative his right﴾. The address is either to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as an incitement and a kindling for others of the Ummah, or to everyone among the responsible who is fit for this, as in His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾. By "the relative" is meant the kinsman, and his right is the maintenance of kinship (silat al-rahim) which Allah commanded and repeated the charge concerning. The scholars differ over whether maintenance is obligatory for relatives, or for some of them, such as parents over children and children over parents, which is well known.

What should be relied upon is that it is obligatory to maintain them with what one's ability reaches and as the condition requires. And ﴿the needy﴾ is conjoined to "the relative," and in this conjunction is evidence that the intended "right" is the financial right. And ﴿the wayfarer﴾ is conjoined to "the needy." The meaning: give whoever is characterized by neediness, or by being a wayfarer, his right.

The reality of the needy and the wayfarer has already been explained in al-Baqarah and at-Tawbah.

What is intended in this verse is giving them charity with what one's ability reaches, of voluntary charity, or of what Allah has prescribed for them of obligatory charity, for they are among the eight categories who are the recipients of zakat.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, commanded what He commanded here, He forbade wastefulness, saying: ﴿And do not squander wastefully﴾. Tabdhir is scattering wealth as seed is scattered, however it falls, without deliberately choosing its places. It is the blameworthy extravagance, because it exceeds the limit that is praiseworthy in the law in spending, or it is spending in what is not right, even if it is little.

Al-Shafi'i said: Tabdhir is spending wealth in what is not its right, and there is no tabdhir in doing good.

Al-Qurtubi said after relating the saying of al-Shafi'i: This is the view of the majority.

Ashhab said, from Malik: Tabdhir is taking wealth from its right and placing it in what is not its right, and it is israf, and it is forbidden, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, the squanderers were brothers of the devils﴾. For this clause is a reason for the prohibition of tabdhir. By brotherhood is meant complete similarity, and avoiding similarity to the devil, even in one trait of his traits, is obligatory; how much more so in what is more general than that, as the generality of "similarity" indicates. And extravagance in spending is from the work of the devil, so when any son of Adam does it, he has obeyed the devil and followed him. ﴿And Satan has ever been to his Lord ungrateful﴾, meaning greatly disbelieving, exceedingly rebellious against the truth; because he, with his disbelief, does nothing but evil, commands nothing but evil, and whispers nothing but what has no good in it.

In this verse there is a branding of the squanderers with similarity to the devils, and then a branding of the species of devil as ungrateful. This requires that the squanderer is similar to the devil, and everyone similar to the devil has the ruling of the devil, and every devil is ungrateful; so the squanderer is ungrateful.

﴿And if you turn away from them﴾. It was mentioned shortly before that the origin of this "imma" is composed of the conditional "in" and the indefinite "ma," and that the entry of the emphatic nun on the condition is because it resembles the prohibition. That is: if you turn away from the relative, the needy, and the wayfarer because of a matter that compelled you to that turning away, ﴿seeking mercy from your Lord﴾, meaning for lack of provision from your Lord. But He placed the effect, which is seeking Allah's mercy, in the place of the cause, which is the lack of provision, because one who lacks provision is one who seeks it. The meaning: and if you turn away from them due to lack of provision from your Lord, hoping that Allah will open it to you, ﴿then speak to them a gentle word﴾, meaning an easy, soft word, like a good promise or an acceptable excuse.

Al-Kisa'i said: "Yassartu lahu al-qawl," meaning I made the speech soft for him.

Al-Farra' said: The meaning of the verse is: if you turn away from the petitioner due to poverty and inability, then speak to them a gentle word; promise them a good promise. It is also possible that the meaning is: if you turn away from them and do not benefit them because you lack the ability, then speak to them a gentle word; and what is intended here is not turning away with the face.

In this verse is Allah's instruction to His servants: when a petitioner asks them for what they do not have, how they should speak and with what they should reply. Indeed he spoke well who said:

"If there is no silver one day with which I can be generous to the askers, then I am a supple cane (lenient in character)."

"The askers never lack goodness from my disposition: either a gift, or a fair refusal."

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the etiquette of refusing after the prohibition of squandering, He clarified the etiquette of spending, saying: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it with complete extension﴾. This prohibition encompasses every responsible person, whether the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) as an allusion to his Ummah and as teaching them, or the address is to everyone among the responsible who is fit for it. The intent is the prohibition for a person to withhold in such a way that he constricts himself and his family, and not to expand in spending in an expansion for which there is no need, such that he becomes a spendthrift. So it is a prohibition against both extremes of excess and deficiency.

From this it is established that moderation is legislated, which is the justice that Allah has urged:

"Do not be in it excessive or deficient; both extremes of the way of purpose are blameworthy."

In this verse Allah, glory be to Him, has likened the state of the miser to the state of one whose hand is chained to his neck, such that he cannot use it, and has likened the state of one who exceeds the limit in expenditure to the state of one who extends his hand with an extension by which nothing that hands grasp is held. In this depiction there is eloquent exaggeration. Then He, glory be to Him, clarified the ruin of the two forbidden extremes, saying: ﴿so you sit blamed﴾, before people, because of the stinginess you are in; ﴿and depleted﴾, because of the extravagance you committed, meaning cut off from aims due to poverty. Al-Mahsur, originally, is one cut off from travel, from "hasarahu al-safar" when the journey has exhausted him; and a camel that is ḥasīr is one whose strength has gone so that it cannot rise. From it is His saying: ﴿Your vision will return to you humbled while it is exhausted﴾, meaning dim and cut off. It has been said: its meaning is regretful over what has passed. This speaker derived it from ḥasrah, which is regret. But there is scrutiny in this, because the agent of ḥasrah is ḥasrān, and mahsūr is not said except of one who is blamed.

Then He consoled His Messenger and the believers, that those whom poverty overtakes are not so because of their lowliness before Allah, glory be to Him, but because of the will of the Creator and Provider, saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord extends provision for whom He wills and restricts it﴾, meaning He expands it for some and restricts it for others, for a profound wisdom, not because whoever is given expanded provision is honored with Him, nor because whoever is restricted in provision is despised by Him.

It has been said that it is also possible that what is meant is that expansion and restriction are only from the command of Allah, whose treasuries never run out; as for His servants, it is upon them to be moderate.

Then He justified what He mentioned of expansion for some and restriction for others with His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is ever, of His servants, Acquainted, Seeing﴾, meaning He knows what they conceal and what they make public; nothing of that is hidden from Him. So He is the All-Knowing of their states, the All-Seeing of the manner of their management in their provisions.

In this verse is evidence that He is the Guarantor of His servants' provision, and therefore He said after it: ﴿And do not kill your children out of fear of poverty﴾. Amlaqa al-rajul: the man was left with nothing but al-malaqat, which are large smooth stones.

Al-Hudhali said, describing a hunter:

"There came upon her an Uqayder with a worn garment, when she passed over the smooth stones, he passed."

Al-Uqayder is the diminutive of al-aqdar, who is the short man, and al-khashif of garments is the worn one; sama means passed; and it is said: amlaqa: when he became poor and time stripped what was in his hand.

Aws said:

"And my poverty: calamities are beating upon me."

Allah, glory be to Him, forbade them from killing their children out of fear of poverty, and they used to do that. Then He clarified to them that their fear of poverty, to the point of reaching the killing of children because of it, has no basis; for Allah, glory be to Him, is the Provider of His servants, who provides for the children as He provides for the fathers, so He said: ﴿We provide for them and for you﴾, and you are not providers for them until you do this deed to them. This verse has passed similarly in al-An'am. Then Allah, glory be to Him, justified the prohibition of killing children for that by His saying: ﴿Indeed, their killing has ever been a great sin﴾. The majority read with a kasra on the kha' and sukun on the ta', with a short hamza (khit'an). Ibn 'Amir read (khata'an) with fatha on the kha' and ta' and the hamza shortened. It is said: khati'a fi dinihi khit'an, if he sinned; and akhta'a, if he took a path of error deliberately or not deliberately.

Al-Azhari said: khati'a khiṭa'an, like atha'ama ya'tham ithman, if he deliberately committed error; and akhta'a, if he did not deliberately intend error, akhta'an and khita'an. The poet said:

"Leave me, for I am only in error and rebellion against me, and I have ruined my wealth."

Al-khata' is the noun, standing in place of al-akhta'; it has two forms: the qasr, which is the better, and the mad, which is rare.

Ibn Kathir read with a kasra on the kha' and fatha on the ta' and mad on the hamza. Al-Nahhas said: I do not know a meaning for this reading, and Abu Hatim likewise considered it an error.

al-Hasan read (khata) with fatha on the kha' and ta', tanwin, without hamza.

When He, glory be to Him, forbade killing children, which calls for the extinction of offspring, He mentioned the prohibition of fornication, which leads to that, because of the mixing of lineages it entails. So He said: ﴿And do not approach fornication﴾. In the prohibition of approaching it by engaging in its preliminaries there is a prohibition of it a fortiori, for when the means to a thing is forbidden, the thing sought through it is forbidden by the implication of the address. Fornication has two forms: the mad and the qasr.

The poet said:

"It was an obligation, as you say, just as fornication was an obligation of stoning."

Then He justified the prohibition of fornication with His saying: ﴿Indeed, it was an abomination﴾, meaning ugly, exceedingly ugly, exceeding the limit; ﴿and evil as a way﴾, meaning a wretched path is its path, because it leads to the Fire. There is no disagreement that it is among the major sins. Evidence concerning its ugliness and warning against it has come, which is well known.

When he finished mentioning the prohibition of killing specifically children and the prohibition of fornication, which leads to what killing children leads to of mixing lineages and their instability, He forbade killing souls that are protected in general, saying: ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾. By "the soul which Allah has forbidden" is meant the one He made protected by the protection of religion or the protection of covenant. By "right" which He excepted is what permits killing protected souls originally, such as apostasy and adultery by one who is married, and retaliation against one who kills intentionally with aggression, and what joins these. The exception is incomplete (mufarragh), meaning: do not kill it for any reason except for a reason that is bound with right, or except as those bound with right. The discussion of this has already passed in al-An'am.

**Al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 17, verses 31–33 (part 2 of 2)**

Then He explained the ruling concerning some who are killed unjustly, saying: ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully﴾, meaning, not for any of the causes that legally justify killing him, ﴿We have certainly given his heir authority﴾, meaning, to whoever among his heirs takes charge of his affair if they are present, or to whoever has authority if they are not present. Sultan (authority) here means the power over the killer: if the heir wishes, he may kill him; if he wishes, he may pardon him; and if he wishes, he may take the blood money (diyah). Then, when He had made clear the permissibility of retaliation (qisas) for the one who has a claim to the blood of the one killed, or for what substitutes for retaliation, He forbade him from exceeding the limit, saying: ﴿so let him not commit excess in killing﴾, meaning, let him not go beyond what Allah has permitted him, so that he does not kill two for one, or a group, or mutilate the killer, or torture him.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read لا يُسْرِفْ with the yā' (the third person), meaning the heir (al-waliyy). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read تُسْرِفْ with the tā' (the second person), which is addressed to the first killer and is a prohibition against killing for him, meaning: do not commit excess in killing, O killer, for upon you is retaliation together with what is upon you of the punishment, wrath and curse of Allah.

Ibn Jarir said: the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to the leaders after him, meaning: do not kill, O Muhammad, anyone other than the killer, and let the leaders after you not do so.

In the recitation of Ubayy (Ubayy ibn Ka'b), it is وَلَا تُسْرِفُوا. Then He gave the reason for the prohibition of excess, saying: ﴿indeed, he has been helped﴾, meaning, supported and aided. This refers to the heir, for Allah, glorified is He, has supported him by establishing retaliation for him, by the proofs He has made manifest and the evidences He has clarified, and He has commanded those in positions of authority to assist him and to uphold his right until he obtains it. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the one killed, meaning: Allah has supported him through his heir. It has been said that this verse is among the first of what was revealed of the Qur'an concerning killing, since it is Meccan.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded on the authority of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying ﴿if you are righteous﴾, that he said: it may happen that a hasty act proceeds from the child toward the parent, so Allah said: ﴿if you are righteous﴾, meaning, if the intention is sincere, ﴿then indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back (awwabin)﴾ for the hasty act that proceeded from him.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman recorded from him, regarding His saying ﴿then indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾, that he said: those who return to good.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Hannad, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi recorded on the authority of al-Dahhak regarding the verse, that he said: those who return from sin to repentance, and from evil deeds to good deeds.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿to those who turn back﴾, that he said: to those who obey and do good.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman recorded from him, that he said: to those who repent often (tawwabin).

Al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also recorded from him, regarding His saying ﴿and give the near relative his right﴾, that he said: He commanded him with the most important of rights, and taught him how to act when he has means, and how to act when he does not have means, so He said: ﴿and if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for﴾, meaning, when they ask you and you have nothing, and you await provision from Allah, ﴿then speak to them a gentle word (qawlan maysuran)﴾, which will be, if Allah wills, like a promise (shibh al-'idah).

Sufyan said: a promise from the Prophet (ﷺ) is a debt.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also recorded from him regarding the verse that he said: it is that you maintain ties with the relative, feed the poor, and treat the wayfarer well.

Ibn Jarir recorded on the authority of Ali ibn al-Husayn that he said to a man from the people of Syria: "Have you recited the Qur'an?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then what have you recited in (Surat) Bani Isra'il: ﴿and give the near relative his right﴾?" He said: "And are you the relatives whose rights Allah commanded to be given?" He said: "Yes."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded on the authority of al-Suddi regarding the verse that he said: "The near relatives (al-qurba) are the relatives of the Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib."

I say: There is nothing in the context that indicates this specification, nor has any evidence pointed to it. The meaning of the Qur'anic wording is clear if the address is to everyone among the community who is fit for it, because its meaning is a command to every responsible person who is able to maintain the ties of kinship: that he give them their right, which is the maintaining of ties that Allah has commanded.

If the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), then if it is in the manner of indirect address (ta'rid) to his community, the matter concerning it is as the first. If it is an address to him without indirection, then his community is his example (uswah), so the command to him to give the near relative his right is a command to every individual of his community.

The apparent meaning is that this address is not specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), by the evidence of what comes before this verse, namely His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him﴾, and what comes after it, namely His saying: ﴿and do not spend wastefully (tabdhir) extravagantly﴾, ﴿indeed the wasteful are brothers of the devils﴾.

There are many hadiths with the same meaning as this verse, which indicates the obligation of maintaining ties of kinship.

Ahmad and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, recorded on the authority of Anas that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have much wealth, and a family, and children, and a household. So inform me how I should spend and how I should act." He said: "Pay the obligatory zakat, for it is a purification that purifies you, and join your relatives, and recognize the right of the questioner, the neighbour and the poor." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, reduce it for me." He said: "Then give the near relative his right, and the poor, and the wayfarer, and do not spend wastefully (tabdhir)." He said: "That is enough for me, O Messenger of Allah."

Al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh recorded on the authority of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿and give the near relative his right﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called Fatimah and gave her Fadak."

Ibn Mardawayh recorded on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said: "When ﴿and give the near relative his right﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) granted Fatimah Fadak as a grant."

Ibn Kathir, after citing this hadith of Abu Sa'id, said the following: "This hadith is problematic, even if its chain were sound, because the verse is Meccan, and Fadak was conquered along with Khaybar in the seventh year after the Hijrah, so how can this be reconciled with that?" End of quotation.

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bukhari in al-Adab, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman recorded on the authority of Ibn Mas'ud regarding His saying ﴿and do not spend wastefully (tabdhir)﴾, that he said: tabdhir is spending wealth in other than its right place.

Ibn Jarir recorded from him, who said: "We, the companions of Muhammad, used to say that tabdhir is spending in other than its right."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Bukhari in al-Adab, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman recorded on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿indeed the wasteful (mubadhdhirin)﴾, that he said: they are those who spend wealth in other than its right place.

Al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman recorded on the authority of Ali, who said: "What you spend on yourself and the people of your household without extravagance (israf) or wastefulness (tabdhir) is for you, and what you give in charity is for you. But what you spend for show and reputation (riya' wa sum'ah), that is the portion of the devil."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh recorded on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿so speak to them a gentle word﴾, that he said: it is the promise.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded on the authority of Sayyar Abu al-Hakam, who said: "Wheat from Iraq was brought to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was generous and bountiful, so he distributed it among the people. This reached a group of the Arabs, who said: 'We come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and ask him,' but they found that he had already finished with it. So Allah revealed ﴿and do not make your hand shackled to your neck﴾, meaning, restrained, ﴿nor extend it fully, lest you sit reproached﴾, meaning, the people reproach you, ﴿destitute (mahsuran)﴾, meaning, with nothing left in your hand."

I say: I do not know how this is possible, for the verse is Meccan, and at that time there were no Arabs intending the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), nor was anything being carried to him from Iraq or from what is nearer to him. Moreover, the conquest of Iraq did not take place until after his death (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir recorded on the authority of al-Minhal ibn Amr that a woman sent her son to the Prophet (ﷺ), and she said: "Say to him: clothe me." He said: "I have nothing." She said: "Go back to him and say: clothe me with your shirt." So he went back to him, and he took off his shirt and gave it to her, and then ﴿and do not make your hand shackled to your neck﴾ was revealed, to the end of the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh recorded a similar account on the authority of Ibn Mas'ud.

Ibn Mardawayh recorded on the authority of Abu Umamah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Aisha, and struck with his hand: "Spend what is on the back of my palm." She said: "Then nothing will remain." He said this three times, and then Allah revealed ﴿and do not make your hand shackled to your neck﴾, to the end of the verse.

This is refuted by the fact that he (ﷺ) did not marry Aisha until after the Hijrah.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and do not make your hand shackled to your neck﴾, that he said: by this is meant stinginess (bukhl).

Both of them also recorded from him regarding the verse that he said: this is about expenditure. He says: do not make it shackled; do not extend it except for good, and do not extend it fully, meaning wastefulness, ﴿so you sit reproached﴾, reproaching himself for what he has lost of his wealth, ﴿destitute (mahsuran)﴾, meaning, all his wealth is gone.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded on the authority of al-Hasan regarding His saying ﴿indeed your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾, that he said: He looks after him; if wealth is better for him, He makes him wealthy, and if poverty is better for him, He makes him poor.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿for fear of poverty (imlaq)﴾, that he said: for fear of destitution and want.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him regarding His saying: khit'an (sin), that he said: it means a sin.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded on the authority of al-Suddi regarding His saying ﴿and do not approach fornication (zina)﴾, that he said: on the day this verse (p-822) was revealed there were no prescribed punishments (hudud), and then the hudud came afterward in Surat al-Nur.

Abu Ya'la and Ibn Mardawayh recorded on the authority of Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he recited: "And do not approach fornication; indeed it is an abomination and an evil way, except for those who repent; indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful." This was mentioned to Umar, so he came to him and asked him. He said: "I took it from the mouth of the Messenger of Allah, and you have no work except the trade in the Baqi'."

There are many hadiths warning against the abomination of fornication.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded on the authority of al-Dahhak regarding His saying ﴿and do not kill the soul﴾, to the end of the verse, that he said: this was in Makkah, and the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) was there, and it is the first thing revealed of the Qur'an concerning killing. The polytheists of Makkah used to assassinate the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so Allah said: whoever among the polytheists kills you, let his killing of you not lead you to kill, for his sake, a father, or a brother, or one of his clan, even if they are polytheists. So do not kill anyone except your killer. This was before Bara'ah (Surat al-Tawbah) was revealed. It was also said that this refers to when the command to fight the polytheists was given, and that is His saying: ﴿so let him not commit excess in killing; indeed he has been helped﴾, meaning, do not kill other than your killer. Today, in that same place among the Muslims, it is not lawful for them to kill anyone except their killer.

Al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan recorded on the authority of Zayd ibn Aslam that in the Jahiliyyah, when a man of one tribe killed a man, they would not be satisfied until they killed for him a man of noble status; if their killer was not of noble status, they would not kill the killer but would kill someone else. So they were admonished regarding that by the words of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿and do not kill the soul﴾, to His saying: ﴿so let him not commit excess in killing﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded through the route of al-Awfi on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have certainly given his heir authority﴾, that he said: it is a clear proof from Allah that He revealed, which the heir of the one killed seeks, namely retaliation (qawd) or the blood money (aql); that is the authority.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded through the route of Mujahid on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿so let him not commit excess in killing﴾, that he said: let him not be excessive in killing.

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded through the route of Abu Salih on the authority of Ibn Abbas, also: let him not kill except the killer of his kinsman.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 17, verses 31–33 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls﴾ means: what is in your hearts of sincerity or its absence in all acts of obedience, and of repentance from a sin that you committed or persistence in it. Included within this generality, at the first level of inclusion, is what is in the soul of righteousness and disobedience toward parents. It has been said that the verse is specific to what is due to the two parents of kindness and what is forbidden to children of disobedience. The first view is better, in consideration of the generality of the wording, so the context's indication neither specifies nor restricts it. ﴿If you are righteous﴾ meaning intending righteousness, repentance from sin, and sincerity in obedience, then what has occurred of the sin from which you have repented will not harm you. ﴿Indeed, He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back (to Him) in repentance﴾ (p-819), meaning those who return from sins to repentance, and from lack of sincerity to pure sincerity, forgiving what has passed from them of speech, deed, or belief. Whoever repents, Allah turns to him in repentance, and whoever returns to Allah, Allah returns to him.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the charge concerning relatives other than the parents, after the charge concerning the two of them, saying: ﴿And give the relative his right﴾. The address is either to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as an incitement and a kindling for others of the Ummah, or to everyone among the responsible who is fit for this, as in His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾. By "the relative" is meant the kinsman, and his right is the maintenance of kinship (silat al-rahim) which Allah commanded and repeated the charge concerning. The scholars differ over whether maintenance is obligatory for relatives, or for some of them, such as parents over children and children over parents, which is well known.

What should be relied upon is that it is obligatory to maintain them with what one's ability reaches and as the condition requires. And ﴿the needy﴾ is conjoined to "the relative," and in this conjunction is evidence that the intended "right" is the financial right. And ﴿the wayfarer﴾ is conjoined to "the needy." The meaning: give whoever is characterized by neediness, or by being a wayfarer, his right.

The reality of the needy and the wayfarer has already been explained in al-Baqarah and at-Tawbah.

What is intended in this verse is giving them charity with what one's ability reaches, of voluntary charity, or of what Allah has prescribed for them of obligatory charity, for they are among the eight categories who are the recipients of zakat.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, commanded what He commanded here, He forbade wastefulness, saying: ﴿And do not squander wastefully﴾. Tabdhir is scattering wealth as seed is scattered, however it falls, without deliberately choosing its places. It is the blameworthy extravagance, because it exceeds the limit that is praiseworthy in the law in spending, or it is spending in what is not right, even if it is little.

Al-Shafi'i said: Tabdhir is spending wealth in what is not its right, and there is no tabdhir in doing good.

Al-Qurtubi said after relating the saying of al-Shafi'i: This is the view of the majority.

Ashhab said, from Malik: Tabdhir is taking wealth from its right and placing it in what is not its right, and it is israf, and it is forbidden, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, the squanderers were brothers of the devils﴾. For this clause is a reason for the prohibition of tabdhir. By brotherhood is meant complete similarity, and avoiding similarity to the devil, even in one trait of his traits, is obligatory; how much more so in what is more general than that, as the generality of "similarity" indicates. And extravagance in spending is from the work of the devil, so when any son of Adam does it, he has obeyed the devil and followed him. ﴿And Satan has ever been to his Lord ungrateful﴾, meaning greatly disbelieving, exceedingly rebellious against the truth; because he, with his disbelief, does nothing but evil, commands nothing but evil, and whispers nothing but what has no good in it.

In this verse there is a branding of the squanderers with similarity to the devils, and then a branding of the species of devil as ungrateful. This requires that the squanderer is similar to the devil, and everyone similar to the devil has the ruling of the devil, and every devil is ungrateful; so the squanderer is ungrateful.

﴿And if you turn away from them﴾. It was mentioned shortly before that the origin of this "imma" is composed of the conditional "in" and the indefinite "ma," and that the entry of the emphatic nun on the condition is because it resembles the prohibition. That is: if you turn away from the relative, the needy, and the wayfarer because of a matter that compelled you to that turning away, ﴿seeking mercy from your Lord﴾, meaning for lack of provision from your Lord. But He placed the effect, which is seeking Allah's mercy, in the place of the cause, which is the lack of provision, because one who lacks provision is one who seeks it. The meaning: and if you turn away from them due to lack of provision from your Lord, hoping that Allah will open it to you, ﴿then speak to them a gentle word﴾, meaning an easy, soft word, like a good promise or an acceptable excuse.

Al-Kisa'i said: "Yassartu lahu al-qawl," meaning I made the speech soft for him.

Al-Farra' said: The meaning of the verse is: if you turn away from the petitioner due to poverty and inability, then speak to them a gentle word; promise them a good promise. It is also possible that the meaning is: if you turn away from them and do not benefit them because you lack the ability, then speak to them a gentle word; and what is intended here is not turning away with the face.

In this verse is Allah's instruction to His servants: when a petitioner asks them for what they do not have, how they should speak and with what they should reply. Indeed he spoke well who said:

"If there is no silver one day with which I can be generous to the askers, then I am a supple cane (lenient in character)."

"The askers never lack goodness from my disposition: either a gift, or a fair refusal."

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the etiquette of refusing after the prohibition of squandering, He clarified the etiquette of spending, saying: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it with complete extension﴾. This prohibition encompasses every responsible person, whether the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) as an allusion to his Ummah and as teaching them, or the address is to everyone among the responsible who is fit for it. The intent is the prohibition for a person to withhold in such a way that he constricts himself and his family, and not to expand in spending in an expansion for which there is no need, such that he becomes a spendthrift. So it is a prohibition against both extremes of excess and deficiency.

From this it is established that moderation is legislated, which is the justice that Allah has urged:

"Do not be in it excessive or deficient; both extremes of the way of purpose are blameworthy."
