Al-Zajjaj said: Everything that Allah has commanded and forbidden is part of the covenant, so it includes what is between the servant and his Lord, and what is between the servants among themselves.

Fulfilling the covenant is carrying out its safeguarding in the legally prescribed manner and the approved rule, except when a specific proof indicates the permissibility of breaking it. ﴿Indeed, the covenant was ever questioned﴾, meaning, questioned about, so the one questioned here is its party. It was also said: the covenant is questioned in order to rebuke the one who breaks it.

﴿And give full measure when you measure﴾, meaning, complete the measure and do not make it deficient at the time you measure for people. ﴿And weigh with an even balance﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the balance of justice, meaning a balance that is one of the balances of dirhams and others. It has two dialects: with the qaf pronounced with a damma (al-qusṭās), and with a kasra (al-qisṭās). It was also said: it is the qabbān (steelyard) called al-qarsṭūn. It was also said: it is justice itself, and this is the language of the Romans. It was also said: it is a Syriac word.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr read (al-qusṭās) with a damma on the qaf.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read it with a kasra on the qaf. The reference in His words "that" points to giving full measure and weight. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "better", meaning: better for you with Allah and with people, from which good remembrance results and people are encouraged to deal with one who is like that. ﴿And better in outcome﴾, meaning better in final result, from ʾāla, when it means to return.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded the reform of the tongue and the heart, so He said: ﴿And do not follow that of which you have no knowledge﴾, meaning, do not follow what you do not know. From your saying qafawtu fulānan, when you follow his trail. From this comes qafiyat al-shi'r (the rhyme of poetry), because it follows every line, and from this comes the well-known tribe called al-Qafa, because they follow the traces of people's footprints.

Ibn Jarir related from a group that they said: qafa and qāfa are like ʿathā and ʿāna (both meaning to go about in a corrupt way).

Mundhir ibn Sa'id al-Ballūṭī said: qafa and qāfa are like jadhaba and jabadha (both meaning to pull).

Al-Kisa'i related from some readers that he read (taqfu) with a damma on the qaf and a sukun on the fa'.

Al-Farra' read it with a fatha on the qaf, and this is a dialect of some Arabs, but Abu Hatim and others denied it.

The meaning of the verse: the prohibition against a person saying what he does not know, or acting on what he has no knowledge of. This is a universal principle. Some exegetes made it specific to certain matters: it was said, do not blame anyone for what you have no knowledge of; it was said, it refers to false testimony; it was said, it refers to slander.

Al-Qutaybi said: the meaning of the verse is: do not follow conjecture and assumptions. This is correct, for what is other than that is knowledge. It was also said: what is meant here by knowledge is firm belief derived from a basis, whether that basis is definitive or speculative.

Abu al-Su'ud said in his tafsir: using it in this meaning is something whose prevalence cannot be denied.

I say: this verse indicates the impermissibility of acting on what is not knowledge. However, it is general and specified by the texts that permit acting on conjecture, such as acting on a general (ʿāmm) text, on the report of a single narrator (khabar al-wāḥid), acting on testimony, ijtihad in the direction of the qiblah, in the compensation for game hunted while in the state of ihram, and similar matters. So it is not excluded from its generality, nor from the generality of ﴿Indeed, assumption does not avail against the truth at all﴾, except what has a proof for the permissibility of acting upon it. So acting on personal opinion (ra'y) in matters of the sharia, if it is due to the absence of a proof in the Book and the Sunnah, then the Prophet (ﷺ) granted leniency in it, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Mu'adh when he sent him as a judge: (By what will you judge? He said: by the Book of Allah. He said: And if you do not find it? He said: then by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah. He said: And if you do not find it? He said: I will strive with my opinion.) This is a hadith suitable to be used as evidence, as we explained in a separate study.

As for hastening to opinion while there is a proof in the Book or the Sunnah, but the holder of opinion fell short of searching and came with his opinion, then it falls under this prohibition at the first level, because it is pure opinion regarding the sharia of Allah, and people have no need of it, since they have the Book of Allah, glorified is He, and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ), and no need called for it. Moreover, the leniency regarding opinion when no proof exists is only a concession for the mujtahid, that it is permissible for him to act upon it. No proof indicates that it is permissible for others to act upon it and to place it in the position of the matters of the sharia. By this it becomes clear to you in the fullest clarity, and it appears to you in the most complete manifestation, that these opinions recorded in the books of positive law (furu') are not from the sharia at all, and the one who acts upon them is on the edge of a crumbling precipice. So the mujtahid who multiplies opinion has followed what he has no knowledge of, and the poor muqallid (imitator) who acts upon the opinion of that mujtahid has acted upon what he has no knowledge of, nor does the one he imitates. ﴿Darknesses, some above others﴾. It has been said that this verse is specific to matters of belief, but there is no proof for that at all.

Then Allah, glorified is He, gave the reason for the prohibition of acting on what is not known, by His words: ﴿Indeed, the hearing and the sight and the heart, all of those will be questioned about﴾. This refers to the three organs. They were treated as rational beings because they are questioned about their states and bear witness against their owners.

Al-Zajjaj said: the Arabs express by "those" (ulā'ika) both what has reason and what does not have reason. Ibn Jarir cited as evidence for the permissibility of this the words of a poet:

"He blamed the dwellings after the abode of al-Liwa, and life after those days."

It was objected that the narration is "after those people (al-aqwām)", and others followed this error, like the author of al-Kashshaf.

The pronoun in (kāna) in His words ﴿was questioned﴾ refers to (kull), and likewise the pronoun in (ʿanhu). It was also said: the pronoun in (kāna) refers to the one who follows, which is implied by His words ﴿and do not follow﴾.

His words "ʿanhu" (about it) are in the position of nominative, since the predicate (musʾūlan) is attributed to it. This was refuted by what al-Nahhas related as a consensus on the impermissibility of placing the deputy of the subject first when it is a prepositional phrase or a genitive.

It was said: the better view is that the subject of (musʾūlan) is an elided pronoun, and what is mentioned explains it.

The meaning of questioning these limbs is that the owner will be asked about what he used them for, because they are instruments, and the one who uses them is the human soul. If he uses them for good, he deserves reward, and if he uses them for evil, he deserves punishment.

It was also said: Allah, glorified is He, will make these limbs speak when they are questioned, and they will tell of what their owner did.

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾. Al-maraḥ: it was said it is intense joy. It was said: arrogance in walking. It was said: a person exceeding his limit. It was said: vanity in walking. It was said: insolence and haughtiness. It was said: vigor.

The apparent meaning here is vanity and boasting. Al-Zajjaj said in explaining the verse: do not walk on the earth in self-admiration, boastful. He mentioned "the earth" even though walking happens only upon it or upon what rests upon it, for emphasis and affirmation. And well did the one who said:

"Do not walk above the earth except in humility, for beneath it are people who are higher than you.
And even if you are in might, safety, and protection, how many people have died who were stronger than you."

Al-maraḥ is a verbal noun used as a state (ḥāl), meaning: possessing exultation. Placing the verbal noun in the place of an adjective contains a kind of emphasis.

The majority read (maraḥan) with a fatha on the ra' as a verbal noun. Ya'qub related from a group that they read it with a kasra, as an active participle.

Then Allah, glorified is He, gave the reason for this prohibition, so He said: ﴿Indeed, you will never tear through the earth﴾. One says "kharaqa al-thawb", meaning he tore it. And "kharaqa al-arḍ" means he cut through it. Al-khark is the wide part of the earth. The meaning: you will never tear through the earth by your walking upon it in arrogance. This contains mockery of the arrogant, self-important one. ﴿And you will never reach the mountains in height﴾, meaning: your power will never reach the point of rivaling the mountains, so that the bulk of your body would carry you to pride and vanity. So you have no strength to tear through the earth by walking upon it, and no greatness in your body to rival the mountains. Then what is it that moves you to what you are engaged in?

(Ṭūlan) is a verbal noun in the position of a state, or a specification, or an object of purpose.

It was also said: what is meant by tearing the earth is piercing it, not cutting it by distance.

Al-Azhari said: kharaqahā means qaṭaʿahā (cut it).

Al-Nahhas said: this is clearer, as if it were derived from al-khark, which is a wide opening. One says: Fulan is more "akhraq" than Fulan, meaning he travels more.

The reference in His words "all of that" is to all that has been mentioned of the commands and prohibitions, or to what He forbade only, from His words ﴿and do not follow﴾ and ﴿do not walk﴾. ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Masruq read (sayyi'uhu) with the adjective sayyi' attached to the pronoun. This reading is supported by His words ﴿disliked﴾, for the bad (sayyi') is the disliked (makrūh). It is also supported by the reading of Ubayy: (kāna sayyi'ātuhu). Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu 'Amr read (sayyi'atan) as the singular of the bad deeds, its accusative placed as the predicate of (kāna), and (makrūhan) is an adjective of (sayyi'atan) by meaning, for it means "bad". Or it is a substitute for (sayyi'atan). It was also said: it is a second predicate of (kāna), taken according to the wording of (kull). Abu 'Ali al-Farisi preferred the substitution, and it has been said regarding its explanation other things that involve strain, which is not hidden.

Al-Zajjaj said: the attachment is better, because the verses that preceded contain what is bad and what is good. So its bad is the disliked, and this strengthens the masculine form in (makrūh). He said: and whoever read with tanwin made "all that" an encompassing of what is forbidden, not of what is good. The meaning: everything that Allah forbade was a bad deed and was disliked. He said: and the disliked, in this reading, is a substitute for the bad deed and not an adjective. The disliked before Allah is that which He hates and does not approve, not that it is not willed absolutely, because the decisive proofs establish that things occur by His will, glorified is He. He mentioned absolute dislike even though among the matters mentioned previously are some major sins, as an indication that mere dislike before the Most High necessitates the listener's restraint and avoidance of it.

The summary: among the characteristics mentioned previously there are what is good, which is what is commanded, and what is disliked, which is what is forbidden. So according to the reading of attachment, the reference is to the prohibited matters, and then the report about these prohibited matters is that they are bad and disliked in that sight.

﴿That is among what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom﴾. The reference is to what was mentioned before, from His words ﴿do not make﴾, to this end, and it ascends to twenty-five obligations. ﴿Among what your Lord has revealed to you﴾, meaning: of its kind or part of it. It is called wisdom because it is a firm (muḥkam) speech, which is what He taught of the laws or of the firm rulings that fall into no corruption.

With the philosophers, wisdom is an expression for knowing the truth for its own sake. The phrase ﴿of wisdom﴾ is attached to an elided verb that occurs as a state, meaning: existing from wisdom; or it is a substitute for the relative pronoun with the preposition repeated; or it is attached to "revealed".

﴿And do not make with Allah another god﴾. Allah, glorified is He, repeated the prohibition of association (shirk) for emphasis, affirmation, and as an alert that it is the head of the characteristics of the religion and its foundation.

It has been said that He, glorified is He, observed a subtle point in this emphasis. He made the first of the two statements result in his being blameworthy and forsaken, which alludes to his state of polytheism in this world. He made the second result in his being cast ﴿into Hell, blameworthy and rejected﴾, which alludes to his state in the Hereafter. The mention of "sitting" there and "casting" here alludes to the fact that a person has the appearance of choice in this world, unlike in the Hereafter. The explanation of "blameworthy" (malum) and "rejected" (madhur) has already been given.

﴿Has your Lord then favoured you with sons, and taken for Himself daughters from among the angels?﴾ Abu 'Ubaydah said: asfakum means khassakum (He singled you out). al-Fadl said: akhlasakum (He chose you exclusively). This is an address to the disbelievers who claimed that the angels are the daughters of God. It contains severe rebuke and a forceful reproof of what these people, who are like cattle, nay, even more astray, were saying. The fa' (then) is a conjunction with an implied prior clause, as with its counterparts that we have mentioned repeatedly. ﴿Indeed you utter a monstrous saying﴾, meaning those who claim that they have the males and God has the females, ﴿a monstrous saying﴾, grave in its enormity and in its audacity against God, to a degree whose extent cannot be measured.

﴿And We have indeed varied in this Qur'an﴾, that is, We have explained the various kinds of speech in it, such as parables and other things, or We have repeated in it. It has also been said that fi (in) is superfluous, and the sense is: "And We have indeed varied this Qur'an." Tasrif (variation) originally means turning a thing from one direction to another. It has also been said that the meaning of tasrif is diversity, i.e., We have varied the admonitions so that they might remember and take heed. The reading of the majority is ṣarrafnā (with shaddah on the rāʾ), while al-Ḥasan read it without shaddah. Then He, exalted is He, gave the reason for this, saying: ﴿that they may take heed﴾, that is, that they may be admonished, reflect with their minds, and ponder in it until they recognise the falsehood of what they say.

Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb, al-A'mash, Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read liyadhkurū (without shaddah on the dhāl), while the rest read it with shaddah (liyadhdhakkarū). Abu 'Ubayd preferred the latter because of the sense of intensification it conveys. The clause ﴿but it only increases them in aversion﴾ is in a position of accusative (naṣb) as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while this variation and admonition only increase them in distance from the truth and in heedlessness of reflecting on what is right, because they believe that the Qur'an is a trick, sorcery, soothsaying and poetry. They do not desist from this error, and there is no restraint to hold them back toward guidance.

Ibn Jarīr narrated from Qatādah, regarding His words ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾, that he said: "They would not mix with them in property, food or mounts, until it was revealed: ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, regarding His words ﴿Indeed the covenant was ever questioned﴾, that he said: "God questions the one who breaks the covenant about his breaking it."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj regarding the verse that he said: "He questions the one who gave the covenant to whom he gave it."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr regarding His words ﴿And give full measure when you measure out﴾, meaning to others, ﴿and weigh with a true balance﴾, meaning the scale. In Byzantine (Rūmī) language, the scale is called qisṭās. ﴿That is better and more favourable in outcome﴾, meaning that fulfilling the measure and the scale is better than shortfall, ﴿and better in result (taʾwīl)﴾, meaning in consequence.

Abu Shaybah, al-Firyābī, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Mujāhid that he said: "al-qisṭās is 'justice' in Byzantine (Rūmiyyah)."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Ḍaḥḥāk that he said: "al-qisṭās is the qabbān (steelyard)."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from al-Ḥasan that he said: "It is iron."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿And do not pursue (taqfu)﴾ that he said: "Do not say (lā taqul)."

Ibn Jarīr narrated from him that he said: "Do not accuse anyone of what you have no knowledge of."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah regarding the verse that he said: "It is false testimony."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from ʿIkrimah regarding His words ﴿Indeed the hearing, the sight and the heart, all of those will be questioned about﴾, that he said: "Their hearing, sight and heart will bear witness against him."

al-Firyābī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿all of those will be questioned about﴾ that he said: "Their hearing, sight and heart will bear witness against him."

al-Firyābī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿all of those will be questioned about﴾ that he said: "On the Day of Resurrection, [it will be said]: 'Was it so, or not?'"

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Qatādah regarding His words ﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾ that he said: "Do not walk in pride and arrogance, for that will not carry you to the mountains, nor will it let you split the earth with your pride and arrogance."

Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "Indeed the Torah is in fifteen verses from the Children of Israel," then he recited: ﴿And do not set up with God another god, lest you be cast into Hell, blameworthy and rejected﴾.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated, through the route of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His words "madḥūran" (rejected) that he said: "expelled (maṭrūdan)."

When Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the prohibition of destroying lives, He followed it with the prohibition of destroying property. The most important property to be guarded and protected is the wealth of the orphan, so He said: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾. The prohibition of approaching it is an emphatic form of the prohibition of directly handling it and destroying it. Then Allah, glorified is He, clarified that the prohibition of approaching it does not mean prohibiting handling it in ways that improve it or preserve it. Rather, it is permissible for the guardian of the orphan to do with the orphan's property what benefits it, and that necessarily involves handling it. So He said: ﴿except in the way that is best﴾, meaning, except by the best of the ways, which is to safeguard it, to seek profit from it, and to strive in what increases it.

Then He mentioned the limit of the prohibition on approaching the orphan's property, so He said: ﴿until he reaches his maturity﴾, meaning: do not approach it except in the best way, until the orphan reaches his maturity.

The majority read (maraḥan) with a fatha on the ra' as a verbal noun. Ya'qub related from a group that they read it with a kasra, as an active participle.

Then Allah, glorified is He, gave the reason for this prohibition, so He said: ﴿Indeed, you will never tear through the earth﴾. One says "kharaqa al-thawb", meaning he tore it. And "kharaqa al-arḍ" means he cut through it. Al-khark is the wide part of the earth. The meaning: you will never tear through the earth by your walking upon it in arrogance. This contains mockery of the arrogant, self-important one. ﴿And you will never reach the mountains in height﴾, meaning: your power will never reach the point of rivaling the mountains, so that the bulk of your body would carry you to pride and vanity. So you have no strength to tear through the earth by walking upon it, and no greatness in your body to rival the mountains. Then what is it that moves you to what you are engaged in?

(Ṭūlan) is a verbal noun in the position of a state, or a specification, or an object of purpose.

It was also said: what is meant by tearing the earth is piercing it, not cutting it by distance.

Al-Azhari said: kharaqahā means qaṭaʿahā (cut it).

Al-Nahhas said: this is clearer, as if it were derived from al-khark, which is a wide opening. One says: Fulan is more "akhraq" than Fulan, meaning he travels more.

The reference in His words "all of that" is to all that has been mentioned of the commands and prohibitions, or to what He forbade only, from His words ﴿and do not follow﴾ and ﴿do not walk﴾. ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Masruq read (sayyi'uhu) with the adjective sayyi' attached to the pronoun. This reading is supported by His words ﴿disliked﴾, for the bad (sayyi') is the disliked (makrūh). It is also supported by the reading of Ubayy: (kāna sayyi'ātuhu). Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu 'Amr read (sayyi'atan) as the singular of the bad deeds, its accusative placed as the predicate of (kāna), and (makrūhan) is an adjective of (sayyi'atan) by meaning, for it means "bad". Or it is a substitute for (sayyi'atan). It was also said: it is a second predicate of (kāna), taken according to the wording of (kull). Abu 'Ali al-Farisi preferred the substitution, and it has been said regarding its explanation other things that involve strain, which is not hidden.

Al-Zajjaj said: the attachment is better, because the verses that preceded contain what is bad and what is good. So its bad is the disliked, and this strengthens the masculine form in (makrūh). He said: and whoever read with tanwin made "all that" an encompassing of what is forbidden, not of what is good. The meaning: everything that Allah forbade was a bad deed and was disliked. He said: and the disliked, in this reading, is a substitute for the bad deed and not an adjective. The disliked before Allah is that which He hates and does not approve, not that it is not willed absolutely, because the decisive proofs establish that things occur by His will, glorified is He. He mentioned absolute dislike even though among the matters mentioned previously are some major sins, as an indication that mere dislike before the Most High necessitates the listener's restraint and avoidance of it.

The summary: among the characteristics mentioned previously there are what is good, which is what is commanded, and what is disliked, which is what is forbidden. So according to the reading of attachment, the reference is to the prohibited matters, and then the report about these prohibited matters is that they are bad and disliked in that sight.

﴿That is among what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom﴾. The reference is to what was mentioned before, from His words ﴿do not make﴾, to this end, and it ascends to twenty-five obligations. ﴿Among what your Lord has revealed to you﴾, meaning: of its kind or part of it. It is called wisdom because it is a firm (muḥkam) speech, which is what He taught of the laws or of the firm rulings that fall into no corruption.

With the philosophers, wisdom is an expression for knowing the truth for its own sake. The phrase ﴿of wisdom﴾ is attached to an elided verb that occurs as a state, meaning: existing from wisdom; or it is a substitute for the relative pronoun with the preposition repeated; or it is attached to "revealed".

﴿And do not make with Allah another god﴾. Allah, glorified is He, repeated the prohibition of association (shirk) for emphasis, affirmation, and as an alert that it is the head of the characteristics of the religion and its foundation.

It has been said that He, glorified is He, observed a subtle point in this emphasis. He made the first of the two statements result in his being blameworthy and forsaken, which alludes to his state of polytheism in this world. He made the second result in his being cast ﴿into Hell, blameworthy and rejected﴾, which alludes to his state in the Hereafter. The mention of "sitting" there and "casting" here alludes to the fact that a person has the appearance of choice in this world, unlike in the Hereafter. The explanation of "blameworthy" (malum) and "rejected" (madhur) has already been given.

﴿Has your Lord then favoured you with sons, and taken for Himself daughters from among the angels?﴾ Abu 'Ubaydah said: asfakum means khassakum (He singled you out). al-Fadl said: akhlasakum (He chose you exclusively). This is an address to the disbelievers who claimed that the angels are the daughters of God. It contains severe rebuke and a forceful reproof of what these people, who are like cattle, nay, even more astray, were saying. The fa' (then) is a conjunction with an implied prior clause, as with its counterparts that we have mentioned repeatedly. ﴿Indeed you utter a monstrous saying﴾, meaning those who claim that they have the males and God has the females, ﴿a monstrous saying﴾, grave in its enormity and in its audacity against God, to a degree whose extent cannot be measured.

﴿And We have indeed varied in this Qur'an﴾, that is, We have explained the various kinds of speech in it, such as parables and other things, or We have repeated in it. It has also been said that fi (in) is superfluous, and the sense is: "And We have indeed varied this Qur'an." Tasrif (variation) originally means turning a thing from one direction to another. It has also been said that the meaning of tasrif is diversity, i.e., We have varied the admonitions so that they might remember and take heed. The reading of the majority is ṣarrafnā (with shaddah on the rāʾ), while al-Ḥasan read it without shaddah. Then He, exalted is He, gave the reason for this, saying: ﴿that they may take heed﴾, that is, that they may be admonished, reflect with their minds, and ponder in it until they recognise the falsehood of what they say.

Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb, al-A'mash, Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read liyadhkurū (without shaddah on the dhāl), while the rest read it with shaddah (liyadhdhakkarū). Abu 'Ubayd preferred the latter because of the sense of intensification it conveys. The clause ﴿but it only increases them in aversion﴾ is in a position of accusative (naṣb) as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while this variation and admonition only increase them in distance from the truth and in heedlessness of reflecting on what is right, because they believe that the Qur'an is a trick, sorcery, soothsaying and poetry. They do not desist from this error, and there is no restraint to hold them back toward guidance.

Ibn Jarīr narrated from Qatādah, regarding His words ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾, that he said: "They would not mix with them in property, food or mounts, until it was revealed: ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, regarding His words ﴿Indeed the covenant was ever questioned﴾, that he said: "God questions the one who breaks the covenant about his breaking it."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj regarding the verse that he said: "He questions the one who gave the covenant to whom he gave it."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr regarding His words ﴿And give full measure when you measure out﴾, meaning to others, ﴿and weigh with a true balance﴾, meaning the scale. In Byzantine (Rūmī) language, the scale is called qisṭās. ﴿That is better and more favourable in outcome﴾, meaning that fulfilling the measure and the scale is better than shortfall, ﴿and better in result (taʾwīl)﴾, meaning in consequence.

Abu Shaybah, al-Firyābī, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Mujāhid that he said: "al-qisṭās is 'justice' in Byzantine (Rūmiyyah)."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Ḍaḥḥāk that he said: "al-qisṭās is the qabbān (steelyard)."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from al-Ḥasan that he said: "It is iron."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿And do not pursue (taqfu)﴾ that he said: "Do not say (lā taqul)."

Ibn Jarīr narrated from him that he said: "Do not accuse anyone of what you have no knowledge of."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah regarding the verse that he said: "It is false testimony."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from ʿIkrimah regarding His words ﴿Indeed the hearing, the sight and the heart, all of those will be questioned about﴾, that he said: "Their hearing, sight and heart will bear witness against him."

al-Firyābī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿all of those will be questioned about﴾ that he said: "Their hearing, sight and heart will bear witness against him."

al-Firyābī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿all of those will be questioned about﴾ that he said: "On the Day of Resurrection, [it will be said]: 'Was it so, or not?'"

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Qatādah regarding His words ﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾ that he said: "Do not walk in pride and arrogance, for that will not carry you to the mountains, nor will it let you split the earth with your pride and arrogance."

Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "Indeed the Torah is in fifteen verses from the Children of Israel," then he recited: ﴿And do not set up with God another god, lest you be cast into Hell, blameworthy and rejected﴾.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated, through the route of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His words "madḥūran" (rejected) that he said: "expelled (maṭrūdan)."

When Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the prohibition of destroying lives, He followed it with the prohibition of destroying property. The most important property to be guarded and protected is the wealth of the orphan, so He said: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾. The prohibition of approaching it is an emphatic form of the prohibition of directly handling it and destroying it. Then Allah, glorified is He, clarified that the prohibition of approaching it does not mean prohibiting handling it in ways that improve it or preserve it. Rather, it is permissible for the guardian of the orphan to do with the orphan's property what benefits it, and that necessarily involves handling it. So He said: ﴿except in the way that is best﴾, meaning, except by the best of the ways, which is to safeguard it, to seek profit from it, and to strive in what increases it.

Then He mentioned the limit of the prohibition on approaching the orphan's property, so He said: ﴿until he reaches his maturity﴾, meaning: do not approach it except in the best way, until the orphan reaches his maturity.

When he reaches his maturity, it becomes permissible for you to hand it over to him, or to dispose of it with his permission. The discussion of this has already preceded in detail in (surah) al-An'am. ﴿And fulfil the covenant﴾: the discussion of this has already passed in more than one place.

Al-Zajjaj said: Everything that Allah has commanded and forbidden is part of the covenant, so it includes what is between the servant and his Lord, and what is between the servants among themselves.

Fulfilling the covenant is carrying out its safeguarding in the legally prescribed manner and the approved rule, except when a specific proof indicates the permissibility of breaking it. ﴿Indeed, the covenant was ever questioned﴾, meaning, questioned about, so the one questioned here is its party. It was also said: the covenant is questioned in order to rebuke the one who breaks it.

﴿And give full measure when you measure﴾, meaning, complete the measure and do not make it deficient at the time you measure for people. ﴿And weigh with an even balance﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the balance of justice, meaning a balance that is one of the balances of dirhams and others. It has two dialects: with the qaf pronounced with a damma (al-qusṭās), and with a kasra (al-qisṭās). It was also said: it is the qabbān (steelyard) called al-qarsṭūn. It was also said: it is justice itself, and this is the language of the Romans. It was also said: it is a Syriac word.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr read (al-qusṭās) with a damma on the qaf.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read it with a kasra on the qaf. The reference in His words "that" points to giving full measure and weight. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "better", meaning: better for you with Allah and with people, from which good remembrance results and people are encouraged to deal with one who is like that. ﴿And better in outcome﴾, meaning better in final result, from ʾāla, when it means to return.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded the reform of the tongue and the heart, so He said: ﴿And do not follow that of which you have no knowledge﴾, meaning, do not follow what you do not know. From your saying qafawtu fulānan, when you follow his trail. From this comes qafiyat al-shi'r (the rhyme of poetry), because it follows every line, and from this comes the well-known tribe called al-Qafa, because they follow the traces of people's footprints.

Ibn Jarir related from a group that they said: qafa and qāfa are like ʿathā and ʿāna (both meaning to go about in a corrupt way).

Mundhir ibn Sa'id al-Ballūṭī said: qafa and qāfa are like jadhaba and jabadha (both meaning to pull).

Al-Kisa'i related from some readers that he read (taqfu) with a damma on the qaf and a sukun on the fa'.

Al-Farra' read it with a fatha on the qaf, and this is a dialect of some Arabs, but Abu Hatim and others denied it.

The meaning of the verse: the prohibition against a person saying what he does not know, or acting on what he has no knowledge of. This is a universal principle. Some exegetes made it specific to certain matters: it was said, do not blame anyone for what you have no knowledge of; it was said, it refers to false testimony; it was said, it refers to slander.

Al-Qutaybi said: the meaning of the verse is: do not follow conjecture and assumptions. This is correct, for what is other than that is knowledge. It was also said: what is meant here by knowledge is firm belief derived from a basis, whether that basis is definitive or speculative.

Abu al-Su'ud said in his tafsir: using it in this meaning is something whose prevalence cannot be denied.

I say: this verse indicates the impermissibility of acting on what is not knowledge. However, it is general and specified by the texts that permit acting on conjecture, such as acting on a general (ʿāmm) text, on the report of a single narrator (khabar al-wāḥid), acting on testimony, ijtihad in the direction of the qiblah, in the compensation for game hunted while in the state of ihram, and similar matters. So it is not excluded from its generality, nor from the generality of ﴿Indeed, assumption does not avail against the truth at all﴾, except what has a proof for the permissibility of acting upon it. So acting on personal opinion (ra'y) in matters of the sharia, if it is due to the absence of a proof in the Book and the Sunnah, then the Prophet (ﷺ) granted leniency in it, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Mu'adh when he sent him as a judge: (By what will you judge? He said: by the Book of Allah. He said: And if you do not find it? He said: then by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah. He said: And if you do not find it? He said: I will strive with my opinion.) This is a hadith suitable to be used as evidence, as we explained in a separate study.

As for hastening to opinion while there is a proof in the Book or the Sunnah, but the holder of opinion fell short of searching and came with his opinion, then it falls under this prohibition at the first level, because it is pure opinion regarding the sharia of Allah, and people have no need of it, since they have the Book of Allah, glorified is He, and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ), and no need called for it. Moreover, the leniency regarding opinion when no proof exists is only a concession for the mujtahid, that it is permissible for him to act upon it. No proof indicates that it is permissible for others to act upon it and to place it in the position of the matters of the sharia. By this it becomes clear to you in the fullest clarity, and it appears to you in the most complete manifestation, that these opinions recorded in the books of positive law (furu') are not from the sharia at all, and the one who acts upon them is on the edge of a crumbling precipice. So the mujtahid who multiplies opinion has followed what he has no knowledge of, and the poor muqallid (imitator) who acts upon the opinion of that mujtahid has acted upon what he has no knowledge of, nor does the one he imitates. ﴿Darknesses, some above others﴾. It has been said that this verse is specific to matters of belief, but there is no proof for that at all.

Then Allah, glorified is He, gave the reason for the prohibition of acting on what is not known, by His words: ﴿Indeed, the hearing and the sight and the heart, all of those will be questioned about﴾. This refers to the three organs. They were treated as rational beings because they are questioned about their states and bear witness against their owners.

Al-Zajjaj said: the Arabs express by "those" (ulā'ika) both what has reason and what does not have reason. Ibn Jarir cited as evidence for the permissibility of this the words of a poet:

"He blamed the dwellings after the abode of al-Liwa, and life after those days."

It was objected that the narration is "after those people (al-aqwām)", and others followed this error, like the author of al-Kashshaf.

The pronoun in (kāna) in His words ﴿was questioned﴾ refers to (kull), and likewise the pronoun in (ʿanhu). It was also said: the pronoun in (kāna) refers to the one who follows, which is implied by His words ﴿and do not follow﴾.

His words "ʿanhu" (about it) are in the position of nominative, since the predicate (musʾūlan) is attributed to it. This was refuted by what al-Nahhas related as a consensus on the impermissibility of placing the deputy of the subject first when it is a prepositional phrase or a genitive.

It was said: the better view is that the subject of (musʾūlan) is an elided pronoun, and what is mentioned explains it.

The meaning of questioning these limbs is that the owner will be asked about what he used them for, because they are instruments, and the one who uses them is the human soul. If he uses them for good, he deserves reward, and if he uses them for evil, he deserves punishment.

It was also said: Allah, glorified is He, will make these limbs speak when they are questioned, and they will tell of what their owner did.

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾. Al-maraḥ: it was said it is intense joy. It was said: arrogance in walking. It was said: a person exceeding his limit. It was said: vanity in walking. It was said: insolence and haughtiness. It was said: vigor.

The apparent meaning here is vanity and boasting. Al-Zajjaj said in explaining the verse: do not walk on the earth in self-admiration, boastful. He mentioned "the earth" even though walking happens only upon it or upon what rests upon it, for emphasis and affirmation. And well did the one who said:

"Do not walk above the earth except in humility, for beneath it are people who are higher than you.
And even if you are in might, safety, and protection, how many people have died who were stronger than you."

This contains mockery of the arrogant, self-important one. ﴿And you will never reach the mountains in height﴾, meaning: your power will never reach the point of rivaling the mountains, so that the bulk of your body would carry you to pride and vanity. Abu Shaybah, al-Firyābī, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Mujāhid that he said: "al-qisṭās is 'justice' in Byzantine (Rūmiyyah)."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Ḍaḥḥāk that he said: "al-qisṭās is the qabbān (steelyard)."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from al-Ḥasan that he said: "It is iron."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿And do not pursue (taqfu)﴾ that he said: "Do not say (lā taqul)."

Ibn Jarīr narrated from him that he said: "Do not accuse anyone of what you have no knowledge of."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah regarding the verse that he said: "It is false testimony."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from ʿIkrimah regarding His words ﴿Indeed the hearing, the sight and the heart, all of those will be questioned about﴾, that he said: "Their hearing, sight and heart will bear witness against him."

al-Firyābī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿all of those will be questioned about﴾ that he said: "Their hearing, sight and heart will bear witness against him."

al-Firyābī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿all of those will be questioned about﴾ that he said: "On the Day of Resurrection, [it will be said]: 'Was it so, or not?'"

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Qatādah regarding His words ﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾ that he said: "Do not walk in pride and arrogance, for that will not carry you to the mountains, nor will it let you split the earth with your pride and arrogance."

Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "Indeed the Torah is in fifteen verses from the Children of Israel," then he recited: ﴿And do not set up with God another god, lest you be cast into Hell, blameworthy and rejected﴾.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated, through the route of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His words "madḥūran" (rejected) that he said: "expelled (maṭrūdan)."

When Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the prohibition of destroying lives, He followed it with the prohibition of destroying property. The most important property to be guarded and protected is the wealth of the orphan, so He said: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾. The prohibition of approaching it is an emphatic form of the prohibition of directly handling it and destroying it. Then Allah, glorified is He, clarified that the prohibition of approaching it does not mean prohibiting handling it in ways that improve it or preserve it. Rather, it is permissible for the guardian of the orphan to do with the orphan's property what benefits it, and that necessarily involves handling it. So He said: ﴿except in the way that is best﴾, meaning, except by the best of the ways, which is to safeguard it, to seek profit from it, and to strive in what increases it.

Then He mentioned the limit of the prohibition on approaching the orphan's property, so He said: ﴿until he reaches his maturity﴾, meaning: do not approach it except in the best way, until the orphan reaches his maturity.

When he reaches his maturity, it becomes permissible for you to hand it over to him, or to dispose of it with his permission. The discussion of this has already preceded in detail in (surah) al-An'am. ﴿And fulfil the covenant﴾: the discussion of this has already passed in more than one place.

Al-Zajjaj said: Everything that Allah has commanded and forbidden is part of the covenant, so it includes what is between the servant and his Lord, and what is between the servants among themselves.

Fulfilling the covenant is carrying out its safeguarding in the legally prescribed manner and the approved rule, except when a specific proof indicates the permissibility of breaking it. ﴿Indeed, the covenant was ever questioned﴾, meaning, questioned about, so the one questioned here is its party. It was also said: the covenant is questioned in order to rebuke the one who breaks it.

﴿And give full measure when you measure﴾, meaning, complete the measure and do not make it deficient at the time you measure for people. ﴿And weigh with an even balance﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the balance of justice, meaning a balance that is one of the balances of dirhams and others. It has two dialects: with the qaf pronounced with a damma (al-qusṭās), and with a kasra (al-qisṭās). It was also said: it is the qabbān (steelyard) called al-qarsṭūn. It was also said: it is justice itself, and this is the language of the Romans. It was also said: it is a Syriac word.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr read (al-qusṭās) with a damma on the qaf.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read it with a kasra on the qaf. The reference in His words "that" points to giving full measure and weight. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "better", meaning: better for you with Allah and with people, from which good remembrance results and people are encouraged to deal with one who is like that. ﴿And better in outcome﴾, meaning better in final result, from ʾāla, when it means to return.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded the reform of the tongue and the heart, so He said: ﴿And do not follow that of which you have no knowledge﴾, meaning, do not follow what you do not know. From your saying qafawtu fulānan, when you follow his trail. From this comes qafiyat al-shi'r (the rhyme of poetry), because it follows every line, and from this comes the well-known tribe called al-Qafa, because they follow the traces of people's footprints.

Ibn Jarir related from a group that they said: qafa and qāfa are like ʿathā and ʿāna (both meaning to go about in a corrupt way).

Mundhir ibn Sa'id al-Ballūṭī said: qafa and qāfa are like jadhaba and jabadha (both meaning to pull).

Al-Kisa'i related from some readers that he read (taqfu) with a damma on the qaf and a sukun on the fa'.

Al-Farra' read it with a fatha on the qaf, and this is a dialect of some Arabs, but Abu Hatim and others denied it.

The meaning of the verse: the prohibition against a person saying what he does not know, or acting on what he has no knowledge of. This is a universal principle. Some exegetes made it specific to certain matters: it was said, do not blame anyone for what you have no knowledge of; it was said, it refers to false testimony; it was said, it refers to slander.

Al-Qutaybi said: the meaning of the verse is: do not follow conjecture and assumptions. This is correct, for what is other than that is knowledge. It was also said: what is meant here by knowledge is firm belief derived from a basis, whether that basis is definitive or speculative.

Abu al-Su'ud said in his tafsir: using it in this meaning is something whose prevalence cannot be denied.

I say: this verse indicates the impermissibility of acting on what is not knowledge. However, it is general and specified by the texts that permit acting on conjecture, such as acting on a general (ʿāmm) text, on the report of a single narrator (khabar al-wāḥid), acting on testimony, ijtihad in the direction of the qiblah, in the compensation for game hunted while in the state of ihram, and similar matters. So it is not excluded from its generality, nor from the generality of ﴿Indeed, assumption does not avail against the truth at all﴾, except what has a proof for the permissibility of acting upon it. So acting on personal opinion (ra'y) in matters of the sharia, if it is due to the absence of a proof in the Book and the Sunnah, then the Prophet (ﷺ) granted leniency in it, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Mu'adh when he sent him as a judge: (By what will you judge? He said: by the Book of Allah. He said: And if you do not find it? He said: then by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah. He said: And if you do not find it? He said: I will strive with my opinion.) This is a hadith suitable to be used as evidence, as we explained in a separate study.

As for hastening to opinion while there is a proof in the Book or the Sunnah, but the holder of opinion fell short of searching and came with his opinion, then it falls under this prohibition at the first level, because it is pure opinion regarding the sharia of Allah, and people have no need of it, since they have the Book of Allah, glorified is He, and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ), and no need called for it. Moreover, the leniency regarding opinion when no proof exists is only a concession for the mujtahid, that it is permissible for him to act upon it. No proof indicates that it is permissible for others to act upon it and to place it in the position of the matters of the sharia. By this it becomes clear to you in the fullest clarity, and it appears to you in the most complete manifestation, that these opinions recorded in the books of positive law (furu') are not from the sharia at all, and the one who acts upon them is on the edge of a crumbling precipice. So the mujtahid who multiplies opinion has followed what he has no knowledge of, and the poor muqallid (imitator) who acts upon the opinion of that mujtahid has acted upon what he has no knowledge of, nor does the one he imitates. ﴿Darknesses, some above others﴾. It has been said that this verse is specific to matters of belief, but there is no proof for that at all.

Then Allah, glorified is He, gave the reason for the prohibition of acting on what is not known, by His words: ﴿Indeed, the hearing and the sight and the heart, all of those will be questioned about﴾. This refers to the three organs. They were treated as rational beings because they are questioned about their states and bear witness against their owners.

Al-Zajjaj said: the Arabs express by "those" (ulā'ika) both what has reason and what does not have reason. Ibn Jarir cited as evidence for the permissibility of this the words of a poet:

"He blamed the dwellings after the abode of al-Liwa, and life after those days."

It was objected that the narration is "after those people (al-aqwām)", and others followed this error, like the author of al-Kashshaf.

The pronoun in (kāna) in His words ﴿was questioned﴾ refers to (kull), and likewise the pronoun in (ʿanhu). It was also said: the pronoun in (kāna) refers to the one who follows, which is implied by His words ﴿and do not follow﴾.

His words "ʿanhu" (about it) are in the position of nominative, since the predicate (musʾūlan) is attributed to it. This was refuted by what al-Nahhas related as a consensus on the impermissibility of placing the deputy of the subject first when it is a prepositional phrase or a genitive.

It was said: the better view is that the subject of (musʾūlan) is an elided pronoun, and what is mentioned explains it.

The meaning of questioning these limbs is that the owner will be asked about what he used them for, because they are instruments, and the one who uses them is the human soul. If he uses them for good, he deserves reward, and if he uses them for evil, he deserves punishment.

It was also said: Allah, glorified is He, will make these limbs speak when they are questioned, and they will tell of what their owner did.

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾. Al-maraḥ: it was said it is intense joy. It was said: arrogance in walking. It was said: a person exceeding his limit. It was said: vanity in walking. It was said: insolence and haughtiness. It was said: vigor.

The apparent meaning here is vanity and boasting. Al-Zajjaj said in explaining the verse: do not walk on the earth in self-admiration, boastful. He mentioned "the earth" even though walking happens only upon it or upon what rests upon it, for emphasis and affirmation. And well did the one who said:

"Do not walk above the earth except in humility, for beneath it are people who are higher than you.
And even if you are in might, safety, and protection, how many people have died who were stronger than you."

Al-maraḥ is a verbal noun used as a state (ḥāl), meaning: possessing exultation. Placing the verbal noun in the place of an adjective contains a kind of emphasis.

The majority read (maraḥan) with a fatha on the ra' as a verbal noun. Ya'qub related from a group that they read it with a kasra, as an active participle.

Then Allah, glorified is He, gave the reason for this prohibition, so He said: ﴿Indeed, you will never tear through the earth﴾. One says "kharaqa al-thawb", meaning he tore it. And "kharaqa al-arḍ" means he cut through it. Al-khark is the wide part of the earth. The meaning: you will never tear through the earth by your walking upon it in arrogance. This contains mockery of the arrogant, self-important one. ﴿And you will never reach the mountains in height﴾, meaning: your power will never reach the point of rivaling the mountains, so that the bulk of your body would carry you to pride and vanity. So you have no strength to tear through the earth by walking upon it, and no greatness in your body to rival the mountains. Then what is it that moves you to what you are engaged in?

(Ṭūlan) is a verbal noun in the position of a state, or a specification, or an object of purpose.

It was also said: what is meant by tearing the earth is piercing it, not cutting it by distance.

Al-Azhari said: kharaqahā means qaṭaʿahā (cut it).

Al-Nahhas said: this is clearer, as if it were derived from al-khark, which is a wide opening. One says: Fulan is more "akhraq" than Fulan, meaning he travels more.

The reference in His words "all of that" is to all that has been mentioned of the commands and prohibitions, or to what He forbade only, from His words ﴿and do not follow﴾ and ﴿do not walk﴾. ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Masruq read (sayyi'uhu) with the adjective sayyi' attached to the pronoun. This reading is supported by His words ﴿disliked﴾, for the bad (sayyi') is the disliked (makrūh). It is also supported by the reading of Ubayy: (kāna sayyi'ātuhu). Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu 'Amr read (sayyi'atan) as the singular of the bad deeds, its accusative placed as the predicate of (kāna), and (makrūhan) is an adjective of (sayyi'atan) by meaning, for it means "bad". Or it is a substitute for (sayyi'atan). It was also said: it is a second predicate of (kāna), taken according to the wording of (kull). Abu 'Ali al-Farisi preferred the substitution, and it has been said regarding its explanation other things that involve strain, which is not hidden.

Al-Zajjaj said: the attachment is better, because the verses that preceded contain what is bad and what is good. So its bad is the disliked, and this strengthens the masculine form in (makrūh). He said: and whoever read with tanwin made "all that" an encompassing of what is forbidden, not of what is good. The meaning: everything that Allah forbade was a bad deed and was disliked. He said: and the disliked, in this reading, is a substitute for the bad deed and not an adjective. The disliked before Allah is that which He hates and does not approve, not that it is not willed absolutely, because the decisive proofs establish that things occur by His will, glorified is He. He mentioned absolute dislike even though among the matters mentioned previously are some major sins, as an indication that mere dislike before the Most High necessitates the listener's restraint and avoidance of it.

The summary: among the characteristics mentioned previously there are what is good, which is what is commanded, and what is disliked, which is what is forbidden. So according to the reading of attachment, the reference is to the prohibited matters, and then the report about these prohibited matters is that they are bad and disliked in that sight.

﴿That is among what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom﴾. The reference is to what was mentioned before, from His words ﴿do not make﴾, to this end, and it ascends to twenty-five obligations. ﴿Among what your Lord has revealed to you﴾, meaning: of its kind or part of it. It is called wisdom because it is a firm (muḥkam) speech, which is what He taught of the laws or of the firm rulings that fall into no corruption.

With the philosophers, wisdom is an expression for knowing the truth for its own sake. The phrase ﴿of wisdom﴾ is attached to an elided verb that occurs as a state, meaning: existing from wisdom; or it is a substitute for the relative pronoun with the preposition repeated; or it is attached to "revealed".

﴿And do not make with Allah another god﴾. Allah, glorified is He, repeated the prohibition of association (shirk) for emphasis, affirmation, and as an alert that it is the head of the characteristics of the religion and its foundation.

It has been said that He, glorified is He, observed a subtle point in this emphasis. He made the first of the two statements result in his being blameworthy and forsaken, which alludes to his state of polytheism in this world. He made the second result in his being cast ﴿into Hell, blameworthy and rejected﴾, which alludes to his state in the Hereafter. The mention of "sitting" there and "casting" here alludes to the fact that a person has the appearance of choice in this world, unlike in the Hereafter. The explanation of "blameworthy" (malum) and "rejected" (madhur) has already been given.

﴿Has your Lord then favoured you with sons, and taken for Himself daughters from among the angels?﴾ Abu 'Ubaydah said: asfakum means khassakum (He singled you out). al-Fadl said: akhlasakum (He chose you exclusively). This is an address to the disbelievers who claimed that the angels are the daughters of God. It contains severe rebuke and a forceful reproof of what these people, who are like cattle, nay, even more astray, were saying. The fa' (then) is a conjunction with an implied prior clause, as with its counterparts that we have mentioned repeatedly. ﴿Indeed you utter a monstrous saying﴾, meaning those who claim that they have the males and God has the females, ﴿a monstrous saying﴾, grave in its enormity and in its audacity against God, to a degree whose extent cannot be measured.

﴿And We have indeed varied in this Qur'an﴾, that is, We have explained the various kinds of speech in it, such as parables and other things, or We have repeated in it. It has also been said that fi (in) is superfluous, and the sense is: "And We have indeed varied this Qur'an." Tasrif (variation) originally means turning a thing from one direction to another. It has also been said that the meaning of tasrif is diversity, i.e., We have varied the admonitions so that they might remember and take heed. The reading of the majority is ṣarrafnā (with shaddah on the rāʾ), while al-Ḥasan read it without shaddah. Then He, exalted is He, gave the reason for this, saying: ﴿that they may take heed﴾, that is, that they may be admonished, reflect with their minds, and ponder in it until they recognise the falsehood of what they say.

Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb, al-A'mash, Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read liyadhkurū (without shaddah on the dhāl), while the rest read it with shaddah (liyadhdhakkarū). Abu 'Ubayd preferred the latter because of the sense of intensification it conveys. The clause ﴿but it only increases them in aversion﴾ is in a position of accusative (naṣb) as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while this variation and admonition only increase them in distance from the truth and in heedlessness of reflecting on what is right, because they believe that the Qur'an is a trick, sorcery, soothsaying and poetry. They do not desist from this error, and there is no restraint to hold them back toward guidance.
