He said: by the Book of Allah. He said: And if you do not find it? He said: then by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah. He said: And if you do not find it? He said: I will strive with my opinion.) This is a hadith suitable to be used as evidence, as we explained in a separate study.

As for hastening to opinion while there is a proof in the Book or the Sunnah, but the holder of opinion fell short of searching and came with his opinion, then it falls under this prohibition at the first level, because it is pure opinion regarding the sharia of Allah, and people have no need of it, since they have the Book of Allah, glorified is He, and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ), and no need called for it. Moreover, the leniency regarding opinion when no proof exists is only a concession for the mujtahid, that it is permissible for him to act upon it. No proof indicates that it is permissible for others to act upon it and to place it in the position of the matters of the sharia. By this it becomes clear to you in the fullest clarity, and it appears to you in the most complete manifestation, that these opinions recorded in the books of positive law (furu') are not from the sharia at all, and the one who acts upon them is on the edge of a crumbling precipice. So the mujtahid who multiplies opinion has followed what he has no knowledge of, and the poor muqallid (imitator) who acts upon the opinion of that mujtahid has acted upon what he has no knowledge of, nor does the one he imitates. ﴿Darknesses, some above others﴾. It has been said that this verse is specific to matters of belief, but there is no proof for that at all.

Then Allah, glorified is He, gave the reason for the prohibition of acting on what is not known, by His words: ﴿Indeed, the hearing and the sight and the heart, all of those will be questioned about﴾. This refers to the three organs. They were treated as rational beings because they are questioned about their states and bear witness against their owners.

Al-Zajjaj said: the Arabs express by "those" (ulā'ika) both what has reason and what does not have reason. Ibn Jarir cited as evidence for the permissibility of this the words of a poet:

"He blamed the dwellings after the abode of al-Liwa, and life after those days."

It was objected that the narration is "after those people (al-aqwām)", and others followed this error, like the author of al-Kashshaf.

The pronoun in (kāna) in His words ﴿was questioned﴾ refers to (kull), and likewise the pronoun in (ʿanhu). It was also said: the pronoun in (kāna) refers to the one who follows, which is implied by His words ﴿and do not follow﴾.

His words "ʿanhu" (about it) are in the position of nominative, since the predicate (musʾūlan) is attributed to it. This was refuted by what al-Nahhas related as a consensus on the impermissibility of placing the deputy of the subject first when it is a prepositional phrase or a genitive.

It was said: the better view is that the subject of (musʾūlan) is an elided pronoun, and what is mentioned explains it.

The meaning of questioning these limbs is that the owner will be asked about what he used them for, because they are instruments, and the one who uses them is the human soul. If he uses them for good, he deserves reward, and if he uses them for evil, he deserves punishment.

It was also said: Allah, glorified is He, will make these limbs speak when they are questioned, and they will tell of what their owner did.

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾. Al-maraḥ: it was said it is intense joy. It was said: arrogance in walking. It was said: a person exceeding his limit. It was said: vanity in walking. It was said: insolence and haughtiness. It was said: vigor.

The apparent meaning here is vanity and boasting. Al-Zajjaj said in explaining the verse: do not walk on the earth in self-admiration, boastful. He mentioned "the earth" even though walking happens only upon it or upon what rests upon it, for emphasis and affirmation. And well did the one who said:

"Do not walk above the earth except in humility, for beneath it are people who are higher than you.
And even if you are in might, safety, and protection, how many people have died who were stronger than you."

Al-maraḥ is a verbal noun used as a state (ḥāl), meaning: possessing exultation. Placing the verbal noun in the place of an adjective contains a kind of emphasis.

The majority read (maraḥan) with a fatha on the ra' as a verbal noun. Ya'qub related from a group that they read it with a kasra, as an active participle.

Then Allah, glorified is He, gave the reason for this prohibition, so He said: ﴿Indeed, you will never tear through the earth﴾. One says "kharaqa al-thawb", meaning he tore it. And "kharaqa al-arḍ" means he cut through it. Al-khark is the wide part of the earth. The meaning: you will never tear through the earth by your walking upon it in arrogance. This contains mockery of the arrogant, self-important one. ﴿And you will never reach the mountains in height﴾, meaning: your power will never reach the point of rivaling the mountains, so that the bulk of your body would carry you to pride and vanity. So you have no strength to tear through the earth by walking upon it, and no greatness in your body to rival the mountains. Then what is it that moves you to what you are engaged in?

(Ṭūlan) is a verbal noun in the position of a state, or a specification, or an object of purpose.

It was also said: what is meant by tearing the earth is piercing it, not cutting it by distance.

Al-Azhari said: kharaqahā means qaṭaʿahā (cut it).

Al-Nahhas said: this is clearer, as if it were derived from al-khark, which is a wide opening. One says: Fulan is more "akhraq" than Fulan, meaning he travels more.

The reference in His words "all of that" is to all that has been mentioned of the commands and prohibitions, or to what He forbade only, from His words ﴿and do not follow﴾ and ﴿do not walk﴾. ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Masruq read (sayyi'uhu) with the adjective sayyi' attached to the pronoun. This reading is supported by His words ﴿disliked﴾, for the bad (sayyi') is the disliked (makrūh). It is also supported by the reading of Ubayy: (kāna sayyi'ātuhu). Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu 'Amr read (sayyi'atan) as the singular of the bad deeds, its accusative placed as the predicate of (kāna), and (makrūhan) is an adjective of (sayyi'atan) by meaning, for it means "bad". Or it is a substitute for (sayyi'atan). It was also said: it is a second predicate of (kāna), taken according to the wording of (kull). Abu 'Ali al-Farisi preferred the substitution, and it has been said regarding its explanation other things that involve strain, which is not hidden.

Al-Zajjaj said: the attachment is better, because the verses that preceded contain what is bad and what is good. So its bad is the disliked, and this strengthens the masculine form in (makrūh). He said: and whoever read with tanwin made "all that" an encompassing of what is forbidden, not of what is good. The meaning: everything that Allah forbade was a bad deed and was disliked. He said: and the disliked, in this reading, is a substitute for the bad deed and not an adjective. The disliked before Allah is that which He hates and does not approve, not that it is not willed absolutely, because the decisive proofs establish that things occur by His will, glorified is He. He mentioned absolute dislike even though among the matters mentioned previously are some major sins, as an indication that mere dislike before the Most High necessitates the listener's restraint and avoidance of it.

The summary: among the characteristics mentioned previously there are what is good, which is what is commanded, and what is disliked, which is what is forbidden. So according to the reading of attachment, the reference is to the prohibited matters, and then the report about these prohibited matters is that they are bad and disliked in that sight.

﴿That is among what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom﴾. The reference is to what was mentioned before, from His words ﴿do not make﴾, to this end, and it ascends to twenty-five obligations. ﴿Among what your Lord has revealed to you﴾, meaning: of its kind or part of it. It is called wisdom because it is a firm (muḥkam) speech, which is what He taught of the laws or of the firm rulings that fall into no corruption.

With the philosophers, wisdom is an expression for knowing the truth for its own sake. The phrase ﴿of wisdom﴾ is attached to an elided verb that occurs as a state, meaning: existing from wisdom; or it is a substitute for the relative pronoun with the preposition repeated; or it is attached to "revealed".

﴿And do not make with Allah another god﴾. Allah, glorified is He, repeated the prohibition of association (shirk) for emphasis, affirmation, and as an alert that it is the head of the characteristics of the religion and its foundation.

It has been said that He, glorified is He, observed a subtle point in this emphasis. He made the first of the two statements result in his being blameworthy and forsaken, which alludes to his state of polytheism in this world. He made the second result in his being cast ﴿into Hell, blameworthy and rejected﴾, which alludes to his state in the Hereafter. The mention of "sitting" there and "casting" here alludes to the fact that a person has the appearance of choice in this world, unlike in the Hereafter. The explanation of "blameworthy" (malum) and "rejected" (madhur) has already been given.

﴿Has your Lord then favoured you with sons, and taken for Himself daughters from among the angels?﴾ Abu 'Ubaydah said: asfakum means khassakum (He singled you out). al-Fadl said: akhlasakum (He chose you exclusively). This is an address to the disbelievers who claimed that the angels are the daughters of God. It contains severe rebuke and a forceful reproof of what these people, who are like cattle, nay, even more astray, were saying. The fa' (then) is a conjunction with an implied prior clause, as with its counterparts that we have mentioned repeatedly. ﴿Indeed you utter a monstrous saying﴾, meaning those who claim that they have the males and God has the females, ﴿a monstrous saying﴾, grave in its enormity and in its audacity against God, to a degree whose extent cannot be measured.

﴿And We have indeed varied in this Qur'an﴾, that is, We have explained the various kinds of speech in it, such as parables and other things, or We have repeated in it. It has also been said that fi (in) is superfluous, and the sense is: "And We have indeed varied this Qur'an." Tasrif (variation) originally means turning a thing from one direction to another. It has also been said that the meaning of tasrif is diversity, i.e., We have varied the admonitions so that they might remember and take heed. The reading of the majority is ṣarrafnā (with shaddah on the rāʾ), while al-Ḥasan read it without shaddah. Then He, exalted is He, gave the reason for this, saying: ﴿that they may take heed﴾, that is, that they may be admonished, reflect with their minds, and ponder in it until they recognise the falsehood of what they say.

Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb, al-A'mash, Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read liyadhkurū (without shaddah on the dhāl), while the rest read it with shaddah (liyadhdhakkarū). Abu 'Ubayd preferred the latter because of the sense of intensification it conveys. The clause ﴿but it only increases them in aversion﴾ is in a position of accusative (naṣb) as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while this variation and admonition only increase them in distance from the truth and in heedlessness of reflecting on what is right, because they believe that the Qur'an is a trick, sorcery, soothsaying and poetry. They do not desist from this error, and there is no restraint to hold them back toward guidance.

Ibn Jarīr narrated from Qatādah, regarding His words ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾, that he said: "They would not mix with them in property, food or mounts, until it was revealed: ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, regarding His words ﴿Indeed the covenant was ever questioned﴾, that he said: "God questions the one who breaks the covenant about his breaking it."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj regarding the verse that he said: "He questions the one who gave the covenant to whom he gave it."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr regarding His words ﴿And give full measure when you measure out﴾, meaning to others, ﴿and weigh with a true balance﴾, meaning the scale. In Byzantine (Rūmī) language, the scale is called qisṭās. ﴿That is better and more favourable in outcome﴾, meaning that fulfilling the measure and the scale is better than shortfall, ﴿and better in result (taʾwīl)﴾, meaning in consequence.

Abu Shaybah, al-Firyābī, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Mujāhid that he said: "al-qisṭās is 'justice' in Byzantine (Rūmiyyah)."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Ḍaḥḥāk that he said: "al-qisṭās is the qabbān (steelyard)."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from al-Ḥasan that he said: "It is iron."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿And do not pursue (taqfu)﴾ that he said: "Do not say (lā taqul)."

Ibn Jarīr narrated from him that he said: "Do not accuse anyone of what you have no knowledge of."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah regarding the verse that he said: "It is false testimony."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from ʿIkrimah regarding His words ﴿Indeed the hearing, the sight and the heart, all of those will be questioned about﴾, that he said: "Their hearing, sight and heart will bear witness against him."

al-Firyābī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿all of those will be questioned about﴾ that he said: "Their hearing, sight and heart will bear witness against him."

al-Firyābī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿all of those will be questioned about﴾ that he said: "On the Day of Resurrection, [it will be said]: 'Was it so, or not?'"

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Qatādah regarding His words ﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾ that he said: "Do not walk in pride and arrogance, for that will not carry you to the mountains, nor will it let you split the earth with your pride and arrogance."

Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "Indeed the Torah is in fifteen verses from the Children of Israel," then he recited: ﴿And do not set up with God another god, lest you be cast into Hell, blameworthy and rejected﴾.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated, through the route of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His words "madḥūran" (rejected) that he said: "expelled (maṭrūdan)."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 17, verses 42–48 (part 1 of 2):**

.

His saying: ﴿Say: If there were gods with Him, as they say﴾. Ibn Kathir and Hafs read *yaqulun* (they say) with a yaʾ (third person), while the rest read it with a taʾ (second person, addressing those who say that there are other gods with God). *Idhan* (then) is the answer to their false statement and the apodosis (*jaza'*) of *law* (if): ﴿they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾, and He is Allah, exalted be He, [seeking] a way, meaning a means of contention and resistance, as kings do with one another in fighting and struggle. It has also been said that the meaning is: then the gods would have sought nearness and closeness to Allah with Him, since they are below Him, and the polytheists only believed that they would bring them closer to Allah.

The first meaning is the apparent one, and similar in meaning is His saying: ﴿If there were in them [the heavens and the earth] gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted﴾.

Then the Exalted purified Himself, and said, exalted be He. *Tasbih* (glorification) means declaring Him free of imperfection, and it has already been discussed. And He is exalted, far removed from what they say of shameful statements and great slander. *ʿUluwwan* means "exaltedly", i.e. *taʿaliyan* (exaltation), but He placed *al-ʿuluww* (height) in the place of *al-taʿaali* (exaltation), as in His saying: ﴿And Allah has brought you forth from the earth as a growth﴾. Then He described the height as greatness, as an intensification of transcendence, and as an indication that between what is necessary in itself and what is contingent in itself, and between the absolutely self-sufficient and the absolutely needy, there is a separation beyond which no addition can be conceived.

Then, exalted be He, He clarified the majesty of His dominion and the greatness of His sovereignty, and said: ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them glorify Him﴾. *Yusabbihu* is read with a yaʾ (third person), and also with a taʾ. He said *fihinna* (in them) with the pronoun for rational beings, because He attributed to them the glorification which is the act of rational beings. Allah, exalted be He, has informed us about the heavens and the earth that they glorify Him, and likewise whoever is in them of His creatures who have intellects, namely the angels, mankind, jinn, and others, as well as the things which do not have intellect. Then He increased this in generality and emphasis, and said: ﴿There is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾. Thus it includes everything that is called a thing, whatever it may be. It has also been said that His saying "and whoever is in them" is to be understood as referring to the angels and the two weighty creatures (jinn and mankind), and that His saying "there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise" is to be understood as referring to what is other than that among the creatures.

The people of knowledge have differed regarding this generality: is it specified or not? One group said: it is not specified, and they understood the glorification as glorification of indication (*dalala*), because every creature bears witness to itself and indicates to others that Allah is the Creator, the Powerful.

Another group said: this glorification is in its literal sense, and the generality is on its apparent meaning.

What is meant is that all creatures glorify Allah, exalted be He, with this glorification whose meaning is declaring Him free of imperfection, even if human beings do not hear that or understand it. This is supported by His saying: ﴿But you do not understand their glorification﴾, for if the intended meaning were the glorification of indication, it would be a matter understood by everyone.

It is answered that what is meant by His saying "you do not understand" are the disbelievers who turn away from consideration.

Another group said: this generality is specified to the angels and the two weighty creatures, excluding inanimate things. It has also been said that it is specific to growing bodies, so plants are included, as this view has been reported from ʿIkrima and al-Hasan. They restricted the glorification of plants to the time of their growth, not after they have been cut. It has been used as evidence for this the hadith (report) that "the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by two graves, and in it [the report]: then he called for a fresh palm frond, split it in two, and said: Indeed, the punishment is lightened for them so long as they have not dried out." The verse is supported in its generality by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] with him in the evening and at sunrise﴾, and His saying: ﴿And indeed among them is that which descends out of fear of Allah﴾, and His saying: ﴿And the mountains crumble to dust﴾, and similar verses. It is also established in the authentic collections that they "used to hear the glorification of food while they were eating with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)". Likewise is the hadith of the trunk of the palm tree moaning, and the hadith that a stone in Makkah used to greet the Prophet (ﷺ). All of these are in the authentic collections. Among them is the glorification of pebbles in the palm of his hand (ﷺ).

Repelling the generality of this verse by mere considerations of improbability is not the practice of one who believes in Allah, exalted be He, and believes in what has come from Him.

The meaning of ﴿except that it glorifies Him with His praise﴾ is: except that it glorifies while being clothed in His praise. ﴿But you do not understand their glorification﴾.

Al-Hasan, Abu ʿAmr, Yaʿqub, Hafs, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *tusabbihu* (glorify) with a taʾ, addressing the audience (second person). The rest read it with a yaʾ. Abu ʿUbayd preferred this reading.

*Innahu kana halīman ghafūran* (Indeed He is ever Forbearing, Forgiving): from His forbearance is granting you respite and not sending His punishment upon you; and from His forgiveness toward you is that He does not take to account whoever among you repents.

When He, exalted be He, finished with the matters of divinity, He began to mention some of the verses of the Qur'an and what happens to those who hear them. So He said: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier﴾. We place between you, O Muhammad, and the polytheists who do not believe in the Hereafter a barrier, i.e. because of their aversion from your recitation and their heedlessness toward you, it is as if there were a barrier between you and them: they pass by you and do not see you. This meaning was mentioned by al-Zajjaj and others. The meaning of *mastur* (hidden) is "concealing" (*satir*).

Al-Akhfash said: he intended "concealing" (*satir*), and the active participle may take the form of the passive participle, as you say: "Indeed you are *mashʾum* (ill-omened) and *maymun* (blessed)", whereas the original forms are *shaʾim* and *yamin*. It has also been said: the meaning of *mastur* is "possessing a covering", like their saying "a *mufʿam* torrent", i.e. one possessing abundance. It has also been said: it is a barrier which eyes cannot see, so it is hidden from them. It has also been said: it is a barrier behind which is another barrier, so it is hidden by something else. It has also been said: what is meant by the hidden barrier is the seal and the covering of nature.

﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾. *Akinna* (coverings) is the plural of *kinan* (covering). Its explanation has already been given in al-Anʿam. It has also been said that this is a relating of what they used to say, namely their saying: "Our hearts are uncovered" ﴿and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a barrier﴾. *An yafqahuhu* (that they understand it) is a purpose clause (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*): i.e. out of aversion to their understanding it, or lest they understand it, i.e. lest they comprehend what it contains of commands, prohibitions, wisdoms and meanings. ﴿And in their ears a deafness﴾, i.e. deafness and heaviness. In the sentence there is an omission, and the sense is: if they hear it.

Among the ugly qualities of the polytheists is that they loved for their gods to be mentioned as Allah, exalted be He, is mentioned. So when they heard the mention of Allah without the mention of their gods, they fled from the assembly. For this reason Allah said: ﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an﴾, i.e. singly, not joined with the mention of their gods. It is a verbal noun (*masdar*) placed in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*). ﴿They turn back on their backs in aversion﴾. *Nufur* is a verbal noun, and the sense is: they fled in flight, or they fled in aversion. It has also been said that it is the plural of *nafir* (fleeing), like *qaʿid* and *quʿud*.

The first is preferable. The verbal noun may also be in the position of a circumstantial accusative, i.e. they turned back fleeing.

﴿We know best what they listen to when they listen to you﴾, i.e. they listen to you while occupied with it, namely mockery of you and of the Qur'an, and idle talk about your mention of your Lord alone. It has also been said: the *ba'* (with) is extra, and the adverbial clause in ﴿when they listen to you﴾ is connected to *aʿlam* (best knows), i.e. We know best the time when they listen to you, and what they listen to with it. In this there is an emphasis of the threat. His saying ﴿and when they are in private consultation﴾ is also connected to *aʿlam*, i.e. and We know best what they confer about among themselves at the time of their private consultation. They used to confer among themselves with denial and mockery. *Yaquluna* (they say) is a substitute for ﴿when they are in private consultation﴾.

﴿If you follow only a man bewitched﴾, i.e. each of them says to the others during their private consultation: you follow only a man who has been bewitched, so that his intellect has become confused and has departed from the limit of balance.

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: *al-maswur* is one whose intellect has gone and been corrupted, from their saying "food is *masur*" when its preparation has been spoiled, and "land is *masura*" when it has received more rain than it should and been ruined by it.

It has also been said: *al-masur* is one who has been deceived, because magic is a trick and deception, and that is because they claimed that Muhammad (ﷺ) was learning from some people, and they were deceiving him with that teaching.

Abu ʿUbayda said: the meaning of *masuran* is that he has a *sahr*, i.e. a lung, so he does not do without food and drink, and so he is like you. The Arabs say of a coward: "his *sahr* has swollen". Every human or other being that eats is *masur*, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*We were shown two places for an unseen matter, and we are nourished with food and with drink.*

i.e. we are nourished and sustained.

Ibn Qutayba said: I do not know what led him to this disliked interpretation, when the early scholars explained it in clear ways.

﴿See how they strike similitudes for you﴾, i.e. they said at one time that you are a soothsayer, at another a magician, at another a poet, and at another a madman, and they went astray from the path of correctness in all of that. ﴿So they cannot find a way﴾ to guidance, or to the criticism which intellects accept and to which assent is given; not the basis of criticism itself. They have done of it what they were able to do. It has also been said: they cannot find an exit, because of the contradiction in their speech, like their saying "a magician, a madman".

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Saʿid ibn Jubayr regarding His saying: ﴿Then they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾, that he said: "in order to remove His dominion."

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu Nuʿaym in *al-Hilya*, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* reported from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Qurt that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), on the night he was taken by night to the Farthest Mosque, had Jibril on his right and Mika'il on his left. He flew with him until he reached the high heavens. When he returned he said: I heard glorification from the high heavens along with much glorification: the high heavens glorified, out of awe of the Possessor of majesty, in fear before the Possessor of loftiness in what is exalted: Glory be to the Most High, the Exalted, glory be to Him and exalted be He."

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Anas that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said while sitting with his companions, when he heard a creaking, and said: The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak. By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, there is not a space of a hand's breadth in it except that there is on it the forehead of an angel prostrating, glorifying with His praise."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu'l-Shaykh in *al-ʿAzama* reported from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of a thing which Nuh commanded to his son? Indeed Nuh said to his son: O my son, I command you to say: Glory be to Allah, for it is the prayer of creation, the glorification of creatures, and by it creatures are provided for." Allah, exalted be He, said: ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾.

Ahmad and Ibn Mardawayh reported a similar report from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Umama who said: "No servant glorifies with a single glorification except that everything Allah has created glorifies [Allah] with it," and he said: ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾. Ibn Kathir said: its chain of narration has weakness in it.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Abu Hurayra who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "An ant bit one of the prophets, so he commanded that the ants' colony be burned, and Allah revealed to him: Because of one ant you burned a nation among the nations which glorify [Allah]."

al-Nasa'i, Abu'l-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAmr who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade killing the frog, and said: its croaking is glorification."

Abu'l-Shaykh in *al-ʿAzama* and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾, that he said: "The crop glorifies, and its reward belongs to its owner; and the garment glorifies, and the dirt says: If you are a believer, then wash me."

Abu'l-Shaykh reported from him that he said: "Everything glorifies except the dog and the donkey."

Ibn Rahawayh in his *Musnad* reported through the route of al-Zuhri who said: "Abu Bakr was brought a crow with its wings spread wide, and he began to spread its wings and say: No game is hunted and no tree is cut except because of the glorification it neglected."

Ahmad in *al-Zuhd* and Abu'l-Shaykh reported it from Maymun ibn Mihran who said: "Abu Bakr al-Siddiq came and mentioned it as his own saying, not as a raised report (*marfu'*)."

Abu Nuʿaym in *al-Hilya* and Ibn Mardawayh reported it from the hadith of Abu Hurayra with similar wording.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from the hadith of Ibn Masʿud with some of its meaning.

Abu'l-Shaykh reported from the hadith of Abu'l-Darda' with its meaning.

Ibn ʿAsakir reported from the hadith of Abu Ruhm something similar.

It was narrated by Ibn al-Mundhir from al-Hasan, who said: "This verse in the Torah is like about a thousand verses: ﴿And there is not a thing but it exalts [Allah] with His praise﴾. He said: In the Torah, the mountains glorify Him, and the trees glorify Him, and such-and-such glorifies Him, and such-and-such glorifies Him."

Ahmad and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Dawud (David) prayed one night until morning. When morning came, he found joy within himself, and a frog called out to him: 'O Dawud, I used to be more diligent than you, and you have just dozed off for a moment.'"

al-Bayhaqi narrated in al-Shuʿab from Sadaqah ibn Yasar, who said: "Dawud was in his prayer niche (mihrab) when he saw a small worm. He reflected on its creation and said: 'Allah does not care about the creation of this.' So Allah made it speak, and it said: 'O Dawud, does your self make you vain? I remember Allah and give thanks to Him more than you, for what Allah has given you.' Allah said: ﴿And there is not a thing but it exalts [Allah] with His praise﴾."

There are in this regard hadiths and reports from the early generations (al-salaf) that explicitly state the glorification of all created things.

Abu Yaʿla, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nuʿaym, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, who said: "When the verse ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ was revealed, Umm Jamil al-ʿAwraʾ came, wailing, with a stone in her hand, saying:

Dhammaman we disobey,
And his religion we despise,
And his command we disobey.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sitting with Abu Bakr beside him. Abu Bakr said: 'This woman has come, and I fear she will see you.' He (ﷺ) said: 'She will not see me.' He then recited a Qur'an with which he sought protection, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a concealed barrier﴾. So she came and stood over Abu Bakr, but did not see the Prophet (ﷺ). She said: 'O Abu Bakr, I have heard that your companion has satirized me.' Abu Bakr said: 'No, by the Lord of this House, he has not satirized you.' So she departed, saying: 'Quraysh knows that I am the daughter of their chief.'" This story has been narrated with different wordings.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a concealed barrier﴾, that he said: "The concealed barrier is coverings over their hearts, so that they do not understand it and do not benefit from it, because they obeyed the Shaytan, and he took possession of them."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Zuhayr ibn Muhammad regarding the verse, that he said: "That is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): when he recited the Qur'an to the polytheists in Makkah, they heard his recitation but did not see him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿They turn away in aversion﴾, that he said: "The shayatin (devils)."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿When they listen to you﴾, that he said: "ʿUtbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabiʿah, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il."

His saying: ﴿Say: If there were gods with Him, as they say﴾. Ibn Kathir and Hafs read *yaqulun* (they say) with a yaʾ (third person), while the rest read it with a taʾ (second person, addressing those who say that there are other gods with God). *Idhan* (then) is the answer to their false statement and the apodosis (*jaza'*) of *law* (if): ﴿they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾, and He is Allah, exalted be He, [seeking] a way, meaning a means of contention and resistance, as kings do with one another in fighting and struggle. It has also been said that the meaning is: then the gods would have sought nearness and closeness to Allah with Him, since they are below Him, and the polytheists only believed that they would bring them closer to Allah.

The first meaning is the apparent one, and similar in meaning is His saying: ﴿If there were in them [the heavens and the earth] gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted﴾.

Then the Exalted purified Himself, and said, exalted be He. *Tasbih* (glorification) means declaring Him free of imperfection, and it has already been discussed. And He is exalted, far removed from what they say of shameful statements and great slander. *ʿUluwwan* means "exaltedly", i.e. *taʿaliyan* (exaltation), but He placed *al-ʿuluww* (height) in the place of *al-taʿaali* (exaltation), as in His saying: ﴿And Allah has brought you forth from the earth as a growth﴾. Then He described the height as greatness, as an intensification of transcendence, and as an indication that between what is necessary in itself and what is contingent in itself, and between the absolutely self-sufficient and the absolutely needy, there is a separation beyond which no addition can be conceived.

Then, exalted be He, He clarified the majesty of His dominion and the greatness of His sovereignty, and said: ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them glorify Him﴾. *Yusabbihu* is read with a yaʾ (third person), and also with a taʾ. He said *fihinna* (in them) with the pronoun for rational beings, because He attributed to them the glorification which is the act of rational beings. Allah, exalted be He, has informed us about the heavens and the earth that they glorify Him, and likewise whoever is in them of His creatures who have intellects, namely the angels, mankind, jinn, and others, as well as the things which do not have intellect. Then He increased this in generality and emphasis, and said: ﴿There is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾. Thus it includes everything that is called a thing, whatever it may be. It has also been said that His saying "and whoever is in them" is to be understood as referring to the angels and the two weighty creatures (jinn and mankind), and that His saying "there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise" is to be understood as referring to what is other than that among the creatures.

The people of knowledge have differed regarding this generality: is it specified or not? One group said: it is not specified, and they understood the glorification as glorification of indication (*dalala*), because every creature bears witness to itself and indicates to others that Allah is the Creator, the Powerful.

Another group said: this glorification is in its literal sense, and the generality is on its apparent meaning.

What is meant is that all creatures glorify Allah, exalted be He, with this glorification whose meaning is declaring Him free of imperfection, even if human beings do not hear that or understand it. This is supported by His saying: ﴿But you do not understand their glorification﴾, for if the intended meaning were the glorification of indication, it would be a matter understood by everyone.

It is answered that what is meant by His saying "you do not understand" are the disbelievers who turn away from consideration.

Another group said: this generality is specified to the angels and the two weighty creatures, excluding inanimate things. It has also been said that it is specific to growing bodies, so plants are included, as this view has been reported from ʿIkrima and al-Hasan. They restricted the glorification of plants to the time of their growth, not after they have been cut. It has been used as evidence for this the hadith (report) that "the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by two graves, and in it [the report]: then he called for a fresh palm frond, split it in two, and said: Indeed, the punishment is lightened for them so long as they have not dried out." The verse is supported in its generality by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] with him in the evening and at sunrise﴾, and His saying: ﴿And indeed among them is that which descends out of fear of Allah﴾, and His saying: ﴿And the mountains crumble to dust﴾, and similar verses. It is also established in the authentic collections that they "used to hear the glorification of food while they were eating with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)". Likewise is the hadith of the trunk of the palm tree moaning, and the hadith that a stone in Makkah used to greet the Prophet (ﷺ). All of these are in the authentic collections. Among them is the glorification of pebbles in the palm of his hand (ﷺ).

Repelling the generality of this verse by mere considerations of improbability is not the practice of one who believes in Allah, exalted be He, and believes in what has come from Him.

The meaning of ﴿except that it glorifies Him with His praise﴾ is: except that it glorifies while being clothed in His praise. ﴿But you do not understand their glorification﴾.

Al-Hasan, Abu ʿAmr, Yaʿqub, Hafs, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *tusabbihu* (glorify) with a taʾ, addressing the audience (second person). The rest read it with a yaʾ. Abu ʿUbayd preferred this reading.

*Innahu kana halīman ghafūran* (Indeed He is ever Forbearing, Forgiving): from His forbearance is granting you respite and not sending His punishment upon you; and from His forgiveness toward you is that He does not take to account whoever among you repents.

When He, exalted be He, finished with the matters of divinity, He began to mention some of the verses of the Qur'an and what happens to those who hear them. So He said: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier﴾. We place between you, O Muhammad, and the polytheists who do not believe in the Hereafter a barrier, i.e. because of their aversion from your recitation and their heedlessness toward you, it is as if there were a barrier between you and them: they pass by you and do not see you. This meaning was mentioned by al-Zajjaj and others. The meaning of *mastur* (hidden) is "concealing" (*satir*).

Al-Akhfash said: he intended "concealing" (*satir*), and the active participle may take the form of the passive participle, as you say: "Indeed you are *mashʾum* (ill-omened) and *maymun* (blessed)", whereas the original forms are *shaʾim* and *yamin*. It has also been said: the meaning of *mastur* is "possessing a covering", like their saying "a *mufʿam* torrent", i.e. one possessing abundance. It has also been said: it is a barrier which eyes cannot see, so it is hidden from them. It has also been said: it is a barrier behind which is another barrier, so it is hidden by something else. It has also been said: what is meant by the hidden barrier is the seal and the covering of nature.

﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾. *Akinna* (coverings) is the plural of *kinan* (covering). Its explanation has already been given in al-Anʿam. It has also been said that this is a relating of what they used to say, namely their saying: "Our hearts are uncovered" ﴿and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a barrier﴾. *An yafqahuhu* (that they understand it) is a purpose clause (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*): i.e. out of aversion to their understanding it, or lest they understand it, i.e. lest they comprehend what it contains of commands, prohibitions, wisdoms and meanings. ﴿And in their ears a deafness﴾, i.e. deafness and heaviness. In the sentence there is an omission, and the sense is: if they hear it.

Among the ugly qualities of the polytheists is that they loved for their gods to be mentioned as Allah, exalted be He, is mentioned. So when they heard the mention of Allah without the mention of their gods, they fled from the assembly. For this reason Allah said: ﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an﴾, i.e. singly, not joined with the mention of their gods. It is a verbal noun (*masdar*) placed in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*). ﴿They turn back on their backs in aversion﴾. *Nufur* is a verbal noun, and the sense is: they fled in flight, or they fled in aversion. It has also been said that it is the plural of *nafir* (fleeing), like *qaʿid* and *quʿud*.

The first is preferable. The verbal noun may also be in the position of a circumstantial accusative, i.e. they turned back fleeing.

﴿We know best what they listen to when they listen to you﴾, i.e. they listen to you while occupied with it, namely mockery of you and of the Qur'an, and idle talk about your mention of your Lord alone. It has also been said: the *ba'* (with) is extra, and the adverbial clause in ﴿when they listen to you﴾ is connected to *aʿlam* (best knows), i.e. We know best the time when they listen to you, and what they listen to with it. In this there is an emphasis of the threat. His saying ﴿and when they are in private consultation﴾ is also connected to *aʿlam*, i.e. and We know best what they confer about among themselves at the time of their private consultation. They used to confer among themselves with denial and mockery. *Yaquluna* (they say) is a substitute for ﴿when they are in private consultation﴾.

﴿If you follow only a man bewitched﴾, i.e. each of them says to the others during their private consultation: you follow only a man who has been bewitched, so that his intellect has become confused and has departed from the limit of balance.

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: *al-maswur* is one whose intellect has gone and been corrupted, from their saying "food is *masur*" when its preparation has been spoiled, and "land is *masura*" when it has received more rain than it should and been ruined by it.

It has also been said: *al-masur* is one who has been deceived, because magic is a trick and deception, and that is because they claimed that Muhammad (ﷺ) was learning from some people, and they were deceiving him with that teaching.

Abu ʿUbayda said: the meaning of *masuran* is that he has a *sahr*, i.e. a lung, so he does not do without food and drink, and so he is like you. The Arabs say of a coward: "his *sahr* has swollen". Every human or other being that eats is *masur*, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*We were shown two places for an unseen matter, and we are nourished with food and with drink.*

i.e. we are nourished and sustained.

Ibn Qutayba said: I do not know what led him to this disliked interpretation, when the early scholars explained it in clear ways.

﴿See how they strike similitudes for you﴾, i.e. they said at one time that you are a soothsayer, at another a magician, at another a poet, and at another a madman, and they went astray from the path of correctness in all of that. ﴿So they cannot find a way﴾ to guidance, or to the criticism which intellects accept and to which assent is given; not the basis of criticism itself. They have done of it what they were able to do. It has also been said: they cannot find an exit, because of the contradiction in their speech, like their saying "a magician, a madman".

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Saʿid ibn Jubayr regarding His saying: ﴿Then they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾, that he said: "in order to remove His dominion."

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu Nuʿaym in *al-Hilya*, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* reported from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Qurt that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), on the night he was taken by night to the Farthest Mosque, had Jibril on his right and Mika'il on his left. He flew with him until he reached the high heavens. When he returned he said: I heard glorification from the high heavens along with much glorification: the high heavens glorified, out of awe of the Possessor of majesty, in fear before the Possessor of loftiness in what is exalted: Glory be to the Most High, the Exalted, glory be to Him and exalted be He."

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Anas that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said while sitting with his companions, when he heard a creaking, and said: The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak. By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, there is not a space of a hand's breadth in it except that there is on it the forehead of an angel prostrating, glorifying with His praise."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu'l-Shaykh in *al-ʿAzama* reported from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of a thing which Nuh commanded to his son? Allah, exalted be He, said: ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Umama who said: "No servant glorifies with a single glorification except that everything Allah has created glorifies [Allah] with it," and he said: ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾. The verse is supported in its generality by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] with him in the evening and at sunrise﴾, and His saying: ﴿And indeed among them is that which descends out of fear of Allah﴾, and His saying: ﴿And the mountains crumble to dust﴾, and similar verses. It is also established in the authentic collections that they "used to hear the glorification of food while they were eating with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)". Likewise is the hadith of the trunk of the palm tree moaning, and the hadith that a stone in Makkah used to greet the Prophet (ﷺ). All of these are in the authentic collections. Among them is the glorification of pebbles in the palm of his hand (ﷺ).

Repelling the generality of this verse by mere considerations of improbability is not the practice of one who believes in Allah, exalted be He, and believes in what has come from Him.

The meaning of ﴿except that it glorifies Him with His praise﴾ is: except that it glorifies while being clothed in His praise. ﴿But you do not understand their glorification﴾.

Al-Hasan, Abu ʿAmr, Yaʿqub, Hafs, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *tusabbihu* (glorify) with a taʾ, addressing the audience (second person). The rest read it with a yaʾ. Abu ʿUbayd preferred this reading.

*Innahu kana halīman ghafūran* (Indeed He is ever Forbearing, Forgiving): from His forbearance is granting you respite and not sending His punishment upon you; and from His forgiveness toward you is that He does not take to account whoever among you repents.

When He, exalted be He, finished with the matters of divinity, He began to mention some of the verses of the Qur'an and what happens to those who hear them. So He said: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier﴾. We place between you, O Muhammad, and the polytheists who do not believe in the Hereafter a barrier, i.e. because of their aversion from your recitation and their heedlessness toward you, it is as if there were a barrier between you and them: they pass by you and do not see you. This meaning was mentioned by al-Zajjaj and others. The meaning of *mastur* (hidden) is "concealing" (*satir*).

Al-Akhfash said: he intended "concealing" (*satir*), and the active participle may take the form of the passive participle, as you say: "Indeed you are *mashʾum* (ill-omened) and *maymun* (blessed)", whereas the original forms are *shaʾim* and *yamin*. It has also been said: the meaning of *mastur* is "possessing a covering", like their saying "a *mufʿam* torrent", i.e. one possessing abundance. It has also been said: it is a barrier which eyes cannot see, so it is hidden from them. It has also been said: it is a barrier behind which is another barrier, so it is hidden by something else. It has also been said: what is meant by the hidden barrier is the seal and the covering of nature.

﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾. *Akinna* (coverings) is the plural of *kinan* (covering). Its explanation has already been given in al-Anʿam. It has also been said that this is a relating of what they used to say, namely their saying: "Our hearts are uncovered" ﴿and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a barrier﴾. *An yafqahuhu* (that they understand it) is a purpose clause (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*): i.e. out of aversion to their understanding it, or lest they understand it, i.e. lest they comprehend what it contains of commands, prohibitions, wisdoms and meanings. ﴿And in their ears a deafness﴾, i.e. deafness and heaviness. In the sentence there is an omission, and the sense is: if they hear it.

Among the ugly qualities of the polytheists is that they loved for their gods to be mentioned as Allah, exalted be He, is mentioned. So when they heard the mention of Allah without the mention of their gods, they fled from the assembly. For this reason Allah said: ﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an﴾, i.e. singly, not joined with the mention of their gods. It is a verbal noun (*masdar*) placed in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*). ﴿They turn back on their backs in aversion﴾. *Nufur* is a verbal noun, and the sense is: they fled in flight, or they fled in aversion. It has also been said that it is the plural of *nafir* (fleeing), like *qaʿid* and *quʿud*.

The first is preferable. The verbal noun may also be in the position of a circumstantial accusative, i.e. they turned back fleeing.

In this there is an emphasis of the threat. His saying ﴿and when they are in private consultation﴾ is also connected to *aʿlam*, i.e. and We know best what they confer about among themselves at the time of their private consultation. They used to confer among themselves with denial and mockery. *Yaquluna* (they say) is a substitute for ﴿when they are in private consultation﴾.

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: *al-maswur* is one whose intellect has gone and been corrupted, from their saying "food is *masur*" when its preparation has been spoiled, and "land is *masura*" when it has received more rain than it should and been ruined by it.

It has also been said: *al-masur* is one who has been deceived, because magic is a trick and deception, and that is because they claimed that Muhammad (ﷺ) was learning from some people, and they were deceiving him with that teaching.

*We were shown two places for an unseen matter, and we are nourished with food and with drink.*

i.e. we are nourished and sustained.

Ibn Qutayba said: I do not know what led him to this disliked interpretation, when the early scholars explained it in clear ways.

﴿See how they strike similitudes for you﴾, i.e. they said at one time that you are a soothsayer, at another a magician, at another a poet, and at another a madman, and they went astray from the path of correctness in all of that. ﴿So they cannot find a way﴾ to guidance, or to the criticism which intellects accept and to which assent is given; not the basis of criticism itself. They have done of it what they were able to do. It has also been said: they cannot find an exit, because of the contradiction in their speech, like their saying "a magician, a madman".

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Saʿid ibn Jubayr regarding His saying: ﴿Then they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾, that he said: "in order to remove His dominion."

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu Nuʿaym in *al-Hilya*, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* reported from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Qurt that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), on the night he was taken by night to the Farthest Mosque, had Jibril on his right and Mika'il on his left. He flew with him until he reached the high heavens. When he returned he said: I heard glorification from the high heavens along with much glorification: the high heavens glorified, out of awe of the Possessor of majesty, in fear before the Possessor of loftiness in what is exalted: Glory be to the Most High, the Exalted, glory be to Him and exalted be He."

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Anas that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said while sitting with his companions, when he heard a creaking, and said: The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak. By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, there is not a space of a hand's breadth in it except that there is on it the forehead of an angel prostrating, glorifying with His praise."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu'l-Shaykh in *al-ʿAzama* reported from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of a thing which Nuh commanded to his son? Indeed Nuh said to his son: O my son, I command you to say: Glory be to Allah, for it is the prayer of creation, the glorification of creatures, and by it creatures are provided for." Allah, exalted be He, said: ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾.

Ahmad and Ibn Mardawayh reported a similar report from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Umama who said: "No servant glorifies with a single glorification except that everything Allah has created glorifies [Allah] with it," and he said: ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾. Ibn Kathir said: its chain of narration has weakness in it.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Abu Hurayra who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "An ant bit one of the prophets, so he commanded that the ants' colony be burned, and Allah revealed to him: Because of one ant you burned a nation among the nations which glorify [Allah]."

al-Nasa'i, Abu'l-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAmr who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade killing the frog, and said: its croaking is glorification."

Abu'l-Shaykh in *al-ʿAzama* and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾, that he said: "The crop glorifies, and its reward belongs to its owner; and the garment glorifies, and the dirt says: If you are a believer, then wash me."

Abu'l-Shaykh reported from him that he said: "Everything glorifies except the dog and the donkey."

Ibn Rahawayh in his *Musnad* reported through the route of al-Zuhri who said: "Abu Bakr was brought a crow with its wings spread wide, and he began to spread its wings and say: No game is hunted and no tree is cut except because of the glorification it neglected."

Ahmad in *al-Zuhd* and Abu'l-Shaykh reported it from Maymun ibn Mihran who said: "Abu Bakr al-Siddiq came and mentioned it as his own saying, not as a raised report (*marfu'*)."

Abu Nuʿaym in *al-Hilya* and Ibn Mardawayh reported it from the hadith of Abu Hurayra with similar wording.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from the hadith of Ibn Masʿud with some of its meaning.

Abu'l-Shaykh reported from the hadith of Abu'l-Darda' with its meaning.

Ibn ʿAsakir reported from the hadith of Abu Ruhm something similar.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 17, verse 42–48 (part 2 of 2):

It was narrated by Ibn al-Mundhir from al-Hasan, who said: "This verse in the Torah is like about a thousand verses: ﴿And there is not a thing but it exalts [Allah] with His praise﴾. He said: In the Torah, the mountains glorify Him, and the trees glorify Him, and such-and-such glorifies Him, and such-and-such glorifies Him."

Ahmad and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Dawud (David) prayed one night until morning. When morning came, he found joy within himself, and a frog called out to him: 'O Dawud, I used to be more diligent than you, and you have just dozed off for a moment.'"

al-Bayhaqi narrated in al-Shuʿab from Sadaqah ibn Yasar, who said: "Dawud was in his prayer niche (mihrab) when he saw a small worm. He reflected on its creation and said: 'Allah does not care about the creation of this.' So Allah made it speak, and it said: 'O Dawud, does your self make you vain? I remember Allah and give thanks to Him more than you, for what Allah has given you.' Allah said: ﴿And there is not a thing but it exalts [Allah] with His praise﴾."

There are in this regard hadiths and reports from the early generations (al-salaf) that explicitly state the glorification of all created things.

Abu Yaʿla, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nuʿaym, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, who said: "When the verse ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ was revealed, Umm Jamil al-ʿAwraʾ came, wailing, with a stone in her hand, saying:

Dhammaman we disobey,
And his religion we despise,
And his command we disobey.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sitting with Abu Bakr beside him. Abu Bakr said: 'This woman has come, and I fear she will see you.' He (ﷺ) said: 'She will not see me.' He then recited a Qur'an with which he sought protection, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a concealed barrier﴾. So she came and stood over Abu Bakr, but did not see the Prophet (ﷺ). She said: 'O Abu Bakr, I have heard that your companion has satirized me.' Abu Bakr said: 'No, by the Lord of this House, he has not satirized you.' So she departed, saying: 'Quraysh knows that I am the daughter of their chief.'" This story has been narrated with different wordings.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a concealed barrier﴾, that he said: "The concealed barrier is coverings over their hearts, so that they do not understand it and do not benefit from it, because they obeyed the Shaytan, and he took possession of them."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Zuhayr ibn Muhammad regarding the verse, that he said: "That is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): when he recited the Qur'an to the polytheists in Makkah, they heard his recitation but did not see him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿They turn away in aversion﴾, that he said: "The shayatin (devils)."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿When they listen to you﴾, that he said: "ʿUtbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabiʿah, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il."

It has also been said that the meaning is: then the gods would have sought nearness and closeness to Allah with Him, since they are below Him, and the polytheists only believed that they would bring them closer to Allah.

Then He described the height as greatness, as an intensification of transcendence, and as an indication that between what is necessary in itself and what is contingent in itself, and between the absolutely self-sufficient and the absolutely needy, there is a separation beyond which no addition can be conceived.

Then, exalted be He, He clarified the majesty of His dominion and the greatness of His sovereignty, and said: ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them glorify Him﴾. *Yusabbihu* is read with a yaʾ (third person), and also with a taʾ. He said *fihinna* (in them) with the pronoun for rational beings, because He attributed to them the glorification which is the act of rational beings. Allah, exalted be He, has informed us about the heavens and the earth that they glorify Him, and likewise whoever is in them of His creatures who have intellects, namely the angels, mankind, jinn, and others, as well as the things which do not have intellect. It is answered that what is meant by His saying "you do not understand" are the disbelievers who turn away from consideration.

It was narrated by Ibn al-Mundhir from al-Hasan, who said: "This verse in the Torah is like about a thousand verses: ﴿And there is not a thing but it exalts [Allah] with His praise﴾. Ahmad and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Dawud (David) prayed one night until morning. When morning came, he found joy within himself, and a frog called out to him: 'O Dawud, I used to be more diligent than you, and you have just dozed off for a moment.'"

His saying: ﴿Say: If there were gods with Him, as they say﴾. Ibn Kathir and Hafs read *yaqulun* (they say) with a yaʾ (third person), while the rest read it with a taʾ (second person, addressing those who say that there are other gods with God). *Idhan* (then) is the answer to their false statement and the apodosis (*jaza'*) of *law* (if): ﴿they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾, and He is Allah, exalted be He, [seeking] a way, meaning a means of contention and resistance, as kings do with one another in fighting and struggle. It has also been said that the meaning is: then the gods would have sought nearness and closeness to Allah with Him, since they are below Him, and the polytheists only believed that they would bring them closer to Allah.

The first meaning is the apparent one, and similar in meaning is His saying: ﴿If there were in them [the heavens and the earth] gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted﴾.

Then the Exalted purified Himself, and said, exalted be He. *Tasbih* (glorification) means declaring Him free of imperfection, and it has already been discussed. And He is exalted, far removed from what they say of shameful statements and great slander. *ʿUluwwan* means "exaltedly", i.e. *taʿaliyan* (exaltation), but He placed *al-ʿuluww* (height) in the place of *al-taʿaali* (exaltation), as in His saying: ﴿And Allah has brought you forth from the earth as a growth﴾. Then He described the height as greatness, as an intensification of transcendence, and as an indication that between what is necessary in itself and what is contingent in itself, and between the absolutely self-sufficient and the absolutely needy, there is a separation beyond which no addition can be conceived.

Then, exalted be He, He clarified the majesty of His dominion and the greatness of His sovereignty, and said: ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them glorify Him﴾. *Yusabbihu* is read with a yaʾ (third person), and also with a taʾ. He said *fihinna* (in them) with the pronoun for rational beings, because He attributed to them the glorification which is the act of rational beings. Allah, exalted be He, has informed us about the heavens and the earth that they glorify Him, and likewise whoever is in them of His creatures who have intellects, namely the angels, mankind, jinn, and others, as well as the things which do not have intellect. Then He increased this in generality and emphasis, and said: ﴿There is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾. Thus it includes everything that is called a thing, whatever it may be. It has also been said that His saying "and whoever is in them" is to be understood as referring to the angels and the two weighty creatures (jinn and mankind), and that His saying "there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise" is to be understood as referring to what is other than that among the creatures.

The people of knowledge have differed regarding this generality: is it specified or not? One group said: it is not specified, and they understood the glorification as glorification of indication (*dalala*), because every creature bears witness to itself and indicates to others that Allah is the Creator, the Powerful.

Another group said: this glorification is in its literal sense, and the generality is on its apparent meaning.

What is meant is that all creatures glorify Allah, exalted be He, with this glorification whose meaning is declaring Him free of imperfection, even if human beings do not hear that or understand it. This is supported by His saying: ﴿But you do not understand their glorification﴾, for if the intended meaning were the glorification of indication, it would be a matter understood by everyone.

It is answered that what is meant by His saying "you do not understand" are the disbelievers who turn away from consideration.

Another group said: this generality is specified to the angels and the two weighty creatures, excluding inanimate things. It has also been said that it is specific to growing bodies, so plants are included, as this view has been reported from ʿIkrima and al-Hasan. They restricted the glorification of plants to the time of their growth, not after they have been cut. It has been used as evidence for this the hadith (report) that "the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by two graves, and in it [the report]: then he called for a fresh palm frond, split it in two, and said: Indeed, the punishment is lightened for them so long as they have not dried out." The verse is supported in its generality by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] with him in the evening and at sunrise﴾, and His saying: ﴿And indeed among them is that which descends out of fear of Allah﴾, and His saying: ﴿And the mountains crumble to dust﴾, and similar verses. It is also established in the authentic collections that they "used to hear the glorification of food while they were eating with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)". Likewise is the hadith of the trunk of the palm tree moaning, and the hadith that a stone in Makkah used to greet the Prophet (ﷺ). All of these are in the authentic collections. Among them is the glorification of pebbles in the palm of his hand (ﷺ).

Repelling the generality of this verse by mere considerations of improbability is not the practice of one who believes in Allah, exalted be He, and believes in what has come from Him.

The meaning of ﴿except that it glorifies Him with His praise﴾ is: except that it glorifies while being clothed in His praise. ﴿But you do not understand their glorification﴾.

Al-Hasan, Abu ʿAmr, Yaʿqub, Hafs, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *tusabbihu* (glorify) with a taʾ, addressing the audience (second person). The rest read it with a yaʾ. Abu ʿUbayd preferred this reading.

*Innahu kana halīman ghafūran* (Indeed He is ever Forbearing, Forgiving): from His forbearance is granting you respite and not sending His punishment upon you; and from His forgiveness toward you is that He does not take to account whoever among you repents.

When He, exalted be He, finished with the matters of divinity, He began to mention some of the verses of the Qur'an and what happens to those who hear them. So He said: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier﴾. We place between you, O Muhammad, and the polytheists who do not believe in the Hereafter a barrier, i.e. because of their aversion from your recitation and their heedlessness toward you, it is as if there were a barrier between you and them: they pass by you and do not see you. This meaning was mentioned by al-Zajjaj and others. The meaning of *mastur* (hidden) is "concealing" (*satir*).

Al-Akhfash said: he intended "concealing" (*satir*), and the active participle may take the form of the passive participle, as you say: "Indeed you are *mashʾum* (ill-omened) and *maymun* (blessed)", whereas the original forms are *shaʾim* and *yamin*. It has also been said: the meaning of *mastur* is "possessing a covering", like their saying "a *mufʿam* torrent", i.e. one possessing abundance. It has also been said: it is a barrier which eyes cannot see, so it is hidden from them. It has also been said: it is a barrier behind which is another barrier, so it is hidden by something else. It has also been said: what is meant by the hidden barrier is the seal and the covering of nature.

﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾. *Akinna* (coverings) is the plural of *kinan* (covering). Its explanation has already been given in al-Anʿam. It has also been said that this is a relating of what they used to say, namely their saying: "Our hearts are uncovered" ﴿and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a barrier﴾. *An yafqahuhu* (that they understand it) is a purpose clause (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*): i.e. out of aversion to their understanding it, or lest they understand it, i.e. lest they comprehend what it contains of commands, prohibitions, wisdoms and meanings. ﴿And in their ears a deafness﴾, i.e. deafness and heaviness. In the sentence there is an omission, and the sense is: if they hear it.

Among the ugly qualities of the polytheists is that they loved for their gods to be mentioned as Allah, exalted be He, is mentioned. So when they heard the mention of Allah without the mention of their gods, they fled from the assembly. For this reason Allah said: ﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an﴾, i.e. singly, not joined with the mention of their gods. It is a verbal noun (*masdar*) placed in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*). ﴿They turn back on their backs in aversion﴾. *Nufur* is a verbal noun, and the sense is: they fled in flight, or they fled in aversion. It has also been said that it is the plural of *nafir* (fleeing), like *qaʿid* and *quʿud*.

The first is preferable. The verbal noun may also be in the position of a circumstantial accusative, i.e. they turned back fleeing.

﴿We know best what they listen to when they listen to you﴾, i.e. they listen to you while occupied with it, namely mockery of you and of the Qur'an, and idle talk about your mention of your Lord alone. It has also been said: the *ba'* (with) is extra, and the adverbial clause in ﴿when they listen to you﴾ is connected to *aʿlam* (best knows), i.e. We know best the time when they listen to you, and what they listen to with it. In this there is an emphasis of the threat. His saying ﴿and when they are in private consultation﴾ is also connected to *aʿlam*, i.e. and We know best what they confer about among themselves at the time of their private consultation. They used to confer among themselves with denial and mockery. *Yaquluna* (they say) is a substitute for ﴿when they are in private consultation﴾.

﴿If you follow only a man bewitched﴾, i.e. each of them says to the others during their private consultation: you follow only a man who has been bewitched, so that his intellect has become confused and has departed from the limit of balance.

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: *al-maswur* is one whose intellect has gone and been corrupted, from their saying "food is *masur*" when its preparation has been spoiled, and "land is *masura*" when it has received more rain than it should and been ruined by it.

It has also been said: *al-masur* is one who has been deceived, because magic is a trick and deception, and that is because they claimed that Muhammad (ﷺ) was learning from some people, and they were deceiving him with that teaching.

Abu ʿUbayda said: the meaning of *masuran* is that he has a *sahr*, i.e. a lung, so he does not do without food and drink, and so he is like you. The Arabs say of a coward: "his *sahr* has swollen". Every human or other being that eats is *masur*, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*We were shown two places for an unseen matter, and we are nourished with food and with drink.*

i.e. we are nourished and sustained.

Ibn Qutayba said: I do not know what led him to this disliked interpretation, when the early scholars explained it in clear ways.

﴿See how they strike similitudes for you﴾, i.e. they said at one time that you are a soothsayer, at another a magician, at another a poet, and at another a madman, and they went astray from the path of correctness in all of that. ﴿So they cannot find a way﴾ to guidance, or to the criticism which intellects accept and to which assent is given; not the basis of criticism itself. They have done of it what they were able to do. It has also been said: they cannot find an exit, because of the contradiction in their speech, like their saying "a magician, a madman".

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Saʿid ibn Jubayr regarding His saying: ﴿Then they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾, that he said: "in order to remove His dominion."

He flew with him until he reached the high heavens. When he returned he said: I heard glorification from the high heavens along with much glorification: the high heavens glorified, out of awe of the Possessor of majesty, in fear before the Possessor of loftiness in what is exalted: Glory be to the Most High, the Exalted, glory be to Him and exalted be He."

It has been used as evidence for this the hadith (report) that "the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by two graves, and in it [the report]: then he called for a fresh palm frond, split it in two, and said: Indeed, the punishment is lightened for them so long as they have not dried out." The verse is supported in its generality by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] with him in the evening and at sunrise﴾, and His saying: ﴿And indeed among them is that which descends out of fear of Allah﴾, and His saying: ﴿And the mountains crumble to dust﴾, and similar verses. It is also established in the authentic collections that they "used to hear the glorification of food while they were eating with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)". Likewise is the hadith of the trunk of the palm tree moaning, and the hadith that a stone in Makkah used to greet the Prophet (ﷺ). All of these are in the authentic collections. Among them is the glorification of pebbles in the palm of his hand (ﷺ).

Repelling the generality of this verse by mere considerations of improbability is not the practice of one who believes in Allah, exalted be He, and believes in what has come from Him.

The meaning of ﴿except that it glorifies Him with His praise﴾ is: except that it glorifies while being clothed in His praise. ﴿But you do not understand their glorification﴾.

Al-Hasan, Abu ʿAmr, Yaʿqub, Hafs, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *tusabbihu* (glorify) with a taʾ, addressing the audience (second person). The rest read it with a yaʾ. Abu ʿUbayd preferred this reading.

*Innahu kana halīman ghafūran* (Indeed He is ever Forbearing, Forgiving): from His forbearance is granting you respite and not sending His punishment upon you; and from His forgiveness toward you is that He does not take to account whoever among you repents.

When He, exalted be He, finished with the matters of divinity, He began to mention some of the verses of the Qur'an and what happens to those who hear them. So He said: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier﴾. We place between you, O Muhammad, and the polytheists who do not believe in the Hereafter a barrier, i.e. because of their aversion from your recitation and their heedlessness toward you, it is as if there were a barrier between you and them: they pass by you and do not see you. This meaning was mentioned by al-Zajjaj and others. The meaning of *mastur* (hidden) is "concealing" (*satir*).

Al-Akhfash said: he intended "concealing" (*satir*), and the active participle may take the form of the passive participle, as you say: "Indeed you are *mashʾum* (ill-omened) and *maymun* (blessed)", whereas the original forms are *shaʾim* and *yamin*. It has also been said: the meaning of *mastur* is "possessing a covering", like their saying "a *mufʿam* torrent", i.e. one possessing abundance. It has also been said: it is a barrier which eyes cannot see, so it is hidden from them. It has also been said: it is a barrier behind which is another barrier, so it is hidden by something else. It has also been said: what is meant by the hidden barrier is the seal and the covering of nature.

﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾. *Akinna* (coverings) is the plural of *kinan* (covering). Its explanation has already been given in al-Anʿam. It has also been said that this is a relating of what they used to say, namely their saying: "Our hearts are uncovered" ﴿and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a barrier﴾. *An yafqahuhu* (that they understand it) is a purpose clause (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*): i.e. out of aversion to their understanding it, or lest they understand it, i.e. lest they comprehend what it contains of commands, prohibitions, wisdoms and meanings. ﴿And in their ears a deafness﴾, i.e. deafness and heaviness. In the sentence there is an omission, and the sense is: if they hear it.

Among the ugly qualities of the polytheists is that they loved for their gods to be mentioned as Allah, exalted be He, is mentioned. So when they heard the mention of Allah without the mention of their gods, they fled from the assembly. For this reason Allah said: ﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an﴾, i.e. singly, not joined with the mention of their gods. It is a verbal noun (*masdar*) placed in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*). ﴿They turn back on their backs in aversion﴾. *Nufur* is a verbal noun, and the sense is: they fled in flight, or they fled in aversion. It has also been said that it is the plural of *nafir* (fleeing), like *qaʿid* and *quʿud*.

The first is preferable. The verbal noun may also be in the position of a circumstantial accusative, i.e. they turned back fleeing.

In this there is an emphasis of the threat. His saying ﴿and when they are in private consultation﴾ is also connected to *aʿlam*, i.e. and We know best what they confer about among themselves at the time of their private consultation. They used to confer among themselves with denial and mockery. *Yaquluna* (they say) is a substitute for ﴿when they are in private consultation﴾.

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: *al-maswur* is one whose intellect has gone and been corrupted, from their saying "food is *masur*" when its preparation has been spoiled, and "land is *masura*" when it has received more rain than it should and been ruined by it.

It has also been said: *al-masur* is one who has been deceived, because magic is a trick and deception, and that is because they claimed that Muhammad (ﷺ) was learning from some people, and they were deceiving him with that teaching.
