i.e. we are nourished and sustained.

They have done of it what they were able to do. It has also been said: they cannot find an exit, because of the contradiction in their speech, like their saying "a magician, a madman".

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Saʿid ibn Jubayr regarding His saying: ﴿Then they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾, that he said: "in order to remove His dominion."

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu Nuʿaym in *al-Hilya*, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* reported from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Qurt that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), on the night he was taken by night to the Farthest Mosque, had Jibril on his right and Mika'il on his left. He flew with him until he reached the high heavens. When he returned he said: I heard glorification from the high heavens along with much glorification: the high heavens glorified, out of awe of the Possessor of majesty, in fear before the Possessor of loftiness in what is exalted: Glory be to the Most High, the Exalted, glory be to Him and exalted be He."

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Anas that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said while sitting with his companions, when he heard a creaking, and said: The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak. By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, there is not a space of a hand's breadth in it except that there is on it the forehead of an angel prostrating, glorifying with His praise."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu'l-Shaykh in *al-ʿAzama* reported from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of a thing which Nuh commanded to his son? Indeed Nuh said to his son: O my son, I command you to say: Glory be to Allah, for it is the prayer of creation, the glorification of creatures, and by it creatures are provided for." Allah, exalted be He, said: ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾.

Ahmad and Ibn Mardawayh reported a similar report from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Umama who said: "No servant glorifies with a single glorification except that everything Allah has created glorifies [Allah] with it," and he said: ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾. Ibn Kathir said: its chain of narration has weakness in it.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Abu Hurayra who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "An ant bit one of the prophets, so he commanded that the ants' colony be burned, and Allah revealed to him: Because of one ant you burned a nation among the nations which glorify [Allah]."

al-Nasa'i, Abu'l-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAmr who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade killing the frog, and said: its croaking is glorification."

Abu'l-Shaykh in *al-ʿAzama* and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾, that he said: "The crop glorifies, and its reward belongs to its owner; and the garment glorifies, and the dirt says: If you are a believer, then wash me."

Abu'l-Shaykh reported from him that he said: "Everything glorifies except the dog and the donkey."

Ibn Rahawayh in his *Musnad* reported through the route of al-Zuhri who said: "Abu Bakr was brought a crow with its wings spread wide, and he began to spread its wings and say: No game is hunted and no tree is cut except because of the glorification it neglected."

Ahmad in *al-Zuhd* and Abu'l-Shaykh reported it from Maymun ibn Mihran who said: "Abu Bakr al-Siddiq came and mentioned it as his own saying, not as a raised report (*marfu'*)."

Abu Nuʿaym in *al-Hilya* and Ibn Mardawayh reported it from the hadith of Abu Hurayra with similar wording.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from the hadith of Ibn Masʿud with some of its meaning.

Abu'l-Shaykh reported from the hadith of Abu'l-Darda' with its meaning.

Ibn ʿAsakir reported from the hadith of Abu Ruhm something similar.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 17, verse 42–48 (part 2 of 2):

It was narrated by Ibn al-Mundhir from al-Hasan, who said: "This verse in the Torah is like about a thousand verses: ﴿And there is not a thing but it exalts [Allah] with His praise﴾. He said: In the Torah, the mountains glorify Him, and the trees glorify Him, and such-and-such glorifies Him, and such-and-such glorifies Him."

Ahmad and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Dawud (David) prayed one night until morning. When morning came, he found joy within himself, and a frog called out to him: 'O Dawud, I used to be more diligent than you, and you have just dozed off for a moment.'"

al-Bayhaqi narrated in al-Shuʿab from Sadaqah ibn Yasar, who said: "Dawud was in his prayer niche (mihrab) when he saw a small worm. He reflected on its creation and said: 'Allah does not care about the creation of this.' So Allah made it speak, and it said: 'O Dawud, does your self make you vain? I remember Allah and give thanks to Him more than you, for what Allah has given you.' Allah said: ﴿And there is not a thing but it exalts [Allah] with His praise﴾."

There are in this regard hadiths and reports from the early generations (al-salaf) that explicitly state the glorification of all created things.

Abu Yaʿla, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nuʿaym, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, who said: "When the verse ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ was revealed, Umm Jamil al-ʿAwraʾ came, wailing, with a stone in her hand, saying:

Dhammaman we disobey,
And his religion we despise,
And his command we disobey.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sitting with Abu Bakr beside him. Abu Bakr said: 'This woman has come, and I fear she will see you.' He (ﷺ) said: 'She will not see me.' He then recited a Qur'an with which he sought protection, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a concealed barrier﴾. So she came and stood over Abu Bakr, but did not see the Prophet (ﷺ). She said: 'O Abu Bakr, I have heard that your companion has satirized me.' Abu Bakr said: 'No, by the Lord of this House, he has not satirized you.' So she departed, saying: 'Quraysh knows that I am the daughter of their chief.'" This story has been narrated with different wordings.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a concealed barrier﴾, that he said: "The concealed barrier is coverings over their hearts, so that they do not understand it and do not benefit from it, because they obeyed the Shaytan, and he took possession of them."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Zuhayr ibn Muhammad regarding the verse, that he said: "That is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): when he recited the Qur'an to the polytheists in Makkah, they heard his recitation but did not see him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿They turn away in aversion﴾, that he said: "The shayatin (devils)."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿When they listen to you﴾, that he said: "ʿUtbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabiʿah, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il."

Then He described the height as greatness, as an intensification of transcendence, and as an indication that between what is necessary in itself and what is contingent in itself, and between the absolutely self-sufficient and the absolutely needy, there is a separation beyond which no addition can be conceived.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Abu Hurayra who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "An ant bit one of the prophets, so he commanded that the ants' colony be burned, and Allah revealed to him: Because of one ant you burned a nation among the nations which glorify [Allah]."

al-Nasa'i, Abu'l-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAmr who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade killing the frog, and said: its croaking is glorification."

Abu'l-Shaykh in *al-ʿAzama* and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾, that he said: "The crop glorifies, and its reward belongs to its owner; and the garment glorifies, and the dirt says: If you are a believer, then wash me."

Abu'l-Shaykh reported from him that he said: "Everything glorifies except the dog and the donkey."

Ibn Rahawayh in his *Musnad* reported through the route of al-Zuhri who said: "Abu Bakr was brought a crow with its wings spread wide, and he began to spread its wings and say: No game is hunted and no tree is cut except because of the glorification it neglected."

Ahmad in *al-Zuhd* and Abu'l-Shaykh reported it from Maymun ibn Mihran who said: "Abu Bakr al-Siddiq came and mentioned it as his own saying, not as a raised report (*marfu'*)."

Abu Nuʿaym in *al-Hilya* and Ibn Mardawayh reported it from the hadith of Abu Hurayra with similar wording.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from the hadith of Ibn Masʿud with some of its meaning.

Abu'l-Shaykh reported from the hadith of Abu'l-Darda' with its meaning.

Ibn ʿAsakir reported from the hadith of Abu Ruhm something similar.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 17, verse 42–48 (part 2 of 2):

It was narrated by Ibn al-Mundhir from al-Hasan, who said: "This verse in the Torah is like about a thousand verses: ﴿And there is not a thing but it exalts [Allah] with His praise﴾. He said: In the Torah, the mountains glorify Him, and the trees glorify Him, and such-and-such glorifies Him, and such-and-such glorifies Him."

Ahmad and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Dawud (David) prayed one night until morning. When morning came, he found joy within himself, and a frog called out to him: 'O Dawud, I used to be more diligent than you, and you have just dozed off for a moment.'"

al-Bayhaqi narrated in al-Shuʿab from Sadaqah ibn Yasar, who said: "Dawud was in his prayer niche (mihrab) when he saw a small worm. He reflected on its creation and said: 'Allah does not care about the creation of this.' So Allah made it speak, and it said: 'O Dawud, does your self make you vain? I remember Allah and give thanks to Him more than you, for what Allah has given you.' Allah said: ﴿And there is not a thing but it exalts [Allah] with His praise﴾."

There are in this regard hadiths and reports from the early generations (al-salaf) that explicitly state the glorification of all created things.

Abu Yaʿla, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nuʿaym, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, who said: "When the verse ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ was revealed, Umm Jamil al-ʿAwraʾ came, wailing, with a stone in her hand, saying:

Dhammaman we disobey,
And his religion we despise,
And his command we disobey.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sitting with Abu Bakr beside him. Abu Bakr said: 'This woman has come, and I fear she will see you.' He (ﷺ) said: 'She will not see me.' He then recited a Qur'an with which he sought protection, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a concealed barrier﴾. So she came and stood over Abu Bakr, but did not see the Prophet (ﷺ). She said: 'O Abu Bakr, I have heard that your companion has satirized me.' Abu Bakr said: 'No, by the Lord of this House, he has not satirized you.' So she departed, saying: 'Quraysh knows that I am the daughter of their chief.'" This story has been narrated with different wordings.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a concealed barrier﴾, that he said: "The concealed barrier is coverings over their hearts, so that they do not understand it and do not benefit from it, because they obeyed the Shaytan, and he took possession of them."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Zuhayr ibn Muhammad regarding the verse, that he said: "That is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): when he recited the Qur'an to the polytheists in Makkah, they heard his recitation but did not see him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿They turn away in aversion﴾, that he said: "The shayatin (devils)."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿When they listen to you﴾, that he said: "ʿUtbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabiʿah, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il."

When He had finished relating the doubts of the people concerning prophethood, He related their doubt concerning the Return (ma'ad), saying: ﴿And they say, "When we are bones and crumbled dust, shall we indeed be raised up in a new creation?"﴾ The interrogative here expresses denial (istinkar) and disbelief in the possibility (istib'ad).

The doubt may be stated thus: when a person dies, his bones dry up, scatter and are dispersed across the corners of the world, and their elements mix with their likes among the (other) elements. How, then, could it be conceived that they be gathered together in their very same individual forms, and that life return to that assembled mass? Glorified is He, Who answered them: restoring the body of the dead to the state of life is something possible. Even if you suppose that his body has become the farthest thing from life and from the moisture of the living, like stones and iron, (the matter is still possible). This is like the saying of one who says, "Do you hope for anything from me, when I am the son of so-and-so?" and he replies, "Be the son of the sultan, or the son of whomever you wish, and I will still demand my right from you."

Rufat (رُفات) is that which has been broken and decayed of anything, like crumbs (futat), debris (hutam) and fragments (rudad). This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah, al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Akhfash. One says of it: rafata al-shay' rafthan, meaning it was smashed, so it is marfut (broken). It was also said: rufat is dust (ghubar), and it was said: it is soil (turab).

﴿Shall we indeed be raised up in a new creation?﴾ He repeated the interrogative, which indicates denial and disbelief, for emphasis and affirmation. The governing element of idha (إذا) is what is indicated by "la-mab'uthun" (لَمَبْعُوثُونَ), not the word itself, because what comes after inna, the hamza and the lam does not govern what precedes them. The sense is: "Shall we, when we are bones and crumbled dust, be resurrected? Shall we indeed be raised up?" The accusative of khalqan (خَلْقًا) is either as a verbal noun (masdar) from a non-identical verb, or as a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning "created," and jadidan (جَدِيدًا) is its adjective.

﴿Say: "Be stones or iron,"﴾ ﴿or a creation﴾ other ﴿than what grows large in your breasts.﴾ Ibn Jarir said: its meaning is, if you find it strange that God should create for you bones and flesh, then be stones or iron yourselves, if you are able to do so. 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: its meaning is that even if you were stones or iron, He would restore you as He originated you, and cause you to die and then give you life.

Al-Nahhas said: this is a good statement, because they are not able to become stones or iron. The meaning is rather that they had acknowledged their Creator yet denied resurrection, so it was said to them: "Consider that you may be whatever you wish; even if you were stones or iron, you would be raised up as you were created the first time."

I say: on this reading we established the answer to the doubt earlier.

﴿Or a creation other than what grows large in your breasts﴾ means: what is greatest in your estimation, of things greater than stones and iron in being remote from life. For you are certainly to be raised up. It was said that what is meant is the heavens, the earth and the mountains, because of their greatness in souls.

A group of scholars and of the Successors (tabi'un) said: what is meant is death, because there is nothing greater in the soul of the son of Adam than it.

The meaning is: "If you were death, God would cause you to die and then raise you up." The distance of this is not hidden, for the sense of the verse is an ascent from stones to iron, and then from iron to what is greater than it in the breasts of the people. Death itself is not something that perceives and feels, such that an ascent from iron to it would take place.

﴿They will say, "Who will restore us?"﴾ when we are bones and crumbled dust, or stones or iron, along with the disparity between the two states. ﴿Say: "He who originated you the first time."﴾ That is, He Who created you and brought you into being at the beginning of your creation, without any previous pattern or any prior form, will restore you.

﴿They will shake their heads at you﴾ meaning they will move them in mockery. It is said: nagha ra'suhu yanghu, yanghida, yunghidu, naghdan and nughudan, meaning it moved. And anghada ra'sahu means he moved it like one who is astonished. From this is the saying of the rajiz (rajaz poet): "He shook his head toward me and raised his brow," and the saying of another rajiz: "Her teeth shook from old age," and another said: "When she saw me, she shook her head for me."

﴿And they say, "When is it?"﴾ that is, the resurrection and the restoration, mockingly and derisively. ﴿Say: "It may be near."﴾ That is, it is near, because "'asa" (عسى, "it may be") in the speech of God is binding in its occurrence. A similar usage is: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near.﴾ And everything that is coming is near.

﴿On the day He calls you﴾: the time-expression is in the accusative governed by a hidden verb, meaning "remember," or it is a substitute for "near," or the sense is: "On the day He calls you, whatever will be will be." The calling (du'a') is a summons to the place of assembly with a speech that all creatures hear. It was said: it is the Blast (sayha) that you will hear, and it will be a summons to them to gather in the place of assembly. ﴿And you will respond with His praise﴾ meaning submitting to Him and praising Him for what He has done with you. It is thus in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause.

It was also said the meaning is: "And you will respond, and the praise is to God," as the poet said: "And I, by the praise of God, have not worn a sinner's garment, nor do I veil myself with treachery."

It has been reported that the disbelievers, when they come out of their graves, say: "Glory be to You, and praise be to You" (p. 828). It was also said: what is meant by the calling here is the resurrection, and by the response is that they are raised up, so the meaning is: "On the day He raises you up, you will be raised, submitting." ﴿And you will think you lingered only a little﴾ meaning at the resurrection you will think that you did not remain in your graves except for a short time. It was also said: between the two blasts, because punishment is withheld from the punished between the two blasts, and that is forty years, during which they sleep. Therefore ﴿they will say, "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting place?"﴾ It was also said: the world will seem trivial in their eyes and small when they see the Day of Resurrection, so they will say this statement.

﴿And say to My servants that they should speak what is best﴾ meaning: say, O Muhammad, to My believing servants that when they argue with the polytheists they should speak the word that is best, better than other good speech, like His saying: ﴿And do not dispute with the People of the Book except in the way that is best﴾ and His saying: ﴿Speak to him gently﴾, because harshness toward them may repel them from responding or lead to what He mentioned: ﴿And do not revile those whom they invoke besides God, lest they revile God in enmity without knowledge.﴾ This was before the revelation of the verse of the sword. It was also said: the meaning is, say to them: they should command what God commanded and forbid what He forbade. It was also said: this verse is only for believers among themselves specifically; the first is preferable, as the occasion of revelation that we will mention, God willing, indicates. ﴿Indeed, Satan incites discord among them﴾ meaning by corruption, by casting enmity and by instigation.

Al-Yazidi said: it is said nazaghā bayna-na, meaning he corrupted.

Another said: nazgh means instigation. ﴿Indeed, Satan has always been to man a clear enemy﴾ meaning openly showing enmity and disclosing it. This is an explanation for what precedes it, and a similar expression has already occurred in al-Baqarah.

﴿Your Lord knows best about you. If He wills, He will have mercy upon you, or if He wills, He will punish you.﴾ It was said this is addressed to the polytheists. The meaning: if He wills, He will grant you success in Islam and so have mercy on you, or He will cause you to die in polytheism and so punish you. It was also said it is addressed to the believers: that is, if He wills He will have mercy on you by protecting you from the disbelievers, or if He wills He will punish you by giving them power over you. It was also said this is an explanation of "the word that is best."

﴿And We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾ meaning We did not appoint you as a trustee to prevent them from disbelief or to compel them into faith. It was also said: We did not make you a surety for them, for which you would be held accountable. From this is the saying of the poet: "I remembered Abu Arwa, so I spent the night as if I were a trustee (wakil) for the restoration of past affairs." That is, a guarantor (kafil).

﴿And your Lord knows best who is in the heavens and the earth﴾ knows them in essence, state and merit. This is more general than His saying: ﴿Your Lord knows best about you﴾, because this includes all that is in the heavens and the earth of His creatures, whereas that is specific to the children of Adam or some of them. This is like a preparation for His saying: ﴿And We have preferred some of the prophets over others﴾, meaning that this preference is with knowledge from Him of who is higher in rank, who is below him, and who deserves additional distinction by the multiplication of his virtues and bounties.

This has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah.

God took Abraham as a close friend (khalil), made Moses one to whom He spoke (kalim), made Jesus His word and spirit, gave Solomon a great kingdom, forgave Muhammad his earlier and later sins, and made him the master of the children of Adam.

In this verse there is a rebuttal to what the disbelievers denied of what the Messenger of God ﷺ related about the elevation of his rank with his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic. Then He mentioned what He preferred Dawud by, saying: ﴿And We gave David the Psalms (Zabur)﴾, meaning a written book (kitab mazbur).

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, do not deny the preference of Muhammad and his being given the Qur'an, for God gave David the Zabur.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿and rufatan﴾ that he said: dust (ghubar).

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning His saying "and rufatan" that he said: soil (turab). And concerning His saying ﴿Say: "Be stones or iron"﴾ he said: whatever you wish, be it; God will restore you as you were.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Umar concerning His saying ﴿or a creation other than what grows large in your breasts﴾ that he said: death; "If you were death, I would give you life."

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir and al-Hakim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas the like of this.

Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah transmitted from al-Hasan the like of this too.

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar, and he added: He said, "Be death, if you are able, for death itself will die."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿So they will shake their heads at you﴾ that he said: they will move them in mockery.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Mujahid concerning His saying ﴿And they say, "When is it?"﴾ that he said: the restoration.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿so you will respond with His praise﴾ that he said: by His command.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning the verse that he said: they will come out of their graves saying, "Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning ﴿so you will respond with His praise﴾ that he said: with knowledge of Him and obedience to Him. ﴿And you will think you lingered only a little﴾, that is, in the world; the world became small in their souls and seemed little when they witnessed the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Sirin concerning His saying ﴿And say to My servants that they should speak what is best﴾ that he said: "There is no god but God."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Jurayj concerning the verse that he said: He pardons evil deeds.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Hasan that he said: He says to him, "May God have mercy on you; may God forgive you."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah that he said: the incitement of Satan is his stirring up of strife (tahrish).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning His saying ﴿And We gave David the Psalms﴾ that he said: We were told that it is a supplication taught to David and a praise and glorification of God, the Mighty and Majestic, in which there is no lawful or unlawful, no obligations and no prescribed punishments.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Rabi' ibn Anas that he said: the Zabur is praise of God, supplication and glorification.

I say: the matter is as Qatadah and al-Rabi' said, for we have examined the Zabur and found it to be sermons (khutab) which David, peace be upon him, delivered and addressed to his Lord, glorified be He, upon entering the sanctuary (kanisah). Its total is one hundred and fifty sermons, each called a mazmur (psalm), with the first mim open, the zay sukun, the second mim damma, and ending with a ra'. In some of these sermons David complains to his Lord about his enemies and seeks victory over them; in others he praises God, glorifies Him and extols Him for the victory and dominance over them that occurred. During the sermon he would play the qithara, which is an instrument of the musical instruments.

Al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur has mentioned here narrations from a group of the early generations which mention words they found in the Zabur that have little benefit, for what the Qur'an contains of admonitions and warnings has sufficed in place of these and other such things.

The doubt may be stated thus: when a person dies, his bones dry up, scatter and are dispersed across the corners of the world, and their elements mix with their likes among the (other) elements. How, then, could it be conceived that they be gathered together in their very same individual forms, and that life return to that assembled mass? Glorified is He, Who answered them: restoring the body of the dead to the state of life is something possible. Even if you suppose that his body has become the farthest thing from life and from the moisture of the living, like stones and iron, (the matter is still possible). This is like the saying of one who says, "Do you hope for anything from me, when I am the son of so-and-so?" and he replies, "Be the son of the sultan, or the son of whomever you wish, and I will still demand my right from you."

Rufat (رُفات) is that which has been broken and decayed of anything, like crumbs (futat), debris (hutam) and fragments (rudad). This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah, al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Akhfash. One says of it: rafata al-shay' rafthan, meaning it was smashed, so it is marfut (broken). It was also said: rufat is dust (ghubar), and it was said: it is soil (turab).

The sense is: "Shall we, when we are bones and crumbled dust, be resurrected? Shall we indeed be raised up?" 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: its meaning is that even if you were stones or iron, He would restore you as He originated you, and cause you to die and then give you life.

Al-Nahhas said: this is a good statement, because they are not able to become stones or iron. The meaning is rather that they had acknowledged their Creator yet denied resurrection, so it was said to them: "Consider that you may be whatever you wish; even if you were stones or iron, you would be raised up as you were created the first time."

I say: on this reading we established the answer to the doubt earlier.

﴿Or a creation other than what grows large in your breasts﴾ means: what is greatest in your estimation, of things greater than stones and iron in being remote from life. For you are certainly to be raised up. It was said that what is meant is the heavens, the earth and the mountains, because of their greatness in souls.

A group of scholars and of the Successors (tabi'un) said: what is meant is death, because there is nothing greater in the soul of the son of Adam than it.

The meaning is: "If you were death, God would cause you to die and then raise you up." The distance of this is not hidden, for the sense of the verse is an ascent from stones to iron, and then from iron to what is greater than it in the breasts of the people. Death itself is not something that perceives and feels, such that an ascent from iron to it would take place.

﴿They will shake their heads at you﴾ meaning they will move them in mockery. It is said: nagha ra'suhu yanghu, yanghida, yunghidu, naghdan and nughudan, meaning it moved. And anghada ra'sahu means he moved it like one who is astonished. From this is the saying of the rajiz (rajaz poet): "He shook his head toward me and raised his brow," and the saying of another rajiz: "Her teeth shook from old age," and another said: "When she saw me, she shook her head for me."

﴿And they say, "When is it?"﴾ that is, the resurrection and the restoration, mockingly and derisively. ﴿Say: "It may be near."﴾ That is, it is near, because "'asa" (عسى, "it may be") in the speech of God is binding in its occurrence. A similar usage is: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near.﴾ And everything that is coming is near.

﴿On the day He calls you﴾: the time-expression is in the accusative governed by a hidden verb, meaning "remember," or it is a substitute for "near," or the sense is: "On the day He calls you, whatever will be will be." The calling (du'a') is a summons to the place of assembly with a speech that all creatures hear. It was said: it is the Blast (sayha) that you will hear, and it will be a summons to them to gather in the place of assembly. ﴿And you will respond with His praise﴾ meaning submitting to Him and praising Him for what He has done with you. It is thus in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause.

It was also said the meaning is: "And you will respond, and the praise is to God," as the poet said: "And I, by the praise of God, have not worn a sinner's garment, nor do I veil myself with treachery."

It has been reported that the disbelievers, when they come out of their graves, say: "Glory be to You, and praise be to You" (p. 828). It was also said: what is meant by the calling here is the resurrection, and by the response is that they are raised up, so the meaning is: "On the day He raises you up, you will be raised, submitting." ﴿And you will think you lingered only a little﴾ meaning at the resurrection you will think that you did not remain in your graves except for a short time. It was also said: between the two blasts, because punishment is withheld from the punished between the two blasts, and that is forty years, during which they sleep. Therefore ﴿they will say, "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting place?"﴾ It was also said: the world will seem trivial in their eyes and small when they see the Day of Resurrection, so they will say this statement.

It was also said: the meaning is, say to them: they should command what God commanded and forbid what He forbade. It was also said: this verse is only for believers among themselves specifically; the first is preferable, as the occasion of revelation that we will mention, God willing, indicates. ﴿Indeed, Satan incites discord among them﴾ meaning by corruption, by casting enmity and by instigation.

Al-Yazidi said: it is said nazaghā bayna-na, meaning he corrupted.

Another said: nazgh means instigation. ﴿Indeed, Satan has always been to man a clear enemy﴾ meaning openly showing enmity and disclosing it. This is an explanation for what precedes it, and a similar expression has already occurred in al-Baqarah.

This has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah.

God took Abraham as a close friend (khalil), made Moses one to whom He spoke (kalim), made Jesus His word and spirit, gave Solomon a great kingdom, forgave Muhammad his earlier and later sins, and made him the master of the children of Adam.

In this verse there is a rebuttal to what the disbelievers denied of what the Messenger of God ﷺ related about the elevation of his rank with his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic. Then He mentioned what He preferred Dawud by, saying: ﴿And We gave David the Psalms (Zabur)﴾, meaning a written book (kitab mazbur).

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, do not deny the preference of Muhammad and his being given the Qur'an, for God gave David the Zabur.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿and rufatan﴾ that he said: dust (ghubar).

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning His saying "and rufatan" that he said: soil (turab). And concerning His saying ﴿Say: "Be stones or iron"﴾ he said: whatever you wish, be it; God will restore you as you were.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Umar concerning His saying ﴿or a creation other than what grows large in your breasts﴾ that he said: death; "If you were death, I would give you life."

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir and al-Hakim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas the like of this.

Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah transmitted from al-Hasan the like of this too.

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar, and he added: He said, "Be death, if you are able, for death itself will die."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿So they will shake their heads at you﴾ that he said: they will move them in mockery.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Mujahid concerning His saying ﴿And they say, "When is it?"﴾ that he said: the restoration.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿so you will respond with His praise﴾ that he said: by His command.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning the verse that he said: they will come out of their graves saying, "Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning ﴿so you will respond with His praise﴾ that he said: with knowledge of Him and obedience to Him. ﴿And you will think you lingered only a little﴾, that is, in the world; the world became small in their souls and seemed little when they witnessed the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Sirin concerning His saying ﴿And say to My servants that they should speak what is best﴾ that he said: "There is no god but God."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Jurayj concerning the verse that he said: He pardons evil deeds.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Hasan that he said: He says to him, "May God have mercy on you; may God forgive you."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah that he said: the incitement of Satan is his stirring up of strife (tahrish).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning His saying ﴿And We gave David the Psalms﴾ that he said: We were told that it is a supplication taught to David and a praise and glorification of God, the Mighty and Majestic, in which there is no lawful or unlawful, no obligations and no prescribed punishments.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Rabi' ibn Anas that he said: the Zabur is praise of God, supplication and glorification.

I say: the matter is as Qatadah and al-Rabi' said, for we have examined the Zabur and found it to be sermons (khutab) which David, peace be upon him, delivered and addressed to his Lord, glorified be He, upon entering the sanctuary (kanisah). Its total is one hundred and fifty sermons, each called a mazmur (psalm), with the first mim open, the zay sukun, the second mim damma, and ending with a ra'. In some of these sermons David complains to his Lord about his enemies and seeks victory over them; in others he praises God, glorifies Him and extols Him for the victory and dominance over them that occurred. During the sermon he would play the qithara, which is an instrument of the musical instruments.

Al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur has mentioned here narrations from a group of the early generations which mention words they found in the Zabur that have little benefit, for what the Qur'an contains of admonitions and warnings has sufficed in place of these and other such things.

When He had finished relating the doubts of the people concerning prophethood, He related their doubt concerning the Return (ma'ad), saying: ﴿And they say, "When we are bones and crumbled dust, shall we indeed be raised up in a new creation?"﴾ The interrogative here expresses denial (istinkar) and disbelief in the possibility (istib'ad).

The doubt may be stated thus: when a person dies, his bones dry up, scatter and are dispersed across the corners of the world, and their elements mix with their likes among the (other) elements. How, then, could it be conceived that they be gathered together in their very same individual forms, and that life return to that assembled mass? Glorified is He, Who answered them: restoring the body of the dead to the state of life is something possible. Even if you suppose that his body has become the farthest thing from life and from the moisture of the living, like stones and iron, (the matter is still possible). This is like the saying of one who says, "Do you hope for anything from me, when I am the son of so-and-so?" and he replies, "Be the son of the sultan, or the son of whomever you wish, and I will still demand my right from you."

Rufat (رُفات) is that which has been broken and decayed of anything, like crumbs (futat), debris (hutam) and fragments (rudad). This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah, al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Akhfash. One says of it: rafata al-shay' rafthan, meaning it was smashed, so it is marfut (broken). It was also said: rufat is dust (ghubar), and it was said: it is soil (turab).

﴿Shall we indeed be raised up in a new creation?﴾ He repeated the interrogative, which indicates denial and disbelief, for emphasis and affirmation. The governing element of idha (إذا) is what is indicated by "la-mab'uthun" (لَمَبْعُوثُونَ), not the word itself, because what comes after inna, the hamza and the lam does not govern what precedes them. The sense is: "Shall we, when we are bones and crumbled dust, be resurrected? Shall we indeed be raised up?" The accusative of khalqan (خَلْقًا) is either as a verbal noun (masdar) from a non-identical verb, or as a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning "created," and jadidan (جَدِيدًا) is its adjective.

﴿Say: "Be stones or iron,"﴾ ﴿or a creation﴾ other ﴿than what grows large in your breasts.﴾ Ibn Jarir said: its meaning is, if you find it strange that God should create for you bones and flesh, then be stones or iron yourselves, if you are able to do so. 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: its meaning is that even if you were stones or iron, He would restore you as He originated you, and cause you to die and then give you life.

Al-Nahhas said: this is a good statement, because they are not able to become stones or iron. The meaning is rather that they had acknowledged their Creator yet denied resurrection, so it was said to them: "Consider that you may be whatever you wish; even if you were stones or iron, you would be raised up as you were created the first time."

I say: on this reading we established the answer to the doubt earlier.

﴿Or a creation other than what grows large in your breasts﴾ means: what is greatest in your estimation, of things greater than stones and iron in being remote from life. For you are certainly to be raised up. It was said that what is meant is the heavens, the earth and the mountains, because of their greatness in souls.

A group of scholars and of the Successors (tabi'un) said: what is meant is death, because there is nothing greater in the soul of the son of Adam than it.

The meaning is: "If you were death, God would cause you to die and then raise you up." The distance of this is not hidden, for the sense of the verse is an ascent from stones to iron, and then from iron to what is greater than it in the breasts of the people. Death itself is not something that perceives and feels, such that an ascent from iron to it would take place.

﴿They will say, "Who will restore us?"﴾ when we are bones and crumbled dust, or stones or iron, along with the disparity between the two states. ﴿Say: "He who originated you the first time."﴾ That is, He Who created you and brought you into being at the beginning of your creation, without any previous pattern or any prior form, will restore you.

﴿They will shake their heads at you﴾ meaning they will move them in mockery. It is said: nagha ra'suhu yanghu, yanghida, yunghidu, naghdan and nughudan, meaning it moved. And anghada ra'sahu means he moved it like one who is astonished. From this is the saying of the rajiz (rajaz poet): "He shook his head toward me and raised his brow," and the saying of another rajiz: "Her teeth shook from old age," and another said: "When she saw me, she shook her head for me."

﴿And they say, "When is it?"﴾ that is, the resurrection and the restoration, mockingly and derisively. ﴿Say: "It may be near."﴾ That is, it is near, because "'asa" (عسى, "it may be") in the speech of God is binding in its occurrence. A similar usage is: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near.﴾ And everything that is coming is near.

﴿On the day He calls you﴾: the time-expression is in the accusative governed by a hidden verb, meaning "remember," or it is a substitute for "near," or the sense is: "On the day He calls you, whatever will be will be." The calling (du'a') is a summons to the place of assembly with a speech that all creatures hear. It was said: it is the Blast (sayha) that you will hear, and it will be a summons to them to gather in the place of assembly. ﴿And you will respond with His praise﴾ meaning submitting to Him and praising Him for what He has done with you. It is thus in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause.

It was also said the meaning is: "And you will respond, and the praise is to God," as the poet said: "And I, by the praise of God, have not worn a sinner's garment, nor do I veil myself with treachery."

It has been reported that the disbelievers, when they come out of their graves, say: "Glory be to You, and praise be to You" (p. 828). It was also said: what is meant by the calling here is the resurrection, and by the response is that they are raised up, so the meaning is: "On the day He raises you up, you will be raised, submitting." ﴿And you will think you lingered only a little﴾ meaning at the resurrection you will think that you did not remain in your graves except for a short time. It was also said: between the two blasts, because punishment is withheld from the punished between the two blasts, and that is forty years, during which they sleep. Therefore ﴿they will say, "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting place?"﴾ It was also said: the world will seem trivial in their eyes and small when they see the Day of Resurrection, so they will say this statement.

﴿And say to My servants that they should speak what is best﴾ meaning: say, O Muhammad, to My believing servants that when they argue with the polytheists they should speak the word that is best, better than other good speech, like His saying: ﴿And do not dispute with the People of the Book except in the way that is best﴾ and His saying: ﴿Speak to him gently﴾, because harshness toward them may repel them from responding or lead to what He mentioned: ﴿And do not revile those whom they invoke besides God, lest they revile God in enmity without knowledge.﴾ This was before the revelation of the verse of the sword. It was also said: the meaning is, say to them: they should command what God commanded and forbid what He forbade. It was also said: this verse is only for believers among themselves specifically; the first is preferable, as the occasion of revelation that we will mention, God willing, indicates. ﴿Indeed, Satan incites discord among them﴾ meaning by corruption, by casting enmity and by instigation.

Al-Yazidi said: it is said nazaghā bayna-na, meaning he corrupted.

Another said: nazgh means instigation. ﴿Indeed, Satan has always been to man a clear enemy﴾ meaning openly showing enmity and disclosing it. This is an explanation for what precedes it, and a similar expression has already occurred in al-Baqarah.

﴿Your Lord knows best about you. If He wills, He will have mercy upon you, or if He wills, He will punish you.﴾ It was said this is addressed to the polytheists. The meaning: if He wills, He will grant you success in Islam and so have mercy on you, or He will cause you to die in polytheism and so punish you. It was also said it is addressed to the believers: that is, if He wills He will have mercy on you by protecting you from the disbelievers, or if He wills He will punish you by giving them power over you. It was also said this is an explanation of "the word that is best."

﴿And We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾ meaning We did not appoint you as a trustee to prevent them from disbelief or to compel them into faith. It was also said: We did not make you a surety for them, for which you would be held accountable. From this is the saying of the poet: "I remembered Abu Arwa, so I spent the night as if I were a trustee (wakil) for the restoration of past affairs." That is, a guarantor (kafil).

﴿And your Lord knows best who is in the heavens and the earth﴾ knows them in essence, state and merit. This is more general than His saying: ﴿Your Lord knows best about you﴾, because this includes all that is in the heavens and the earth of His creatures, whereas that is specific to the children of Adam or some of them.
