Nothing that you used to invoke besides Him, whether an idol, a jinn, an angel, or a human, is found to rescue you, ﴿except Him alone﴾. You then place your hope in His mercy and rescue. The exception here is *munqati'* (disconnected). The meaning of the verse is that the disbelievers believe about their idols and all their other objects of worship only that they benefit them in circumstances other than this one. In this situation, however, each of them knows by innate nature, with a knowledge he cannot repel, that the idols and the like have no power to act. ﴿But when He brings you safely to land, you turn away﴾ from sincerity to Allah and His oneness, and return to invoking your idols and seeking aid from them. ﴿And man has ever been ungrateful﴾, i.e., greatly ungrateful for the blessing of Allah. This is a causal explanation of what preceded it. The meaning is that in times of hardship they cling to Allah's mercy, and in times of ease they turn away from Him.

Then He, glorified is He, rebuked them for their bad conduct, saying: ﴿Do you feel secure that He will not cause the side of the land to swallow you?﴾ The *hamza* is interrogative for denial, and the *fa'* (then) is conjunctive upon an omitted clause, whose estimated sense is: "Have you been delivered, and so you felt secure, and this led you to turn away?" Thus He made clear to them that He is able to destroy them on land, even if they are saved from the sea.

*Al-khasf* (swallowing) is when the earth collapses upon something. It is said: *bi'r khasif* (a well that is caved in) when its base has collapsed; *ayn khasif* (a sunken eye) means one whose pupil is sunk deep in the head; *khasafat 'ayn al-ma'* (the spring of water sank) when its water has receded; and *khasafat al-shams* (the sun was eclipsed) when it set out of sight of the earth. *Janib al-barr* (the side of the land) means the region of the earth. He called it "side" because after the swallowing it becomes a side; and also because the sea is a side of the earth and the land is a side.

It has been said that they were on the sea shore, and its shore is the side of the land, so they felt secure there from the dangers of the sea. Thus He warned them of what they felt secure from on land, just as He warned them of what they feared from the sea.

﴿Or send upon you a violent wind of stones﴾. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Qutaybi said: *al-Hasb* means throwing, i.e., a violent wind that casts [stones], namely a wind that hurls small pebbles. Al-Zajjaj said: *al-Hasib* is dust in which there are pebbles, so *al-hasib* is that which has pebbles, like *laabin* (milky) and *tamir* (dated). It has been said: *al-hasib* is stones from the sky that pelt them, as was done to the people of Lot. The cloud that throws hail is also called *hasib*, and from this is al-Farazdaq's saying:

*Facing the mountains of Syria, they strike us with a hail like scattered cotton-carding.*

﴿Then you will not find for yourselves any protector﴾, i.e., a guardian and helper who would protect you from the might of Allah.

﴿Or do you feel secure that He will not return you to it another time﴾, i.e., to the sea again, by stirring up your motives and multiplying your needs to ride it. He used *fi* (in) rather than saying *ila* (to) the sea, to indicate their settling in it. ﴿Then send upon you a violent wind of storm﴾. *Al-qasif* is the strong wind that breaks forcefully, from *qasafa al-shay'* (he broke the thing forcefully), meaning he broke it violently; *al-qasf* is breaking. Or it is the wind that has a *qasif*, i.e., a loud sound, from their saying: "a thundering thunder" (*ra'd qasif*), meaning very loud. ﴿And drown you﴾. Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Ruways and Mujahid read *fa-tughriqakum* (with a *ta'* at the beginning), with the wind as its subject. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Wardan read *fa-yughriqakum* with a *ya'* and with shadda on the *ra'*. Abu Ja'far also read *al-riyah* (the winds). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read with *nun* (we) in all these verbs.

The rest read with *ya'* in all of them as well. The *ba'* in ﴿because you disbelieved﴾ denotes causation, i.e., because of your disbelief. ﴿Then you will not find for yourselves against Us any avenger for it﴾, i.e., a pursuer who would demand from us what we have done. Al-Zajjaj said: you will not find anyone to follow us in denouncing what has befallen you. Al-Nahhas said: it is from *al-tha'r* (vengeance), and so it is said of anyone who seeks vengeance or other things: *tabi'* and *tabi'* (a pursuer).

﴿And We have certainly honoured the children of Adam﴾. This is a general statement mentioning the blessing that Allah has bestowed upon the children of Adam, i.e., We have honoured them all. This honour includes that He created them in this good form and singled them out with what He has specifically granted them of foods, drinks and clothing, in a manner that none of the other kinds of animals possesses the like of.

Ibn Jarir relates from a group that this honour is that they eat with their hands, while the other animals eat with the mouth; al-Nahhas relates it similarly. It has been said: He distinguished them with speech, intellect and discernment. It has been said: He honoured men with beards and women with long hair. Ibn Jarir said: He honoured them by giving them dominion over all creation and subjecting all creation to them. It has been said: with speech, writing and understanding. There is no obstacle to understanding the honour mentioned in the verse as encompassing all of these things.

The greatest of the qualities of honour is intellect, for by it they have gained dominion over all the animals, distinguished between good and evil, expanded in foods and drinks, and acquired wealth by which they have caused the attainment of matters that animals cannot attain. By it they were able to build dwellings that protect them from what they fear, and to produce garments that shield them from heat and cold. It has been said: their honour is that He made Muhammad (ﷺ) one of them.

﴿And We carried them on land and sea﴾. This is a specification of some kinds of honour. He, glorified is He, carried them on land by means of beasts, and at sea by means of ships. It has been said: We carried them in both [land and sea], in that We did not swallow them up nor drown them.

﴿And provided for them of the good things﴾, i.e., delicious foods and drinks and all that they enjoy and benefit from. ﴿And We preferred them over many of those We created with a [marked] preference﴾. He, glorified is He, left this "many" general and did not explain its kinds. This conveys that He, glorified is He, favoured the children of Adam over many of His creatures. Some scholars have taken "many" here to mean "all," but this is a forced interpretation for which there is no need.

Many scholars have busied themselves with matters for which there is no need and from which no benefit follows, namely the question of whether the angels are superior to the prophets or the prophets to the angels. Among the proofs by which those who prefer the prophets over the angels have held is this verse, but it offers no evidence for their claim, given what you have come to know of the generality of "many" and the failure to specify it. The partisanship in this question is what drove some of the Ash'aris to interpret "many" here as "all," so that the preference over the angels might be established for them. Some of the Mu'tazilites have also taken this verse as evidence for the superiority of the angels over the prophets, but there is no evidence in it for that. At most, the only thing it establishes is that man was not preferred over them. It is therefore possible that they are equal to man, and possible that they are superior to him. With such possibilities, the inference is not complete. The emphasis conveyed by the phrase ﴿with a [marked] preference﴾ indicates the greatness of this preference and that it holds a firm place. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿hasiban﴾ (a violent wind of stones): he said, "A rain of stones."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada, who said: "Stones from the sky."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿qasifan min al-rih﴾ (a violent wind of storm): he said, "The one that drowns."

Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, who said: "The *qasif* and the *'asif* are in the sea."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿qasifan﴾: he said, "'Asifan" (a violent wind). And regarding His saying ﴿Then you will not find for yourselves against Us any avenger for it﴾: he said, "A helper."

Al-Bayhaqi related it through another route, from Ibn 'Amr as a *mawquf* (a statement of a companion) report, and said: "This is the sound one."

It is said: *bi'r khasif* (a well that is caved in) when its base has collapsed; *ayn khasif* (a sunken eye) means one whose pupil is sunk deep in the head; *khasafat 'ayn al-ma'* (the spring of water sank) when its water has receded; and *khasafat al-shams* (the sun was eclipsed) when it set out of sight of the earth. *Janib al-barr* (the side of the land) means the region of the earth. He called it "side" because after the swallowing it becomes a side; and also because the sea is a side of the earth and the land is a side.

It has been said that they were on the sea shore, and its shore is the side of the land, so they felt secure there from the dangers of the sea. Thus He warned them of what they felt secure from on land, just as He warned them of what they feared from the sea.

﴿Or send upon you a violent wind of stones﴾. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Qutaybi said: *al-Hasb* means throwing, i.e., a violent wind that casts [stones], namely a wind that hurls small pebbles. Al-Zajjaj said: *al-Hasib* is dust in which there are pebbles, so *al-hasib* is that which has pebbles, like *laabin* (milky) and *tamir* (dated). It has been said: *al-hasib* is stones from the sky that pelt them, as was done to the people of Lot. The cloud that throws hail is also called *hasib*, and from this is al-Farazdaq's saying:

*Facing the mountains of Syria, they strike us with a hail like scattered cotton-carding.*

﴿Then you will not find for yourselves any protector﴾, i.e., a guardian and helper who would protect you from the might of Allah.

﴿Or do you feel secure that He will not return you to it another time﴾, i.e., to the sea again, by stirring up your motives and multiplying your needs to ride it. He used *fi* (in) rather than saying *ila* (to) the sea, to indicate their settling in it. ﴿Then send upon you a violent wind of storm﴾. *Al-qasif* is the strong wind that breaks forcefully, from *qasafa al-shay'* (he broke the thing forcefully), meaning he broke it violently; *al-qasf* is breaking. Or it is the wind that has a *qasif*, i.e., a loud sound, from their saying: "a thundering thunder" (*ra'd qasif*), meaning very loud. ﴿And drown you﴾. Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Ruways and Mujahid read *fa-tughriqakum* (with a *ta'* at the beginning), with the wind as its subject. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Wardan read *fa-yughriqakum* with a *ya'* and with shadda on the *ra'*. Abu Ja'far also read *al-riyah* (the winds). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read with *nun* (we) in all these verbs.

The rest read with *ya'* in all of them as well. The *ba'* in ﴿because you disbelieved﴾ denotes causation, i.e., because of your disbelief. ﴿Then you will not find for yourselves against Us any avenger for it﴾, i.e., a pursuer who would demand from us what we have done. Al-Zajjaj said: you will not find anyone to follow us in denouncing what has befallen you. Al-Nahhas said: it is from *al-tha'r* (vengeance), and so it is said of anyone who seeks vengeance or other things: *tabi'* and *tabi'* (a pursuer).

Ibn Jarir relates from a group that this honour is that they eat with their hands, while the other animals eat with the mouth; al-Nahhas relates it similarly. It has been said: He distinguished them with speech, intellect and discernment. It has been said: He honoured men with beards and women with long hair. Ibn Jarir said: He honoured them by giving them dominion over all creation and subjecting all creation to them. It has been said: with speech, writing and understanding. There is no obstacle to understanding the honour mentioned in the verse as encompassing all of these things.

The greatest of the qualities of honour is intellect, for by it they have gained dominion over all the animals, distinguished between good and evil, expanded in foods and drinks, and acquired wealth by which they have caused the attainment of matters that animals cannot attain. By it they were able to build dwellings that protect them from what they fear, and to produce garments that shield them from heat and cold. It has been said: their honour is that He made Muhammad (ﷺ) one of them.

﴿And We carried them on land and sea﴾. This is a specification of some kinds of honour. He, glorified is He, carried them on land by means of beasts, and at sea by means of ships. It has been said: We carried them in both [land and sea], in that We did not swallow them up nor drown them.

﴿And provided for them of the good things﴾, i.e., delicious foods and drinks and all that they enjoy and benefit from. ﴿And We preferred them over many of those We created with a [marked] preference﴾. He, glorified is He, left this "many" general and did not explain its kinds. This conveys that He, glorified is He, favoured the children of Adam over many of His creatures. Some scholars have taken "many" here to mean "all," but this is a forced interpretation for which there is no need.

Many scholars have busied themselves with matters for which there is no need and from which no benefit follows, namely the question of whether the angels are superior to the prophets or the prophets to the angels. Among the proofs by which those who prefer the prophets over the angels have held is this verse, but it offers no evidence for their claim, given what you have come to know of the generality of "many" and the failure to specify it. The partisanship in this question is what drove some of the Ash'aris to interpret "many" here as "all," so that the preference over the angels might be established for them. Some of the Mu'tazilites have also taken this verse as evidence for the superiority of the angels over the prophets, but there is no evidence in it for that. For it has not been established that the angels are among the small group excluded from this "many." Even if we concede that, there is nothing in what is excluded from this "many" that indicates they are superior to the children of Adam. At most, the only thing it establishes is that man was not preferred over them. It is therefore possible that they are equal to man, and possible that they are superior to him. With such possibilities, the inference is not complete. The emphasis conveyed by the phrase ﴿with a [marked] preference﴾ indicates the greatness of this preference and that it holds a firm place. Therefore, the children of Adam should receive it with gratitude and beware of ingratitude toward it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿yuzji﴾ (drives): he said, "yujri" (runs). They also related from Qatada, who said: "He moves them through the sea."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿hasiban﴾ (a violent wind of stones): he said, "A rain of stones."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada, who said: "Stones from the sky."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿qasifan min al-rih﴾ (a violent wind of storm): he said, "The one that drowns."

Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, who said: "The *qasif* and the *'asif* are in the sea."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿qasifan﴾: he said, "'Asifan" (a violent wind). And regarding His saying ﴿Then you will not find for yourselves against Us any avenger for it﴾: he said, "A helper."

Al-Tabarani, al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab*, and al-Khatib in his *Tarikh* related from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is nothing more honoured by Allah on the Day of Resurrection than the son of Adam." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, not even the angels?" He said: "Not even the angels. The angels are compelled, in the position of the sun and the moon." Al-Bayhaqi related it through another route, from Ibn 'Amr as a *mawquf* (a statement of a companion) report, and said: "This is the sound one."

Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* related from Abu Hurayra, who said: "The believer is more honoured by Allah than His angels."

Al-Tabarani related from Ibn 'Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The angels said: 'O Lord, You have given the children of Adam the world, in which they eat, drink and wear clothing, while we glorify You with Your praise and do not eat, drink or play. So, just as You have given them the world, give us the Hereafter.' He said: 'I will not make the righteous offspring of those whom I created with My own hand like those to whom I said "Be," and it was.'"

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir related it from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "The angels said..."

The chain of al-Tabarani is thus: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Sadaqa al-Baghdadi narrated to us; Ibrahim ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Khalid al-Misisi narrated to us; Hajjaj ibn Muhammad narrated to us; Abu Ghassan Muhammad ibn Mutarrif ibn Sulaym narrated to us, from 'Ata' ibn Yasar, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), and he mentioned it.

Ibn 'Asakir related through the route of 'Urwa ibn Ruwaym, who said: "Anas ibn Malik narrated to me from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," and he mentioned something similar to the first hadith of Ibn 'Amr, with an addition.

Al-Bayhaqi also related something similar in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* through another route, from 'Urwa ibn Ruwaym, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said..." and he mentioned it.

Al-Hakim in *al-Tarikh* and al-Daylami related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Honour is eating with the fingers."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 17, verses 71–75 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿On the Day We shall call every people with their imam﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it means the Day of Resurrection, and it is in the accusative on the basis of the meaning "remember the Day We call."

It has been read as *yadʻū* with the yāʼ (the verb in the active voice), and as *yudʻā* in the passive. The *bāʼ* in *bi-imāmihim* is for attachment (*ilṣāq*), as when you say, "I call you by your name." It is also permissible for it to be connected to an omitted word that serves as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), the sense being: "We call every people while being accompanied by their imam," that is, "they are called and their imam is among them," like "a rider with his troops." The first is preferable.

In linguistic usage, *imām* (leader, model) is everything that is followed, whether a prophet, a person of rank in religion, or a book.

The exegetes differed in specifying the imam by whom every people is called. Ibn ʻAbbas, al-Ḥasan, Qatada and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it is the book of each person, in which his deeds are recorded; that is, every person is called with the book of his deeds (p-835). This is supported by His saying: ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa 69:19], and so on.

Ibn Zayd said: the imam is the Book sent down to them. So the People of the Torah are called with the Torah, the People of the Gospel with the Gospel, and the People of the Qur'an with the Qur'an, and it is said: "O People of the Torah! O People of the Gospel! O People of the Qur'an!"

Mujahid and Qatada said: their imam is their prophet, so it is said: "Bring forward the followers of Abraham! Bring forward the followers of Moses! Bring forward the followers of Jesus! Bring forward the followers of Muhammad!" This is also the view of al-Zajjaj.

ʻAli ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: the imam is the imam of their age, so the people of every age are called with the imam whose command they obeyed and whose prohibition they heeded.

al-Ḥasan and Abu al-ʻĀliya said: what is meant by their imam is their deeds, so it is said, for example: "Where are the strivers? Where are the patient? Where are the fasters? Where are the worshippers?" and similar. This is narrated from Ibn ʻAbbas and Abu Hurayra.

Abu ʻUbayda said: what is meant by their imam is the master of their school of thought, so it is said, for example: "Where are the followers of the scholar So-and-so, son of So-and-so?" This is a far-fetched view.

Muhammad ibn Kaʻb said: *bi-imāmihim* means "with their mothers," the plural of *umm* being *imām* like *khuff* and *khifāf*. This is very far-fetched.

It has also been said: the imam is every trait that appears in a person, whether good, such as knowledge, generosity and courage, or bad, its opposites. The one who motivates those actions is an inner disposition that is like the imam. al-Rāzī mentioned this meaning in his tafsir.

﴿So whoever is given his record in his right hand﴾ from among those who are called. The singling out of the right hand is for honour and good tidings. ﴿Those﴾: the demonstrative refers to *man* (whoever) according to its meaning.

It has been said: the reason for the plural is to indicate that they are gathered together in a sublime state, or to signal that their reading of their books will be done collectively, not individually. ﴿They shall read their book﴾, which was given to them, ﴿and they will not be wronged a fatil﴾, that is, they will not be deprived of their rewards by the measure of a *fatīl*, which is the thin skin in the cleft of a date-stone, or it is a metaphor for the least thing.

He did not mention the people of the left hand explicitly, but He mentioned what indicates their wretched state, saying: ﴿And whoever is blind in this [world]﴾, that is, whoever among those called was blind in this world, meaning deprived of insight.

al-Naysabūrī said: there is no disagreement that what is meant by this blindness is blindness of the heart. As for His saying: ﴿he will be blind in the Hereafter﴾, it may mean blindness of the eye, as in His saying: ﴿And We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾ and ﴿He will say, "My Lord, why have You raised me blind, when I was [once] seeing?"﴾ [Ṭāhā 20:124–125]. In this there is an increase in punishment. It may also mean blindness of the heart.

It has been said: what is meant by "the Hereafter" is the work of the Hereafter, that is, he is blind in the work or affair of the Hereafter. It has been said: what is meant is one who was blind to the blessings with which Allah favoured him in this world, so he is blind to the blessings of the Hereafter. It has been said: whoever was blind in this world, in which repentance is accepted, will be blind in the Hereafter, in which there is no repentance. It has been said: whoever was blind in this world to the proofs of Allah will be blind in the Hereafter.

It has been said that His saying ﴿he is blind in the Hereafter﴾ is an elative (*afʻal tafḍīl*), meaning "more blind." This is based on it being blindness of the heart, since this is not said of blindness of the eye.

al-Khalīl and Sībawayh said: because it is created in the manner of a hand or a foot, one does not say *mā aʻmāhu* ("how blind he is!"), just as one does not say *mā aydāhu*.

al-Akhfash said: this form is not used of it because it has more than the usual number of letters.

al-Farrāʼ related from some Arabs that he heard them say: *mā aswada shaʻarahu* ("how black his hair is!"). From this is the poet's verse:

*Amma al-mulūku fa-anta al-yawma alʼamuhum*
*lu'man wa-abyaḍuhum sirbāla ṭabbākh*

As for the kings, today you are the most base of them in baseness, and the whitest of them in the garment of a cook.

The discussion is fully treated in grammar works.

Ḥamza, al-Kisāʼī, Abu Bakr and Khalaf read *aʻmā* with *imāla* (the fronting of the vowel) in both places, while Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqūb and the rest read it without *imāla*. Abu ʻUbayd applied *imāla* to the first but not the second.

﴿And more astray in way﴾, meaning that this one is more astray in way than the blind, because he has no path to guidance, unlike the blind man, who may find guidance in some circumstances.

Then, when He had enumerated in the preceding verses the kinds of blessings bestowed on the children of Adam, He followed this with what serves as a warning against being deceived by the whisperings of the wretched, saying: ﴿And indeed, they were about to tempt you away from that which We revealed to you﴾. The particle *in* is the light form of the heavy *inna*, its omitted subject being a pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr shaʼn*). The *lām* is the one that distinguishes it from the negative. The meaning: indeed, the matter is that they came close to deceiving you, tempting you away. The root of *fitna* is testing, and from it comes "the goldsmith tested (*fatana*) the gold." It was then used for anyone who removes a thing from its limit and direction. This is because giving them what they asked for would contravene the judgment of the Qur'an and be a fabrication against Allah, the substitution of a promise for a threat, and other such things. ﴿from that which We revealed to you﴾: of commands, prohibitions, promises and threats. ﴿to fabricate against Us other than it﴾: to invent speech against Us other than what We revealed to you, of what the disbelievers of Quraysh proposed to you. ﴿And then they would have taken you as a friend﴾, that is, if you had followed their desires, they would have taken you as a friend for themselves, meaning they would have been loyal to you and befriended you. It is derived from *khilla* (friendship), with the *kh* vowelled with a *fatḥa*.

﴿And if We had not made you firm﴾ upon the truth and protected you from agreeing with them, ﴿you would have almost inclined to them﴾, that is, you would have come close to inclining towards them even slightly. *Rukūn* is slight inclining, and for this He said: ﴿a little﴾. But the infallibility (*ʻiṣma*) overtook him, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, and prevented him from coming near even the lowest degree of inclining towards them, let alone actual inclining. This is evidence that he, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, did not intend to comply with them. al-Qushayrī and others mentioned this meaning. It has also been said: the meaning is: "And they were about to inform on you that you had inclined to their words," so their act is attributed to him figuratively and by extension, as when you say to a man, "You nearly killed yourself," meaning that people nearly killed you because of what you did. al-Mahdawī mentioned this meaning.

Then He threatened him in that matter with the most severe threat, saying: ﴿Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] in life and double [punishment] in death﴾, that is, if you had come close to inclining towards them, you would have received double the punishment that anyone else who does this would receive in both abodes. The meaning: a punishment doubled in life and a punishment doubled in death, that is, multiplied. Then the qualified noun was omitted, the adjective was put in its place and made into a construct phrase, because the error of a great person is great, as He said: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits an obvious immorality, the punishment will be doubled for her, twofold﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 33:30]. The *ḍiʻf* (double) of a thing is its like, though *ḍiʻf* may also mean a portion, as in His saying: ﴿for each is double﴾ [al-Aʻrāf 7:38], that is, a portion.

al-Rāzī said: the sum of the matter is that if you had let the promptings of Satan enter your heart and had resolved to incline your intention, you would have deserved a doubling of punishment upon you in this world and the next, and your punishment would have been double the punishment of the polytheist in this world and double his punishment in the next. ﴿Then you would not find for yourself against Us any helper﴾ (p-836), who would support you and repel this punishment from you.

al-Naysabūrī said: know that nearness to temptation does not indicate falling into it, and the warning against disobedience does not indicate undertaking it. Therefore the verse does not imply any criticism of infallibility.

﴿And indeed, they were about to unsettle you from the land﴾: the discussion of this is like the discussion of ﴿And indeed, they were about to tempt you﴾. That is, the matter is that they came close to driving you out of the land of Makkah so that you would leave it. But this did not happen from them; rather, Allah prevented them from it until he emigrated by the command of his Lord, and after they had intended it. It has also been said: the expulsion is used figuratively for the intention to expel. ﴿And then they would not have remained after you except for a little while﴾: this is coordinated with *layastafizzūnaka* (they would have unsettled you), that is, they would not have remained after your expulsion except for a short time. Then they were punished with a punishment that uprooted them all.

ʻAṭāʼ ibn Abi Rabāḥ read *lā yulabbathū* with the doubled *bāʼ*.

It is also read *lā yalbathū* with the accusative, by applying *idhan* (then) as an operator, the sentence being coordinated with the sentence *wa-in kādū* and not only with the predicate.

Nāfiʻ, Ibn Kathīr, Abu Bakr and Abu ʻAmr read *khalfaka* (after you), and its meaning is "after you."

Ibn ʻĀmir, Ḥafṣ, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʼī read *khilāfaka*, and its meaning is also "after you."

Ibn al-Anbārī said: *khilāfaka* means "in opposition to you." Abu Ḥātim preferred the second reading, because of His saying: ﴿Those who were left behind rejoiced in their remaining behind, contrary (*khilāfa*) to the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Tawba 9:81].

Among what indicates that *khilāf* means *baʻda* (after) is the poet's verse:

*ʻAfat al-diyāru khilāfahā fa-kaʼannamā*
*basaṭa al-shawāṭib baynahunna ḥaṣīrā*

The dwellings were effaced after them, as if the palm-strip-cutters had spread a mat among them.

It is said: *shaṭabat al-mar'atu al-jarīd* when she split the palm-frond in order to make a mat from it.

Abu ʻUbayda said: then the *shāṭiba* (the one who splits) hands it to the *muthaqqiba* (the one who pierces).

﴿A practice of those We sent before you of Our messengers﴾: *sunnata* is in the accusative as a verbal noun, that is, "Allah has ordained a practice." Al-Farrāʼ said: that is, "they will be punished as the practice of those We sent before," and when the preposition was dropped, the verb governed the noun. It has been said: the meaning is "Our practice is the practice of those We sent before you."

al-Zajjaj said: he says that this practice of Ours concerning those We sent to before you is that when they expelled their prophet from among them or killed him, the punishment would descend upon them. ﴿And you will not find any alteration in Our practice﴾, that is, what Allah has established as a custom cannot be altered by anyone, nor can anyone change it.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʻAbbas, concerning His saying ﴿On the Day We shall call every people with their imam﴾, that he said: "The imam of guidance and the imam of misguidance."

Ibn Abi Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khaṭīb in his *Tārīkh* related from Anas concerning the verse that he said: "Their prophet."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid the like of it. Ibn Jarīr related from Ibn ʻAbbas concerning the verse that he said: "With the book of their deeds."

Ibn Mardawayh related from ʻAlī concerning the verse that he said: "Every people will be called with the imam of their time, the Book of their Lord, and the sunna of their Prophet."

al-Tirmidhī, who graded it as ḥasan, al-Bazzār, Ibn Abi Ḥātim, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Ḥākim, who declared it ṣaḥīḥ, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying ﴿On the Day We shall call every people with their imam﴾, that he said: "One of them will be called and his book will be given to him in his right hand, and his body will be extended for him to sixty cubits, and his face will become white, and a crown of pearls will be placed on his head, shining. He will set off to his companions, and they will see him from afar and say: 'O Allah, bring us this one and bless us in this one,' until he comes to them and says: 'Rejoice, for each of you has one like this.' As for the disbeliever, his face will turn black, and his body will be extended for him to sixty cubits in the form of Adam, and he will be crowned. His companions will see him and say: 'We seek refuge in Allah from the evil of this one. O Allah, do not bring us this one.' He will come to them and they will say: 'O Allah, disgrace him!' He will say: 'May Allah remove you far away, for each of you has one like this.'"

al-Bazzār said after relating it: "It is not narrated except through this route."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 17, verses 71–75 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh, in *al-ʿAẓama*, related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿And whoever is blind in this [world]﴾. He said: Whoever is blind in this world to what he sees of My power, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, the mountains, the seas, the people, the animals and similar things, ( ﴿then he﴾ ) regarding what I have described to him, ( ﴿in the Hereafter﴾ ) and he has not seen it, ﴿[will be] blind and further astray from the way.﴾ He said: more distant from proof.

Al-Firyabi and Ibn Abi Hatim related a similar statement through the chain of ʿIkrimah from him.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him: Whoever is blind to the power of Allah in this world, he will be blind in the Hereafter.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, also saying: "Umayyah ibn Khalaf, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham and some men of Quraysh came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Come, touch our gods and we will enter your religion with you.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was distressed by the separation from his people and loved their Islam, so he became softened toward them, and Allah revealed: ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you away from that which We have revealed to you﴾ up to His words: ﴿a helper.﴾"

Ibn Mardawayh related through the chain of al-Kalbi, from Yadhan, from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, the like of this.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to touch the Black Stone, and they said: 'We will not let you touch it until you touch our gods.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'What harm is there if I do it, while Allah knows what is contrary to it in me?' So Allah revealed: ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you...﴾ the verse."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Shihab a similar account.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Jubayr ibn Nufayr that "Quraysh came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said to him: 'If you have been sent to us, then drive away those who have followed you from the scum of the people and their clients, so that we may be your companions.' He inclined toward them, so Allah revealed to him: ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you...﴾ the verse."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi, who said: Allah revealed ﴿By the star when it falls﴾ [al-Najm: 1]. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited to them this verse: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-ʿUzza﴾ [al-Najm: 19], and Satan then cast upon him: "Those are the exalted cranes, and indeed their intercession is hoped for." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) recited the rest of the surah and prostrated. So Allah revealed: ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you away from that which We revealed to you﴾ the verse. He remained anxious and grieved until Allah revealed: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger or prophet except that when he spoke [i.e., recited], Satan threw [something] into his recitation﴾ [al-Hajj: 52]—the verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas that "Thaqif said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Give us a respite of one year, until gifts are offered to our gods. When we receive what is offered to the gods, we will keep it, then we will embrace Islam and break the gods.' He intended to grant them a delay, so this was revealed: ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you...﴾ the verse."

Ibn Jarir related from him regarding His words ﴿double [punishment] of life and double [punishment] of death﴾: it means double the punishment of this world and the Hereafter.

Al-Bayhaqi related from al-Hasan regarding the verse that he said: it is the punishment of the grave. He also related the like of this from ʿAtaʾ.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, who said: The polytheists said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The prophets used to dwell in al-Sham, so what is your business with Madinah?" He intended to leave, so Allah revealed: ﴿And indeed, they almost drove you out of the land...﴾ the verse.

Ibn Jarir related from Hadrami that it had reached him that some of the Jews said something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* and Ibn ʿAsakir related from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm that "the Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'If you are a prophet, then go to al-Sham, for al-Sham is the land of the gathering and the land of the prophets.' The Prophet (ﷺ) accepted what they said and resolved to campaign toward Tabuk, intending nothing but al-Sham. When he reached Tabuk, Allah revealed to him verses from Surat Bani Isra'il after the surah had been completed: ﴿And indeed, they almost drove you out of the land...﴾ up to His words: ( *tahwilan* ) [a transformation]. So He commanded him to return to Madinah, and said: 'In it is your living, in it is your dying, and from it you will be resurrected.' Gabriel said to him: 'Ask your Lord, for every prophet has a request.' He said: 'What do you command me to ask?' He said: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance and to exit a sound exit, and grant me from Yourself a supporting authority﴾. These [verses] were revealed to him on his return from Tabuk."

Ibn Kathir said: There is scrutiny in this chain, and the apparent view is that it is not authentic, for the Prophet (ﷺ) did not campaign to Tabuk because of the statement of the Jews; rather he campaigned in compliance with His words: ﴿Fight those of the disbelievers who are near to you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 123]. He also campaigned in order to take retribution against those who killed his companions at Mu'tah.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿And indeed, they almost drove you out of the land﴾, that he said: The people of Makkah resolved to expel the Prophet (ﷺ) from Makkah, and they did so afterward, so Allah destroyed them on the day of Badr. They did not remain after him except a little while until Allah destroyed them on the day of Badr. This was the *sunnah* (the established way) of Allah regarding the messengers: when their people did to them the like of that, [Allah would destroy them].

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿And then they would not remain after you except a little﴾ that he said: By "a little" He means the day of their seizure at Badr, and that was the "little" in which they remained after him.

His saying: ﴿On the Day We shall call every people with their imam﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it means the Day of Resurrection, and it is in the accusative on the basis of the meaning "remember the Day We call."

It has been read as *yadʻū* with the yāʼ (the verb in the active voice), and as *yudʻā* in the passive. The *bāʼ* in *bi-imāmihim* is for attachment (*ilṣāq*), as when you say, "I call you by your name." It is also permissible for it to be connected to an omitted word that serves as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), the sense being: "We call every people while being accompanied by their imam," that is, "they are called and their imam is among them," like "a rider with his troops." The first is preferable.

In linguistic usage, *imām* (leader, model) is everything that is followed, whether a prophet, a person of rank in religion, or a book.

The exegetes differed in specifying the imam by whom every people is called. Ibn ʻAbbas, al-Ḥasan, Qatada and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it is the book of each person, in which his deeds are recorded; that is, every person is called with the book of his deeds (p-835). This is supported by His saying: ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa 69:19], and so on.

Ibn Zayd said: the imam is the Book sent down to them. So the People of the Torah are called with the Torah, the People of the Gospel with the Gospel, and the People of the Qur'an with the Qur'an, and it is said: "O People of the Torah! O People of the Gospel! O People of the Qur'an!"

Mujahid and Qatada said: their imam is their prophet, so it is said: "Bring forward the followers of Abraham! Bring forward the followers of Moses! Bring forward the followers of Jesus! Bring forward the followers of Muhammad!" This is also the view of al-Zajjaj.

ʻAli ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: the imam is the imam of their age, so the people of every age are called with the imam whose command they obeyed and whose prohibition they heeded.

al-Ḥasan and Abu al-ʻĀliya said: what is meant by their imam is their deeds, so it is said, for example: "Where are the strivers? Where are the patient? Where are the fasters? Where are the worshippers?" and similar. This is narrated from Ibn ʻAbbas and Abu Hurayra.

Abu ʻUbayda said: what is meant by their imam is the master of their school of thought, so it is said, for example: "Where are the followers of the scholar So-and-so, son of So-and-so?" This is a far-fetched view.

Muhammad ibn Kaʻb said: *bi-imāmihim* means "with their mothers," the plural of *umm* being *imām* like *khuff* and *khifāf*. This is very far-fetched.

It has also been said: the imam is every trait that appears in a person, whether good, such as knowledge, generosity and courage, or bad, its opposites. The one who motivates those actions is an inner disposition that is like the imam. al-Rāzī mentioned this meaning in his tafsir.

﴿So whoever is given his record in his right hand﴾ from among those who are called. The singling out of the right hand is for honour and good tidings. ﴿Those﴾: the demonstrative refers to *man* (whoever) according to its meaning.

It has been said: the reason for the plural is to indicate that they are gathered together in a sublime state, or to signal that their reading of their books will be done collectively, not individually. ﴿They shall read their book﴾, which was given to them, ﴿and they will not be wronged a fatil﴾, that is, they will not be deprived of their rewards by the measure of a *fatīl*, which is the thin skin in the cleft of a date-stone, or it is a metaphor for the least thing.

He did not mention the people of the left hand explicitly, but He mentioned what indicates their wretched state, saying: ﴿And whoever is blind in this [world]﴾, that is, whoever among those called was blind in this world, meaning deprived of insight.

al-Naysabūrī said: there is no disagreement that what is meant by this blindness is blindness of the heart. As for His saying: ﴿he will be blind in the Hereafter﴾, it may mean blindness of the eye, as in His saying: ﴿And We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾ and ﴿He will say, "My Lord, why have You raised me blind, when I was [once] seeing?"﴾ [Ṭāhā 20:124–125]. In this there is an increase in punishment. It may also mean blindness of the heart.

It has been said: what is meant by "the Hereafter" is the work of the Hereafter, that is, he is blind in the work or affair of the Hereafter. It has been said: what is meant is one who was blind to the blessings with which Allah favoured him in this world, so he is blind to the blessings of the Hereafter. It has been said: whoever was blind in this world, in which repentance is accepted, will be blind in the Hereafter, in which there is no repentance. It has been said: whoever was blind in this world to the proofs of Allah will be blind in the Hereafter.

Then they were punished with a punishment that uprooted them all.

ʻAṭāʼ ibn Abi Rabāḥ read *lā yulabbathū* with the doubled *bāʼ*.

It is also read *lā yalbathū* with the accusative, by applying *idhan* (then) as an operator, the sentence being coordinated with the sentence *wa-in kādū* and not only with the predicate.

Nāfiʻ, Ibn Kathīr, Abu Bakr and Abu ʻAmr read *khalfaka* (after you), and its meaning is "after you."

Ibn ʻĀmir, Ḥafṣ, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʼī read *khilāfaka*, and its meaning is also "after you."

Ibn al-Anbārī said: *khilāfaka* means "in opposition to you." Abu Ḥātim preferred the second reading, because of His saying: ﴿Those who were left behind rejoiced in their remaining behind, contrary (*khilāfa*) to the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Tawba 9:81].

Among what indicates that *khilāf* means *baʻda* (after) is the poet's verse:

*ʻAfat al-diyāru khilāfahā fa-kaʼannamā*
*basaṭa al-shawāṭib baynahunna ḥaṣīrā*

The dwellings were effaced after them, as if the palm-strip-cutters had spread a mat among them.

It is said: *shaṭabat al-mar'atu al-jarīd* when she split the palm-frond in order to make a mat from it.

Abu ʻUbayda said: then the *shāṭiba* (the one who splits) hands it to the *muthaqqiba* (the one who pierces).

﴿A practice of those We sent before you of Our messengers﴾: *sunnata* is in the accusative as a verbal noun, that is, "Allah has ordained a practice." Al-Farrāʼ said: that is, "they will be punished as the practice of those We sent before," and when the preposition was dropped, the verb governed the noun. It has been said: the meaning is "Our practice is the practice of those We sent before you."

al-Zajjaj said: he says that this practice of Ours concerning those We sent to before you is that when they expelled their prophet from among them or killed him, the punishment would descend upon them. ﴿And you will not find any alteration in Our practice﴾, that is, what Allah has established as a custom cannot be altered by anyone, nor can anyone change it.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʻAbbas, concerning His saying ﴿On the Day We shall call every people with their imam﴾, that he said: "The imam of guidance and the imam of misguidance."

Ibn Abi Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khaṭīb in his *Tārīkh* related from Anas concerning the verse that he said: "Their prophet."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid the like of it. Ibn Jarīr related from Ibn ʻAbbas concerning the verse that he said: "With the book of their deeds."

Ibn Mardawayh related from ʻAlī concerning the verse that he said: "Every people will be called with the imam of their time, the Book of their Lord, and the sunna of their Prophet."

al-Tirmidhī, who graded it as ḥasan, al-Bazzār, Ibn Abi Ḥātim, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Ḥākim, who declared it ṣaḥīḥ, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying ﴿On the Day We shall call every people with their imam﴾, that he said: "One of them will be called and his book will be given to him in his right hand, and his body will be extended for him to sixty cubits, and his face will become white, and a crown of pearls will be placed on his head, shining. He will set off to his companions, and they will see him from afar and say: 'O Allah, bring us this one and bless us in this one,' until he comes to them and says: 'Rejoice, for each of you has one like this.' As for the disbeliever, his face will turn black, and his body will be extended for him to sixty cubits in the form of Adam, and he will be crowned. His companions will see him and say: 'We seek refuge in Allah from the evil of this one. O Allah, do not bring us this one.' He will come to them and they will say: 'O Allah, disgrace him!' He will say: 'May Allah remove you far away, for each of you has one like this.'"

al-Bazzār said after relating it: "It is not narrated except through this route."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 17, verses 71–75 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh, in *al-ʿAẓama*, related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿And whoever is blind in this [world]﴾. He said: Whoever is blind in this world to what he sees of My power, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, the mountains, the seas, the people, the animals and similar things, ( ﴿then he﴾ ) regarding what I have described to him, ( ﴿in the Hereafter﴾ ) and he has not seen it, ﴿[will be] blind and further astray from the way.﴾ He said: more distant from proof.

Al-Firyabi and Ibn Abi Hatim related a similar statement through the chain of ʿIkrimah from him.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him: Whoever is blind to the power of Allah in this world, he will be blind in the Hereafter.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, also saying: "Umayyah ibn Khalaf, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham and some men of Quraysh came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Come, touch our gods and we will enter your religion with you.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was distressed by the separation from his people and loved their Islam, so he became softened toward them, and Allah revealed: ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you away from that which We have revealed to you﴾ up to His words: ﴿a helper.﴾"

Ibn Mardawayh related through the chain of al-Kalbi, from Yadhan, from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, the like of this.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to touch the Black Stone, and they said: 'We will not let you touch it until you touch our gods.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'What harm is there if I do it, while Allah knows what is contrary to it in me?' So Allah revealed: ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you...﴾ the verse."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Shihab a similar account.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Jubayr ibn Nufayr that "Quraysh came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said to him: 'If you have been sent to us, then drive away those who have followed you from the scum of the people and their clients, so that we may be your companions.' He inclined toward them, so Allah revealed to him: ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you...﴾ the verse."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi, who said: Allah revealed ﴿By the star when it falls﴾ [al-Najm: 1]. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited to them this verse: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-ʿUzza﴾ [al-Najm: 19], and Satan then cast upon him: "Those are the exalted cranes, and indeed their intercession is hoped for." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) recited the rest of the surah and prostrated. So Allah revealed: ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you away from that which We revealed to you﴾ the verse. He remained anxious and grieved until Allah revealed: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger or prophet except that when he spoke [i.e., recited], Satan threw [something] into his recitation﴾ [al-Hajj: 52]—the verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas that "Thaqif said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Give us a respite of one year, until gifts are offered to our gods. When we receive what is offered to the gods, we will keep it, then we will embrace Islam and break the gods.' He intended to grant them a delay, so this was revealed: ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you...﴾ the verse."

Ibn Jarir related from him regarding His words ﴿double [punishment] of life and double [punishment] of death﴾: it means double the punishment of this world and the Hereafter.

Al-Bayhaqi related from al-Hasan regarding the verse that he said: it is the punishment of the grave. He also related the like of this from ʿAtaʾ.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, who said: The polytheists said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The prophets used to dwell in al-Sham, so what is your business with Madinah?" He intended to leave, so Allah revealed: ﴿And indeed, they almost drove you out of the land...﴾ the verse.

Ibn Jarir related from Hadrami that it had reached him that some of the Jews said something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* and Ibn ʿAsakir related from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm that "the Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'If you are a prophet, then go to al-Sham, for al-Sham is the land of the gathering and the land of the prophets.' The Prophet (ﷺ) accepted what they said and resolved to campaign toward Tabuk, intending nothing but al-Sham. When he reached Tabuk, Allah revealed to him verses from Surat Bani Isra'il after the surah had been completed: ﴿And indeed, they almost drove you out of the land...﴾ up to His words: ( *tahwilan* ) [a transformation]. So He commanded him to return to Madinah, and said: 'In it is your living, in it is your dying, and from it you will be resurrected.' Gabriel said to him: 'Ask your Lord, for every prophet has a request.' He said: 'What do you command me to ask?' He said: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance and to exit a sound exit, and grant me from Yourself a supporting authority﴾. These [verses] were revealed to him on his return from Tabuk."

Ibn Kathir said: There is scrutiny in this chain, and the apparent view is that it is not authentic, for the Prophet (ﷺ) did not campaign to Tabuk because of the statement of the Jews; rather he campaigned in compliance with His words: ﴿Fight those of the disbelievers who are near to you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 123]. He also campaigned in order to take retribution against those who killed his companions at Mu'tah.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿And indeed, they almost drove you out of the land﴾, that he said: The people of Makkah resolved to expel the Prophet (ﷺ) from Makkah, and they did so afterward, so Allah destroyed them on the day of Badr. They did not remain after him except a little while until Allah destroyed them on the day of Badr. This was the *sunnah* (the established way) of Allah regarding the messengers: when their people did to them the like of that, [Allah would destroy them].

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿And then they would not remain after you except a little﴾ that he said: By "a little" He means the day of their seizure at Badr, and that was the "little" in which they remained after him.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 17, verses 71–75 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿On the Day We shall call every people with their imam﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it means the Day of Resurrection, and it is in the accusative on the basis of the meaning "remember the Day We call."

It has been read as *yadʻū* with the yāʼ (the verb in the active voice), and as *yudʻā* in the passive. The *bāʼ* in *bi-imāmihim* is for attachment (*ilṣāq*), as when you say, "I call you by your name." It is also permissible for it to be connected to an omitted word that serves as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), the sense being: "We call every people while being accompanied by their imam," that is, "they are called and their imam is among them," like "a rider with his troops." The first is preferable.

In linguistic usage, *imām* (leader, model) is everything that is followed, whether a prophet, a person of rank in religion, or a book.

The exegetes differed in specifying the imam by whom every people is called. Ibn ʻAbbas, al-Ḥasan, Qatada and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it is the book of each person, in which his deeds are recorded; that is, every person is called with the book of his deeds (p-835). This is supported by His saying: ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa 69:19], and so on.

Ibn Zayd said: the imam is the Book sent down to them. So the People of the Torah are called with the Torah, the People of the Gospel with the Gospel, and the People of the Qur'an with the Qur'an, and it is said: "O People of the Torah! O People of the Gospel! O People of the Qur'an!"

Mujahid and Qatada said: their imam is their prophet, so it is said: "Bring forward the followers of Abraham! Bring forward the followers of Moses! Bring forward the followers of Jesus! Bring forward the followers of Muhammad!" This is also the view of al-Zajjaj.

ʻAli ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: the imam is the imam of their age, so the people of every age are called with the imam whose command they obeyed and whose prohibition they heeded.

al-Ḥasan and Abu al-ʻĀliya said: what is meant by their imam is their deeds, so it is said, for example: "Where are the strivers? Where are the patient? Where are the fasters? Where are the worshippers?" and similar. This is narrated from Ibn ʻAbbas and Abu Hurayra.

Abu ʻUbayda said: what is meant by their imam is the master of their school of thought, so it is said, for example: "Where are the followers of the scholar So-and-so, son of So-and-so?" This is a far-fetched view.

Muhammad ibn Kaʻb said: *bi-imāmihim* means "with their mothers," the plural of *umm* being *imām* like *khuff* and *khifāf*. This is very far-fetched.

It has also been said: the imam is every trait that appears in a person, whether good, such as knowledge, generosity and courage, or bad, its opposites. The one who motivates those actions is an inner disposition that is like the imam. al-Rāzī mentioned this meaning in his tafsir.

﴿So whoever is given his record in his right hand﴾ from among those who are called. The singling out of the right hand is for honour and good tidings. ﴿Those﴾: the demonstrative refers to *man* (whoever) according to its meaning.

It has been said: the reason for the plural is to indicate that they are gathered together in a sublime state, or to signal that their reading of their books will be done collectively, not individually. ﴿They shall read their book﴾, which was given to them, ﴿and they will not be wronged a fatil﴾, that is, they will not be deprived of their rewards by the measure of a *fatīl*, which is the thin skin in the cleft of a date-stone, or it is a metaphor for the least thing.

He did not mention the people of the left hand explicitly, but He mentioned what indicates their wretched state, saying: ﴿And whoever is blind in this [world]﴾, that is, whoever among those called was blind in this world, meaning deprived of insight.

al-Naysabūrī said: there is no disagreement that what is meant by this blindness is blindness of the heart. As for His saying: ﴿he will be blind in the Hereafter﴾, it may mean blindness of the eye, as in His saying: ﴿And We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾ and ﴿He will say, "My Lord, why have You raised me blind, when I was [once] seeing?"﴾ [Ṭāhā 20:124–125]. In this there is an increase in punishment. It may also mean blindness of the heart.

It has been said: what is meant by "the Hereafter" is the work of the Hereafter, that is, he is blind in the work or affair of the Hereafter. It has been said: what is meant is one who was blind to the blessings with which Allah favoured him in this world, so he is blind to the blessings of the Hereafter. It has been said: whoever was blind in this world, in which repentance is accepted, will be blind in the Hereafter, in which there is no repentance. It has been said: whoever was blind in this world to the proofs of Allah will be blind in the Hereafter.

It has been said that His saying ﴿he is blind in the Hereafter﴾ is an elative (*afʻal tafḍīl*), meaning "more blind." This is based on it being blindness of the heart, since this is not said of blindness of the eye.

al-Khalīl and Sībawayh said: because it is created in the manner of a hand or a foot, one does not say *mā aʻmāhu* ("how blind he is!"), just as one does not say *mā aydāhu*.

al-Akhfash said: this form is not used of it because it has more than the usual number of letters.

al-Farrāʼ related from some Arabs that he heard them say: *mā aswada shaʻarahu* ("how black his hair is!"). From this is the poet's verse:

*Amma al-mulūku fa-anta al-yawma alʼamuhum*
*lu'man wa-abyaḍuhum sirbāla ṭabbākh*

As for the kings, today you are the most base of them in baseness, and the whitest of them in the garment of a cook.

The discussion is fully treated in grammar works.

Ḥamza, al-Kisāʼī, Abu Bakr and Khalaf read *aʻmā* with *imāla* (the fronting of the vowel) in both places, while Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqūb and the rest read it without *imāla*. Abu ʻUbayd applied *imāla* to the first but not the second.

﴿And more astray in way﴾, meaning that this one is more astray in way than the blind, because he has no path to guidance, unlike the blind man, who may find guidance in some circumstances.

Then, when He had enumerated in the preceding verses the kinds of blessings bestowed on the children of Adam, He followed this with what serves as a warning against being deceived by the whisperings of the wretched, saying: ﴿And indeed, they were about to tempt you away from that which We revealed to you﴾. The particle *in* is the light form of the heavy *inna*, its omitted subject being a pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr shaʼn*). The *lām* is the one that distinguishes it from the negative. The meaning: indeed, the matter is that they came close to deceiving you, tempting you away. The root of *fitna* is testing, and from it comes "the goldsmith tested (*fatana*) the gold." It was then used for anyone who removes a thing from its limit and direction. This is because giving them what they asked for would contravene the judgment of the Qur'an and be a fabrication against Allah, the substitution of a promise for a threat, and other such things. ﴿from that which We revealed to you﴾: of commands, prohibitions, promises and threats. ﴿to fabricate against Us other than it﴾: to invent speech against Us other than what We revealed to you, of what the disbelievers of Quraysh proposed to you. ﴿And then they would have taken you as a friend﴾, that is, if you had followed their desires, they would have taken you as a friend for themselves, meaning they would have been loyal to you and befriended you. It is derived from *khilla* (friendship), with the *kh* vowelled with a *fatḥa*.

﴿And if We had not made you firm﴾ upon the truth and protected you from agreeing with them, ﴿you would have almost inclined to them﴾, that is, you would have come close to inclining towards them even slightly. *Rukūn* is slight inclining, and for this He said: ﴿a little﴾. But the infallibility (*ʻiṣma*) overtook him, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, and prevented him from coming near even the lowest degree of inclining towards them, let alone actual inclining. This is evidence that he, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, did not intend to comply with them. al-Qushayrī and others mentioned this meaning. It has also been said: the meaning is: "And they were about to inform on you that you had inclined to their words," so their act is attributed to him figuratively and by extension, as when you say to a man, "You nearly killed yourself," meaning that people nearly killed you because of what you did. al-Mahdawī mentioned this meaning.

Then He threatened him in that matter with the most severe threat, saying: ﴿Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] in life and double [punishment] in death﴾, that is, if you had come close to inclining towards them, you would have received double the punishment that anyone else who does this would receive in both abodes. The meaning: a punishment doubled in life and a punishment doubled in death, that is, multiplied. Then the qualified noun was omitted, the adjective was put in its place and made into a construct phrase, because the error of a great person is great, as He said: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits an obvious immorality, the punishment will be doubled for her, twofold﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 33:30]. The *ḍiʻf* (double) of a thing is its like, though *ḍiʻf* may also mean a portion, as in His saying: ﴿for each is double﴾ [al-Aʻrāf 7:38], that is, a portion.

al-Rāzī said: the sum of the matter is that if you had let the promptings of Satan enter your heart and had resolved to incline your intention, you would have deserved a doubling of punishment upon you in this world and the next, and your punishment would have been double the punishment of the polytheist in this world and double his punishment in the next. ﴿Then you would not find for yourself against Us any helper﴾ (p-836), who would support you and repel this punishment from you.

al-Naysabūrī said: know that nearness to temptation does not indicate falling into it, and the warning against disobedience does not indicate undertaking it. Therefore the verse does not imply any criticism of infallibility.

﴿And indeed, they were about to unsettle you from the land﴾: the discussion of this is like the discussion of ﴿And indeed, they were about to tempt you﴾. That is, the matter is that they came close to driving you out of the land of Makkah so that you would leave it. But this did not happen from them; rather, Allah prevented them from it until he emigrated by the command of his Lord, and after they had intended it. It has also been said: the expulsion is used figuratively for the intention to expel. ﴿And then they would not have remained after you except for a little while﴾: this is coordinated with *layastafizzūnaka* (they would have unsettled you), that is, they would not have remained after your expulsion except for a short time. Then they were punished with a punishment that uprooted them all.
