The second is that it is a healing from apparent illnesses through incantations (*ruqa*), seeking refuge (*ta'awwudh*), and the like. There is no barrier to taking *shifa'* in both senses, either by the generality of metaphor (*ʿumum al-majaz*) or by treating a homonym (*mushtarak*) as carrying both of its meanings.

Then He, glorified is He, stated that it is a mercy for the believers, because of the beneficial sciences it contains, which include what is good for the religion and for the world, and because of the great reward in reciting and reflecting upon it, which is a cause of the mercy, forgiveness and good pleasure of God, glorified is He. A similar verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing. But as for those who do not believe, there is deafness in their ears, and it is blindness for them."﴾ [Fussilat: 44]

Then, when He, glorified is He, mentioned the benefit the Qur'an contains for His believing servants, He mentioned the harm it contains for everyone else, and said: ﴿And it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss.﴾ That is: the Qur'an, all of it or every part of it, does not increase the wrongdoers, who put denial in the place of affirmation and doubt and suspicion in the place of certainty and tranquility, ﴿except in loss﴾, that is, in destruction. This is because hearing the Qur'an enrages them, provokes them, and calls them to commit even more abominations out of rebellion and obstinacy, and at that point they are destroyed. It is also said that *al-khasar* means deficiency, as in His saying: ﴿so it increased them in defilement upon their defilement﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125].

Then He, glorified is He, drew attention to the disclosure of some of the blameworthy dispositions with which man was created, and said: ﴿And when We bestow favour upon man﴾, that is, upon this kind, with blessings that call for gratitude, such as health and wealth, ﴿he turns away﴾ from giving thanks to God and from remembering Him, ﴿and distances himself [*nā'a bi-janibihi*]﴾. *Al-nay'* is distance, and the *ba'* is either for transitivity or for accompaniment. This is an emphasis on turning away, because turning away from a thing means turning the face of one's side (*'ard al-wajh*) away from it, that is, its direction. Distancing with the side means bending one's flank away from it and turning one's back to it. It is not far-fetched that what is meant by turning away here is turning away from supplication and entreaty, which he used to do when affliction and trial came upon him, and that what is meant by distancing with the side is arrogance and withdrawing oneself from discharging the rights of blessings.

Ibn 'Amir, in the transmission of Ibn Dhakwan, and Abu Ja'far recited *nā'a*, like *bā'a*, with the *hamza* moved later, by metathesis (*al-qalb*). Hamza recited *nā'ā* with *imala* of both fathas, and al-Kisa'i agreed with him. Shu'ba and al-Susi applied *imala* to the *hamza* only. The rest recited both with *fath*.

﴿And when evil touches him﴾, from illness or poverty, ﴿he is ever despairing, extremely hopeless of the mercy of God.﴾ The meaning is that if he attains worldly aims and achieves what he desires, he forgets the One who is worshipped; and if something of that escapes him, grief overcomes him and despair dominates him. Both of these traits are ugly and blameworthy. What is in this verse is not contradicted by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when evil touches him, he is one of abundant supplication﴾ [Fussilat: 51], nor by similar verses, because that is the characteristic of another group among them, other than the group mentioned in this verse. It is not far-fetched to say that there is no contradiction between the two verses: it may be that, together with his intense despair and great hopelessness, he frequently supplicates with his tongue.

﴿Say: "Each acts according to his own manner [*shakilatihi*]."﴾ *Al-shakila* (manner), said al-Farra', is the way or path. It is also said to mean direction, nature, religion, intention, or innate disposition. It is derived from *al-shakl* (form), as one says: "You are not of my form or of my manner." *Al-shakl* is the like and the equal.

The meaning is that every person acts according to what suits the character he has become accustomed to, and this is a reproach to the disbeliever and a praise of the believer. ﴿Your Lord knows best who is best guided in the way.﴾ Because He is the Creator of you, and the Knower of what you are created with of dispositions and of what you differ in of ways. It is He who distinguishes between the believer, who does not turn away when blessed and does not despair when tested, and the disbeliever, whose habit is insolence at blessings and despair at afflictions.

Then, since the discourse had drifted to mention of man and what he was created with, He, glorified is He, mentioned the question that people asked the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, about the *ruh* (spirit). He said: ﴿And they ask you about the spirit.﴾ People have differed about the *ruh* that was asked about. It is said that it is the spirit that governs the body, by which life exists. This is the view of most exegetes.

Al-Farra' said: the spirit by which man lives is something God, glorified is He, did not inform any of His creatures about, and He did not give knowledge of it to any of His servants. So He said: ﴿Say: "The spirit is of the command of my Lord."﴾ That is: you do not know it. It is also said that the spirit being asked about is Gabriel. It is said to be Jesus. It is said to be the Qur'an. It is said to be an angel of great creation. It is said to be a creation like the creation of the children of Adam. And other views have been said which carry no benefit and whose inclusion is of no use. The apparent view is the first, and the cause of the revelation of this verse, and the identity of those who asked the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, about the spirit, will come later. Apparently the question was about the reality of the spirit, because knowing the reality of a thing is more important and prior to knowing one of its states.

Then God, glorified is He, commanded him to answer those who asked him about the spirit, and said: ﴿Say: "The spirit is of the command of my Lord."﴾ The *min* here is explanatory (*bayaniyya*). *Al-amr* means matter or affair, and the idafa (construct) is for specification. That is: it is of the kind of things God has kept to Himself knowledge of, things He has not made known to His servants. It is also said that the meaning of "of the command of my Lord" is: of His revelation and His speech, not of the speech of human beings.

In this verse there is a rebuke, most forceful, to those who plunge into the question of the spirit, who burden themselves to explain what its form is and to clarify its reality, and a most powerful deterrent for them. They have prolonged discourse on this subject beyond what the matter can bear. Most of it, indeed all of it, is among the superfluities that bring no benefit to religion or to the world.

Some researchers have related that the opinions of those who differ about the spirit reached one thousand eight hundred opinions. So consider this empty superfluity and this fruitless toil devoid of benefit, after they knew that God, glorified is He, has kept its knowledge to Himself, and did not inform His prophets of it, nor did He permit them to ask about it or to investigate its reality, let alone their communities who follow them. How strange it is, by God, that the opinions of the people of superfluity should reach this limit, which they did not reach, nor even part of it, in other matters on which God has permitted discussion and has not kept its knowledge to Himself.

Then God, glorified is He, concluded this verse with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little.﴾ That is: the knowledge that God has taught you is nothing but a small amount in comparison with the knowledge of the Creator, glorified is He, even if you have been given a large share of knowledge. Indeed, the knowledge of the prophets, peace be upon them, in comparison with the knowledge of God, glorified is He, is nothing but what a bird takes in its beak from the sea, as in the hadith of Musa and al-Khidr, peace be upon them both.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "*Duluk al-shams* is its setting (*ghurubuha*). The Arabs say, when the sun sets: *dalakat al-shams* (the sun has declined)."

Ibn Abi Shayba and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ali, who said: "*Duluquha* is its setting."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said, regarding ﴿at the decline of the sun﴾: "The departure of the sun (*zawal al-shams*)."

al-Bazzar, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Daylami transmitted from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: '*Dulūk al-shams* is its departure (*zawaluha*).'" al-Suyuti graded its chain as weak. Malik transmitted it in the Muwatta', and 'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted it from Ibn 'Umar as his own statement.

'Abd al-Razzaq transmitted from him, who said: "*Duluk al-shams* is its inclination (*ziyaguha*) after midday."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "*Duluquha* is its departure (*zawaluha*)."

Ibn Abi Shayba and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him, regarding God's saying ﴿at the decline of the sun﴾, that he said: "When the shade (*al-fay'*) begins to move."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Abu Mas'ud and 'Uqba ibn 'Amr, who both said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: 'Gabriel came to me at the decline of the sun, when it had passed its zenith, and led me in the noon prayer (*al-zuhr*).'"

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Abu Barza al-Aslami, who said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, used to pray the noon prayer when the sun had passed its zenith, then he recited: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted something similar from a hadith of Anas. Among what is cited as evidence that *al-duluk* is the zenith of midday is what Ibn Jarir transmitted from Jabir, who said: "I invited the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and whomever of his companions wished to be fed at my house. Then they left when the sun had passed its zenith. The Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, went out and said: 'Go out, O Abu Bakr, for this is the time when the sun has declined (*dalakat*).'" There is an unknown narrator in its chain. However, Ibn Jarir transmitted it from him by another route, from Sahl ibn Bakkar, from Abu 'Awana, from al-Aswad ibn Qays, from Nubayh al-'Anbari, from Jabir, and mentioned something similar, traced to the Prophet (*marfu'an*).

al-Tabarani transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud regarding God's saying ﴿until the darkness of the night﴾, that he said: "Until the late evening prayer (*al-'isha' al-akhira*)."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "*Ghasaq al-layl* is the gathering of the night and its darkness."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him, who said: "*Ghasaq al-layl* is the beginning of the night."

'Abd al-Razzaq transmitted from Abu Hurayra, who said: "*Duluk al-shams* is when the sun leaves the middle of the sky, and *ghasaq al-layl* is the setting of the sun."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding God's saying ﴿and the Qur'an of dawn﴾, that he said: "It is the dawn prayer (*salat al-subh*)."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* transmitted from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, regarding God's saying: ﴿and the Qur'an of dawn; indeed, the Qur'an of dawn is ever witnessed﴾. He said: "The angels of the night and the angels of the day witness it, and they gather in it." It is in the two *Sahihs* from him, as a marfu' report, with the wording: "The angels of the night and the angels of the day gather at the dawn prayer." Then Abu Hurayra said: "Recite, if you wish: ﴿and the Qur'an of dawn; indeed, the Qur'an of dawn is ever witnessed﴾."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Tabarani transmitted something similar from Ibn Mas'ud as a mawquf report.

(p. 840)

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu al-Darda', who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾. He said: "The angels of the night and the angels of the day witness it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿as an additional [prayer] for you﴾, that he said: "That is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ). He was commanded to pray the night vigil, and it was made obligatory upon him."

al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Aishah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Three things are obligatory upon me, and for you they are a sunnah: the witr, the siwak, and the night prayer."

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Umamah, regarding His words: ﴿as an additional [prayer] for you﴾, that he said: "It was an additional [prayer] for the Prophet (ﷺ), and for you it is a virtue." In another wording: "The additional prayer was only specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Hurairah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His words: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾, and when he was asked about it, he said: "It is the praiseworthy station, in which I will intercede for my ummah."

Ahmad (p-841), Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ka'b ibn Malik that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "People will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection, and I and my ummah will be on a hill, and my Lord will clothe me in a green garment. Then I will be given permission, and I will say what Allah wills me to say. That is the praiseworthy station."

al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: "On the Day of Resurrection every nation will follow its prophet, saying: 'O so-and-so, intercede! O so-and-so, intercede!' until the intercession reaches the Prophet (ﷺ). That is the day on which Allah will raise him to a praiseworthy station."

He also narrated something similar to it from him, as a marfu' report. The narrations on this subject are very numerous and firmly established in the two Sahihs and elsewhere, so we will not lengthen by mentioning them. Whoever wishes for a full survey should examine the hadiths on intercession, including the intercession of the mothers and others.

al-Tabarani narrated, regarding His words: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾, that he said: "He will seat him between Himself and Jibril, and he will intercede for his ummah. That is the praiseworthy station."

al-Daylami narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: (﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾) he said: 'He will seat me with Him upon the throne.'" It is necessary to investigate the chain of narration of these two hadiths.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sahih, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, al-Bayhaqi and al-Diya in al-Mukhtarah narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was in Makkah, and then he was commanded to emigrate. So Allah revealed: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance and to exit a sound exit, and grant me from Yourself a supporting authority﴾."

al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Qatadah regarding His words: (﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter﴾), the verse, that he said: "Allah brought him out of Makkah with a sound exit, and brought him into Madinah with a sound entrance."

He said: The Prophet of Allah knew that he had no capacity for this matter except through an authority, so he asked for a supporting authority for the Book of Allah, His limits and His obligations, and for establishing the Book of Allah. For authority is a might from Allah, which He placed among His servants. Were it not for that, some of them would raid others, and the strong among them would devour the weak.

al-Khatib narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "By Allah, what Allah restrains by authority is greater than what He restrains by the Qur'an."

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) entered Makkah, and around the House were three hundred and sixty idols. He began striking them with a stick in his hand, saying: ﴿Truth has come and falsehood has vanished; indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish﴾, and ﴿Truth has come, and falsehood can neither originate nor restore﴾ [Saba': 49]." There are hadiths on this subject as well.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His words: (﴿And turns away with his side﴾), that he said: "He withdrew."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: (﴿was ever despairing﴾), that he said: "Despairing." And regarding His words: ﴿Each acts according to his manner﴾, he said: "according to his side."

Hannad and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Hasan, who said: "According to his manner, according to his intention."

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "I was walking with the Prophet (ﷺ) among the ruins of Madinah, and he was leaning on a palm-frond stalk. He passed by a group of Jews, and some of them said to others: 'Ask him about the spirit.' Some of them said: 'Do not ask him.' They said: 'O Muhammad, what is the spirit?' He continued leaning on the stalk, so I thought he was receiving revelation. Then he said: ﴿They ask you about the spirit. Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord, and you have been given of knowledge only a little﴾."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sahih, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Hibban, Abu al-Shaykh in al-Azamah, al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Quraysh said to the Jews: 'Give us something to ask this man.' They said: 'Ask him about the spirit.' So it was revealed: ﴿They ask you about the spirit. Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord, and you have been given of knowledge only a little﴾. They said: 'We have been given much knowledge; we have been given the Torah, and whoever has been given the Torah has been given much good.' So Allah revealed: ﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord are exhausted, even if We brought the like of it as a supplement﴾ [al-Kahf: 109]." There are hadiths and reports on this subject.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 17, verses 78–85 (part 1 of 3):

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the divine matters, the Return and the Recompense, He followed them with mention of the noblest acts of worship, which is the prayer (ṣalāh). So He said: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾. The exegetes have agreed that what is meant by this verse is the obligatory prayers.

The scholars differed over the meaning of *dulūk* (decline) mentioned in this verse, in two views. The first is that it is the sun's passing from the middle of the sky (zawāl). This was said by ʿUmar, his son, Abū Hurayrah, Abū Barzah, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, al-Shaʿbī, ʿAṭāʾ, Mujāhid, Qatādah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Abū Jaʿfar al-Bāqir, and Ibn Jarīr chose it.

The second view is that it is the sun's setting (ghurūb). This was said by ʿAlī, Ibn Masʿūd and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, and it is related from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Al-Farrāʾ said: The *dulūk* of the sun is from its zawāl until its ghurūb.

Al-Azharī said: The meaning of *dulūk* in the speech of the Arabs is zawāl (passing). For this reason the sun when it passes the middle of the day is called *dālikah*, and when it sets it is called *dālikah*, because in both states it is passing.

He said: My view is that it is its passing at midday, so that the verse includes the five prayers. The meaning is: establish the prayer from the time of the sun's decline ﴿until the darkness of the night﴾, which includes the Ẓuhr and the ʿAṣr, and the two prayers of the darkness of the night, which are the ʿIshāʾ (two prayers). Then He said: ﴿and the Qurʾān of dawn﴾, which makes five prayers.

Abū ʿUbayd said: Its *dulūk* is its setting. It is said: *daladat bi-rāḥ*, meaning the sun set. Quṭrub cited as evidence for this the words of a poet:

*This is the station of the two feet of Rabāḥ;*
*she crept on until she set at Barāḥ.*

(Barāḥ is one of the names of the sun, on the pattern of *ḥadhām* and *qaṭām*.) From the same usage is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

*Lamps which are not the rising stars that lead them,*
*nor the setting ones, the dawāliq.*

That is, the sinking ones.

*Ghasaq al-layl* is the gathering of darkness.

Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj said: It is said *ghasaqa al-layl* and *aghsaqa*, when it comes with its darkness. Abū ʿUbayd said: *al-ghasaq* is the blackness of the night.

Qays ibn al-Ruqayyāt said:

*Indeed this night has become dark,*
*and I have complained of worry and sleeplessness.*

It is also said: *ghasaq al-layl* is the disappearance of the twilight (shafaq). From this is the verse of Zuhayr:

*She kept giving with her hands while heedless,*
*until darkness and ghasaq gathered in heaps.*

The root of the word is from flowing; it is said *ghasaqat* when it flowed.

Al-Farrāʾ reported *ghasaqa al-layl* and *aghsaqa*, *ẓalama* and *aẓlama*, *dajā* and *adjā*, *ghabisha* and *aghbisha*. Whoever holds that the time of the Ẓuhr extends from the zawāl until the ghurūb has used this end-point as evidence, namely His words ﴿until the darkness of the night﴾. This was related from al-Awzāʿī and Abū Ḥanīfah. Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī permitted it in a case of necessity. However, authentic and mass-transmitted (mutawātir, i.e., reported by so many chains that their authenticity is certain) hadiths have come from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) specifying the times of the prayers, so the general wording of this verse must be interpreted in the light of what the Sunnah (the Prophetic tradition) has clarified. Therefore we will not lengthen the discussion with this.

His words ﴿and the Qurʾān of dawn﴾: the accusative of *qurʾān* is because it is coordinated with *al-ṣalāh* (the prayer), meaning: and establish the Qurʾān of dawn. This was said by al-Farrāʾ.

Al-Zajjāj and the Basrans said: its accusative is by way of incitement (*ighrāʾ*), meaning: keep to the Qurʾān of dawn.

The exegetes said: what is meant by the Qurʾān of dawn is the dawn prayer (ṣalāt al-ṣubḥ).

Al-Zajjāj said: In this there is a great benefit, indicating that prayer is not valid except with recitation, to the extent that the prayer itself is called "Qurʾān." The authentic hadiths indicate that there is no prayer except with the Opening of the Book (al-Fātiḥah). In some hadiths coming from a sound channel: "and a Qurʾān along with it." And there is what indicates the obligation of al-Fātiḥah in every rakʿah. I have written about this in my works with a refined treatment.

Then He, glory be to Him, gave the reason for this with His words: ﴿Indeed the Qurʾān of dawn is ever witnessed﴾, meaning: the angels of the night and the angels of the day witness it, as is related in the authentic hadith. (p-٨٣٨) Most of the exegetes said this.

﴿And from the night, perform the tahajjud with it as a supererogatory (nāfilah) for you﴾. The *min* (from) here is partitive, and its accusative is as an adverb of time by an implied verb, meaning: stand for part of the night and perform the tahajjud with it. The pronoun in *bihi* refers to the Qurʾān. What has been said, that it is in the accusative by way of incitement, with the sense "upon you part of the night," is very far-fetched.

Tahajjud is derived from *hujūd*.

Abū ʿUbaydah and Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: it is one of the words with opposite meanings (*aḍdād*), because it is said *hajada al-rajul* when he slept, and *hajada* when he stayed awake. From its use for staying awake is the verse of a poet:

*Lo, she visited while the people of Mina were wakeful;*
*would that her phantom returned to Mina.*

That is, awake. From its use for sleep is the verse of another:

*Lo, she came to us while the companions were asleep,*
*then she spent the night giving generously with bountiful gifts.*

That is, sleeping.

Al-Azharī said: *hujūd* originally means sleeping at night, but the form *tafaʿʿul* came to it for the sake of avoidance, as in *taʾaththama* and *taḥarraja*, meaning he avoided sin and difficulty. So the one who performs tahajjud is one who avoids sleep and stands in the night.

It is also related from al-Azharī that he said: the *mutahajjid* is one who rises from sleep to the prayer. Thus al-Wāḥidī related it from him, restricting tahajjud to rising from sleep. Mujāhid, ʿAlqamah and al-Aswad said likewise, saying: tahajjud is after sleep.

Al-Layth said: *tahajjada* means he woke up for prayer.

﴿as a supererogatory (nāfilah) for you﴾: the meaning of *nāfilah* in the language is an addition beyond the basic requirement. So the meaning is that it is for the Prophet (ﷺ) an addition beyond the obligations. The command to tahajjud, although its apparent sense is obligation, the explicit statement that it is a *nāfilah* is a clear indication that the command is not binding. It was also said that what is meant by *nāfilah* here is that it is an obligation additional to the five obligatory prayers for him (ﷺ). This is refuted by the explicit use of the word *nāfilah*. It was also said: the night prayer was obligatory for him (ﷺ), then the obligation was abrogated (naskh, i.e., the cancellation of a earlier ruling by a later one), so standing in the night became voluntary. On this view is understood what has come in the hadith that it was obligatory for him and voluntary for his community.

Al-Wāḥidī said: The night prayer was an extra for the Prophet (ﷺ) specifically, for raising his ranks, not for expiating sins, since he was forgiven his earlier and later sins; for us it is not a supererogatory act, because of the multitude of our sins; rather we perform it to expiate them. He said: This is the view of all the exegetes.

The summary is that although the address in this verse, in His words ﴿Establish the prayer﴾, is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), the command to him is a command to his community. So it is a general law. Among this is the encouragement to the night prayer, which encompasses the whole community. The explicit statement that it is a *nāfilah* indicates that it is not obligatory. So tahajjud at night is recommended and legislated for every responsible person.

Then He, glory be to Him, promised him for establishing the obligatory and supererogatory prayers, saying: ﴿It may be that your Lord raises you to a praiseworthy station﴾. We have mentioned in several places that *ʿasā* (it may be) from the Generous One is an expectation that is certain to occur. The accusative of *maqāman* is as an adverb of place by an implied verb, or by embedding in *yabʿathaka* the sense of *iqāmah* (establishing). It is also permitted that it be in the accusative as a circumstantial state, meaning: He raises you possessing a praiseworthy station. The meaning of the station being praiseworthy is that everyone who knows of it praises it.

The station has been differently identified in several views. The first is that it is the station which the Prophet (ﷺ) occupies to intercede (shafāʿah) for people on the Day of Resurrection, so that their Lord, glory be to Him, may relieve them of what they are in. This view is the one indicated by the sound proofs in the interpretation of the verse, and Ibn Jarīr related it from most of the people of interpretation (taʾwīl).

Al-Wāḥidī said: The consensus of the exegetes is that the praiseworthy station is the station of intercession.

The second view: the praiseworthy station is the Prophet (ﷺ) being given the banner of praise (liwāʾ al-ḥamd) on the Day of Resurrection.

It is possible to say that this does not contradict the first view, since there is no contradiction between his standing in the station of intercession and his holding the banner of praise.

The third view: the praiseworthy station is that God, glory be to Him, seats Muhammad (ﷺ) with Him upon His Throne (kursī). Ibn Jarīr related this from a group including Mujāhid, and a hadith has come concerning it.

Al-Naqqāsh related from Abū Dāwūd al-Sijistānī that he said: Whoever denies this hadith is in our view an accused (one whose reliability is in question). The people of knowledge have never ceased narrating this hadith.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: Mujāhid, although he is one of the Imams in interpretation, has two views that are abandoned by the people of knowledge: one is this, and the second is his interpretation of ﴿faces on that day radiant, looking at their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyāmah 75:22–23], which he said means waiting for the reward, and is not sight. End of quote. In any case, this view does not contradict the first, since it is possible that God, glory be to Him, seats him in this seat and he intercedes that intercession.

The fourth view: it is unrestricted in every station that brings praise from kinds of honours. This was mentioned by the author of al-Kashshāf (al-Zamakhsharī) and those who follow him in exegesis. It is answered that the sound hadiths coming in specifying this praiseworthy station are mass-transmitted, so turning to them is required. The verse has no general wording such that one would say: the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific occasion. As for his saying that it is unrestricted in everything that brings praise, the meaning is that it is general in everything of that kind, but the general is expressed by the wording of the unrestricted, as he mentioned in the case of the slaughter of the cow; and for this reason he said here.

It was also said: what is meant is intercession, which is one kind of what the word *maqām* (station) covers.

The difference between the general of alternatives (*ʿumūm badalī*) and the comprehensive general (*ʿumūm shumūlī*) is well known, so we will not lengthen by mentioning it.

﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance and cause me to exit a sound exit﴾. The majority read *mudkhala ṣidqin* and *mukhraja ṣidqin* with a *ḍammah* on both the *mīm*s.

Al-Ḥasan, Abū al-ʿĀliyah and Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim read them with a *fatḥah* on both. These are two verbal nouns (maṣdar) meaning the entering and the exiting. The attribution to *ṣidq* (truthfulness) is for the sake of intensification, like *ḥātim al-jūd* (the very epitome of generosity), meaning an entering worthy of being called an entering, in which one sees nothing disliked.

Al-Wāḥidī said: Attributing them to *ṣidq* is a praise of both, and everything you attribute to *ṣidq* is praise.

The exegetes differed over the meaning of the verse. It was said: it was revealed when he was commanded to emigrate, meaning entering Medina and exiting Mecca; Ibn Jarīr chose this. It was said: the meaning is: cause me to die a true death, and resurrect me on the Day of Resurrection with a true resurrection. It was said: the meaning is: cause me to enter what You have commanded me, and exit what You have forbidden me. It was said: its entering is into a place of security and its exiting is from among the polytheists; this is like the first view. It was said: what is meant is entering with honour and exiting with victory. It was said: the meaning is: cause me to enter the grave at death with a sound entering, and exit from it at resurrection with a sound exiting. It was said: cause me to enter wherever You cause me to enter in truth, and exit in truth. It was said: the verse is general in everything it covers of affairs, so it is a supplication, and its meaning is: My Lord, set right for me my course in all affairs and my conduct in them (p-٨٣٩).

﴿And grant me from Yourself an authority, a helper﴾, meaning: a clear, overpowering proof by which You will help me against all who oppose me. It was also said: grant me from Yourself a kingdom and a strong might. It seems that he (ﷺ) knew that he had no capacity for this matter except through an authority, so he asked for an authority to help him. This was said by al-Ḥasan and Qatādah, and Ibn Jarīr chose it.

Ibn Kathīr said: This is the stronger view, because the truth necessarily requires subjugation of whoever opposes and rivals it. For this reason the Most High says: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Book and the Balance so that people may uphold justice; and We sent down iron, in which is great might and benefits for people, and so that God may know who helps Him and His messengers unseen﴾ [al-Ḥadīd 57:25]. And in the hadith: "Indeed God restrains by the authority what He does not restrain by the Qurʾān," meaning: He prevents by the authority from committing indecencies and sins what He does not prevent in many people by the Qurʾān, along with its severe warning and stern threat. And this is what actually happens. End of quote.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 17, verses 78–85 (part 2 of 3):

﴿And say: "The truth has come and falsehood has vanished."﴾ By "the truth" is meant Islam. It is also said to mean the Qur'an, and it is said to mean jihad. There is no barrier to understanding the verse as including all of these, and as including whatever is true, whatever it may be. By "falsehood" is meant polytheism (shirk). It is also said to mean Satan. It is not far-fetched to understand it as anything that stands opposite the truth, without distinguishing one kind of falsehood from another.

The meaning of *zahaqa* is that it perished and vanished. From it comes *zuhuq al-nafs* (the departure of the soul), which is its perishing. ﴿Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish.﴾ That is, this is its nature: it perishes and does not endure, whereas the truth is always enduring.

﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers.﴾ The majority of readers recited *nunazzilu* with the *nun*. Abu 'Amr recited it with the lighter form (*al-takhfif*). Mujahid recited it with a *ya'* (yā' taḥtiyya) and the lighter form, and al-Marwazi transmitted this from Hafs. The *min* here is for the starting point of the action (*ibtida' al-ghaya*). It may also be for specifying the kind (*bayan al-jins*). It is also said to be for partitioning (*al-tab'id*). Some exegetes rejected this, because it would imply that some of it contains no healing. Ibn 'Atiyya answered that what is partitioned is its sending down (*inzaluhu*).

The scholars differed over the meaning of its being a healing, on two views. The first is that it is a healing for the hearts, through the removal of ignorance from them, the dispelling of doubt, and the lifting of the veil from matters that point to God, glorified is He. The second is that it is a healing from apparent illnesses through incantations (*ruqa*), seeking refuge (*ta'awwudh*), and the like. There is no barrier to taking *shifa'* in both senses, either by the generality of metaphor (*ʿumum al-majaz*) or by treating a homonym (*mushtarak*) as carrying both of its meanings.

Then He, glorified is He, stated that it is a mercy for the believers, because of the beneficial sciences it contains, which include what is good for the religion and for the world, and because of the great reward in reciting and reflecting upon it, which is a cause of the mercy, forgiveness and good pleasure of God, glorified is He. A similar verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing. But as for those who do not believe, there is deafness in their ears, and it is blindness for them."﴾ [Fussilat: 44]

Then, when He, glorified is He, mentioned the benefit the Qur'an contains for His believing servants, He mentioned the harm it contains for everyone else, and said: ﴿And it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss.﴾ That is: the Qur'an, all of it or every part of it, does not increase the wrongdoers, who put denial in the place of affirmation and doubt and suspicion in the place of certainty and tranquility, ﴿except in loss﴾, that is, in destruction. This is because hearing the Qur'an enrages them, provokes them, and calls them to commit even more abominations out of rebellion and obstinacy, and at that point they are destroyed. It is also said that *al-khasar* means deficiency, as in His saying: ﴿so it increased them in defilement upon their defilement﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125].

Then He, glorified is He, drew attention to the disclosure of some of the blameworthy dispositions with which man was created, and said: ﴿And when We bestow favour upon man﴾, that is, upon this kind, with blessings that call for gratitude, such as health and wealth, ﴿he turns away﴾ from giving thanks to God and from remembering Him, ﴿and distances himself [*nā'a bi-janibihi*]﴾. *Al-nay'* is distance, and the *ba'* is either for transitivity or for accompaniment. This is an emphasis on turning away, because turning away from a thing means turning the face of one's side (*'ard al-wajh*) away from it, that is, its direction. Distancing with the side means bending one's flank away from it and turning one's back to it. It is not far-fetched that what is meant by turning away here is turning away from supplication and entreaty, which he used to do when affliction and trial came upon him, and that what is meant by distancing with the side is arrogance and withdrawing oneself from discharging the rights of blessings.

Ibn 'Amir, in the transmission of Ibn Dhakwan, and Abu Ja'far recited *nā'a*, like *bā'a*, with the *hamza* moved later, by metathesis (*al-qalb*). Hamza recited *nā'ā* with *imala* of both fathas, and al-Kisa'i agreed with him. Shu'ba and al-Susi applied *imala* to the *hamza* only. The rest recited both with *fath*.

﴿And when evil touches him﴾, from illness or poverty, ﴿he is ever despairing, extremely hopeless of the mercy of God.﴾ The meaning is that if he attains worldly aims and achieves what he desires, he forgets the One who is worshipped; and if something of that escapes him, grief overcomes him and despair dominates him. Both of these traits are ugly and blameworthy. What is in this verse is not contradicted by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when evil touches him, he is one of abundant supplication﴾ [Fussilat: 51], nor by similar verses, because that is the characteristic of another group among them, other than the group mentioned in this verse. It is not far-fetched to say that there is no contradiction between the two verses: it may be that, together with his intense despair and great hopelessness, he frequently supplicates with his tongue.

﴿Say: "Each acts according to his own manner [*shakilatihi*]."﴾ *Al-shakila* (manner), said al-Farra', is the way or path. It is also said to mean direction, nature, religion, intention, or innate disposition. It is derived from *al-shakl* (form), as one says: "You are not of my form or of my manner." *Al-shakl* is the like and the equal.

The meaning is that every person acts according to what suits the character he has become accustomed to, and this is a reproach to the disbeliever and a praise of the believer. ﴿Your Lord knows best who is best guided in the way.﴾ Because He is the Creator of you, and the Knower of what you are created with of dispositions and of what you differ in of ways. It is He who distinguishes between the believer, who does not turn away when blessed and does not despair when tested, and the disbeliever, whose habit is insolence at blessings and despair at afflictions.

Then, since the discourse had drifted to mention of man and what he was created with, He, glorified is He, mentioned the question that people asked the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, about the *ruh* (spirit). He said: ﴿And they ask you about the spirit.﴾ People have differed about the *ruh* that was asked about. It is said that it is the spirit that governs the body, by which life exists. This is the view of most exegetes.

Al-Farra' said: the spirit by which man lives is something God, glorified is He, did not inform any of His creatures about, and He did not give knowledge of it to any of His servants. So He said: ﴿Say: "The spirit is of the command of my Lord."﴾ That is: you do not know it. It is also said that the spirit being asked about is Gabriel. It is said to be Jesus. It is said to be the Qur'an. It is said to be an angel of great creation. It is said to be a creation like the creation of the children of Adam. And other views have been said which carry no benefit and whose inclusion is of no use. The apparent view is the first, and the cause of the revelation of this verse, and the identity of those who asked the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, about the spirit, will come later. Apparently the question was about the reality of the spirit, because knowing the reality of a thing is more important and prior to knowing one of its states.

Then God, glorified is He, commanded him to answer those who asked him about the spirit, and said: ﴿Say: "The spirit is of the command of my Lord."﴾ The *min* here is explanatory (*bayaniyya*). *Al-amr* means matter or affair, and the idafa (construct) is for specification. That is: it is of the kind of things God has kept to Himself knowledge of, things He has not made known to His servants. It is also said that the meaning of "of the command of my Lord" is: of His revelation and His speech, not of the speech of human beings.

In this verse there is a rebuke, most forceful, to those who plunge into the question of the spirit, who burden themselves to explain what its form is and to clarify its reality, and a most powerful deterrent for them. They have prolonged discourse on this subject beyond what the matter can bear. Most of it, indeed all of it, is among the superfluities that bring no benefit to religion or to the world.

Some researchers have related that the opinions of those who differ about the spirit reached one thousand eight hundred opinions. So consider this empty superfluity and this fruitless toil devoid of benefit, after they knew that God, glorified is He, has kept its knowledge to Himself, and did not inform His prophets of it, nor did He permit them to ask about it or to investigate its reality, let alone their communities who follow them. How strange it is, by God, that the opinions of the people of superfluity should reach this limit, which they did not reach, nor even part of it, in other matters on which God has permitted discussion and has not kept its knowledge to Himself.

Then God, glorified is He, concluded this verse with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little.﴾ That is: the knowledge that God has taught you is nothing but a small amount in comparison with the knowledge of the Creator, glorified is He, even if you have been given a large share of knowledge. Indeed, the knowledge of the prophets, peace be upon them, in comparison with the knowledge of God, glorified is He, is nothing but what a bird takes in its beak from the sea, as in the hadith of Musa and al-Khidr, peace be upon them both.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "*Duluk al-shams* is its setting (*ghurubuha*). The Arabs say, when the sun sets: *dalakat al-shams* (the sun has declined)."

Ibn Abi Shayba and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ali, who said: "*Duluquha* is its setting."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said, regarding ﴿at the decline of the sun﴾: "The departure of the sun (*zawal al-shams*)."

al-Bazzar, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Daylami transmitted from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: '*Dulūk al-shams* is its departure (*zawaluha*).'" al-Suyuti graded its chain as weak. Malik transmitted it in the Muwatta', and 'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted it from Ibn 'Umar as his own statement.

'Abd al-Razzaq transmitted from him, who said: "*Duluk al-shams* is its inclination (*ziyaguha*) after midday."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "*Duluquha* is its departure (*zawaluha*)."

Ibn Abi Shayba and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him, regarding God's saying ﴿at the decline of the sun﴾, that he said: "When the shade (*al-fay'*) begins to move."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Abu Mas'ud and 'Uqba ibn 'Amr, who both said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: 'Gabriel came to me at the decline of the sun, when it had passed its zenith, and led me in the noon prayer (*al-zuhr*).'"

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Abu Barza al-Aslami, who said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, used to pray the noon prayer when the sun had passed its zenith, then he recited: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted something similar from a hadith of Anas. Among what is cited as evidence that *al-duluk* is the zenith of midday is what Ibn Jarir transmitted from Jabir, who said: "I invited the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and whomever of his companions wished to be fed at my house. Then they left when the sun had passed its zenith. The Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, went out and said: 'Go out, O Abu Bakr, for this is the time when the sun has declined (*dalakat*).'" There is an unknown narrator in its chain. However, Ibn Jarir transmitted it from him by another route, from Sahl ibn Bakkar, from Abu 'Awana, from al-Aswad ibn Qays, from Nubayh al-'Anbari, from Jabir, and mentioned something similar, traced to the Prophet (*marfu'an*).

al-Tabarani transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud regarding God's saying ﴿until the darkness of the night﴾, that he said: "Until the late evening prayer (*al-'isha' al-akhira*)."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "*Ghasaq al-layl* is the gathering of the night and its darkness."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him, who said: "*Ghasaq al-layl* is the beginning of the night."

'Abd al-Razzaq transmitted from Abu Hurayra, who said: "*Duluk al-shams* is when the sun leaves the middle of the sky, and *ghasaq al-layl* is the setting of the sun."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding God's saying ﴿and the Qur'an of dawn﴾, that he said: "It is the dawn prayer (*salat al-subh*)."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* transmitted from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, regarding God's saying: ﴿and the Qur'an of dawn; indeed, the Qur'an of dawn is ever witnessed﴾. He said: "The angels of the night and the angels of the day witness it, and they gather in it." It is in the two *Sahihs* from him, as a marfu' report, with the wording: "The angels of the night and the angels of the day gather at the dawn prayer." Then Abu Hurayra said: "Recite, if you wish: ﴿and the Qur'an of dawn; indeed, the Qur'an of dawn is ever witnessed﴾."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Tabarani transmitted something similar from Ibn Mas'ud as a mawquf report.

(p. 840)

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu al-Darda', who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾. He said: "The angels of the night and the angels of the day witness it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿as an additional [prayer] for you﴾, that he said: "That is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ). He was commanded to pray the night vigil, and it was made obligatory upon him."

al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Aishah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Three things are obligatory upon me, and for you they are a sunnah: the witr, the siwak, and the night prayer."

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Umamah, regarding His words: ﴿as an additional [prayer] for you﴾, that he said: "It was an additional [prayer] for the Prophet (ﷺ), and for you it is a virtue." In another wording: "The additional prayer was only specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Hurairah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His words: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾, and when he was asked about it, he said: "It is the praiseworthy station, in which I will intercede for my ummah."

Ahmad (p-841), Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ka'b ibn Malik that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "People will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection, and I and my ummah will be on a hill, and my Lord will clothe me in a green garment. Then I will be given permission, and I will say what Allah wills me to say. That is the praiseworthy station."

al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: "On the Day of Resurrection every nation will follow its prophet, saying: 'O so-and-so, intercede! O so-and-so, intercede!' until the intercession reaches the Prophet (ﷺ). That is the day on which Allah will raise him to a praiseworthy station."

He also narrated something similar to it from him, as a marfu' report. The narrations on this subject are very numerous and firmly established in the two Sahihs and elsewhere, so we will not lengthen by mentioning them. Whoever wishes for a full survey should examine the hadiths on intercession, including the intercession of the mothers and others.

al-Tabarani narrated, regarding His words: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾, that he said: "He will seat him between Himself and Jibril, and he will intercede for his ummah. That is the praiseworthy station."

al-Daylami narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: (﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾) he said: 'He will seat me with Him upon the throne.'" It is necessary to investigate the chain of narration of these two hadiths.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sahih, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, al-Bayhaqi and al-Diya in al-Mukhtarah narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was in Makkah, and then he was commanded to emigrate. So Allah revealed: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance and to exit a sound exit, and grant me from Yourself a supporting authority﴾."

al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Qatadah regarding His words: (﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter﴾), the verse, that he said: "Allah brought him out of Makkah with a sound exit, and brought him into Madinah with a sound entrance."

He said: The Prophet of Allah knew that he had no capacity for this matter except through an authority, so he asked for a supporting authority for the Book of Allah, His limits and His obligations, and for establishing the Book of Allah. For authority is a might from Allah, which He placed among His servants. Were it not for that, some of them would raid others, and the strong among them would devour the weak.

al-Khatib narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "By Allah, what Allah restrains by authority is greater than what He restrains by the Qur'an."

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) entered Makkah, and around the House were three hundred and sixty idols. He began striking them with a stick in his hand, saying: ﴿Truth has come and falsehood has vanished; indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish﴾, and ﴿Truth has come, and falsehood can neither originate nor restore﴾ [Saba': 49]." There are hadiths on this subject as well.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His words: (﴿And turns away with his side﴾), that he said: "He withdrew."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: (﴿was ever despairing﴾), that he said: "Despairing." And regarding His words: ﴿Each acts according to his manner﴾, he said: "according to his side."

Hannad and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Hasan, who said: "According to his manner, according to his intention."

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "I was walking with the Prophet (ﷺ) among the ruins of Madinah, and he was leaning on a palm-frond stalk. He passed by a group of Jews, and some of them said to others: 'Ask him about the spirit.' Some of them said: 'Do not ask him.' They said: 'O Muhammad, what is the spirit?' He continued leaning on the stalk, so I thought he was receiving revelation. Then he said: ﴿They ask you about the spirit. Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord, and you have been given of knowledge only a little﴾."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sahih, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Hibban, Abu al-Shaykh in al-Azamah, al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Quraysh said to the Jews: 'Give us something to ask this man.' They said: 'Ask him about the spirit.' So it was revealed: ﴿They ask you about the spirit. Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord, and you have been given of knowledge only a little﴾. They said: 'We have been given much knowledge; we have been given the Torah, and whoever has been given the Torah has been given much good.' So Allah revealed: ﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord are exhausted, even if We brought the like of it as a supplement﴾ [al-Kahf: 109]." There are hadiths and reports on this subject.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 17, verses 78–85 (part 1 of 3):

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the divine matters, the Return and the Recompense, He followed them with mention of the noblest acts of worship, which is the prayer (ṣalāh). So He said: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾. The exegetes have agreed that what is meant by this verse is the obligatory prayers.

The scholars differed over the meaning of *dulūk* (decline) mentioned in this verse, in two views. The first is that it is the sun's passing from the middle of the sky (zawāl). This was said by ʿUmar, his son, Abū Hurayrah, Abū Barzah, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, al-Shaʿbī, ʿAṭāʾ, Mujāhid, Qatādah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Abū Jaʿfar al-Bāqir, and Ibn Jarīr chose it.

The second view is that it is the sun's setting (ghurūb). This was said by ʿAlī, Ibn Masʿūd and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, and it is related from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Al-Farrāʾ said: The *dulūk* of the sun is from its zawāl until its ghurūb.

Al-Azharī said: The meaning of *dulūk* in the speech of the Arabs is zawāl (passing). For this reason the sun when it passes the middle of the day is called *dālikah*, and when it sets it is called *dālikah*, because in both states it is passing.

He said: My view is that it is its passing at midday, so that the verse includes the five prayers. The meaning is: establish the prayer from the time of the sun's decline ﴿until the darkness of the night﴾, which includes the Ẓuhr and the ʿAṣr, and the two prayers of the darkness of the night, which are the ʿIshāʾ (two prayers). Then He said: ﴿and the Qurʾān of dawn﴾, which makes five prayers.

Abū ʿUbayd said: Its *dulūk* is its setting. It is said: *daladat bi-rāḥ*, meaning the sun set. Quṭrub cited as evidence for this the words of a poet:

*This is the station of the two feet of Rabāḥ;*
*she crept on until she set at Barāḥ.*

(Barāḥ is one of the names of the sun, on the pattern of *ḥadhām* and *qaṭām*.) From the same usage is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

*Lamps which are not the rising stars that lead them,*
*nor the setting ones, the dawāliq.*

That is, the sinking ones.

*Ghasaq al-layl* is the gathering of darkness.

Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj said: It is said *ghasaqa al-layl* and *aghsaqa*, when it comes with its darkness. Abū ʿUbayd said: *al-ghasaq* is the blackness of the night.

Qays ibn al-Ruqayyāt said:

*Indeed this night has become dark,*
*and I have complained of worry and sleeplessness.*

It is also said: *ghasaq al-layl* is the disappearance of the twilight (shafaq). From this is the verse of Zuhayr:

*She kept giving with her hands while heedless,*
*until darkness and ghasaq gathered in heaps.*

The root of the word is from flowing; it is said *ghasaqat* when it flowed.

Al-Farrāʾ reported *ghasaqa al-layl* and *aghsaqa*, *ẓalama* and *aẓlama*, *dajā* and *adjā*, *ghabisha* and *aghbisha*. Whoever holds that the time of the Ẓuhr extends from the zawāl until the ghurūb has used this end-point as evidence, namely His words ﴿until the darkness of the night﴾. This was related from al-Awzāʿī and Abū Ḥanīfah. Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī permitted it in a case of necessity. However, authentic and mass-transmitted (mutawātir, i.e., reported by so many chains that their authenticity is certain) hadiths have come from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) specifying the times of the prayers, so the general wording of this verse must be interpreted in the light of what the Sunnah (the Prophetic tradition) has clarified. Therefore we will not lengthen the discussion with this.

His words ﴿and the Qurʾān of dawn﴾: the accusative of *qurʾān* is because it is coordinated with *al-ṣalāh* (the prayer), meaning: and establish the Qurʾān of dawn. This was said by al-Farrāʾ.

Al-Zajjāj and the Basrans said: its accusative is by way of incitement (*ighrāʾ*), meaning: keep to the Qurʾān of dawn.

The exegetes said: what is meant by the Qurʾān of dawn is the dawn prayer (ṣalāt al-ṣubḥ).

Al-Zajjāj said: In this there is a great benefit, indicating that prayer is not valid except with recitation, to the extent that the prayer itself is called "Qurʾān." The authentic hadiths indicate that there is no prayer except with the Opening of the Book (al-Fātiḥah). In some hadiths coming from a sound channel: "and a Qurʾān along with it." And there is what indicates the obligation of al-Fātiḥah in every rakʿah. I have written about this in my works with a refined treatment.

Then He, glory be to Him, gave the reason for this with His words: ﴿Indeed the Qurʾān of dawn is ever witnessed﴾, meaning: the angels of the night and the angels of the day witness it, as is related in the authentic hadith. (p-٨٣٨) Most of the exegetes said this.

﴿And from the night, perform the tahajjud with it as a supererogatory (nāfilah) for you﴾. The *min* (from) here is partitive, and its accusative is as an adverb of time by an implied verb, meaning: stand for part of the night and perform the tahajjud with it. The pronoun in *bihi* refers to the Qurʾān. What has been said, that it is in the accusative by way of incitement, with the sense "upon you part of the night," is very far-fetched.

Tahajjud is derived from *hujūd*.

Abū ʿUbaydah and Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: it is one of the words with opposite meanings (*aḍdād*), because it is said *hajada al-rajul* when he slept, and *hajada* when he stayed awake. From its use for staying awake is the verse of a poet:

*Lo, she visited while the people of Mina were wakeful;*
*would that her phantom returned to Mina.*

That is, awake. From its use for sleep is the verse of another:

*Lo, she came to us while the companions were asleep,*
*then she spent the night giving generously with bountiful gifts.*

That is, sleeping.

Al-Azharī said: *hujūd* originally means sleeping at night, but the form *tafaʿʿul* came to it for the sake of avoidance, as in *taʾaththama* and *taḥarraja*, meaning he avoided sin and difficulty. So the one who performs tahajjud is one who avoids sleep and stands in the night.

It is also related from al-Azharī that he said: the *mutahajjid* is one who rises from sleep to the prayer. Thus al-Wāḥidī related it from him, restricting tahajjud to rising from sleep. Mujāhid, ʿAlqamah and al-Aswad said likewise, saying: tahajjud is after sleep.

Al-Layth said: *tahajjada* means he woke up for prayer.

﴿as a supererogatory (nāfilah) for you﴾: the meaning of *nāfilah* in the language is an addition beyond the basic requirement. So the meaning is that it is for the Prophet (ﷺ) an addition beyond the obligations. The command to tahajjud, although its apparent sense is obligation, the explicit statement that it is a *nāfilah* is a clear indication that the command is not binding. It was also said that what is meant by *nāfilah* here is that it is an obligation additional to the five obligatory prayers for him (ﷺ). This is refuted by the explicit use of the word *nāfilah*. It was also said: the night prayer was obligatory for him (ﷺ), then the obligation was abrogated (naskh, i.e., the cancellation of a earlier ruling by a later one), so standing in the night became voluntary. On this view is understood what has come in the hadith that it was obligatory for him and voluntary for his community.

Al-Wāḥidī said: The night prayer was an extra for the Prophet (ﷺ) specifically, for raising his ranks, not for expiating sins, since he was forgiven his earlier and later sins; for us it is not a supererogatory act, because of the multitude of our sins; rather we perform it to expiate them. He said: This is the view of all the exegetes.

The summary is that although the address in this verse, in His words ﴿Establish the prayer﴾, is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), the command to him is a command to his community. So it is a general law. Among this is the encouragement to the night prayer, which encompasses the whole community. The explicit statement that it is a *nāfilah* indicates that it is not obligatory. So tahajjud at night is recommended and legislated for every responsible person.

Then He, glory be to Him, promised him for establishing the obligatory and supererogatory prayers, saying: ﴿It may be that your Lord raises you to a praiseworthy station﴾. We have mentioned in several places that *ʿasā* (it may be) from the Generous One is an expectation that is certain to occur. The accusative of *maqāman* is as an adverb of place by an implied verb, or by embedding in *yabʿathaka* the sense of *iqāmah* (establishing). It is also permitted that it be in the accusative as a circumstantial state, meaning: He raises you possessing a praiseworthy station. The meaning of the station being praiseworthy is that everyone who knows of it praises it.

The station has been differently identified in several views. The first is that it is the station which the Prophet (ﷺ) occupies to intercede (shafāʿah) for people on the Day of Resurrection, so that their Lord, glory be to Him, may relieve them of what they are in. This view is the one indicated by the sound proofs in the interpretation of the verse, and Ibn Jarīr related it from most of the people of interpretation (taʾwīl).

Al-Wāḥidī said: The consensus of the exegetes is that the praiseworthy station is the station of intercession.

The second view: the praiseworthy station is the Prophet (ﷺ) being given the banner of praise (liwāʾ al-ḥamd) on the Day of Resurrection.

It is possible to say that this does not contradict the first view, since there is no contradiction between his standing in the station of intercession and his holding the banner of praise.

The third view: the praiseworthy station is that God, glory be to Him, seats Muhammad (ﷺ) with Him upon His Throne (kursī). Ibn Jarīr related this from a group including Mujāhid, and a hadith has come concerning it.

Al-Naqqāsh related from Abū Dāwūd al-Sijistānī that he said: Whoever denies this hadith is in our view an accused (one whose reliability is in question). The people of knowledge have never ceased narrating this hadith.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: Mujāhid, although he is one of the Imams in interpretation, has two views that are abandoned by the people of knowledge: one is this, and the second is his interpretation of ﴿faces on that day radiant, looking at their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyāmah 75:22–23], which he said means waiting for the reward, and is not sight. End of quote. In any case, this view does not contradict the first, since it is possible that God, glory be to Him, seats him in this seat and he intercedes that intercession.

The fourth view: it is unrestricted in every station that brings praise from kinds of honours. This was mentioned by the author of al-Kashshāf (al-Zamakhsharī) and those who follow him in exegesis. It is answered that the sound hadiths coming in specifying this praiseworthy station are mass-transmitted, so turning to them is required. The verse has no general wording such that one would say: the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific occasion. As for his saying that it is unrestricted in everything that brings praise, the meaning is that it is general in everything of that kind, but the general is expressed by the wording of the unrestricted, as he mentioned in the case of the slaughter of the cow; and for this reason he said here.

It was also said: what is meant is intercession, which is one kind of what the word *maqām* (station) covers.

The difference between the general of alternatives (*ʿumūm badalī*) and the comprehensive general (*ʿumūm shumūlī*) is well known, so we will not lengthen by mentioning it.

﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance and cause me to exit a sound exit﴾. The majority read *mudkhala ṣidqin* and *mukhraja ṣidqin* with a *ḍammah* on both the *mīm*s.

Al-Ḥasan, Abū al-ʿĀliyah and Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim read them with a *fatḥah* on both. These are two verbal nouns (maṣdar) meaning the entering and the exiting. The attribution to *ṣidq* (truthfulness) is for the sake of intensification, like *ḥātim al-jūd* (the very epitome of generosity), meaning an entering worthy of being called an entering, in which one sees nothing disliked.

Al-Wāḥidī said: Attributing them to *ṣidq* is a praise of both, and everything you attribute to *ṣidq* is praise.

The exegetes differed over the meaning of the verse. It was said: it was revealed when he was commanded to emigrate, meaning entering Medina and exiting Mecca; Ibn Jarīr chose this. It was said: the meaning is: cause me to die a true death, and resurrect me on the Day of Resurrection with a true resurrection. It was said: the meaning is: cause me to enter what You have commanded me, and exit what You have forbidden me. It was said: its entering is into a place of security and its exiting is from among the polytheists; this is like the first view. It was said: what is meant is entering with honour and exiting with victory. It was said: the meaning is: cause me to enter the grave at death with a sound entering, and exit from it at resurrection with a sound exiting. It was said: cause me to enter wherever You cause me to enter in truth, and exit in truth. It was said: the verse is general in everything it covers of affairs, so it is a supplication, and its meaning is: My Lord, set right for me my course in all affairs and my conduct in them (p-٨٣٩).

﴿And grant me from Yourself an authority, a helper﴾, meaning: a clear, overpowering proof by which You will help me against all who oppose me. It was also said: grant me from Yourself a kingdom and a strong might. It seems that he (ﷺ) knew that he had no capacity for this matter except through an authority, so he asked for an authority to help him. This was said by al-Ḥasan and Qatādah, and Ibn Jarīr chose it.

Ibn Kathīr said: This is the stronger view, because the truth necessarily requires subjugation of whoever opposes and rivals it. For this reason the Most High says: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Book and the Balance so that people may uphold justice; and We sent down iron, in which is great might and benefits for people, and so that God may know who helps Him and His messengers unseen﴾ [al-Ḥadīd 57:25]. And in the hadith: "Indeed God restrains by the authority what He does not restrain by the Qurʾān," meaning: He prevents by the authority from committing indecencies and sins what He does not prevent in many people by the Qurʾān, along with its severe warning and stern threat. And this is what actually happens. End of quote.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 17, verses 78–85 (part 2 of 3):

﴿And say: "The truth has come and falsehood has vanished."﴾ By "the truth" is meant Islam. It is also said to mean the Qur'an, and it is said to mean jihad. There is no barrier to understanding the verse as including all of these, and as including whatever is true, whatever it may be. By "falsehood" is meant polytheism (shirk). It is also said to mean Satan. It is not far-fetched to understand it as anything that stands opposite the truth, without distinguishing one kind of falsehood from another.

The meaning of *zahaqa* is that it perished and vanished. From it comes *zuhuq al-nafs* (the departure of the soul), which is its perishing. ﴿Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish.﴾ That is, this is its nature: it perishes and does not endure, whereas the truth is always enduring.

﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers.﴾ The majority of readers recited *nunazzilu* with the *nun*. Abu 'Amr recited it with the lighter form (*al-takhfif*). Mujahid recited it with a *ya'* (yā' taḥtiyya) and the lighter form, and al-Marwazi transmitted this from Hafs. The *min* here is for the starting point of the action (*ibtida' al-ghaya*). It may also be for specifying the kind (*bayan al-jins*). It is also said to be for partitioning (*al-tab'id*). Some exegetes rejected this, because it would imply that some of it contains no healing. Ibn 'Atiyya answered that what is partitioned is its sending down (*inzaluhu*).

The scholars differed over the meaning of its being a healing, on two views. The first is that it is a healing for the hearts, through the removal of ignorance from them, the dispelling of doubt, and the lifting of the veil from matters that point to God, glorified is He. The second is that it is a healing from apparent illnesses through incantations (*ruqa*), seeking refuge (*ta'awwudh*), and the like. There is no barrier to taking *shifa'* in both senses, either by the generality of metaphor (*ʿumum al-majaz*) or by treating a homonym (*mushtarak*) as carrying both of its meanings.

Then He, glorified is He, stated that it is a mercy for the believers, because of the beneficial sciences it contains, which include what is good for the religion and for the world, and because of the great reward in reciting and reflecting upon it, which is a cause of the mercy, forgiveness and good pleasure of God, glorified is He. A similar verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing. But as for those who do not believe, there is deafness in their ears, and it is blindness for them."﴾ [Fussilat: 44]

Then, when He, glorified is He, mentioned the benefit the Qur'an contains for His believing servants, He mentioned the harm it contains for everyone else, and said: ﴿And it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss.﴾ That is: the Qur'an, all of it or every part of it, does not increase the wrongdoers, who put denial in the place of affirmation and doubt and suspicion in the place of certainty and tranquility, ﴿except in loss﴾, that is, in destruction. This is because hearing the Qur'an enrages them, provokes them, and calls them to commit even more abominations out of rebellion and obstinacy, and at that point they are destroyed. It is also said that *al-khasar* means deficiency, as in His saying: ﴿so it increased them in defilement upon their defilement﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125].

Then He, glorified is He, drew attention to the disclosure of some of the blameworthy dispositions with which man was created, and said: ﴿And when We bestow favour upon man﴾, that is, upon this kind, with blessings that call for gratitude, such as health and wealth, ﴿he turns away﴾ from giving thanks to God and from remembering Him, ﴿and distances himself [*nā'a bi-janibihi*]﴾. *Al-nay'* is distance, and the *ba'* is either for transitivity or for accompaniment. This is an emphasis on turning away, because turning away from a thing means turning the face of one's side (*'ard al-wajh*) away from it, that is, its direction. Distancing with the side means bending one's flank away from it and turning one's back to it. It is not far-fetched that what is meant by turning away here is turning away from supplication and entreaty, which he used to do when affliction and trial came upon him, and that what is meant by distancing with the side is arrogance and withdrawing oneself from discharging the rights of blessings.

Ibn 'Amir, in the transmission of Ibn Dhakwan, and Abu Ja'far recited *nā'a*, like *bā'a*, with the *hamza* moved later, by metathesis (*al-qalb*). Hamza recited *nā'ā* with *imala* of both fathas, and al-Kisa'i agreed with him. Shu'ba and al-Susi applied *imala* to the *hamza* only. The rest recited both with *fath*.

﴿And when evil touches him﴾, from illness or poverty, ﴿he is ever despairing, extremely hopeless of the mercy of God.﴾ The meaning is that if he attains worldly aims and achieves what he desires, he forgets the One who is worshipped; and if something of that escapes him, grief overcomes him and despair dominates him. Both of these traits are ugly and blameworthy. What is in this verse is not contradicted by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when evil touches him, he is one of abundant supplication﴾ [Fussilat: 51], nor by similar verses, because that is the characteristic of another group among them, other than the group mentioned in this verse. It is not far-fetched to say that there is no contradiction between the two verses: it may be that, together with his intense despair and great hopelessness, he frequently supplicates with his tongue.

﴿Say: "Each acts according to his own manner [*shakilatihi*]."﴾ *Al-shakila* (manner), said al-Farra', is the way or path. It is also said to mean direction, nature, religion, intention, or innate disposition. It is derived from *al-shakl* (form), as one says: "You are not of my form or of my manner." *Al-shakl* is the like and the equal.

The meaning is that every person acts according to what suits the character he has become accustomed to, and this is a reproach to the disbeliever and a praise of the believer. ﴿Your Lord knows best who is best guided in the way.﴾ Because He is the Creator of you, and the Knower of what you are created with of dispositions and of what you differ in of ways. It is He who distinguishes between the believer, who does not turn away when blessed and does not despair when tested, and the disbeliever, whose habit is insolence at blessings and despair at afflictions.

Then, since the discourse had drifted to mention of man and what he was created with, He, glorified is He, mentioned the question that people asked the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, about the *ruh* (spirit). He said: ﴿And they ask you about the spirit.﴾ People have differed about the *ruh* that was asked about. It is said that it is the spirit that governs the body, by which life exists. This is the view of most exegetes.

Al-Farra' said: the spirit by which man lives is something God, glorified is He, did not inform any of His creatures about, and He did not give knowledge of it to any of His servants. So He said: ﴿Say: "The spirit is of the command of my Lord."﴾ That is: you do not know it. It is also said that the spirit being asked about is Gabriel. It is said to be Jesus. It is said to be the Qur'an. It is said to be an angel of great creation. It is said to be a creation like the creation of the children of Adam. And other views have been said which carry no benefit and whose inclusion is of no use. The apparent view is the first, and the cause of the revelation of this verse, and the identity of those who asked the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, about the spirit, will come later. Apparently the question was about the reality of the spirit, because knowing the reality of a thing is more important and prior to knowing one of its states.

Then God, glorified is He, commanded him to answer those who asked him about the spirit, and said: ﴿Say: "The spirit is of the command of my Lord."﴾ The *min* here is explanatory (*bayaniyya*). *Al-amr* means matter or affair, and the idafa (construct) is for specification. That is: it is of the kind of things God has kept to Himself knowledge of, things He has not made known to His servants. It is also said that the meaning of "of the command of my Lord" is: of His revelation and His speech, not of the speech of human beings.

In this verse there is a rebuke, most forceful, to those who plunge into the question of the spirit, who burden themselves to explain what its form is and to clarify its reality, and a most powerful deterrent for them. They have prolonged discourse on this subject beyond what the matter can bear. Most of it, indeed all of it, is among the superfluities that bring no benefit to religion or to the world.

Some researchers have related that the opinions of those who differ about the spirit reached one thousand eight hundred opinions. So consider this empty superfluity and this fruitless toil devoid of benefit, after they knew that God, glorified is He, has kept its knowledge to Himself, and did not inform His prophets of it, nor did He permit them to ask about it or to investigate its reality, let alone their communities who follow them. How strange it is, by God, that the opinions of the people of superfluity should reach this limit, which they did not reach, nor even part of it, in other matters on which God has permitted discussion and has not kept its knowledge to Himself.
