The position of ﴿upon their faces﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) from the pronoun of the object. ﴿Blind﴾ (*'umyan*) is accusative as a circumstantial phrase, and ﴿mute and deaf﴾ (*bukman wa summan*) are conjoined to it. The *abkam* is one who does not speak, and the *asamm* is one who does not hear. This is a condition in which they are raised, in the most hideous form and the most dreadful sight. God has combined for them blindness of sight, inability to speak, and inability to hear, along with being dragged upon their faces. Then, beyond all this, ﴿their refuge is Hell﴾ That is: the place to which they return. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial phrase, or it is a resumed sentence with no position. ﴿Whenever it subsides, We increase for them the blaze﴾ That is: whenever its flame dies down. It is said: "The fire subsided (*khabat*), subsiding in subsidence (*khabwan*)" when it becomes extinguished and its flame quiets.

Ibn Qutaybah (d. 276 AH) said: the meaning of ﴿We increase for them the blaze﴾ is intensification (*tasa''ur*), which is blazing.

It has been said that the subsiding of the fire implies a lightening of the punishment for its people, so how can this be reconciled with His saying: ﴿The punishment will not be lightened for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 162]? It is answered that what is meant by the absence of lightening is that no perceptible interval of time occurs between the subsiding and the re-intensifying. It has also been said that it subsides without any lightening of their punishment from it.

﴿That﴾ That is: the punishment ﴿is their recompense﴾ which God has made obligatory for them and which they deserved from Him. The *ba'* in His saying ﴿because they denied Our signs﴾ indicates cause, that is: because of their denial of them, for they did not affirm the revealed signs nor reflect on the signs of creation. The demonstrative ﴿that﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is ﴿their recompense﴾, while ﴿because they denied﴾ is another predicate. It is also permissible for ﴿their recompense﴾ to be a second subject whose predicate is what follows it, and the whole sentence is the predicate of the first subject.

﴿And they said, "When we are bones and crumbled particles..."﴾ The *hamza* here is interrogative for denial. The exegesis of this verse has already been given in this surah. The word *khalqan* (creation) in His saying ﴿Will we really be resurrected in a new creation?﴾ is either a verbal noun from a verb of the same root (*masdar*) or a circumstantial phrase, meaning: created.

So He, glory be to Him, brought an argument that restrains them from denial and turns them back from rejection.

He said: ﴿Do they not see that God, who created the heavens and the earth, is able to create the likes of them?﴾ That is: the One who is able to create this is more able to restore what is lesser than it. It has also been said that the meaning is that He is able to annihilate them and bring others into existence. On the first view, *khalq* (creation) means restoration (*i'adah*); on this view it has its literal meaning.

The clause ﴿And He has appointed for them a term about which there is no doubt﴾ is conjoined to ﴿Do they not see﴾, and the meaning is: they have known by the evidence of reason that whoever is able to create the heavens and the earth is able to create the likes of them, because they are not stronger in creation than they. As He said: ﴿Are you more difficult to create, or is the heaven?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 27]. ﴿And He has appointed for them a term about which there is no doubt﴾ This is death or the Resurrection. It is possible that the *waw* is for resumption of speech. It has also been said that there is inversion in the sentence, meaning: "Do they not see that God, who created the heavens and the earth and appointed for them a term about which there is no doubt, is able to create the likes of them?" ﴿But the wrongdoers refused except denial﴾ That is: the polytheists refused except to deny. In this the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, to pass judgment on them as wrongdoers and transgressors of limits.

Then, since these disbelievers requested that rivers and springs be made to flow through their lands so that their livelihoods would expand, God, glory be to Him, made clear that they would not be content, but would remain in their stinginess and niggardliness. He said: ﴿Say, "If you possessed the treasuries of my Lord's mercy..."﴾ The word ﴿you﴾ (*antum*) is nominative as the subject of a verb omitted and explained by what follows, meaning: "If you possessed—you would possess." The separate pronoun is a substitute (*badal*) for the attached pronoun, which is the *waw*. The treasuries of His mercy, glory be to Him, are the treasuries of provisions.

Al-Zajjaj said: God informed them that if they owned the treasuries of provisions, they would withhold out of stinginess and miserliness, which is fear of spending; that is, fear that they would spend and then become poor. In omitting the verb that the word ﴿you﴾ is the subject of, and in presenting the statement in the form of a subject and predicate, there is an indication that they are the ones especially characterized by niggardliness.

The lexicographers said: *anfaqa*, *asram*, *a'dama*, and *aqtara* mean "his wealth became little." So the meaning is: you would have withheld out of fear of the scarcity of wealth. ﴿And man is ever tight-fisted﴾ That is: stingy, restricting others.

It is said: *qatara 'ala 'iyalihi* (he was stingy with his dependents), *yaqturu* and *yuqattiru*, *qatran* and *qutur*: he restricted them in their provision. It is also permissible that what is meant is that man is ever [p. 845] of little wealth. The apparent meaning is that what is intended is an emphasis in describing him with niggardliness, because man is not of little wealth in general; rather some of them have much wealth. Unless what is meant is that the whole human species is of little wealth in relation to the treasuries of God and what is with Him.

This verse has been interpreted in two ways. One: it was revealed specifically concerning the polytheists, and this is the view of al-Hasan (al-Basri). The second: it is general, and this is the view of the majority, as reported by al-Mawardi (d. 450 AH).

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others have related from Anas, who said: It was said: "O Messenger of God, how will people be gathered upon their faces?" He said: "The One who made them walk upon their feet is able to make them walk upon their faces."

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it *hasan*), Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in three categories: one category walking, one category riding, and one category upon their faces." Then he mentioned something similar to the hadith of Anas.

There are other hadiths on this topic.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿Their refuge is Hell﴾, that he said: it means that they are its fuel.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related through 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from him, regarding His saying ﴿Whenever it subsides﴾, that he said: it became quiet.

These same authorities also related from him regarding the verse: he said: Whenever it burns them, it kindles them as fuel. When it has burned them so that nothing of them remains, it becomes glowing embers that blaze, and that is its subsiding. Then when they are changed into a new creation, it returns to them.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ata' regarding His saying ﴿treasuries of my Lord's mercy﴾ that he said: it is provision.

He also related from 'Ikrimah regarding His saying ﴿Then you would have withheld out of fear of spending﴾ that he said: "Then" means: you would not have fed anyone anything.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿fear of spending﴾ that he said: poverty. ﴿And man is ever tight-fisted﴾ he said: stingy.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding ﴿fear of spending﴾ that he said: fear of destitution. ﴿And man is ever tight-fisted﴾ he said: stingy and withholding.

We gave Moses nine clear signs. (That is, indications showing his prophethood.)

It has been said that the connection between this verse and what precedes it is that the miracles mentioned are, as it were, equal to those things which the disbelievers of Quraysh demanded, and even greater than them. So the non-answering of what they asked for in signs was only due to the absence of benefit in destroying them if they did not believe in them.

Most exegetes said: the nine signs are the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the staff, the hand, the years (of drought), and the decrease of fruits.

Al-Hasan replaced the years of drought and the decrease of fruits with the sea and the mountain.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: they are the five mentioned in al-A'raf, plus the sea, the staff, the stone, and the obliteration of their wealth.

The discussion of these signs has already been covered in full, and the hadith of Safwan ibn 'Assal listing these nine signs will come. ﴿So ask the Children of Israel﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Nuhayk read (fa-sa'ala), in the form of a report, meaning: Moses asked Pharaoh to release the Children of Israel, let them go free, and send them with him. The others read (﴿fa-s'al﴾), in the imperative, meaning: ask them, O Muhammad, when (﴿he came to them﴾) Moses. The asking is a request for testimony, for greater reassurance and certainty, because when proofs converge that is stronger. Those asked are the believers among the Children of Israel, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his companions. ﴿Pharaoh said to him, "I think you, O Moses, are indeed bewitched."﴾ The fa' here is the fa' of explanation (al-fa' al-fasiha), meaning: Moses manifested before Pharaoh the clear signs We had given him, and conveyed to him what he had been sent with, and then Pharaoh said to him.

The (mashur) is the one who has been bewitched and whose mind has been confused.

Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra' said: it means the sorcerer, so the passive form was used in place of the active form.

﴿He said, "You know well that none has sent down these but the Lord of the heavens and the earth as clear proofs."﴾ He means the signs he had shown. (Anzala, "sent down," here means "brought into being.") (﴿as clear proofs﴾) means indications by which His power and oneness may be inferred, and (basa'ir, "clear proofs") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

Al-Kisa'i read the (ta') of (''ʿalimta'', "you know") with a damma, making it Moses' speech, and this was reported from 'Ali. The rest read it with a fatha, addressed to Pharaoh.

The reasoning for the first reading is that Pharaoh did not know this, and only Moses knew it.

The reasoning for the majority reading is that Pharaoh did know it, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They denied them, though their souls acknowledged them, out of injustice and arrogance﴾ [al-Naml: 14]. Abu 'Ubayd said: what we adopt is the fatha on the ta', and it is more correct in meaning, because Moses would not say "I know," when he is the one calling. Something similar was reported from al-Zajjaj.

﴿And indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed.﴾ The (zann, "thinking") here means certainty. (Tubur) means destruction and loss.

Al-Kumayt said:
"And Qada'a, in the days, saw an opinion that was doomed and persistent."
That is: ruined and lost. It was also said that (al-mathbur) means the cursed. From this is the poet's saying:
"O our people, do not seek to be stubborn in folly, for folly and rebellion are cursed."
That is: cursed. It was also said that (al-mathbur) is the one deficient in intellect. It was also said that it means the one prevented from good; one says: "What prevented you (ma tharaka) from such and such," meaning what held you back from it. The lexicographers related this. It was also said that it means the bewitched.

1 ﴿So he wanted to drive them out of the land﴾, that is: Pharaoh wanted to expel the Children of Israel and Moses and remove them from the land, meaning the land of Egypt, by banishing them from it. It was also said he wanted to kill them, and on this view "the land" means land in general. The meaning of (istifzaz, "driving out") has been mentioned shortly before. ﴿Then We drowned him and those with him, all of them.﴾ So destruction by drowning befell him and them, and We did not leave any of them.

1 ﴿And We said after him to the Children of Israel, "Dwell in the land."﴾ (p. 846) That is: after drowning him and those with him. The land here means the land of Egypt, from which he had wanted to drive them out. ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter comes﴾, that is: the final abode, which is the Resurrection, or the final return, or the final Hour. (﴿We will bring you together in a mingled throng﴾.) Al-Jawhari said: (al-lafif) is what gathers of people from various tribes. It is said: "The people came with their lafif," meaning with their mixed groups. So the meaning here is: We will bring you forth from your graves mingled from every place, the believer mixed with the disbeliever.

Al-Asma'i said: (al-lafif) is a plural with no singular, and it is like a collective noun.

﴿And with truth We sent it down, and with truth it descended.﴾ The pronoun refers to the Qur'an. The meaning of "with truth We sent it down" is: We revealed it accompanied by truth. The meaning of "and with truth it descended" is: it descended with the truth in it. It was also said: the second is what remains. The first (bi'l-haqq, "with truth") means "together with" (ma'a), that is: together with the truth We sent it down, as in the saying "the emir rode with his sword," meaning together with his sword. "And with truth it descended" means: with Muhammad, as you say, "I descended upon Zayd."

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the (ba') in both places means (ma'a, "together with"). It was also said that the meaning could be: and with truth We decreed that it should descend, and so it descended, or that We sent it down from heaven only as preserved, and it descended upon the Messenger only as preserved from the confusion of the devils. The fronting in both places serves to restrict.

﴿And We did not send you except as a bringer of good tidings and a warner.﴾ That is: a bringer of good tidings with Paradise for whoever obeys, and a warner, frightening with the Fire, for whoever disobeys.

(﴿And a Qur'an We have divided﴾). The accusative of (qur'anan, "a Qur'an") is governed by a hidden verb which the following clause explains. 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Qatada, Abu Raja' and al-Sha'bi read (farraqnahu) with the doubled letter, meaning: We sent it down piece by piece, not all at once.

The majority read (faraqnahu) with the light form, meaning: We made it clear and explained it, and We distinguished in it between truth and falsehood.

al-Zajjaj said: He divided it in revelation so that people might understand it.

Abu 'Ubayd said: the light form is more pleasing to me, because its explanation is: "We made it clear," and the doubled form has no meaning except that it was sent down in parts.

What supports this is what Tha'lab related from Ibn al-A'rabi, that he said: "faraqtu" (lightened) is used for separating speech, and "farraqtu" (doubled) is used for separating bodies.

Then Allah mentioned the reason for His saying (faraqnahu, "We divided it"). He said: ﴿So that you may recite it to the people at a measured pace﴾, that is: over an extended period, piece by piece, according to the first reading, or We sent it down verse by verse and surah by surah.

Its meaning according to the second reading (﴿at a measured pace﴾) is: with deliberation and slowness in recitation, for that is closer to understanding and easier for memorization.

The readers agreed on the damma of the mim in (mukth, "measured pace") except Ibn Muhaysin, who read it with a fatha on the mim.

(﴿And We sent it down in gradual revelation﴾). The emphasis by the verbal noun is for intensification. The meaning is: We sent it down in stages, divided, for the benefit this holds; if they had been commanded all the obligations at one time, they would have recoiled and been unable to bear them.

1 ﴿Say, "Believe in it or do not believe."﴾ Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to say to the disbelievers who demanded signs: "Believe in it or do not believe." So your belief in it and your refusal of it do not increase it or decrease it.

In this there is a severe warning to them, and a command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to turn away from them and to disregard them. Then He gave the reason with His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it﴾, that is: the scholars who had read the earlier books before the Qur'an was sent down, and who knew the reality of revelation and the signs of prophethood, such as Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, Waraqa ibn Nawfal, and 'Abd Allah ibn Salam. ﴿When it is recited to them﴾, that is: the Qur'an, ﴿they fall down upon their faces prostrating﴾, that is: they fall on their faces, prostrating to Allah the Exalted.

He specified the falling (khurur, "falling down") as being upon the chins (li'l-adhqan, "to the chins"), meaning upon them, because the dhaqan, which is the junction of the two jaws, is the first part that touches the ground.

al-Zajjaj said: because the dhaqan is the junction of the two jaws, and as a person begins falling down for prostration, the first part of his face that touches the ground is the chin.

It was also said that the intended meaning is placing the beard in the dust, for that is the utmost submission. The use of (li) in (li'l-adhqan) rather than (ʿalā, "upon") indicates specificity, as though they singled out their chins for falling, or singled out falling for their chins.

It was also said that the pronoun in His saying (min qablihi, "before it") refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), but what we mentioned, that it refers to the Qur'an, is better, because the context indicates that. In this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Its summary is: if these ignorant people, who have no knowledge, no understanding of the books of Allah or His prophets, do not believe in it, then do not be concerned about that, for people of knowledge have believed in it, humbled themselves before it, and submitted to it when it was recited to them, with a submission whose effect is evident in that they fall on their chins prostrating to Allah.

﴿And they say, "Glory be to our Lord."﴾ That is: they say in their prostration glorifying our Lord above what the ignorant say of denial, or glorifying Him above breaking His promise. ﴿Indeed the promise of our Lord was ever fulfilled.﴾ (In) here is the lightened form of the heavy (inna), and the lam is the lam that distinguishes it.

Then He mentioned that they fell down upon their chins weeping, so He said: ﴿And they fall down upon their chins weeping﴾. He repeated the mention of falling upon the chins because the causes differ: the first is for glorifying and exalting Allah the Exalted, and the second is for weeping under the effect of the Qur'an's admonitions in their hearts and their increased humility. For this reason He said: ﴿And it increases them﴾, that is: hearing the Qur'an, or the Qur'an through their hearing of it, in humility, meaning softness of heart and moistness of the eye.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying (﴿nine signs﴾) that he mentioned what we have mentioned from most exegetes.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he said: his hand, his staff, his tongue, the sea, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood.

al-Tayalisi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Qani', al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Abu Nu'aym, al-Bayhaqi, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Safwan ibn 'Assal that: "Two Jews said to one another, 'Come, let us go to this Prophet and ask him.' So they came to him and asked him about the saying of Allah: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses nine clear signs﴾. He said: 'Do not associate anything with Allah, do not commit adultery, do not be extravagant, do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, do not steal, do not practice sorcery, do not walk with an innocent person to a ruler so that he kills him, do not consume usury, do not slander a chaste woman'—or he said: 'do not flee from the battlefield' (Shu'ba was unsure)—'and upon you, O Jews, specifically, is that you do not transgress on the Sabbath.' So they kissed his hands and feet and said: 'We testify that you are the Prophet of Allah.' He said: 'What prevents you from accepting Islam?' They said: 'David supplicated Allah that a prophet should never cease from his offspring, and we fear that if we accept Islam the Jews will kill us.'"

(p. 847) Ibn Abi al-Dunya, in his book on the blame of anger, related from Anas ibn Malik that he was asked about the saying: ﴿And indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed﴾, and he said: "Opposed," and said: "The prophets are too noble to be cursed or reviled."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas concerning (﴿mathbur﴾) that he said: "Cursed."

al-Shirazi, in al-Alqab, and Ibn Mardawayh related from him that he said: "Little of intellect."

Ibn Jarir related from him also (﴿lafif﴾) that he said: "All together."

al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn 'Abbas that he read (﴿and a Qur'an We have divided﴾) with the doubled letter, and said: "The Qur'an descended to the lowest heaven in the Night of Power in Ramadan all at once. Whenever the polytheists introduced something, Allah sent them an answer, and He divided it over twenty years."

Something similar has been related from him through several chains.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him (﴿We divided it﴾) that he said: "We distinguished it." (﴿At a measured pace﴾): "Over a period." (﴿They fall upon their chins﴾): He says: "Upon their faces."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid regarding ﴿When it is recited to them﴾ that he said: "It is their book."

Its meaning according to the second reading (﴿at a measured pace﴾) is: with deliberation and slowness in recitation, for that is closer to understanding and easier for memorization.

The readers agreed on the damma of the mim in (mukth, "measured pace") except Ibn Muhaysin, who read it with a fatha on the mim.

(﴿And We sent it down in gradual revelation﴾). The emphasis by the verbal noun is for intensification. The meaning is: We sent it down in stages, divided, for the benefit this holds; if they had been commanded all the obligations at one time, they would have recoiled and been unable to bear them.

For this reason He said: ﴿And it increases them﴾, that is: hearing the Qur'an, or the Qur'an through their hearing of it, in humility, meaning softness of heart and moistness of the eye.

Ibn Jarir related from him also (﴿lafif﴾) that he said: "All together."

al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn 'Abbas that he read (﴿and a Qur'an We have divided﴾) with the doubled letter, and said: "The Qur'an descended to the lowest heaven in the Night of Power in Ramadan all at once. Something similar has been related from him through several chains.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him (﴿We divided it﴾) that he said: "We distinguished it." (﴿At a measured pace﴾): "Over a period." (﴿They fall upon their chins﴾): He says: "Upon their faces."

(﴿We will bring you together in a mingled throng﴾.) Al-Jawhari said: (al-lafif) is what gathers of people from various tribes. It is said: "The people came with their lafif," meaning with their mixed groups. So the meaning here is: We will bring you forth from your graves mingled from every place, the believer mixed with the disbeliever.

Al-Asma'i said: (al-lafif) is a plural with no singular, and it is like a collective noun.

﴿And with truth We sent it down, and with truth it descended.﴾ The pronoun refers to the Qur'an. The meaning of "with truth We sent it down" is: We revealed it accompanied by truth. The meaning of "and with truth it descended" is: it descended with the truth in it. It was also said: the second is what remains. The first (bi'l-haqq, "with truth") means "together with" (ma'a), that is: together with the truth We sent it down, as in the saying "the emir rode with his sword," meaning together with his sword. "And with truth it descended" means: with Muhammad, as you say, "I descended upon Zayd."

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the (ba') in both places means (ma'a, "together with"). It was also said that the meaning could be: and with truth We decreed that it should descend, and so it descended, or that We sent it down from heaven only as preserved, and it descended upon the Messenger only as preserved from the confusion of the devils. The fronting in both places serves to restrict.

﴿And We did not send you except as a bringer of good tidings and a warner.﴾ That is: a bringer of good tidings with Paradise for whoever obeys, and a warner, frightening with the Fire, for whoever disobeys.

(﴿And a Qur'an We have divided﴾). The accusative of (qur'anan, "a Qur'an") is governed by a hidden verb which the following clause explains. 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Qatada, Abu Raja' and al-Sha'bi read (farraqnahu) with the doubled letter, meaning: We sent it down piece by piece, not all at once.

The majority read (faraqnahu) with the light form, meaning: We made it clear and explained it, and We distinguished in it between truth and falsehood.

al-Zajjaj said: He divided it in revelation so that people might understand it.

Abu 'Ubayd said: the light form is more pleasing to me, because its explanation is: "We made it clear," and the doubled form has no meaning except that it was sent down in parts.

What supports this is what Tha'lab related from Ibn al-A'rabi, that he said: "faraqtu" (lightened) is used for separating speech, and "farraqtu" (doubled) is used for separating bodies.

Then Allah mentioned the reason for His saying (faraqnahu, "We divided it"). He said: ﴿So that you may recite it to the people at a measured pace﴾, that is: over an extended period, piece by piece, according to the first reading, or We sent it down verse by verse and surah by surah.

Its meaning according to the second reading (﴿at a measured pace﴾) is: with deliberation and slowness in recitation, for that is closer to understanding and easier for memorization.

The readers agreed on the damma of the mim in (mukth, "measured pace") except Ibn Muhaysin, who read it with a fatha on the mim.

(﴿And We sent it down in gradual revelation﴾). The emphasis by the verbal noun is for intensification. The meaning is: We sent it down in stages, divided, for the benefit this holds; if they had been commanded all the obligations at one time, they would have recoiled and been unable to bear them.

1 ﴿Say, "Believe in it or do not believe."﴾ Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to say to the disbelievers who demanded signs: "Believe in it or do not believe." So your belief in it and your refusal of it do not increase it or decrease it.

In this there is a severe warning to them, and a command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to turn away from them and to disregard them. Then He gave the reason with His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it﴾, that is: the scholars who had read the earlier books before the Qur'an was sent down, and who knew the reality of revelation and the signs of prophethood, such as Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, Waraqa ibn Nawfal, and 'Abd Allah ibn Salam. ﴿When it is recited to them﴾, that is: the Qur'an, ﴿they fall down upon their faces prostrating﴾, that is: they fall on their faces, prostrating to Allah the Exalted.

He specified the falling (khurur, "falling down") as being upon the chins (li'l-adhqan, "to the chins"), meaning upon them, because the dhaqan, which is the junction of the two jaws, is the first part that touches the ground.

al-Zajjaj said: because the dhaqan is the junction of the two jaws, and as a person begins falling down for prostration, the first part of his face that touches the ground is the chin.

It was also said that the intended meaning is placing the beard in the dust, for that is the utmost submission. The use of (li) in (li'l-adhqan) rather than (ʿalā, "upon") indicates specificity, as though they singled out their chins for falling, or singled out falling for their chins.

It was also said that the pronoun in His saying (min qablihi, "before it") refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), but what we mentioned, that it refers to the Qur'an, is better, because the context indicates that. In this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Its summary is: if these ignorant people, who have no knowledge, no understanding of the books of Allah or His prophets, do not believe in it, then do not be concerned about that, for people of knowledge have believed in it, humbled themselves before it, and submitted to it when it was recited to them, with a submission whose effect is evident in that they fall on their chins prostrating to Allah.

﴿And they say, "Glory be to our Lord."﴾ That is: they say in their prostration glorifying our Lord above what the ignorant say of denial, or glorifying Him above breaking His promise. ﴿Indeed the promise of our Lord was ever fulfilled.﴾ (In) here is the lightened form of the heavy (inna), and the lam is the lam that distinguishes it.

Then He mentioned that they fell down upon their chins weeping, so He said: ﴿And they fall down upon their chins weeping﴾. He repeated the mention of falling upon the chins because the causes differ: the first is for glorifying and exalting Allah the Exalted, and the second is for weeping under the effect of the Qur'an's admonitions in their hearts and their increased humility. For this reason He said: ﴿And it increases them﴾, that is: hearing the Qur'an, or the Qur'an through their hearing of it, in humility, meaning softness of heart and moistness of the eye.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying (﴿nine signs﴾) that he mentioned what we have mentioned from most exegetes.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he said: his hand, his staff, his tongue, the sea, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood.

al-Tayalisi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Qani', al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Abu Nu'aym, al-Bayhaqi, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Safwan ibn 'Assal that: "Two Jews said to one another, 'Come, let us go to this Prophet and ask him.' So they came to him and asked him about the saying of Allah: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses nine clear signs﴾. He said: 'Do not associate anything with Allah, do not commit adultery, do not be extravagant, do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, do not steal, do not practice sorcery, do not walk with an innocent person to a ruler so that he kills him, do not consume usury, do not slander a chaste woman'—or he said: 'do not flee from the battlefield' (Shu'ba was unsure)—'and upon you, O Jews, specifically, is that you do not transgress on the Sabbath.' So they kissed his hands and feet and said: 'We testify that you are the Prophet of Allah.' He said: 'What prevents you from accepting Islam?' They said: 'David supplicated Allah that a prophet should never cease from his offspring, and we fear that if we accept Islam the Jews will kill us.'"

(p. 847) Ibn Abi al-Dunya, in his book on the blame of anger, related from Anas ibn Malik that he was asked about the saying: ﴿And indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed﴾, and he said: "Opposed," and said: "The prophets are too noble to be cursed or reviled."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas concerning (﴿mathbur﴾) that he said: "Cursed."

al-Shirazi, in al-Alqab, and Ibn Mardawayh related from him that he said: "Little of intellect."

Ibn Jarir related from him also (﴿lafif﴾) that he said: "All together."

al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn 'Abbas that he read (﴿and a Qur'an We have divided﴾) with the doubled letter, and said: "The Qur'an descended to the lowest heaven in the Night of Power in Ramadan all at once. Whenever the polytheists introduced something, Allah sent them an answer, and He divided it over twenty years."

Something similar has been related from him through several chains.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him (﴿We divided it﴾) that he said: "We distinguished it." (﴿At a measured pace﴾): "Over a period." (﴿They fall upon their chins﴾): He says: "Upon their faces."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid regarding ﴿When it is recited to them﴾ that he said: "It is their book."

We gave Moses nine clear signs. (That is, indications showing his prophethood.)

It has been said that the connection between this verse and what precedes it is that the miracles mentioned are, as it were, equal to those things which the disbelievers of Quraysh demanded, and even greater than them. So the non-answering of what they asked for in signs was only due to the absence of benefit in destroying them if they did not believe in them.

Most exegetes said: the nine signs are the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the staff, the hand, the years (of drought), and the decrease of fruits.

Al-Hasan replaced the years of drought and the decrease of fruits with the sea and the mountain.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: they are the five mentioned in al-A'raf, plus the sea, the staff, the stone, and the obliteration of their wealth.

The discussion of these signs has already been covered in full, and the hadith of Safwan ibn 'Assal listing these nine signs will come. ﴿So ask the Children of Israel﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Nuhayk read (fa-sa'ala), in the form of a report, meaning: Moses asked Pharaoh to release the Children of Israel, let them go free, and send them with him. The others read (﴿fa-s'al﴾), in the imperative, meaning: ask them, O Muhammad, when (﴿he came to them﴾) Moses. The asking is a request for testimony, for greater reassurance and certainty, because when proofs converge that is stronger. Those asked are the believers among the Children of Israel, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his companions. ﴿Pharaoh said to him, "I think you, O Moses, are indeed bewitched."﴾ The fa' here is the fa' of explanation (al-fa' al-fasiha), meaning: Moses manifested before Pharaoh the clear signs We had given him, and conveyed to him what he had been sent with, and then Pharaoh said to him.

The (mashur) is the one who has been bewitched and whose mind has been confused.

Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra' said: it means the sorcerer, so the passive form was used in place of the active form.

﴿He said, "You know well that none has sent down these but the Lord of the heavens and the earth as clear proofs."﴾ He means the signs he had shown. (Anzala, "sent down," here means "brought into being.") (﴿as clear proofs﴾) means indications by which His power and oneness may be inferred, and (basa'ir, "clear proofs") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

Al-Kisa'i read the (ta') of (''ʿalimta'', "you know") with a damma, making it Moses' speech, and this was reported from 'Ali. The rest read it with a fatha, addressed to Pharaoh.

The reasoning for the first reading is that Pharaoh did not know this, and only Moses knew it.

The reasoning for the majority reading is that Pharaoh did know it, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They denied them, though their souls acknowledged them, out of injustice and arrogance﴾ [al-Naml: 14]. Abu 'Ubayd said: what we adopt is the fatha on the ta', and it is more correct in meaning, because Moses would not say "I know," when he is the one calling. Something similar was reported from al-Zajjaj.

﴿And indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed.﴾ The (zann, "thinking") here means certainty. (Tubur) means destruction and loss.

Al-Kumayt said:
"And Qada'a, in the days, saw an opinion that was doomed and persistent."
That is: ruined and lost. It was also said that (al-mathbur) means the cursed. From this is the poet's saying:
"O our people, do not seek to be stubborn in folly, for folly and rebellion are cursed."
That is: cursed. It was also said that (al-mathbur) is the one deficient in intellect. It was also said that it means the one prevented from good; one says: "What prevented you (ma tharaka) from such and such," meaning what held you back from it. The lexicographers related this. It was also said that it means the bewitched.

1 ﴿So he wanted to drive them out of the land﴾, that is: Pharaoh wanted to expel the Children of Israel and Moses and remove them from the land, meaning the land of Egypt, by banishing them from it. It was also said he wanted to kill them, and on this view "the land" means land in general. The meaning of (istifzaz, "driving out") has been mentioned shortly before. ﴿Then We drowned him and those with him, all of them.﴾ So destruction by drowning befell him and them, and We did not leave any of them.

He, glorified is He, wished to teach His servants the manner of supplication and humility, so He said: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful (al-Rahman). Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾ Its meaning is that the two are equal in permissibility of use and in the goodness of calling upon Him by either of them. For this reason He said: ( ﴿Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾ ) The tanwin in (ayyan) is a replacement for the omitted genitive noun, and (ma) is added to emphasize the indefiniteness in (ayyan). The pronoun in (lahu) refers to the One named. The original wording would have been: "Whichever you call upon, it is good," but in its place He put ( ﴿to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ ) for emphasis, and to indicate that if all His names are good, then these two names are good. The meaning of the goodness of the names is that each is self-sufficient in attributes of majesty and generosity. This was mentioned by al-Naysaburi, and Abu al-Su'ud followed him.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah informed them that their calling upon Allah and their calling upon al-Rahman return to one matter. The reason for the revelation of the verse will be mentioned later, and through it the intended meaning becomes clear. Then He mentioned another manner of supplication, saying: ﴿And do not recite your prayer aloud, nor be silent in it﴾, that is, the recitation of your prayer, with the omission of a noun, since it is known that loudness and quietness are attributes of the voice and not of the acts of prayer. So this is the mention of the whole and the intention of a part. It is said: "His voice faded (khafata sawtuhu khufutan)" when his speech ceased, weakened and became still; "the crop faded (khafata al-zar'u)" when it withered; and "the man spoke quietly (khafata al-rajul bi-qira'atihi)" when he did not raise his voice in it. It is also said that the meaning is: "Do not recite aloud throughout your prayer, nor be silent throughout it," and the first is preferable. ﴿And seek a way between these﴾, that is, between the loud and the quiet indicated by the two verbs. (Sabilan) means a path moderate between the two matters, so that it is neither loud nor silent. According to the second interpretation, the meaning of that is a prohibition against reciting aloud in all prayers, and a prohibition against being silent in all prayers, and a command to make some of them loud, which is the night prayer, and to be quiet in the day prayer. Some people held that this verse has been abrogated (mansukha) by His saying: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret﴾ [al-A'raf: 55].

When He commanded that He not be mentioned or called upon except by His most beautiful names, He drew attention to the manner of praising Him, saying: ﴿And say: Praise be to Allah, who has not taken a son﴾, as the Jews and Christians say, and as those polytheists who say that the angels are the daughters of Allah say; exalted is He far above that with a great exaltation. ﴿And He has no partner in the dominion﴾, that is, no associate with Him in His kingdom and lordship, as the Dualists and others of the sects who affirm a plurality of gods claim. ﴿And He has no protector out of weakness﴾, that is, He does not need anyone's support because of any humiliation that would befall Him; so He is free from any protector or helper.

Al-Zajjaj said: That is, He does not need to be helped by another. In the midst of the praise, mention of these sublime attributes indicates that the one deserving of praise is the one who possesses these attributes, because He is the One able to create and to bestow blessings, since offspring is a cause of cowardice and miserliness; and also because it entails the origination of the father, since he would be begotten from a part of his own parts, and the originated thing is not able to bestow complete favor. Partnership in dominion is only conceivable for one who cannot be independent in it, and one who cannot be independent is incapable, let alone complete what he has, let alone maintain the order of what he is upon. Moreover, partnership necessitates conflict between the two partners, so one partner may prevent the other from bestowing good upon his allies, and it leads to corruption: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22]. And one who needs a protector to prevent him from humiliation and to help him against whoever wishes to humiliate him is weak, unable to do what the one who is self-sufficient can do. ﴿And magnify Him with magnification﴾, that is, glorify Him greatly, and describe Him as greater than everything.

He, glorified is He, wished to teach His servants the manner of supplication and humility, so He said: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful (al-Rahman). Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾ Its meaning is that the two are equal in permissibility of use and in the goodness of calling upon Him by either of them. For this reason He said: ( ﴿Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾ ) The tanwin in (ayyan) is a replacement for the omitted genitive noun, and (ma) is added to emphasize the indefiniteness in (ayyan). The pronoun in (lahu) refers to the One named. The original wording would have been: "Whichever you call upon, it is good," but in its place He put ( ﴿to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ ) for emphasis, and to indicate that if all His names are good, then these two names are good. The meaning of the goodness of the names is that each is self-sufficient in attributes of majesty and generosity. This was mentioned by al-Naysaburi, and Abu al-Su'ud followed him.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah informed them that their calling upon Allah and their calling upon al-Rahman return to one matter. The reason for the revelation of the verse will be mentioned later, and through it the intended meaning becomes clear. Then He mentioned another manner of supplication, saying: ﴿And do not recite your prayer aloud, nor be silent in it﴾, that is, the recitation of your prayer, with the omission of a noun, since it is known that loudness and quietness are attributes of the voice and not of the acts of prayer. So this is the mention of the whole and the intention of a part. It is said: "His voice faded (khafata sawtuhu khufutan)" when his speech ceased, weakened and became still; "the crop faded (khafata al-zar'u)" when it withered; and "the man spoke quietly (khafata al-rajul bi-qira'atihi)" when he did not raise his voice in it. It is also said that the meaning is: "Do not recite aloud throughout your prayer, nor be silent throughout it," and the first is preferable. ﴿And seek a way between these﴾, that is, between the loud and the quiet indicated by the two verbs. (Sabilan) means a path moderate between the two matters, so that it is neither loud nor silent. According to the second interpretation, the meaning of that is a prohibition against reciting aloud in all prayers, and a prohibition against being silent in all prayers, and a command to make some of them loud, which is the night prayer, and to be quiet in the day prayer. Some people held that this verse has been abrogated (mansukha) by His saying: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret﴾ [al-A'raf: 55].

When He commanded that He not be mentioned or called upon except by His most beautiful names, He drew attention to the manner of praising Him, saying: ﴿And say: Praise be to Allah, who has not taken a son﴾, as the Jews and Christians say, and as those polytheists who say that the angels are the daughters of Allah say; exalted is He far above that with a great exaltation. ﴿And He has no partner in the dominion﴾, that is, no associate with Him in His kingdom and lordship, as the Dualists and others of the sects who affirm a plurality of gods claim. ﴿And He has no protector out of weakness﴾, that is, He does not need anyone's support because of any humiliation that would befall Him; so He is free from any protector or helper.

Al-Zajjaj said: That is, He does not need to be helped by another. In the midst of the praise, mention of these sublime attributes indicates that the one deserving of praise is the one who possesses these attributes, because He is the One able to create and to bestow blessings, since offspring is a cause of cowardice and miserliness; and also because it entails the origination of the father, since he would be begotten from a part of his own parts, and the originated thing is not able to bestow complete favor. Partnership in dominion is only conceivable for one who cannot be independent in it, and one who cannot be independent is incapable, let alone complete what he has, let alone maintain the order of what he is upon.
